question: Why is بِسْمِ written with or without its alif?

positions.position: The alif of bism is omitted because the familiar phrase is frequent and shortened.
positions.reasons: AKHFASH (author): The alif is omitted in writing bism because the phrase is frequent and the prefixed bāʾ already supplies the linkage; it remains in bismi al-Raḥmān and similar phrases. THALABI (أبو خالد بن يزيد المرادي): Abu Khalid ibn Yazid al-Muradi says the alif of ism was dropped for frequent use and its length was transferred to the bā; where ism retains alif, the bā keeps its ordinary form. MAWARDI (author): The connective alif is omitted in spelling and pronunciation because of frequent use and joining; by contrast it remains written in 96:1 because that wording is less frequent. | mentions 96:1 WAHIDI-BASIT (author): The written alif is dropped from bism Allāh because the familiar phrase is unmistakable and Arabic favors brevity when meaning is clear; unlike the less frequent formula in al-Wāqiʿa, al-Ḥāqqa. BAGHAWI (author): The alif in ism is omitted for lightness because the expression is used very frequently. BAGHAWI-FULL (author): The alif is omitted from ism for ease and frequent use; al-Qutaybi explains the lengthened ba as an honorific opening, and Umar b. Abd al-Aziz ordered careful lettering. KASHSHAF-FULL (author): The alif in bism is omitted in writing because connected use is frequent; the lengthened bā compensates for it, and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz told his scribe to lengthen the bā. | mentions 96:1 IBNATIYYA (author): The alif is omitted from the written basmala for brevity and ease because the phrase is so frequently used. IBNATIYYA (الكسائي وسعيد الأخفش، ويحيى بن زياد): Al-Kisa'i and Sa'id al-Akhfash omit the alif in bism al-Rahman and bism al-Qahir; Yahya b. Ziyad says omission applies only with Allah because that phrase is especially frequent. Ibn Atiyya says the alif remains with other names. TABRISI (author): The hamzat al-waṣl of ism drops in connected pronunciation and is omitted in writing here because the basmala is frequent and unambiguous, unlike the less frequent Qur'anic form in 96:1. | mentions 96:1 QURTUBI (author): The alif in ism is omitted in the basmala through frequent use; it remains in the less common “Read in the name of your Lord.” | mentions 96:1 BAYDAWI (أصحابنا البصريون): Basran grammarians derive ism from a form whose ending was dropped for frequent use; hamzat al-waṣl allows its consonant-initial form to begin a word. BAYDAWI (author): The written alif is omitted by orthographic convention due to frequency, and the bāʾ is lengthened in compensation. BAYDAWI-FULL (author): The written alif is omitted from بسم through frequent use, with the bāʾ lengthened in its place. BAYDAWI-FULL (أصحابنا البصريين): The Basrans derive اسم from a shortened form whose ending was dropped through frequent use; its beginning was made still and hamzat al-waṣl added to start it with a vowel. NASAFI (author): The alif of ism is omitted in this written basmala because it is frequent and unpronounced; the bā’ is lengthened to compensate, and ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-‘Aziz instructed his scribe to lengthen the bā’, distinguish the sīns, and round the mīm. | mentions 96:1 NASAFI-FULL (عمر بن عبد العزيز): Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz instructed his scribe to lengthen the ba, make the sin strokes clear, and round the mim; the written alif is omitted here through frequent use. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): The basmala's deleted verb is one rhetorical omission, and the alifs of bismillāh and raḥmān are also omitted in writing because of frequent use. BURHAN (علماء الظاهر): The outward scholars explain the omission as abbreviation from frequent use: the alif of ism is dropped only when appended to Allah and preceded by ba according to the majority. ALUSI (author): The written basmala omits the alif of ism; explanations include frequent usage, the bāʾ replacing the initial hamza, and whether the governing word is stated. | mentions 96:1 ELMALILI (author): In the basmala’s special orthography the alif of ism is omitted and the opening bāʾ is lengthened; frequent use explains this abbreviation, while the writing also hints at the force of connection.

positions.position: Ibn Sirin disliked extending the ba to the mim before writing the sin.
positions.reasons: DURR (محمد بن سيرين): Ibn Sirin disliked extending the ba to the mim before writing the sin. DURR (محمد بن سيرين): Ibn Sirin strongly disapproved of extending the basmala's ba before writing its sin. DURR-FULL (محمد بن سيرين): Ibn Sirin disliked connecting the ba directly to the mim before writing the sin. DURR-FULL (محمد بن سيرين): Ibn Sirin strongly opposed extending the ba to the mim without first writing the sin.

positions.position: Mujahid and al-Sha'bi disliked a ritually impure person writing the basmala.
positions.reasons: DURR (مجاهد والشعبي): Mujahid and al-Sha'bi disliked a ritually impure person writing the basmala. DURR-FULL (مجاهد والشعبي): Mujahid and al-Shabi disliked a ritually impure person writing the basmala.

positions.position: A weak report says God forgives one who writes the basmala beautifully out of reverence.
positions.reasons: DURR (أنس): A weak report says God forgives one who writes the basmala beautifully out of reverence. DURR-FULL (أنس): A weak report says God forgives one who writes the basmala beautifully out of reverence for Him.

positions.position: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz struck a scribe for writing the mim before the sin and dismissed another who omitted the sin.
positions.reasons: DURR (عمر بن عبد العزيز): Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz struck a scribe for writing the mim before the sin and dismissed another who omitted the sin. DURR-FULL (عمر بن عبد العزيز): Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz punished and dismissed a scribe for writing the mim before the sin or omitting the sin.

positions.position: The Kufans derive ism from wasm, “mark,” and posit a compensatory hamza; al-Ālūsī rejects this as unsupported and prefers the Basran derivation.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (الكوفيون): The Kufans derive ism from wasm, “mark,” and posit a compensatory hamza; al-Ālūsī rejects this as unsupported and prefers the Basran derivation. ALUSI-FULL (الكوفيون): The Kufans derive ism from wasm, a mark identifying its referent; al-Alusi rejects the derivation because its compensatory hamza and morphology lack a sound parallel.

positions.position: Agreement that everything between the muṣḥaf’s covers is Qur’an proves the basmala is Qur’anic, which is uncontested; it does not prove it must be recited at each written opening.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): Agreement that everything between the muṣḥaf’s covers is Qur’an proves the basmala is Qur’anic, which is uncontested; it does not prove it must be recited at each written opening. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Agreement that everything between the covers is Qur'an establishes that the basmala is Qur'an, which is undisputed, but does not establish that it must be recited at each written location.

positions.position: Reciters and codex scribes omit the alif in the familiar basmala because its meaning is obvious and Arabic usage favors brevity in repeated, familiar expressions.
positions.reasons: FARRA (القراء): Reciters and codex scribes omit the alif in the familiar basmala because its meaning is obvious and Arabic usage favors brevity in repeated, familiar expressions.

positions.position: Do not omit the alif of ism with a name other than Allah or with a preposition other than bi; lām and kāf do not follow this spelling convention.
positions.reasons: FARRA (author): Do not omit the alif of ism with a name other than Allah or with a preposition other than bi; lām and kāf do not follow this spelling convention.

positions.position: Arabic speakers shorten frequent expressions even more, as in aysh ʿindak and the altered form of shayʾ.
positions.reasons: FARRA (author): Arabic speakers shorten frequent expressions even more, as in aysh ʿindak and the altered form of shayʾ.

positions.position: The claim that alif was dropped because bāʾ cannot be paused on is disproved by other non-pauseable letters that Arabs still write in similar forms.
positions.reasons: FARRA (author): The claim that alif was dropped because bāʾ cannot be paused on is disproved by other non-pauseable letters that Arabs still write in similar forms.

positions.position: The alif in ism is hamzat waṣl: sumayy shows that it is not pronounced and is dropped.
positions.reasons: AKHFASH (author): The alif in ism is hamzat waṣl: sumayy shows that it is not pronounced and is dropped.

positions.position: Hamzat waṣl lets speech begin despite initial sukūn, then is unnecessary when joined to what precedes it; 5:12, 2:60, 36:14, 19:28, 111:4.
positions.reasons: AKHFASH (author): Hamzat waṣl lets speech begin despite initial sukūn, then is unnecessary when joined to what precedes it; 5:12, 2:60, 36:14, 19:28, 111:4.

positions.position: The alif remains when ism is attached to something other than God or when a different preposition precedes it.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-BASIT (author): The alif remains when ism is attached to something other than God or when a different preposition precedes it.

positions.position: The alif is also absent in pronunciation because it is a connecting hamza, for which the preceding bāʾ suffices.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-BASIT (author): The alif is also absent in pronunciation because it is a connecting hamza, for which the preceding bāʾ suffices.

positions.position: It was written to separate surahs and seek blessing by beginning with it, as people begin important acts with it.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF (author): It was written to separate surahs and seek blessing by beginning with it, as people begin important acts with it.

positions.position: Ism begins with a helping hamza initially because its first consonant is quiescent; in connected speech no addition is needed.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF (author): Ism begins with a helping hamza initially because its first consonant is quiescent; in connected speech no addition is needed.

positions.position: Some omit the helping hamza and instead move the quiescent consonant, saying sim or sum.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF (author): Some omit the helping hamza and instead move the quiescent consonant, saying sim or sum.

positions.position: Ism has a deleted ending like yad and dam; asma and sammaytu show its original sumu and derivation from elevation.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF (author): Ism has a deleted ending like yad and dam; asma and sammaytu show its original sumu and derivation from elevation.

positions.position: Naming raises the named one's standing; nabz derives from a word meaning raised voice and also means upper palm bark.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF (author): Naming raises the named one's standing; nabz derives from a word meaning raised voice and also means upper palm bark.

positions.position: The written alif is dropped by analogy with connected pronunciation; the bā is lengthened to compensate for the omission.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF (author): The written alif is dropped by analogy with connected pronunciation; the bā is lengthened to compensate for the omission.

positions.position: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz told his scribe to lengthen bā, show tooth-like strokes, and round mīm.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF (عمر بن عبد العزيز): Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz told his scribe to lengthen bā, show tooth-like strokes, and round mīm.

positions.position: The noun ism begins with a consonant cluster, so speakers add a connecting hamza at utterance onset; some instead pronounce sim or sum by moving the initial consonant.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL (author): The noun ism begins with a consonant cluster, so speakers add a connecting hamza at utterance onset; some instead pronounce sim or sum by moving the initial consonant.

positions.position: Ism is a noun with a deleted ending, originally sumw, derived from elevation because naming raises and publicizes the named one.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL (author): Ism is a noun with a deleted ending, originally sumw, derived from elevation because naming raises and publicizes the named one.

positions.position: The word nabz for a nickname is related to nabr, raising the voice; nabz also names the outer peel of a palm tree.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL (author): The word nabz for a nickname is related to nabr, raising the voice; nabz also names the outer peel of a palm tree.

positions.position: Allah is the most striking and frequently used of God's names, usually preceding the others, which generally function as attributes.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (author): Allah is the most striking and frequently used of God's names, usually preceding the others, which generally function as attributes.

positions.position: The mark derivation drops wāw and adds a compensatory alif; the rise derivation has two analyses, one treating ism as a reshaped imperative and one deriving it from sumw with the final wāw deleted and hamza added because a word
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The mark derivation drops wāw and adds a compensatory alif; the rise derivation has two analyses, one treating ism as a reshaped imperative and one deriving it from sumw with the final wāw deleted and hamza added because a word cannot begin with a consonant cluster.

positions.position: Al-Akhfash compares the reshaping to al-ān, which he says came from the past verb āna yaʾīn and received the definite article.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الأخفش): Al-Akhfash compares the reshaping to al-ān, which he says came from the past verb āna yaʾīn and received the definite article.

positions.position: Arabic has several variants for 'name': Arabs use forms including ism and sim, with additional forms explained by whether the hamza is pronounced or dropped and by differing roots.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Arabic has several variants for 'name': Arabs use forms including ism and sim, with additional forms explained by whether the hamza is pronounced or dropped and by differing roots.

positions.position: Al-Kisāʾī says speakers pronounce the hamza with either kasra or ḍamma; when dropped, the resulting form varies according to the dialect's original vowel.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الكسائي): Al-Kisāʾī says speakers pronounce the hamza with either kasra or ḍamma; when dropped, the resulting form varies according to the dialect's original vowel.

positions.position: Thaʿlab ties the forms to whether 'name' derives from the root meaning to rise or become elevated.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (ثعلب): Thaʿlab ties the forms to whether 'name' derives from the root meaning to rise or become elevated.

positions.position: Al-Mubarrad reports hearing Arabs use several vowel and form variants for the word 'name.'
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (المبرد): Al-Mubarrad reports hearing Arabs use several vowel and form variants for the word 'name.'

positions.position: Al-Razi gives the Basran counterargument: if the word came from 'mark,' its diminutive and plural should be wasīm and awsām, not the attested forms.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (البصريون): Al-Razi gives the Basran counterargument: if the word came from 'mark,' its diminutive and plural should be wasīm and awsām, not the attested forms.

positions.position: A report says ʿAlī praised careful writing of the basmala, saying a man was forgiven for writing it well.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (علي بن أبي طالب): A report says ʿAlī praised careful writing of the basmala, saying a man was forgiven for writing it well.

positions.position: ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn interprets “when you mention your Lord alone in the Qurʾān” as saying the basmala.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (علي بن الحسين): ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn interprets “when you mention your Lord alone in the Qurʾān” as saying the basmala. | mentions 17:46

positions.position: Abū Bakr al-Khaṭīb prefers writing the basmala at the start of poetry collections.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (أبو بكر الخطيب): Abū Bakr al-Khaṭīb prefers writing the basmala at the start of poetry collections.

positions.position: Al-Farrāʾ reads the bāʾ as an imperative: begin in God’s name.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (الفراء): Al-Farrāʾ reads the bāʾ as an imperative: begin in God’s name.

positions.position: Al-Zajjāj reads the bāʾ as a statement: I began in God’s name.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (الزجاج): Al-Zajjāj reads the bāʾ as a statement: I began in God’s name.

positions.position: Al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ explain bismillah as bi-ism al-ilāh, with hamza deletion and lām assimilation.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (الكسائي والفراء): Al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ explain bismillah as bi-ism al-ilāh, with hamza deletion and lām assimilation.

positions.position: Forms asmāʾ, asāmī, samā, and samīt support this derivation; poetry attests the form samy.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (author): Forms asmāʾ, asāmī, samā, and samīt support this derivation; poetry attests the form samy.

positions.position: The Kufans derive ism from sima, “mark”: its original was wasm, with initial wāw deleted and hamzat al-waṣl added to reduce irregularity.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (الكوفيون): The Kufans derive ism from sima, “mark”: its original was wasm, with initial wāw deleted and hamzat al-waṣl added to reduce irregularity.

positions.position: Sam and sim are also forms; a poem attests sam in the phrase “in the name of the one in every sūra.”
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (author): Sam and sim are also forms; a poem attests sam in the phrase “in the name of the one in every sūra.”

positions.position: Ibn Abbas says whoever omits the basmala has omitted 114 verses from God’s Book.
positions.reasons: NASAFI (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas says whoever omits the basmala has omitted 114 verses from God’s Book.

positions.position: Ism begins with a silent consonant, so an initial hamza is added when starting speech but omitted in connected speech; some instead move the first consonant and say sim. Its ending is deleted, its original form is sumuw, and its
positions.reasons: NASAFI (author): Ism begins with a silent consonant, so an initial hamza is added when starting speech but omitted in connected speech; some instead move the first consonant and say sim. Its ending is deleted, its original form is sumuw, and its derivation denotes elevation because naming publicizes and honors the named.

positions.position: The noun ism has a prosthetic hamza for initial pronunciation, can be shortened to sim, and derives from deleted-final form samw, “elevation”: naming raises and publicizes the named one's mention.
positions.reasons: NASAFI-FULL (author): The noun ism has a prosthetic hamza for initial pronunciation, can be shortened to sim, and derives from deleted-final form samw, “elevation”: naming raises and publicizes the named one's mention.

positions.position: Al-Kisāʾī and al-Akhfash allow dropping the alif in bi-sm with other divine names; al-Farrāʾ restricts deletion to the full basmala.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (الكسائي والأخفش): Al-Kisāʾī and al-Akhfash allow dropping the alif in bi-sm with other divine names; al-Farrāʾ restricts deletion to the full basmala.

positions.position: Al-Kisāʾī and al-Akhfash allow dropping the alif from bism with any divine name.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الكسائي والأخفش): Al-Kisāʾī and al-Akhfash allow dropping the alif from bism with any divine name.

positions.position: The initial hamza is hamzat al-wasl, usually omitted in connected speech but retained by poetic necessity; ism is one of ten words beginning with it.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): The initial hamza is hamzat al-wasl, usually omitted in connected speech but retained by poetic necessity; ism is one of ten words beginning with it.

positions.position: Al-Kisa'i and al-Akhfash reportedly allow dropping the hamza when ism is annexed to another divine name, as in bism rabbika or bism al-khaliq.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (الكسائي والأخفش): Al-Kisa'i and al-Akhfash reportedly allow dropping the hamza when ism is annexed to another divine name, as in bism rabbika or bism al-khaliq.

positions.position: This derivation changes initial waw to hamza, like ishaah and i'aah from wishah and wi'aah; the name then has the pattern fa'al meaning worshipped or wondered at.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): This derivation changes initial waw to hamza, like ishaah and i'aah from wishah and wi'aah; the name then has the pattern fa'al meaning worshipped or wondered at.

positions.position: The omitted alif in bism signals the name’s elevated, unique rank and its connection to God, whose name gathers all names; the spelling also evokes manifestation and hiddenness.
positions.reasons: BURHAN (author): The omitted alif in bism signals the name’s elevated, unique rank and its connection to God, whose name gathers all names; the spelling also evokes manifestation and hiddenness.

positions.position: Al-Kisaʾi does not require the preceding ba and permits deletion in forms such as bism al-malik; the majority requires ba.
positions.reasons: BURHAN (الكسائي): Al-Kisaʾi does not require the preceding ba and permits deletion in forms such as bism al-malik; the majority requires ba.

positions.position: In sound and broken plurals, a surplus alif is deleted when the detailed meaning is latent and retained when it is manifest.
positions.reasons: BURHAN (author): In sound and broken plurals, a surplus alif is deleted when the detailed meaning is latent and retained when it is manifest.

positions.position: The basmala has nineteen written letters but eighteen pronounced, signaling protection from Hell's nineteen keepers and the drawing of mercy through the five prayers and witr, among the greatest devotions.
positions.reasons: BIQAI (author): The basmala has nineteen written letters but eighteen pronounced, signaling protection from Hell's nineteen keepers and the drawing of mercy through the five prayers and witr, among the greatest devotions.

positions.position: The basmala has nineteen written and eighteen spoken letters, alluding to the nineteen guardians of Hell and to mercy drawn by the five prayers and witr.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (author): The basmala has nineteen written and eighteen spoken letters, alluding to the nineteen guardians of Hell and to mercy drawn by the five prayers and witr.

positions.position: Sa'id ibn Jubayr says every written work, even poetry, should begin with the basmala.
positions.reasons: DURR (سعيد بن جبير): Sa'id ibn Jubayr says every written work, even poetry, should begin with the basmala.

positions.position: Al-Zuhri says established practice is not to write the basmala before poetry, disagreeing with Sa'id ibn Jubayr.
positions.reasons: DURR (الزهري): Al-Zuhri says established practice is not to write the basmala before poetry, disagreeing with Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

positions.position: Al-Sha'bi says people disliked placing the basmala before poetry and reports consensus against doing so.
positions.reasons: DURR (الشعبي): Al-Sha'bi says people disliked placing the basmala before poetry and reports consensus against doing so.

positions.position: Ibn Abbas transmits the calligraphic instruction not to extend the ba to the mim before writing the sin.
positions.reasons: DURR (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas transmits the calligraphic instruction not to extend the ba to the mim before writing the sin.

positions.position: Anas reports a direction to elongate al-Rahman when writing the basmala.
positions.reasons: DURR (النبي): Anas reports a direction to elongate al-Rahman when writing the basmala.

positions.position: Ibn Awn corrected a scribe who wrote bm, insisting on the sin lest someone sin unknowingly.
positions.reasons: DURR (ابن عون): Ibn Awn corrected a scribe who wrote bm, insisting on the sin lest someone sin unknowingly.

positions.position: Muadh reports Muhammad and al-Hasan disliked writing the extended ba without the sin.
positions.reasons: DURR (محمد والحسن): Muadh reports Muhammad and al-Hasan disliked writing the extended ba without the sin.

positions.position: Al-Zuhri says the basmala should not be written before poetry; al-Shabi reports dislike and consensus on that practice.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (الزهري): Al-Zuhri says the basmala should not be written before poetry; al-Shabi reports dislike and consensus on that practice.

positions.position: Matar al-Warraq says the Prophet directed Muawiya to connect the ba and sin and forbade lengthening any divine name in writing or recitation.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (مطر الوراق): Matar al-Warraq says the Prophet directed Muawiya to connect the ba and sin and forbade lengthening any divine name in writing or recitation.

positions.position: Ali says a man was forgiven for taking care over the writing of the basmala.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (علي بن أبي طالب): Ali says a man was forgiven for taking care over the writing of the basmala.

positions.position: Al-Zuhri reports that the Prophet prohibited extending the basmala in writing.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (الزهري): Al-Zuhri reports that the Prophet prohibited extending the basmala in writing.

positions.position: Muslim ibn Yasar disliked writing “bm” in place of the basmala because that drops the sin; other reports describe reprimands and punishment for the same omission.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (مسلم بن يسار): Muslim ibn Yasar disliked writing “bm” in place of the basmala because that drops the sin; other reports describe reprimands and punishment for the same omission.

positions.position: When Ibn Awn wrote “bm” for Ibn Sirin, Ibn Sirin demanded that he write the sin, warning against unwitting sin.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (ابن عون): When Ibn Awn wrote “bm” for Ibn Sirin, Ibn Sirin demanded that he write the sin, warning against unwitting sin.

positions.position: A mursal report says the Prophet condemned writing the basmala on the ground and instructed that it be placed in its proper place.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): A mursal report says the Prophet condemned writing the basmala on the ground and instructed that it be placed in its proper place.

positions.position: A marfu report promises that one who lifts a paper bearing the basmala out of reverence is counted among the truthful and brings relief to parents, even if unbelievers.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (أنس): A marfu report promises that one who lifts a paper bearing the basmala out of reverence is counted among the truthful and brings relief to parents, even if unbelievers.

positions.position: Umm Khalid claims she was the first to write the basmala.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (أم خالد بن خالد بن سعيد بن العاص): Umm Khalid claims she was the first to write the basmala.

positions.position: The Basrans derive ism from sumūw, “height,” with a deleted wāw; its function is to raise what is named from obscurity into recognition.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): The Basrans derive ism from sumūw, “height,” with a deleted wāw; its function is to raise what is named from obscurity into recognition.

positions.position: Abu Hurayra transmits the Prophet's instruction not to omit the basmala because it is one of the Fatiha's verses.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (أبو هريرة): Abu Hurayra transmits the Prophet's instruction not to omit the basmala because it is one of the Fatiha's verses.

positions.position: Razi argues that because the basmala is Qur'an in al-Naml and appears repeatedly in Qur'anic script, it is Qur'an wherever repeated.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (الفخر الرازي): Razi argues that because the basmala is Qur'an in al-Naml and appears repeatedly in Qur'anic script, it is Qur'an wherever repeated. | mentions 27:30

positions.position: He says denying the basmala's Qur'anic status because it is written in the muṣḥaf is intellectually unsound and contrary to fairness and faith.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): He says denying the basmala's Qur'anic status because it is written in the muṣḥaf is intellectually unsound and contrary to fairness and faith.

positions.position: Basran grammarians count ism among nouns whose first letter is quiescent, requiring a helping hamza when pronounced initially.
