positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (ابن إسحاق وأبو عمر والنضر والمبرد): Competing derivations connect Allāh to rising, concealment, fear, bewilderment, worship, or rest; Abū Ḥayyān reports these without choosing among them.

positions.position: If Allāh derives from al-ilāh, al- marks predominance: ilāh can name true or false deities, while Allāh names only the true deity; the comparison to al-Najm is challenged.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (author): If Allāh derives from al-ilāh, al- marks predominance: ilāh can name true or false deities, while Allāh names only the true deity; the comparison to al-Najm is challenged.

positions.position: On the other proposed derivations, al- is an inseparable extra article; omitting it in lāh abūka is anomalous.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (author): On the other proposed derivations, al- is an inseparable extra article; omitting it in lāh abūka is anomalous.

positions.position: Al-Suhaylī explains “you worship only names” as a metaphor for idols with false, unreal names, so their worship is effectively worship of invented names.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (السهيلي): Al-Suhaylī explains “you worship only names” as a metaphor for idols with false, unreal names, so their worship is effectively worship of invented names. | mentions 12:40

positions.position: Al-Suhaylī reads the worship of names besides God as a striking metaphor: the idolaters worship names they invented, not real entities.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (السهيلي): Al-Suhaylī reads the worship of names besides God as a striking metaphor: the idolaters worship names they invented, not real entities. | mentions 12:40

positions.position: Those who derive Allah from divinity cite that God is worshipped in heaven and earth and is a god in both realms.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): Those who derive Allah from divinity cite that God is worshipped in heaven and earth and is a god in both realms. | mentions 6:3, 43:84

positions.position: Al-Khalil explains that all creation is captivated by God, using a form of the root “to worship.”
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (الخليل بن أحمد): Al-Khalil explains that all creation is captivated by God, using a form of the root “to worship.”

positions.position: In the opening invocation, Allah is the ever-living witness who knows everything and permits all events; His mercy encompasses creation, while His special grace perfects the worship of His devotees.
positions.reasons: BIQAI (author): In the opening invocation, Allah is the ever-living witness who knows everything and permits all events; His mercy encompasses creation, while His special grace perfects the worship of His devotees.

positions.position: Since people are gathered to know God for worship, invoking His name at every movement and stillness leads to watchfulness, reverent fear, and belief that affairs originate from and return to Him; hence the Fātiḥa begins with the basmala.
positions.reasons: BIQAI (author): Since people are gathered to know God for worship, invoking His name at every movement and stillness leads to watchfulness, reverent fear, and belief that affairs originate from and return to Him; hence the Fātiḥa begins with the basmala.

positions.position: Here, “name” means God's supreme attributes.
positions.reasons: BIQAI (author): Here, “name” means God's supreme attributes.

positions.position: Al-Ḥarālī mystically explains Allah as the name toward which hearts turn when intellect reaches its limit: they are bewildered by Him and find in Him sufficiency from everything.
positions.reasons: BIQAI (أبو الحسن الحرالي): Al-Ḥarālī mystically explains Allah as the name toward which hearts turn when intellect reaches its limit: they are bewildered by Him and find in Him sufficiency from everything.

positions.position: Their order follows existence: creation, then universal blessings, then the particular blessing of worship. The two attributes encourage, while the second's implication folds in punishment as a restrained warning.
positions.reasons: BIQAI (author): Their order follows existence: creation, then universal blessings, then the particular blessing of worship. The two attributes encourage, while the second's implication folds in punishment as a restrained warning.

positions.position: The sūra establishes praise as encompassing all perfections and gratitude as magnifying the Benefactor.
positions.reasons: BIQAI (author): The sūra establishes praise as encompassing all perfections and gratitude as magnifying the Benefactor.

positions.position: In the authentic report in Muslim and the four Sunan, God says the Fatiha is divided between Himself and His servant: He answers praise, glorification and worship, and grants the servant's final requests.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (أبو هريرة): In the authentic report in Muslim and the four Sunan, God says the Fatiha is divided between Himself and His servant: He answers praise, glorification and worship, and grants the servant's final requests.

positions.position: Ibn Abbas explains the basmala as a command to read in God's name and defines Allah by divinity and worship.
positions.reasons: DURR (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas explains the basmala as a command to read in God's name and defines Allah by divinity and worship.

positions.position: The Prophet tells Ubayy three verses belong to God, three to the servant, and the worship-and-help verse is shared.
positions.reasons: DURR (النبي): The Prophet tells Ubayy three verses belong to God, three to the servant, and the worship-and-help verse is shared.

positions.position: Allah means the one possessing divinity and worship, worshipped by all creation.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (ابن عباس): Allah means the one possessing divinity and worship, worshipped by all creation.

positions.position: Naẓir al-Jaysh praises the preceding derivation as unsurpassed; al-Alusi finds it acceptable except for claiming al-ilāh means any object of worship.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (ناظر الجيش): Naẓir al-Jaysh praises the preceding derivation as unsurpassed; al-Alusi finds it acceptable except for claiming al-ilāh means any object of worship.

positions.position: Al-Balqini insists al-ilāh applies only to the true God and says applying it to another is unbelief; al-Alusi considers this objection open to reply.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (البلقيني): Al-Balqini insists al-ilāh applies only to the true God and says applying it to another is unbelief; al-Alusi considers this objection open to reply.

positions.position: Those who cannot humble their pride before God’s infinite manifestation and say they searched for God but did not find Him proclaim failure in the name of science and philosophy.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Those who cannot humble their pride before God’s infinite manifestation and say they searched for God but did not find Him proclaim failure in the name of science and philosophy.

positions.position: Sensing God requires the heart to discern Him and apprehend the realized relation between them.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Sensing God requires the heart to discern Him and apprehend the realized relation between them.

positions.position: Names include both proper and common nouns and names of entities and attributes; the distinctions matter when discussing God’s beautiful names.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Names include both proper and common nouns and names of entities and attributes; the distinctions matter when discussing God’s beautiful names.

positions.position: Allah is the proper personal name of the true object of worship; through this name and the divine attributes the Qurʾān introduces God and our relation to Him.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Allah is the proper personal name of the true object of worship; through this name and the divine attributes the Qurʾān introduces God and our relation to Him.

positions.position: Every person has an innate, simple, unbounded inner assent to God that is more truthful and powerful than finite senses, consciousness, reason, and thought because it encompasses them.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Every person has an innate, simple, unbounded inner assent to God that is more truthful and powerful than finite senses, consciousness, reason, and thought because it encompasses them.

positions.position: People’s forgetfulness of this primordial awareness is a source of error; the universe is full of divine signs and the Qurʾān recalls them with miraculous eloquence, hence its name al-Dhikr.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): People’s forgetfulness of this primordial awareness is a source of error; the universe is full of divine signs and the Qurʾān recalls them with miraculous eloquence, hence its name al-Dhikr.

positions.position: No other object of worship is called Allah, and the name has no dual or plural; many divine names are allowed, and a proper divine name in another language is possible, though familiar Turkish names are not equivalent.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): No other object of worship is called Allah, and the name has no dual or plural; many divine names are allowed, and a proper divine name in another language is possible, though familiar Turkish names are not equivalent. | mentions 19:65

positions.position: Unlike idols, fire, the sun, rulers, or other things made into gods by worshippers, God remains intrinsically worthy of worship whether people recognize Him or not; even deniers are compelled to serve Him unknowingly.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Unlike idols, fire, the sun, rulers, or other things made into gods by worshippers, God remains intrinsically worthy of worship whether people recognize Him or not; even deniers are compelled to serve Him unknowingly.

positions.position: That meaning cannot apply generally: saying one eats in God's name is improper, though saying one eats food God bestowed would be sound; worship is for God but not done as His deputy.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): That meaning cannot apply generally: saying one eats in God's name is improper, though saying one eats food God bestowed would be sound; worship is for God but not done as His deputy.

positions.position: Because God is the deity of everything, the divine name implies every perfection; it names the necessary existent who possesses all perfections, while lexically it remains the established name derived from ilah.
positions.reasons: TABATABAI (author): Because God is the deity of everything, the divine name implies every perfection; it names the necessary existent who possesses all perfections, while lexically it remains the established name derived from ilah.

positions.position: Al-Ridha explains bismillah as marking oneself with a mark of God, namely worship; the author sees it as a consequence of beginning worship in God's name.
positions.reasons: TABATABAI (الإمام الرضا): Al-Ridha explains bismillah as marking oneself with a mark of God, namely worship; the author sees it as a consequence of beginning worship in God's name.

question: What distinguishes ٱللَّهِ among divine names?

positions.position: Ibn Abbas identifies Allah as God's greatest name.
positions.reasons: DURR (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas identifies Allah as God's greatest name. DURR (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas says the basmala is a name of God and close to God's greatest name. DURR-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas identifies Allah as God's greatest name. DURR-FULL (الشعبي): Al-Shabi identifies the greatest name as “Ya Allah.”

positions.position: Jabir ibn Zayd says Allah is the Greatest Name because every Qur'anic sura begins with it before any other name.
positions.reasons: IBNABIHATIM (أبو الشعثاء جابر بن زيد): Jabir ibn Zayd says Allah is the Greatest Name because every Qur'anic sura begins with it before any other name. DURR (جابر بن يزيد): Jabir ibn Yazid says Allah is the greatest name because the Qur'an begins with it before every other name.

positions.position: Abu Hanifa is reported to say Allah is God’s greatest name because no one shares it.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (أبو حنيفة): Abu Hanifa is reported to say Allah is God’s greatest name because no one shares it. MAWARDI-FULL (أبو حنيفة): He identifies Allah as the Greatest Name because no one shares this name.

positions.position: Al-Hasan says al-Rahman is a name reserved from ordinary appropriation.
positions.reasons: DURR (الحسن): Al-Hasan says al-Rahman is a name reserved from ordinary appropriation. DURR-FULL (الحسن): Al-Hasan says al-Rahman is a name reserved for God.

positions.position: Allah is the greatest name encompassing all names; its veiled inner reality is accessible only to purified people living on lawful sustenance through faith.
positions.reasons: TUSTARI (author): Allah is the greatest name encompassing all names; its veiled inner reality is accessible only to purified people living on lawful sustenance through faith.

positions.position: Al-Ṭabarī considers ʿAṭāʾ’s explanation plausible: God uniquely combines the two names to distinguish His name, even if their individual meanings differ or overlap.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): Al-Ṭabarī considers ʿAṭāʾ’s explanation plausible: God uniquely combines the two names to distinguish His name, even if their individual meanings differ or overlap.

positions.position: ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī says al-Raḥmān was an exclusive divine name, then was separated from God’s name when Musaylima appropriated it.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (عطاء الخراساني): ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī says al-Raḥmān was an exclusive divine name, then was separated from God’s name when Musaylima appropriated it.

positions.position: Ṭabarī explains that God’s unique name remains exclusive even if people bear names such as Saʿīd while being its opposite.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): Ṭabarī explains that God’s unique name remains exclusive even if people bear names such as Saʿīd while being its opposite.

positions.position: The Prophet calls the basmala one of God's names and compares its nearness to Allah's name with the closeness of the eye's black and white.
positions.reasons: IBNABIHATIM (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): The Prophet calls the basmala one of God's names and compares its nearness to Allah's name with the closeness of the eye's black and white.

positions.position: Invoking any divine name gives the invoker some personal share, but the name Allah calls only to oneness and contains no deficiency.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (محمد بن موسى الواسطي): Invoking any divine name gives the invoker some personal share, but the name Allah calls only to oneness and contains no deficiency.

positions.position: Unlike other names, which imply compensation when invoked, Allah is a name reserved uniquely for the Real.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (بعضهم): Unlike other names, which imply compensation when invoked, Allah is a name reserved uniquely for the Real.

positions.position: No one truly says Allah except God, since every other speaker says it from a personal share and shares cannot reach realities.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (الشبلي): No one truly says Allah except God, since every other speaker says it from a personal share and shares cannot reach realities.

positions.position: All names' meanings are contained in Allah, but Allah's name derives from none; God alone bears it, though creatures share derivations of other names.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (بعضهم): All names' meanings are contained in Allah, but Allah's name derives from none; God alone bears it, though creatures share derivations of other names.

positions.position: The name Allah manifests divine awe and majesty.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (أبو العباس بن عطاء): The name Allah manifests divine awe and majesty.

positions.position: They say Allah is exclusive to God because it contains lordship and encompasses all meanings; its successive deletions yield li-llāh, lah, and huwa.
positions.reasons: THALABI (الخليل بن أحمد وجماعة): They say Allah is exclusive to God because it contains lordship and encompasses all meanings; its successive deletions yield li-llāh, lah, and huwa.

positions.position: When applied to another being, the source says the form must be qualified or indefinite; Allah and al-ilāh are reserved for God, as in the Israelites’ request for a god.
positions.reasons: THALABI (author): When applied to another being, the source says the form must be qualified or indefinite; Allah and al-ilāh are reserved for God, as in the Israelites’ request for a god. | mentions 7:138

positions.position: Allah is God’s most exclusive name, since no other is called by it; the phrase asking whether He has a like is the broader interpretation because it covers names and deeds.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (author): Allah is God’s most exclusive name, since no other is called by it; the phrase asking whether He has a like is the broader interpretation because it covers names and deeds.

positions.position: Allah is God's most particular name because no one besides Him has borne it.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI-FULL (author): Allah is God's most particular name because no one besides Him has borne it.

positions.position: A second interpretation asks whether anyone comparable to Him is known; this is broader because it applies to both name and act.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI-FULL (author): A second interpretation asks whether anyone comparable to Him is known; this is broader because it applies to both name and act.

positions.position: Rahman functions as an exclusive, established epithet for God, like Allah, and is not ordinarily used of anyone else.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL (author): Rahman functions as an exclusive, established epithet for God, like Allah, and is not ordinarily used of anyone else.

positions.position: Al-Rida says the basmala is nearer to God's Greatest Name than the black of the eye is to its white.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (علي بن موسى الرضا): Al-Rida says the basmala is nearer to God's Greatest Name than the black of the eye is to its white.

positions.position: Allah is an exclusive divine name and is not applied to anyone besides God.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (author): Allah is an exclusive divine name and is not applied to anyone besides God.

positions.position: One analysis derives Allah from lah; the article marks glorification and exaltation, not definiteness, since God's names are already definite.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (سيبويه): One analysis derives Allah from lah; the article marks glorification and exaltation, not definiteness, since God's names are already definite.

positions.position: Al-Razi rejects 'Possessor of Majesty and Honor' as the greatest name because majesty and honor denote negative and relational attributes, not the unique essence.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Razi rejects 'Possessor of Majesty and Honor' as the greatest name because majesty and honor denote negative and relational attributes, not the unique essence. | mentions 55:27

positions.position: Al-Razi cites a prophetic report urging frequent invocation of the Possessor of Majesty and Honor as support for that candidate name.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Razi cites a prophetic report urging frequent invocation of the Possessor of Majesty and Honor as support for that candidate name.

positions.position: The testimony of faith uniquely uses Allah: replacing it with another divine name would not, in Rāzī’s account, take a non-Muslim into Islam.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The testimony of faith uniquely uses Allah: replacing it with another divine name would not, in Rāzī’s account, take a non-Muslim into Islam.

positions.position: If an essence-name can be assigned, it must be the greatest name and remembrance because their honor follows the honor of what is known and remembered.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): If an essence-name can be assigned, it must be the greatest name and remembrance because their honor follows the honor of what is known and remembered.

positions.position: A prophet or angel who encountered that name while its meaning was manifest might be obeyed by all physical and spiritual realms.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A prophet or angel who encountered that name while its meaning was manifest might be obeyed by all physical and spiritual realms.

positions.position: Ibn al-ʿArabī says disagreement turns on whether “no prayer” negates validity or completeness; Qurṭubī prefers general negation.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (ابن العربي): Ibn al-ʿArabī says disagreement turns on whether “no prayer” negates validity or completeness; Qurṭubī prefers general negation.

positions.position: Saʿīd reports forgiveness for a person who kissed a paper bearing God’s name and placed it on his eyes.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (سعيد): Saʿīd reports forgiveness for a person who kissed a paper bearing God’s name and placed it on his eyes.

positions.position: Ibn al-ʿArabī calls Mālik’s post-recitation rule for al-Fātiḥa unsupported by transmitted evidence or sound reasoning.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (ابن العربي): Ibn al-ʿArabī calls Mālik’s post-recitation rule for al-Fātiḥa unsupported by transmitted evidence or sound reasoning.

positions.position: Allah is the greatest, most comprehensive divine name, unique to God and not pluralized; 19:65 may mean no one bears that name.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (author): Allah is the greatest, most comprehensive divine name, unique to God and not pluralized; 19:65 may mean no one bears that name. | mentions 19:65

positions.position: Ibn al-ʿArabī reports al-Raḥmān may be the greatest name of God.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (ابن العربي): Ibn al-ʿArabī reports al-Raḥmān may be the greatest name of God.

positions.position: Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr notes uncertainty over the narrator’s name; Qurṭubī lists variants but identifies him as a leading Anṣārī.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (ابن عبد البر): Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr notes uncertainty over the narrator’s name; Qurṭubī lists variants but identifies him as a leading Anṣārī.

positions.position: Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr and Ibn al-Qāsim prefer cancelling the missed unit and replacing it.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (ابن عبد البر وابن القاسم): Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr and Ibn al-Qāsim prefer cancelling the missed unit and replacing it.

positions.position: Bayḍāwī prefers that Allāh was originally descriptive but became name-like through exclusive use, allowing predicates while excluding descriptive use and partners.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (author): Bayḍāwī prefers that Allāh was originally descriptive but became name-like through exclusive use, allowing predicates while excluding descriptive use and partners.

positions.position: Al-Raḥmān precedes as God's exclusive name, the true ultimate benefactor; others give from mixed motives and only mediate blessings God creates and enables.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (author): Al-Raḥmān precedes as God's exclusive name, the true ultimate benefactor; others give from mixed motives and only mediate blessings God creates and enables.

positions.position: The cited poem attests the use of لاه as God's name among tribal elders.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL (author): The cited poem attests the use of لاه as God's name among tribal elders.

positions.position: Although one might expect the less to precede the greater, الرحمن comes first because worldly mercy precedes the afterlife and because the name has become exclusive to God.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL (author): Although one might expect the less to precede the greater, الرحمن comes first because worldly mercy precedes the afterlife and because the name has become exclusive to God.

positions.position: The stronger view is that الله was originally descriptive, as derivation and the sense of “God in the heavens” indicate, but exclusive usage made it function like a proper name.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL (author): The stronger view is that الله was originally descriptive, as derivation and the sense of “God in the heavens” indicate, but exclusive usage made it function like a proper name. | mentions 6:3

positions.position: On a qualitative reading, الرحمن covers both worlds while الرحيم covers this world, since all afterlife blessings are immense but worldly blessings range from great to small.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL (author): On a qualitative reading, الرحمن covers both worlds while الرحيم covers this world, since all afterlife blessings are immense but worldly blessings range from great to small.

positions.position: Al-Bayḍāwī's stronger grammatical view is that الرحمن is indeclinable, despite its exclusive association with God and the usual feminine patterns of its class.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL (author): Al-Bayḍāwī's stronger grammatical view is that الرحمن is indeclinable, despite its exclusive association with God and the usual feminine patterns of its class.

positions.position: These particular names teach that only the true God deserves to be invoked for every need: He owns all blessings, immediate and future, great and small, and alone enables their delivery and use.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL (author): These particular names teach that only the true God deserves to be invoked for every need: He owns all blessings, immediate and future, great and small, and alone enables their delivery and use.

positions.position: Al-Suhaylī says omitting the verb after the basmala keeps God's name alone at the start and makes the spoken form mirror the heart's exclusive remembrance.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (السهيلي): Al-Suhaylī says omitting the verb after the basmala keeps God's name alone at the start and makes the spoken form mirror the heart's exclusive remembrance.

positions.position: Others assign each name a distinct object: mercy is universal to believers and unbelievers in this world but reserved for believers in the next; a reversed report also circulates, and the author doubts this distinction alone.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): Others assign each name a distinct object: mercy is universal to believers and unbelievers in this world but reserved for believers in the next; a reversed report also circulates, and the author doubts this distinction alone.

positions.position: A report says the basmala is one of God's names, extremely close to the Greatest Name, like the closeness between the black and white of the eye.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (ابن عباس): A report says the basmala is one of God's names, extremely close to the Greatest Name, like the closeness between the black and white of the eye.

positions.position: Al-Sha'bi gives the greatest name as Ya Allah.
positions.reasons: DURR (الشعبي): Al-Sha'bi gives the greatest name as Ya Allah.

positions.position: Al-Bayhaqi says rqiqan in the transmitted text is likely a scribal error for rafiqan, a divine name.
positions.reasons: DURR (البيهقي): Al-Bayhaqi says rqiqan in the transmitted text is likely a scribal error for rafiqan, a divine name.

positions.position: Safwan says jinn share human property and clothing, so God's name should be said when removing or putting them on; God's name is a seal.
positions.reasons: DURR (صفوان بن سليم): Safwan says jinn share human property and clothing, so God's name should be said when removing or putting them on; God's name is a seal.

positions.position: A report says the basmala is a name of God, nearly as close to His greatest name as the pupil is to the white of the eye.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): A report says the basmala is a name of God, nearly as close to His greatest name as the pupil is to the white of the eye.

positions.position: Jabir ibn Yazid also says Allah is the greatest name, since the Quran places it before every other name.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (جابر بن يزيد): Jabir ibn Yazid also says Allah is the greatest name, since the Quran places it before every other name.

positions.position: Al-Bayḍāwī says Allāh began as an adjective but became proper through exclusive use; al-Ālūsī rejects his arguments from description, the heavenly predicate, and derivation.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (البيضاوي): Al-Bayḍāwī says Allāh began as an adjective but became proper through exclusive use; al-Ālūsī rejects his arguments from description, the heavenly predicate, and derivation. | mentions 6:3

positions.position: The exclusive declaration “no god but God” supports a proper name: an adjective or generic noun would not itself prevent sharing, even if conventionally reserved.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): The exclusive declaration “no god but God” supports a proper name: an adjective or generic noun would not itself prevent sharing, even if conventionally reserved. | mentions 2:163

positions.position: Alusi prefers estimating a preceding verb: putting it after ba, ism, Allah, or the attributes would split grammatical units or make mercy appear an exclusive cause of recitation.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi prefers estimating a preceding verb: putting it after ba, ism, Allah, or the attributes would split grammatical units or make mercy appear an exclusive cause of recitation.

positions.position: With a preceding verb, the formula still implies restriction: one reads with God's help or blessing because He is the Merciful, excluding those outside that stated cause in this rhetorical context.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): With a preceding verb, the formula still implies restriction: one reads with God's help or blessing because He is the Merciful, excluding those outside that stated cause in this rhetorical context.

positions.position: Al-Sayyid al-Sanad treats both forms as names of the divine essence, with al-ilāh usable of another before deletion but Allah exclusive afterward.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (السيد السند): Al-Sayyid al-Sanad treats both forms as names of the divine essence, with al-ilāh usable of another before deletion but Allah exclusive afterward.

positions.position: Al-Raḍī says both forms are exclusive to God, though before assimilation the word is an established common proper name and afterward a fully specific proper name.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (الرضي): Al-Raḍī says both forms are exclusive to God, though before assimilation the word is an established common proper name and afterward a fully specific proper name.

positions.position: Ibn Malik argues Allah was formed with the article from the outset, not from al-ilāh, because the forms differ in both morphology and meaning.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (ابن مالك): Ibn Malik argues Allah was formed with the article from the outset, not from al-ilāh, because the forms differ in both morphology and meaning.

positions.position: Al-Bayḍawi treats Allah as originally a descriptor that became a name through exclusive usage; he argues its essence cannot be directly conceived and cites usage and derivation.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (البيضاوي): Al-Bayḍawi treats Allah as originally a descriptor that became a name through exclusive usage; he argues its essence cannot be directly conceived and cites usage and derivation. | mentions 6:3

positions.position: The Prophet's moral character and mission as mercy to the worlds ground his selection and training; God taught him to begin with the divine name and its exclusive relation.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): The Prophet's moral character and mission as mercy to the worlds ground his selection and training; God taught him to begin with the divine name and its exclusive relation. | mentions 68:4, 21:107

positions.position: Rahmān is an exclusive divine name and a dominant adjective of essence rather than action; it can occur with or without its described noun, but does not take a preposition as a verb would.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Rahmān is an exclusive divine name and a dominant adjective of essence rather than action; it can occur with or without its described noun, but does not take a preposition as a verb would.

positions.position: This fronting makes the beginning exclusive to Allah's name, rejecting the pagan practice of starting with Lat or Uzza and expressing tawhid.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): This fronting makes the beginning exclusive to Allah's name, rejecting the pagan practice of starting with Lat or Uzza and expressing tawhid.

positions.position: Al-Sadiq, and separately al-Ridha in reports cited by al-Ayyashi and al-Uyun, say the basmala is nearer to God's greatest name than the eye's pupil is to its white; its explanation is deferred.
positions.reasons: TABATABAI (الصادق): Al-Sadiq, and separately al-Ridha in reports cited by al-Ayyashi and al-Uyun, say the basmala is nearer to God's greatest name than the eye's pupil is to its white; its explanation is deferred.

positions.position: Rahman is an exclusive divine name for limitless, undeserved grace toward every creature throughout all time, like rain falling and sunlight warming all things.
positions.reasons: KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): Rahman is an exclusive divine name for limitless, undeserved grace toward every creature throughout all time, like rain falling and sunlight warming all things.

positions.position: Allāh is the most universal and all-embracing Divine Name, yet uniquely applies only to God, unlike other Divine Names.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (author): Allāh is the most universal and all-embracing Divine Name, yet uniquely applies only to God, unlike other Divine Names.

question: What inward meanings do the letters of ٱللَّهِ carry?

positions.position: The final alif in Allāh is variously said to be omitted to distinguish its spelling from lāhū, to lighten it, or because of a spelling convention.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (author): The final alif in Allāh is variously said to be omitted to distinguish its spelling from lāhū, to lighten it, or because of a spelling convention. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): The final alif in Allah is said to be omitted in writing to distinguish it from lāh, or simply for brevity, or because of a spelling convention.

positions.position: They retain the alif in fa-sabbih bi-ismi rabbika because this name is not used with the preposition as frequently as Allah’s name; 87:1.
positions.reasons: FARRA (author): They retain the alif in fa-sabbih bi-ismi rabbika because this name is not used with the preposition as frequently as Allah’s name; 87:1.

positions.position: The letters signify oneness, then the erasure of indication and of that erasure in the disclosure of hāʾ.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (بعضهم): The letters signify oneness, then the erasure of indication and of that erasure in the disclosure of hāʾ.

positions.position: Dropping letters from Allah leaves successive divine indications—lillah, lahu, then hāʾ—which is the utmost signification.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (بعضهم): Dropping letters from Allah leaves successive divine indications—lillah, lahu, then hāʾ—which is the utmost signification.

positions.position: Uttering Allah through letters cannot truly name Him, since He exceeds letters, concepts, and imaginings; the formula is accepted because no other mode of affirming oneness is possible.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (بعضهم): Uttering Allah through letters cannot truly name Him, since He exceeds letters, concepts, and imaginings; the formula is accepted because no other mode of affirming oneness is possible.

positions.position: The visible letters are not God Himself; when the letters disappear, the indication is that He is God.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (بعض البغداديين): The visible letters are not God Himself; when the letters disappear, the indication is that He is God.

positions.position: The ultimate goal is God; the supplication asks for guidance to Him, steadfastness in His presence, freedom from substitutes, and settlement at the encounter.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (حكيم من الحكماء): The ultimate goal is God; the supplication asks for guidance to Him, steadfastness in His presence, freedom from substitutes, and settlement at the encounter.

positions.position: God first called servants to the single name Allah; people of realities need that name, while further descriptions in the chapter serve successively lower ranks.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (أبو سعيد الخراز): God first called servants to the single name Allah; people of realities need that name, while further descriptions in the chapter serve successively lower ranks.

positions.position: Every divine name may be emulated except Allah, which is for attachment to God rather than taking on His name.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (بعضهم): Every divine name may be emulated except Allah, which is for attachment to God rather than taking on His name.

positions.position: In Allah, the two lām letters and hāʾ are connected while alif is separate, indicating that the reference to God is not made through the servant's own self.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (بعضهم): In Allah, the two lām letters and hāʾ are connected while alif is separate, indicating that the reference to God is not made through the servant's own self.

positions.position: The four letters form a complete, unique name: alif is the pillar of oneness, the two lām letters signify the Tablet of the Pen and of Prophecy, and hāʾ is the utmost indication; God exceeds apprehension.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (جعفر): The four letters form a complete, unique name: alif is the pillar of oneness, the two lām letters signify the Tablet of the Pen and of Prophecy, and hāʾ is the utmost indication; God exceeds apprehension.

positions.position: Al-Shāfiʿī, al-Shaʿbī, and a view attributed to ʿAbd Allāh say it was revealed as the first verse of al-Fātiḥa and is a verse in every sura except al-Tawba; written repetitions and the Naml occurrence are their evidence.
positions.reasons: THALABI (الشافعي والشعبي وعبد الله): Al-Shāfiʿī, al-Shaʿbī, and a view attributed to ʿAbd Allāh say it was revealed as the first verse of al-Fātiḥa and is a verse in every sura except al-Tawba; written repetitions and the Naml occurrence are their evidence. | mentions 27:30, 55:13, 77:15

positions.position: The source notes a heavy pronunciation of the lām in Allah, with the tongue pressed to the palate in reverence for the name.
positions.reasons: THALABI (author): The source notes a heavy pronunciation of the lām in Allah, with the tongue pressed to the palate in reverence for the name.

positions.position: Al-Zajjaj says emphatic pronunciation of Allah's lām is Sunna; Arabs all use it, showing inherited usage.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF (الزجاج): Al-Zajjaj says emphatic pronunciation of Allah's lām is Sunna; Arabs all use it, showing inherited usage.

positions.position: Al-Zajjaj says pronouncing Allah's lām emphatically is a sunnah; universal Arab practice shows it was inherited generation after generation.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL (الزجاج): Al-Zajjaj says pronouncing Allah's lām emphatically is a sunnah; universal Arab practice shows it was inherited generation after generation.

positions.position: The final alif of Allah is said to be omitted to distinguish its script from al-Lat, for ease, or as a dialect form; Ibn al-A'rabi's verse is cited for the latter.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (author): The final alif of Allah is said to be omitted to distinguish its script from al-Lat, for ease, or as a dialect form; Ibn al-A'rabi's verse is cited for the latter.

positions.position: The written name Allah is the most striking and most frequently used of God's names, usually preceding the others, which tend to function as attributes.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): The written name Allah is the most striking and most frequently used of God's names, usually preceding the others, which tend to function as attributes.

positions.position: Explanations for omitting the final alif in Allah include avoiding confusion with al-Lat, lightening, or dialect; a verse by Ibn al-Aʿrabi illustrates the form.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): Explanations for omitting the final alif in Allah include avoiding confusion with al-Lat, lightening, or dialect; a verse by Ibn al-Aʿrabi illustrates the form.

positions.position: Removing the initial alif from Allah yields lillāh, attested in Qur’anic phrases about God’s armies and treasuries.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Removing the initial alif from Allah yields lillāh, attested in Qur’anic phrases about God’s armies and treasuries. | mentions 48:4, 63:7

positions.position: Further deletion yields lahu and then huwa; the wāw is extra because it drops in the dual and plural forms.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Further deletion yields lahu and then huwa; the wāw is extra because it drops in the dual and plural forms. | mentions 39:63, 64:1, 112:1, 40:65

positions.position: The alif in 'Allah' is not omitted in ordinary pronunciation, though poetic necessity permits its omission at a pause, as in the cited anonymous verse.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The alif in 'Allah' is not omitted in ordinary pronunciation, though poetic necessity permits its omission at a pause, as in the cited anonymous verse.

positions.position: Qutayba alone is reported to permit imāla of 'Allah' in some transmissions.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (قتيبة): Qutayba alone is reported to permit imāla of 'Allah' in some transmissions.

positions.position: God is spelled with two lām letters unlike alladhī: the divine name is inflected, while the relative pronoun is indeclinable because it requires a relative clause; its dual form further separates it from particles.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): God is spelled with two lām letters unlike alladhī: the divine name is inflected, while the relative pronoun is indeclinable because it requires a relative clause; its dual form further separates it from particles.

positions.position: A single lām would make 'Allah' visually confusable with 'ilāh,' whereas writing out both lām letters avoids ambiguity.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A single lām would make 'Allah' visually confusable with 'ilāh,' whereas writing out both lām letters avoids ambiguity.

positions.position: Because pronouncing God's name emphatically signals greatness, omitting a lām in its spelling would conflict with that reverence.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Because pronouncing God's name emphatically signals greatness, omitting a lām in its spelling would conflict with that reverence.

positions.position: The alif before hāʾ is omitted in writing to avoid visually repetitive letters, paralleling avoidance of repeated identical sounds in recitation.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The alif before hāʾ is omitted in writing to avoid visually repetitive letters, paralleling avoidance of repeated identical sounds in recitation.

positions.position: Al-Akhfash says ism shifts the phrase from an oath to an invocation for blessing; the underlying phrase is bi-Allah.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (الأخفش): Al-Akhfash says ism shifts the phrase from an oath to an invocation for blessing; the underlying phrase is bi-Allah.

positions.position: Al-Kisāʾī and Saʿīd al-Akhfash also omit the alif before al-Raḥmān and al-Qāhir; Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb omits it only before Allah.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (الكسائي وسعيد الأخفش): Al-Kisāʾī and Saʿīd al-Akhfash also omit the alif before al-Raḥmān and al-Qāhir; Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb omits it only before Allah.

positions.position: Deleting Allāh's alif is an error that invalidates prayer and does not establish an explicit oath, though poetic necessity may require it.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (author): Deleting Allāh's alif is an error that invalidates prayer and does not establish an explicit oath, though poetic necessity may require it.

positions.position: Most reciters emphasize the lām of Allah after fatḥa or ḍamma and lighten it after kasra; some lighten it in every context and others emphasize it throughout.
positions.reasons: NASAFI (الجمهور): Most reciters emphasize the lām of Allah after fatḥa or ḍamma and lighten it after kasra; some lighten it in every context and others emphasize it throughout.

positions.position: The lām of Allah is generally emphatic after fatḥa or ḍamma and light after kasra; some readers lighten it in every position, others always emphasize it, while the first pattern is the majority practice.
positions.reasons: NASAFI-FULL (author): The lām of Allah is generally emphatic after fatḥa or ḍamma and light after kasra; some readers lighten it in every position, others always emphasize it, while the first pattern is the majority practice.

positions.position: The alif is omitted in writing in bi-sm Allāh and in raḥmān because of frequent use.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (author): The alif is omitted in writing in bi-sm Allāh and in raḥmān because of frequent use.

positions.position: Ba is also discussed as extra in the construction beginning a-wa-lam yaraw anna Allah and similar expressions.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): Ba is also discussed as extra in the construction beginning a-wa-lam yaraw anna Allah and similar expressions. | mentions 46:33

positions.position: The author rebuts al-Khalil: if hamza replaced waw, the original forms should remain pronounceable, and the word should pluralize as awliha; neither occurs.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): The author rebuts al-Khalil: if hamza replaced waw, the original forms should remain pronounceable, and the word should pluralize as awliha; neither occurs.

positions.position: Al-Khalil can answer that the replacement became obligatory because this name has unique grammatical properties and its plural preserves that replacement.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (الخليل): Al-Khalil can answer that the replacement became obligatory because this name has unique grammatical properties and its plural preserves that replacement.

positions.position: Whether the article in Allah is original depends on whether the name is derived; if derived it is original, otherwise added.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): Whether the article in Allah is original depends on whether the name is derived; if derived it is original, otherwise added.

positions.position: The alif was omitted in writing to distinguish Allah from the idol al-Lat; another explanation invokes the word al-lāh, while a third calls the spelling a rare form fixed by frequent use.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): The alif was omitted in writing to distinguish Allah from the idol al-Lat; another explanation invokes the word al-lāh, while a third calls the spelling a rare form fixed by frequent use.

positions.position: The lām of Allah is emphatic except after kasra; al-Zamakhshari's unqualified statement should be understood this way, while Abu al-Baqa's report of always-light pronunciation is rejected.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): The lām of Allah is emphatic except after kasra; al-Zamakhshari's unqualified statement should be understood this way, while Abu al-Baqa's report of always-light pronunciation is rejected.

positions.position: Readers disagree about the lām after an imāla-like open vowel; al-Susi has one reading with a light lām in hatta nara Allah jahratan.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): Readers disagree about the lām after an imāla-like open vowel; al-Susi has one reading with a light lām in hatta nara Allah jahratan.

positions.position: Al-Suhayli and Ibn al-Arabi unusually say the article is original; the author objects that this would make the pattern fa'al regularly take tanwin, which Allah does not.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (السهيلي وابن العربي): Al-Suhayli and Ibn al-Arabi unusually say the article is original; the author objects that this would make the pattern fa'al regularly take tanwin, which Allah does not.

positions.position: Abu Zayd al-Balkhi reports that Allah is a Syriac loan from laha; a poem preserves the supposed original form lahi.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (أبو زيد البلخي): Abu Zayd al-Balkhi reports that Allah is a Syriac loan from laha; a poem preserves the supposed original form lahi.

positions.position: A strange proposal derives the name from the pronoun hu plus a possessive lām and article; the author says it resembles mysticism, not linguistic scholarship.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): A strange proposal derives the name from the pronoun hu plus a possessive lām and article; the author says it resembles mysticism, not linguistic scholarship.

positions.position: The lām is emphatic after fatḥa or ḍamma according to common recitation practice; deletion of the alif is reported in pause, but retention is more eloquent.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): The lām is emphatic after fatḥa or ḍamma according to common recitation practice; deletion of the alif is reported in pause, but retention is more eloquent.

positions.position: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ reports dropping Allāh’s alif; al-Taysīr confines it to pause, and some jurists call it erroneous enough to invalidate prayer or an explicit oath.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ reports dropping Allāh’s alif; al-Taysīr confines it to pause, and some jurists call it erroneous enough to invalidate prayer or an explicit oath.

positions.position: Sound hadiths support its names al-Ruqya, al-Shifāʾ, and al-Shāfiya; it is also called al-Ṣalāh because it is required or recommended in prayer.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Sound hadiths support its names al-Ruqya, al-Shifāʾ, and al-Shāfiya; it is also called al-Ṣalāh because it is required or recommended in prayer.

positions.position: Other accounts say it descended both when prayer became obligatory in Mecca and when the qibla changed in Medina, or that parts are Meccan and Medinan; he calls the latter weak.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Other accounts say it descended both when prayer became obligatory in Mecca and when the qibla changed in Medina, or that parts are Meccan and Medinan; he calls the latter weak.

positions.position: Many Sufis favor this mystical account, which al-Alusi says is close to their spiritual mode of interpretation.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (الصوفية): Many Sufis favor this mystical account, which al-Alusi says is close to their spiritual mode of interpretation.

positions.position: Readers generally velarize Allah’s lām after an a or u vowel, though an unrestricted form is reported; deleting the alif is less eloquent and, in one view, invalid in prayer or an oath.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (القراء): Readers generally velarize Allah’s lām after an a or u vowel, though an unrestricted form is reported; deleting the alif is less eloquent and, in one view, invalid in prayer or an oath.

positions.position: Ibn Arabi reads the letters and patterns of Allah mystically, finding signs in the alif, lām, and changing vowels; al-Alusi directs readers to the esoteric writings.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (ابن عربي): Ibn Arabi reads the letters and patterns of Allah mystically, finding signs in the alif, lām, and changing vowels; al-Alusi directs readers to the esoteric writings.

positions.position: A mystical letter reading assigns hidden and manifest alifs in Allah and Rahman to essence and knowledge, with other letters indicating divine attributes; life is their necessary condition.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): A mystical letter reading assigns hidden and manifest alifs in Allah and Rahman to essence and knowledge, with other letters indicating divine attributes; life is their necessary condition.

positions.position: Basmala is a coined noun formed by blending letters from bismi and Allāh; naḥt creates a compact expression from a frequently spoken phrase.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): Basmala is a coined noun formed by blending letters from bismi and Allāh; naḥt creates a compact expression from a frequently spoken phrase.

positions.position: Arabic forms the regular verbal noun basmala and the active participle from basmala; no passive participle is attested.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): Arabic forms the regular verbal noun basmala and the active participle from basmala; no passive participle is attested.

positions.position: Forms such as bāqiya, ṭāghiya, khāṭiʾa, and ḥāqqa can function as verbal nouns; Ibn ʿAbbās glosses al-ṭāghiya as the people’s transgression.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (ابن عباس): Forms such as bāqiya, ṭāghiya, khāṭiʾa, and ḥāqqa can function as verbal nouns; Ibn ʿAbbās glosses al-ṭāghiya as the people’s transgression.

question: Which names may be used of God, and how?

positions.position: Arabic convention places a referent’s name before its attributes; Ṭabarī applies that order to the divine names.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): Arabic convention places a referent’s name before its attributes; Ṭabarī applies that order to the divine names. TAB-FULL (author): Arabic convention places a referent’s name before its attributes; Ṭabarī applies that order to the divine names.

positions.position: Poetic usage confirms verbal nouns can take other noun forms: ʿaṭāʾika means iʿṭāʾika, ṭūl means iṭāla, and muṣāb means iṣāba.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): Poetic usage confirms verbal nouns can take other noun forms: ʿaṭāʾika means iʿṭāʾika, ṭūl means iṭāla, and muṣāb means iṣāba.

positions.position: Accordingly, the name stands for naming: the phrase means that one begins an action or recitation by naming God.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): Accordingly, the name stands for naming: the phrase means that one begins an action or recitation by naming God.

positions.position: Because the name itself is inaccessible in reality, pleasures are even more inaccessible, teaching creatures their inability to name God's essence.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (بعضهم): Because the name itself is inaccessible in reality, pleasures are even more inaccessible, teaching creatures their inability to name God's essence.

positions.position: A name can stand for its referent because speech or address attached to the name is in reality attached to the named thing.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (author): A name can stand for its referent because speech or address attached to the name is in reality attached to the named thing.

positions.position: The preferred reading is begin by naming God: the command teaches opening actions with God's name, as in eating, drinking, and slaughter, rather than merely reporting His majesty.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (author): The preferred reading is begin by naming God: the command teaches opening actions with God's name, as in eating, drinking, and slaughter, rather than merely reporting His majesty.

positions.position: Adam answers Moses that God chose him, revealed the Torah, and had decreed Adam's act before creating him; Adam thus prevails over Moses three times.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النبي): Adam answers Moses that God chose him, revealed the Torah, and had decreed Adam's act before creating him; Adam thus prevails over Moses three times.

positions.position: A supplication invoking every name God gave or kept hidden asks that the Quran enliven the heart and remove grief; God replaces the supplicant's sorrow with joy.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النبي): A supplication invoking every name God gave or kept hidden asks that the Quran enliven the heart and remove grief; God replaces the supplicant's sorrow with joy.

positions.position: Qadim originally denotes long duration rather than absence of a beginning, as in an old date-palm and an old error; it does not by itself prove eternity.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Qadim originally denotes long duration rather than absence of a beginning, as in an old date-palm and an old error; it does not by itself prove eternity. | mentions 36:39, 12:95

positions.position: Abadi denotes duration into the future.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Abadi denotes duration into the future.

positions.position: The cited Prophetic saying calls the sacred months one single month followed by three consecutive months, illustrating the root sense of succession.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النبي): The cited Prophetic saying calls the sacred months one single month followed by three consecutive months, illustrating the root sense of succession.

positions.position: One position makes divine names strictly revelatory: no name or attribute may be applied unless it occurs in the Qur'an or an authentic hadith.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (بعض العلماء): One position makes divine names strictly revelatory: no name or attribute may be applied unless it occurs in the Qur'an or an authentic hadith.

positions.position: The opposing position permits any expression whose meaning befits God's majesty and attributes.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (بعض العلماء): The opposing position permits any expression whose meaning befits God's majesty and attributes.

positions.position: Al-Ghazālī distinguishes names from descriptions: names of God require textual warrant, but descriptive attributes do not.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الغزالي): Al-Ghazālī distinguishes names from descriptions: names of God require textual warrant, but descriptive attributes do not.

positions.position: Proponents of strict textual warrant argue that some apparently laudatory human labels, such as physician or jurist, are not used for God, so naming is restricted.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أصحاب التوقيف): Proponents of strict textual warrant argue that some apparently laudatory human labels, such as physician or jurist, are not used for God, so naming is restricted.

positions.position: Razi begins answering the example of “physician,” “jurist,” “certain,” and “clarifying,” arguing that each term has a meaning that makes it unsuitable for God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi begins answering the example of “physician,” “jurist,” “certain,” and “clarifying,” arguing that each term has a meaning that makes it unsuitable for God.

positions.position: A report says that when Abū Bakr fell ill and someone offered to bring a physician, he replied that the physician had made him ill.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A report says that when Abū Bakr fell ill and someone offered to bring a physician, he replied that the physician had made him ill.

positions.position: They cite “God's are the beautiful names, so call upon Him by them”: every name denoting praise and majesty is beautiful and permitted.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (القائلون بأنه لا حاجة إلى التوقيف): They cite “God's are the beautiful names, so call upon Him by them”: every name denoting praise and majesty is beautiful and permitted. | mentions 7:180

positions.position: They argue that valid meanings matter more than particular words, so forbidding a suitable expression is pointless.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (القائلون بأنه لا حاجة إلى التوقيف): They argue that valid meanings matter more than particular words, so forbidding a suitable expression is pointless.

positions.position: Al-Ghazālī reasons that if giving someone a name can be poor etiquette, naming God is even more sensitive, whereas varied descriptive expressions are permitted.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الغزالي): Al-Ghazālī reasons that if giving someone a name can be poor etiquette, naming God is even more sensitive, whereas varied descriptive expressions are permitted.

positions.position: Razi cites the Prophet's saying that people are like mines of gold and silver; he gives no chain or grading.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): Razi cites the Prophet's saying that people are like mines of gold and silver; he gives no chain or grading.

positions.position: He also cites the Prophet's saying that spirits are troops joined in affinity; no chain or grading is supplied.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): He also cites the Prophet's saying that spirits are troops joined in affinity; no chain or grading is supplied.

positions.position: Al-Suhrawardī reportedly had a disciple undertake one or two forty-day retreats, recited the ninety-nine names to him, then assigned a name-based remembrance if one especially moved him.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أبو النجيب البغدادي السهروردي): Al-Suhrawardī reportedly had a disciple undertake one or two forty-day retreats, recited the ninety-nine names to him, then assigned a name-based remembrance if one especially moved him.

positions.position: If a disciple showed no response, al-Suhrawardī told him to return to worldly duties because he was not made for this path.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أبو النجيب البغدادي السهروردي): If a disciple showed no response, al-Suhrawardī told him to return to worldly duties because he was not made for this path.

positions.position: Razi calls this sensible: differing souls each suit a particular state, and a matching practice readily brings that soul from potentiality into actuality.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi calls this sensible: differing souls each suit a particular state, and a matching practice readily brings that soul from potentiality into actuality.

positions.position: Razi closes his survey of divine names and opens a new chapter on the name Allah.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi closes his survey of divine names and opens a new chapter on the name Allah.

positions.position: Al-Khalīl says Allah and al-ilāh are specific to God; other uses are either in a construct phrase or indefinite, as in the Israelites’ request for idols.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الخليل): Al-Khalīl says Allah and al-ilāh are specific to God; other uses are either in a construct phrase or indefinite, as in the Israelites’ request for idols. | mentions 7:138

positions.position: The name Allah encompasses all divine attributes, whereas calling God by a specific name such as al-Raḥmān or al-ʿAlīm identifies one attribute.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The name Allah encompasses all divine attributes, whereas calling God by a specific name such as al-Raḥmān or al-ʿAlīm identifies one attribute.

positions.position: If a name is established before proving its referent, it is a proper name rather than a direct proper designation; once established after proof, it directly names the reality, illustrated by the name Ülker for blind and sighted people.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): If a name is established before proving its referent, it is a proper name rather than a direct proper designation; once established after proof, it directly names the reality, illustrated by the name Ülker for blind and sighted people.

positions.position: The discussion of whether God’s essence-name can be a proper designation distinguishes manifestations of essence, attributes, and effects; divine names are restricted to revelation, and direct self-manifestation is possible at least to God Himself.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): The discussion of whether God’s essence-name can be a proper designation distinguishes manifestations of essence, attributes, and effects; divine names are restricted to revelation, and direct self-manifestation is possible at least to God Himself.

positions.position: Some call Allāh the All-Encompassing Name, comprising all divine Names and Attributes.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (author): Some call Allāh the All-Encompassing Name, comprising all divine Names and Attributes. | mentions 112:1

positions.position: Jaʿfar calls the basmalah the greatest Quranic verse; Shiite scholars consequently treat it as a verse of the Fātiḥah and every sūrah beginning with it.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq): Jaʿfar calls the basmalah the greatest Quranic verse; Shiite scholars consequently treat it as a verse of the Fātiḥah and every sūrah beginning with it.

positions.position: Some scholars count the basmalah as a verse separate from the sūrahs that begin with it.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (author): Some scholars count the basmalah as a verse separate from the sūrahs that begin with it.

positions.position: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that revelation of the basmalah taught the Prophet where one sūrah ends and the next begins.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (Ibn ʿAbbās): Ibn ʿAbbās reports that revelation of the basmalah taught the Prophet where one sūrah ends and the next begins.

positions.position: The basmalah, or its shortened form, consecrates licit actions because all things should be done for God’s sake and in His Name.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (author): The basmalah, or its shortened form, consecrates licit actions because all things should be done for God’s sake and in His Name.

question: What can be known or said of God's essence?

positions.position: Mercy may mean God's willing good for its recipients, which makes it an attribute of essence.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI (author): Mercy may mean God's willing good for its recipients, which makes it an attribute of essence. ABUHAYYAN (قوم): Some theologians define divine mercy as God's will to bring good to whomever He wills, making it an attribute of essence. SAMIN-DURR (author): Mercy can mean tenderness, making divine mercy figuratively God's beneficence and an attribute of action; the author prefers the view that it is God's willing good, a real attribute of essence.

positions.position: Abu ʿAmr derives the name from bewilderment: minds are perplexed by God’s essence, greatness, and unknowable nature.
positions.reasons: THALABI (أبو عمرو بن العلاء): Abu ʿAmr derives the name from bewilderment: minds are perplexed by God’s essence, greatness, and unknowable nature. TABRISI (أبو عمرو): Abu Amr derives the name from bewilderment: minds are bewildered by the essence of God's greatness.

positions.position: Alternatively, mercy is withholding deserved punishment and giving good to the undeserving, which makes it an attribute of action.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI (author): Alternatively, mercy is withholding deserved punishment and giving good to the undeserving, which makes it an attribute of action. BAGHAWI-FULL (author): Mercy is either God’s willing good for its recipients, an attribute of essence, or withholding deserved punishment and giving unearned good, an attribute of action.

positions.position: Al-Ashʿarī regards a name as an attribute, which divides into what is the same as the named, other than it, or neither same nor other.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (أبو الحسن الأشعري): Al-Ashʿarī regards a name as an attribute, which divides into what is the same as the named, other than it, or neither same nor other. BAYDAWI-FULL (الشيخ أبو الحسن الأشعري): Al-Ashʿarī treats the name as an attribute and divides attributes into what is identical with the named essence, other than it, or neither it nor other than it.

positions.position: Commands to glorify God’s name mean to say Glory be to God, whereas commands to glorify Him mean declaring His essence and attributes free of imperfection.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): Commands to glorify God’s name mean to say Glory be to God, whereas commands to glorify Him mean declaring His essence and attributes free of imperfection. | mentions 56:74, 76:26, 87:1 IBNASHUR-FULL (author): “Glorify in the name of your Lord” means to say “Glory be to God,” while the command “glorify Him” directs praise to God's essence and attributes. | mentions 56:74, 76:26

positions.position: The opening formula signals love as the beginning.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (أبو القاسم الحكيم): The opening formula signals love as the beginning.

positions.position: The letters signify God's inspiration of prophecy to prophets, nearness and intimacy to knowers, and enduring compassionate attention to seekers.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (العباس بن عطاء): The letters signify God's inspiration of prophecy to prophets, nearness and intimacy to knowers, and enduring compassionate attention to seekers.

positions.position: The prophets appear and pass away through God; His manifestation beautifies beauty, and His illumination opens and makes things generous.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (بعضهم): The prophets appear and pass away through God; His manifestation beautifies beauty, and His illumination opens and makes things generous.

positions.position: Knowers empty and purify their hearts for God; their first gift is annihilation of all besides Him and exclusive affiliation to Him rather than Adam.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (الجنيد): Knowers empty and purify their hearts for God; their first gift is annihilation of all besides Him and exclusive affiliation to Him rather than Adam.

positions.position: The formula preserves created forms: opening by God's essence would dissolve creation, except prophets and saints; the name illuminates knowers' hearts.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (بعضهم): The formula preserves created forms: opening by God's essence would dissolve creation, except prophets and saints; the name illuminates knowers' hearts.

positions.position: Bismillah marks the people of reality, who adorn themselves only with the Real and swear only by Him.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (بعضهم): Bismillah marks the people of reality, who adorn themselves only with the Real and swear only by Him.

positions.position: He assigns the letters the meanings of God's secret among knowers, peace upon them, and His love for them.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (أبو بكر بن طاهر): He assigns the letters the meanings of God's secret among knowers, peace upon them, and His love for them.

positions.position: A report attributed to the Prophet, explicitly qualified as possibly unauthentic, maps the letters to God's splendor, radiance, and majesty.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): A report attributed to the Prophet, explicitly qualified as possibly unauthentic, maps the letters to God's splendor, radiance, and majesty.

positions.position: Ordinary utterance of Allah is habitual; when God takes charge of a speaker who is veiled from self-awareness, faults and slips disappear.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (بعضهم): Ordinary utterance of Allah is habitual; when God takes charge of a speaker who is veiled from self-awareness, faults and slips disappear.

positions.position: He describes a seeker who has forgotten personal interests and needs, loses ordinary self-description, becomes filled with hidden divine light, and ultimately cannot utter the name in the limit of nearness.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (أبو سعيد الخراز): He describes a seeker who has forgotten personal interests and needs, loses ordinary self-description, becomes filled with hidden divine light, and ultimately cannot utter the name in the limit of nearness.

positions.position: Alif signifies God's self-subsistence and separation from creation; letters depend upon it, while it depends on none.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (بعضهم): Alif signifies God's self-subsistence and separation from creation; letters depend upon it, while it depends on none.

positions.position: The author identifies name with the named, the existent thing, its essence, and itself, citing the announcement that a boy’s name is Yaḥyā and then addressing him as Yaḥyā.
positions.reasons: THALABI (author): The author identifies name with the named, the existent thing, its essence, and itself, citing the announcement that a boy’s name is Yaḥyā and then addressing him as Yaḥyā. | mentions 19:7

positions.position: Another gloss describes God’s essence as His power to subdue.
positions.reasons: THALABI (قوم): Another gloss describes God’s essence as His power to subdue.

positions.position: Abu Bakr al-Warrāq gives the terse gloss “He is.”
positions.reasons: THALABI (أبو بكر الوراق): Abu Bakr al-Warrāq gives the terse gloss “He is.”

positions.position: On the first derivation ilāh is an attribute of action; on the preferred derivation it is an attribute of the divine essence.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI-FULL (author): On the first derivation ilāh is an attribute of action; on the preferred derivation it is an attribute of the divine essence.

positions.position: Some regard the names as synonyms meaning “possessor of mercy”; their repetition encourages hope among those who seek God.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI (author): Some regard the names as synonyms meaning “possessor of mercy”; their repetition encourages hope among those who seek God.

positions.position: A name such as Zayd or lion can mean its referent, as in Zayd stands, or the word itself, as in lion has three letters; only in the first use does the name mean the named.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (author): A name such as Zayd or lion can mean its referent, as in Zayd stands, or the word itself, as in lion has three letters; only in the first use does the name mean the named.

positions.position: Many scholars take name to mean the named essence in 87:1, 55:78 and 53:23; they cite Labid's line about the name of peace as a greeting.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (أكثر أهل العلم): Many scholars take name to mean the named essence in 87:1, 55:78 and 53:23; they cite Labid's line about the name of peace as a greeting. | mentions 87:1, 55:78, 53:23

positions.position: More commonly, ism denotes the verbal name itself: examples include Adam being taught the names, the hadith of God's ninety-nine names, and grammarians' technical usage.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (author): More commonly, ism denotes the verbal name itself: examples include Adam being taught the names, the hadith of God's ninety-nine names, and grammarians' technical usage. | mentions 2:31

positions.position: A final derivation takes it from lah, meaning hidden: God is hidden in modality from minds but manifest through signs and proofs.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (author): A final derivation takes it from lah, meaning hidden: God is hidden in modality from minds but manifest through signs and proofs.

positions.position: Each deviant Muslim sect errs across many questions concerning God’s essence, attributes, rulings, acts and names, as well as compulsion, decree, justice, reward, resurrection, promises, threats, legal status and imamate.
positions.reasons: RAZI (author): Each deviant Muslim sect errs across many questions concerning God’s essence, attributes, rulings, acts and names, as well as compulsion, decree, justice, reward, resurrection, promises, threats, legal status and imamate.

positions.position: Al-Razi rejects al-Ḥayy al-Qayyūm as greatest because 'Living' is a cognitive and active attribute and 'Self-subsisting Sustainer' combines negation with relation.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Razi rejects al-Ḥayy al-Qayyūm as greatest because 'Living' is a cognitive and active attribute and 'Self-subsisting Sustainer' combines negation with relation. | mentions 2:255

positions.position: Al-Razi rejects the view that every divine name is equally greatest, since a name denoting the unique essence is nobler.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (من يقول إن أسماء الله كلها عظيمة): Al-Razi rejects the view that every divine name is equally greatest, since a name denoting the unique essence is nobler.

positions.position: Al-Razi says the disagreement concerns wording only, not whether God exists or has a real essence, and it entails neither disbelief nor condemnation.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Razi says the disagreement concerns wording only, not whether God exists or has a real essence, and it entails neither disbelief nor condemnation.

positions.position: A thing is anything that can be known and reported about; God's essence can be known and reported about, so it qualifies.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A thing is anything that can be known and reported about; God's essence can be known and reported about, so it qualifies.

positions.position: With part-based names excluded, seven attribute-based kinds remain; al-Razi begins with names denoting a real attribute belonging to God's unique essence.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): With part-based names excluded, seven attribute-based kinds remain; al-Razi begins with names denoting a real attribute belonging to God's unique essence.

positions.position: Most scholars permit calling God 'a thing'; their first proof is the Qur'an's question about which thing is greatest in testimony, answered by saying God witnesses.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الجمهور): Most scholars permit calling God 'a thing'; their first proof is the Qur'an's question about which thing is greatest in testimony, answered by saying God witnesses. | mentions 6:19

positions.position: They also cite 'Everything perishes except His face,' understanding His face as His essence; the exception implies that God is included under 'thing.'
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): They also cite 'Everything perishes except His face,' understanding His face as His essence; the exception implies that God is included under 'thing.' | mentions 28:88

positions.position: The Qur'an uses 'self' of God when God says He knows what is in His self and warns people about His self.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The Qur'an uses 'self' of God when God says He knows what is in His self and warns people about His self. | mentions 5:116, 3:28

positions.position: ʿĀʾisha reports that the Prophet taught a glorification using the number of His creatures, the ink of His words, His self's pleasure, and the weight of His Throne.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (عائشة): ʿĀʾisha reports that the Prophet taught a glorification using the number of His creatures, the ink of His words, His self's pleasure, and the weight of His Throne.

positions.position: Al-Anṣārī al-Harawī reports from ʿĀʾisha that the Prophet said the greatest reward belongs to a righteous minister who obeys a ruler in God's cause.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (عائشة): Al-Anṣārī al-Harawī reports from ʿĀʾisha that the Prophet said the greatest reward belongs to a righteous minister who obeys a ruler in God's cause.

positions.position: Abū Hurayra reports the Prophet saying that Abraham lied only three times, twice in God's cause.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أبو هريرة): Abū Hurayra reports the Prophet saying that Abraham lied only three times, twice in God's cause.

positions.position: Abū Dharr reports that the Prophet called struggle against one's self and desires in God's cause the best jihad.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أبو ذر): Abū Dharr reports that the Prophet called struggle against one's self and desires in God's cause the best jihad.

positions.position: Dhāt denotes the relation of a subject to an attribute; attributes cannot regress infinitely through further attributes, so they must belong to a self-subsisting essence, making the term true of God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Dhāt denotes the relation of a subject to an attribute; attributes cannot regress infinitely through further attributes, so they must belong to a self-subsisting essence, making the term true of God.

positions.position: In these reports, 'in God's dhāt' means seeking God's pleasure, not referring to His essence or nature.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): In these reports, 'in God's dhāt' means seeking God's pleasure, not referring to His essence or nature.

positions.position: The phrase His light marks possession, like a thing attributed to its owner, and therefore means God creates light rather than being light in essence.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The phrase His light marks possession, like a thing attributed to its owner, and therefore means God creates light rather than being light in essence. | mentions 24:35

positions.position: Philosophers call God a substance because they define substance as a self-subsisting essence independent of a substrate; they read its root as manifestness and say God is most manifest through proofs.
