positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الفلاسفة): Philosophers call God a substance because they define substance as a self-subsisting essence independent of a substrate; they read its root as manifestness and say God is most manifest through proofs.

positions.position: The text groups Christians with philosophers in applying the term substance to God, while noting the theologians reject the term.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النصارى): The text groups Christians with philosophers in applying the term substance to God, while noting the theologians reject the term.

positions.position: Theologians say Muslims unanimously avoid calling God a substance, so the term must be avoided.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (المتكلمون): Theologians say Muslims unanimously avoid calling God a substance, so the term must be avoided.

positions.position: God is the one most deserving of the name lasting; the Quran also uses the word for Paradise's fruit.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): God is the one most deserving of the name lasting; the Quran also uses the word for Paradise's fruit. | mentions 13:35

positions.position: Necessary existent in itself means that God's essence and reality entail His existence, making Him incapable of nonexistence or perishing.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Necessary existent in itself means that God's essence and reality entail His existence, making Him incapable of nonexistence or perishing.

positions.position: Every necessary existent is eternal, but an eternally caused thing could be eternal without being necessary in itself.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Every necessary existent is eternal, but an eternally caused thing could be eternal without being necessary in itself.

positions.position: The Persian word khuda means self-arrived: it combines self and came, indicating that God came to existence through Himself rather than another.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The Persian word khuda means self-arrived: it combines self and came, indicating that God came to existence through Himself rather than another.

positions.position: Kain is used in the Quran for God's attributes, though not for His essence; supplications attributed to the Prophet do use it of God's essence.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Kain is used in the Quran for God's attributes, though not for His essence; supplications attributed to the Prophet do use it of God's essence.

positions.position: Some say no beginning is a positive attribute because negating prior nonexistence amounts to affirming existence.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Some say no beginning is a positive attribute because negating prior nonexistence amounts to affirming existence.

positions.position: Others say no beginning is privative: it negates being preceded by nonexistence, a positive condition distinct from nonexistence itself.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Others say no beginning is privative: it negates being preceded by nonexistence, a positive condition distinct from nonexistence itself.

positions.position: Razi answers that if being preceded by nonexistence were an additional positive property, that property would itself be originated and require another such property without end.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi answers that if being preceded by nonexistence were an additional positive property, that property would itself be originated and require another such property without end.

positions.position: Sarmadi derives from succession: since time persists through successive parts, the literal term implies succession, impossible for God; use it metaphorically only if scripture or hadith uses it.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Sarmadi derives from succession: since time persists through successive parts, the literal term implies succession, impossible for God; use it metaphorically only if scripture or hadith uses it.

positions.position: Mustamirr derives from passing and suits time, which persists as parts pass successively, but not God, whose persistence is intrinsic rather than successive.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Mustamirr derives from passing and suits time, which persists as parts pass successively, but not God, whose persistence is intrinsic rather than successive.

positions.position: Extended likewise describes time and temporal things because their parts unfold in sequence; of God it is metaphorical.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Extended likewise describes time and temporal things because their parts unfold in sequence; of God it is metaphorical.

positions.position: They argue a self-complete essence needs no attributes, while an incomplete essence perfected by another cannot be divine.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (المعتزلة والفلاسفة): They argue a self-complete essence needs no attributes, while an incomplete essence perfected by another cannot be divine.

positions.position: They infer from God's condemnation of Christian trinitarianism that affirming attributes is unbelief, since Christians combine one essence with attributes rather than affirming three gods.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (المعتزلة والفلاسفة): They infer from God's condemnation of Christian trinitarianism that affirming attributes is unbelief, since Christians combine one essence with attributes rather than affirming three gods.

positions.position: They argue an attribute cannot be necessary in itself, since only one necessary existent exists and an attribute depends on its subject.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (المعتزلة والفلاسفة): They argue an attribute cannot be necessary in itself, since only one necessary existent exists and an attribute depends on its subject.

positions.position: They argue an attribute cannot be possible in itself: if caused by another, God's necessary essence would depend on it; if caused by God's essence, God would be both agent and recipient.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (المعتزلة والفلاسفة): They argue an attribute cannot be possible in itself: if caused by another, God's necessary essence would depend on it; if caused by God's essence, God would be both agent and recipient.

positions.position: They add that a produced effect cannot depend on its cause after it exists, which would be circular; dependence during or before production makes the attribute originated.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (المعتزلة والفلاسفة): They add that a produced effect cannot depend on its cause after it exists, which would be circular; dependence during or before production makes the attribute originated.

positions.position: They say originated attributes cannot subsist in God: either His essence suffices for them and they should be eternally present or absent, or their dependence makes the necessary God contingent.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (المعتزلة والفلاسفة): They say originated attributes cannot subsist in God: either His essence suffices for them and they should be eternally present or absent, or their dependence makes the necessary God contingent.

positions.position: If attributes originated, God existed as God before they appeared, showing that they are unnecessary for divinity.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (المعتزلة والفلاسفة): If attributes originated, God existed as God before they appeared, showing that they are unnecessary for divinity.

positions.position: They argue attributes are either dispensable additions or necessities that make God dependent on something else.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (المعتزلة والفلاسفة): They argue attributes are either dispensable additions or necessities that make God dependent on something else.

positions.position: God must be knowing, powerful, and living; the necessary conceptual distinction between God's essence and His being knowing or powerful shows these are not identical.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): God must be knowing, powerful, and living; the necessary conceptual distinction between God's essence and His being knowing or powerful shows these are not identical.

positions.position: These arguments establish that God has attributes, but they might be relational: power is capacity to produce, and knowledge is awareness, each grounded in the divine essence.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): These arguments establish that God has attributes, but they might be relational: power is capacity to produce, and knowledge is awareness, each grounded in the divine essence.

positions.position: Razi rejects that proof: God's essence is distinct from other essences in itself, and differences in receptivity would require another attribute without end.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi rejects that proof: God's essence is distinct from other essences in itself, and differences in receptivity would require another attribute without end.

positions.position: A third group defines living as not being unable to know and have power; Razi accepts that this negates a negation, but asks why the resulting positive cannot be the essence itself.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A third group defines living as not being unable to know and have power; Razi accepts that this negates a negation, but asks why the resulting positive cannot be the essence itself.

positions.position: The argument that one can conceive God's essence while doubting that He is living fails because the divine essence is known only indirectly, not in itself.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The argument that one can conceive God's essence while doubting that He is living fails because the divine essence is known only indirectly, not in itself.

positions.position: No one may question God's actions and judgments; He does whatever He wills.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): No one may question God's actions and judgments; He does whatever He wills. | mentions 21:23, 11:107

positions.position: Since negations across God's essence, attributes, and actions are limitless, names arising from this class are limitless too.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Since negations across God's essence, attributes, and actions are limitless, names arising from this class are limitless too.

positions.position: Quddus describes God's essence as unlike deficient natures; Salam describes His freedom from deficient attributes.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Quddus describes God's essence as unlike deficient natures; Salam describes His freedom from deficient attributes.

positions.position: Quranic negations concern God's essence, attributes, or actions; negating every unlike essence or attribute yields an unlimited number of negative descriptions.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Quranic negations concern God's essence, attributes, or actions; negating every unlike essence or attribute yields an unlimited number of negative descriptions.

positions.position: God's self-sufficiency means He needs nothing in His essence or real and negative attributes; the Lord is rich, possessed of mercy.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): God's self-sufficiency means He needs nothing in His essence or real and negative attributes; the Lord is rich, possessed of mercy. | mentions 47:38, 6:133

positions.position: Defects to be negated fall under the opposites of knowledge, power, self-sufficiency, and unity.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Defects to be negated fall under the opposites of knowledge, power, self-sufficiency, and unity.

positions.position: The discussion also includes negating partners, opposites, and peers under divine unity.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The discussion also includes negating partners, opposites, and peers under divine unity.

positions.position: Proper names function as signs for a particular essence; in God's case the sign is intellectual, and intellectual indication can encompass negative attributes.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Proper names function as signs for a particular essence; in God's case the sign is intellectual, and intellectual indication can encompass negative attributes.

positions.position: The ritual formula says “God is greater,” never “God is more magnificent,” which Razi treats as evidence that the terms differ.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The ritual formula says “God is greater,” never “God is more magnificent,” which Razi treats as evidence that the terms differ.

positions.position: Words from k-b-r, including “greater” and “the Magnificent,” are used of God, unlike the unattested “self-magnifying” form from ʿ-ẓ-m.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Words from k-b-r, including “greater” and “the Magnificent,” are used of God, unlike the unattested “self-magnifying” form from ʿ-ẓ-m.

positions.position: Presence varies endlessly by nearness and degree of manifestation; every degree is absence relative to a fuller one, so presence and absence are both unbounded.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Presence varies endlessly by nearness and degree of manifestation; every degree is absence relative to a fuller one, so presence and absence are both unbounded.

positions.position: Conceiving a compound requires attending to its parts, but a simple noncomposite essence cannot be brought before the mind through an operation; hence simple conception is pure unity.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Conceiving a compound requires attending to its parts, but a simple noncomposite essence cannot be brought before the mind through an operation; hence simple conception is pure unity.

positions.position: Saying “O He” is pure conception of the divine reality, free of composition and multiplicity, and therefore the highest form of unity.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Saying “O He” is pure conception of the divine reality, free of composition and multiplicity, and therefore the highest form of unity.

positions.position: Because no definition reaches God's essence, “O He” directs mind and spirit toward its light in hope of a glimpse.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Because no definition reaches God's essence, “O He” directs mind and spirit toward its light in hope of a glimpse.

positions.position: Awe of a mighty king can erase awareness of hunger, pain, and even family; a glimpse of divine majesty similarly leaves only Hu and makes its recitation an imitation of that state.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Awe of a mighty king can erase awareness of hunger, pain, and even family; a glimpse of divine majesty similarly leaves only Hu and makes its recitation an imitation of that state.

positions.position: Razi asks God to grant the reciter the state toward which this remembrance points.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi asks God to grant the reciter the state toward which this remembrance points.

positions.position: Every contingent essence depends on its cause even to be an essence; without God's effect there is no essence, existence, reality, or fixed status.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Every contingent essence depends on its cause even to be an essence; without God's effect there is no essence, existence, reality, or fixed status.

positions.position: Written talismanic formulas point to words, which point to mental meanings; if they mean nothing they are useless, while meaningful formulas must concern God rather than something else.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Written talismanic formulas point to words, which point to mental meanings; if they mean nothing they are useless, while meaningful formulas must concern God rather than something else.

positions.position: Since meaningful remembrance of God is already delimited, familiar supplications should be more effective than unknown formulas; differences among languages matter little.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Since meaningful remembrance of God is already delimited, familiar supplications should be more effective than unknown formulas; differences among languages matter little.

positions.position: An objection says weak souls gain little from known prayers, but mysterious words may inspire awe and fear, detach them from the bodily world, and strengthen spiritual influence.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (قائل): An objection says weak souls gain little from known prayers, but mysterious words may inspire awe and fear, detach them from the bodily world, and strengthen spiritual influence.

positions.position: Razi presents that objection as the reason unknown incantations might affect ordinary people, though his initial reasoning favors known supplications.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi presents that objection as the reason unknown incantations might affect ordinary people, though his initial reasoning favors known supplications.

positions.position: These dispositions are rooted in each soul; spiritual discipline can weaken a trait's dominance but cannot change the soul's original nature.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): These dispositions are rooted in each soul; spiritual discipline can weaken a trait's dominance but cannot change the soul's original nature.

positions.position: They also say a proper name functions like pointing, which is impossible for God, and distinguishes one individual from another similar in essence, which God cannot have.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (القائلون بأنه ليس اسم علم): They also say a proper name functions like pointing, which is impossible for God, and distinguishes one individual from another similar in essence, which God cannot have.

positions.position: A proper name designates a particular essence without requiring sensory pointing or a second similar being; neither objection rules out applying one to God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A proper name designates a particular essence without requiring sensory pointing or a second similar being; neither objection rules out applying one to God.

positions.position: A sixth etymology from lāha yalūhu means concealment: God's essence is hidden from intellects by its very perfection.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A sixth etymology from lāha yalūhu means concealment: God's essence is hidden from intellects by its very perfection.

positions.position: A discerning thinker says God is hidden from intellects by the intensity of His manifestation and concealed by the fullness of His light.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (بعض المحققين): A discerning thinker says God is hidden from intellects by the intensity of His manifestation and concealed by the fullness of His light.

positions.position: The essence of divine self-sufficiency is concealed from intellects; God is hidden through power, while creatures are veiled as the overpowered.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The essence of divine self-sufficiency is concealed from intellects; God is hidden through power, while creatures are veiled as the overpowered.

positions.position: Names can be classified as Arabic or Persian, whereas God's essence is above language.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Names can be classified as Arabic or Persian, whereas God's essence is above language.

positions.position: Al-Razi classifies names as names of the essence, a constituent part, an intrinsic quality, or a relation alone.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Razi classifies names as names of the essence, a constituent part, an intrinsic quality, or a relation alone.

positions.position: Other categories designate a negative or privative state, a real attribute together with a relation, or a real attribute together with negation.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Other categories designate a negative or privative state, a real attribute together with a relation, or a real attribute together with negation.

positions.position: The remaining kinds combine a relation with negation, or all three of intrinsic quality, relation, and negation; examples include 'First' and 'Self-subsisting Sustainer.'
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The remaining kinds combine a relation with negation, or all three of intrinsic quality, relation, and negation; examples include 'First' and 'Self-subsisting Sustainer.'

positions.position: He says these nine categories exhaust names applied to God or created things, then opens the question whether God has a name for His unique essence.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): He says these nine categories exhaust names applied to God or created things, then opens the question whether God has a name for His unique essence.

positions.position: Human thought knows God only as existent, everlasting, possessed of negative attributes, or possessed of relational attributes; the unique essence differs from all four and so is unknown.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Human thought knows God only as existent, everlasting, possessed of negative attributes, or possessed of relational attributes; the unique essence differs from all four and so is unknown.

positions.position: Human concepts arise from the five senses, bodily states, intellectual concepts such as existence and possibility, or combinations; since God's essence differs from these, it is inconceivable to creatures.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Human concepts arise from the five senses, bodily states, intellectual concepts such as existence and possibility, or combinations; since God's essence differs from these, it is inconceivable to creatures.

positions.position: God's essence causes all its real, relational, and negative properties; if the essence were known, all those properties would necessarily be known, which they are not.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): God's essence causes all its real, relational, and negative properties; if the essence were known, all those properties would necessarily be known, which they are not.

positions.position: Some argue that finite creaturely intellects cannot reach the infinite God, so only God knows God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (بعضهم): Some argue that finite creaturely intellects cannot reach the infinite God, so only God knows God.

positions.position: God differs from creation by His own essence, not through an added property: if the difference required another property, regress or circularity would result.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): God differs from creation by His own essence, not through an added property: if the difference required another property, regress or circularity would result.

positions.position: God's essence is not identical with power or knowledge, since these are relational notions while His essence is independently subsistent.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): God's essence is not identical with power or knowledge, since these are relational notions while His essence is independently subsistent.

positions.position: Ancient philosophers deny that God has a name for His unique essence because naming directs a hearer to a referent, but no creature knows that essence; they allow names for knowable consequences such as eternal and necessary.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (قدماء الفلاسفة): Ancient philosophers deny that God has a name for His unique essence because naming directs a hearer to a referent, but no creature knows that essence; they allow names for knowable consequences such as eternal and necessary.

positions.position: Others say God could grant a close servant knowledge of His unique essence, in which case naming that essence would be possible; the issue rests on the preceding premises.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Others say God could grant a close servant knowledge of His unique essence, in which case naming that essence would be possible; the issue rests on the preceding premises.

positions.position: Some scholars say the basmala encompasses the revealed law because it indicates the divine essence and attributes.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (بعض العلماء): Some scholars say the basmala encompasses the revealed law because it indicates the divine essence and attributes.

positions.position: Alternatively, bāʾ denotes accompaniment: “I read while blessed by God's name.”
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (author): Alternatively, bāʾ denotes accompaniment: “I read while blessed by God's name.”

positions.position: If ism means the spoken word, it differs from its referent: transient sounds vary across peoples and eras and may be multiple or singular, unlike the named entity.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (author): If ism means the spoken word, it differs from its referent: transient sounds vary across peoples and eras and may be multiple or singular, unlike the named entity.

positions.position: If ism means the entity itself, it is the named thing, though this sense is not established in common usage.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (author): If ism means the entity itself, it is the named thing, though this sense is not established in common usage.

positions.position: In Qur'anic commands to glorify God's name, “name” means the word: as God's essence and attributes must be kept from defects, so must their names from obscenity and discourtesy.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (author): In Qur'anic commands to glorify God's name, “name” means the word: as God's essence and attributes must be kept from defects, so must their names from obscenity and discourtesy. | mentions 55:78, 87:1

positions.position: Alternatively, “name” is an insertion without independent meaning, as in the poet's line “then the name of peace be upon you both.”
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (author): Alternatively, “name” is an insertion without independent meaning, as in the poet's line “then the name of peace be upon you both.”

positions.position: “In God's name” rather than “by God” invokes blessing and aid through mention of His name, or distinguishes seeking blessing from swearing.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (author): “In God's name” rather than “by God” invokes blessing and aid through mention of His name, or distinguishes seeking blessing from swearing.

positions.position: The unqualified essence is unknowable to humans and cannot be named; a merely proper-name reading also fails to explain “He is God in the heavens.”
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (author): The unqualified essence is unknowable to humans and cannot be named; a merely proper-name reading also fails to explain “He is God in the heavens.” | mentions 6:3

positions.position: Another analysis treats اسم as pleonastic, as in the cited poetic expression.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL (author): Another analysis treats اسم as pleonastic, as in the cited poetic expression.

positions.position: Some regard الله as the proper name of God's unique essence because it alone accepts His attributes and cannot imply a partner in the confession of divine unity.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL (author): Some regard الله as the proper name of God's unique essence because it alone accepts His attributes and cannot imply a partner in the confession of divine unity.

positions.position: Allah is a name rather than an attribute: one predicates unity and self-sufficiency of God but does not call another thing ‘a god’; divine attributes require a named subject to qualify.
positions.reasons: NASAFI (author): Allah is a name rather than an attribute: one predicates unity and self-sufficiency of God but does not call another thing ‘a god’; divine attributes require a named subject to qualify.

positions.position: Al-Khalil, al-Zajjaj, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, and al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl deny that the name Allah has a derivation.
positions.reasons: NASAFI (الخليل والزجاج ومحمد بن الحسن والحسين بن الفضل): Al-Khalil, al-Zajjaj, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, and al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl deny that the name Allah has a derivation.

positions.position: One derivation connects Allah with alih, ‘to be bewildered’: minds are dazed by trying to know God, which explains the spread of error and rarity of sound reflection.
positions.reasons: NASAFI (قيل): One derivation connects Allah with alih, ‘to be bewildered’: minds are dazed by trying to know God, which explains the spread of error and rarity of sound reflection.

positions.position: The nineteenth letter signifies the human world as a distinct realm because humanity’s nobility and comprehensiveness gather the whole cosmos, as Gabriel is distinguished among angels.
positions.reasons: QASHANI (author): The nineteenth letter signifies the human world as a distinct realm because humanity’s nobility and comprehensiveness gather the whole cosmos, as Gabriel is distinguished among angels. | mentions 2:98

positions.position: Three hidden alifs complete the twenty-two letters and signify the divine world in respect of essence, attributes, and acts: three in detailed consideration, one in realization.
positions.reasons: QASHANI (author): Three hidden alifs complete the twenty-two letters and signify the divine world in respect of essence, attributes, and acts: three in detailed consideration, one in realization.

positions.position: The three written alifs signify those worlds appearing in the supreme human manifestation while the divine world remains veiled.
positions.reasons: QASHANI (author): The three written alifs signify those worlds appearing in the supreme human manifestation while the divine world remains veiled.

positions.position: Lengthening bāʾ compensates for the hidden alif: divinity is concealed in diffusive mercy and appears in human form, knowable only to its people, hence the indefinite form.
positions.reasons: QASHANI (author): Lengthening bāʾ compensates for the hidden alif: divinity is concealed in diffusive mercy and appears in human form, knowable only to its people, hence the indefinite form.

positions.position: A hadith says God created Adam in His image; the author explains a hierarchy of veils from essence by attributes, from attributes by acts, and from acts by beings and effects.
positions.reasons: QASHANI (author): A hadith says God created Adam in His image; the author explains a hierarchy of veils from essence by attributes, from attributes by acts, and from acts by beings and effects.

positions.position: Disclosure of acts beyond the veil of created effects yields trust; disclosure of attributes beyond acts yields contentment and surrender; disclosure of essence beyond attributes yields annihilation in unity and absolute unification.
positions.reasons: QASHANI (author): Disclosure of acts beyond the veil of created effects yields trust; disclosure of attributes beyond acts yields contentment and surrender; disclosure of essence beyond attributes yields annihilation in unity and absolute unification.

positions.position: Names are the determinate forms by which divine attributes and essence are known: their identities signify attributes and essence, existence signifies His face, and their individuation His unity.
positions.reasons: QASHANI (author): Names are the determinate forms by which divine attributes and essence are known: their identities signify attributes and essence, existence signifies His face, and their individuation His unity.

positions.position: Allah names the divine essence absolutely, without reference either to its being qualified by attributes or to its lack of attributes.
positions.reasons: QASHANI (author): Allah names the divine essence absolutely, without reference either to its being qualified by attributes or to its lack of attributes.

positions.position: The All-Merciful grants existence and perfection universally according to wisdom and each recipient’s capacity at the beginning.
positions.reasons: QASHANI (author): The All-Merciful grants existence and perfection universally according to wisdom and each recipient’s capacity at the beginning.

positions.position: The Especially Merciful grants the human kind its particular spiritual perfection at the end; the perfected human form gathers universal and special mercy and manifests the divine essence and all attributes.
positions.reasons: QASHANI (author): The Especially Merciful grants the human kind its particular spiritual perfection at the end; the perfected human form gathers universal and special mercy and manifests the divine essence and all attributes.

positions.position: The Prophet says he was given comprehensive speech and sent to complete noble character; existent things are realities, while noble character’s states and sources of action are gathered in the universal human being.
positions.reasons: QASHANI (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): The Prophet says he was given comprehensive speech and sent to complete noble character; existent things are realities, while noble character’s states and sources of action are gathered in the universal human being.

positions.position: Divine mercy may figuratively mean beneficence, an attribute of action; another view defines it as willing good, an attribute of essence, raising the dispute over whether attributes of action are originated or eternal.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (author): Divine mercy may figuratively mean beneficence, an attribute of action; another view defines it as willing good, an attribute of essence, raising the dispute over whether attributes of action are originated or eternal.

positions.position: Another account says mercy is tenderness that prompts kindness; for God it means kindness alone, as a report contrasts divine beneficence with human tenderness.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): Another account says mercy is tenderness that prompts kindness; for God it means kindness alone, as a report contrasts divine beneficence with human tenderness.

positions.position: He argues that “glorify the name of your Lord” and “names you invented” can use name for the divine essence or idols, not merely their words.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): He argues that “glorify the name of your Lord” and “names you invented” can use name for the divine essence or idols, not merely their words. | mentions 87:1, 12:40

positions.position: Some take ism here as God’s essence because help cannot be sought through a bare word and none of the ninety-nine names is literally “name”; al-Ālūsī distinguishes constructions with bi-
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Some take ism here as God’s essence because help cannot be sought through a bare word and none of the ninety-nine names is literally “name”; al-Ālūsī distinguishes constructions with bi-

positions.position: Others say seeking blessing applies to a name even if seeking help applies to the named essence; they cite the distinction between swearing and auspicious invocation.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Others say seeking blessing applies to a name even if seeking help applies to the named essence; they cite the distinction between swearing and auspicious invocation.

positions.position: Many prefer estimating the verb after the basmala because God's name precedes the act in essence; Alusi links this to an a priori proof and cites a gnostic who sees God before every thing.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Many prefer estimating the verb after the basmala because God's name precedes the act in essence; Alusi links this to an a priori proof and cites a gnostic who sees God before every thing.

positions.position: Muʿtazilites object that identity would make the referent multiply with its names, although names change and arise after their referents; al-Alusi says these objections address only the created signifier sense.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (المعتزلة): Muʿtazilites object that identity would make the referent multiply with its names, although names change and arise after their referents; al-Alusi says these objections address only the created signifier sense.

positions.position: Those objections do not refute identity when name means the essence itself; al-Alusi traces the Muʿtazilite claim of distinction to a doctrinal error.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Those objections do not refute identity when name means the essence itself; al-Alusi traces the Muʿtazilite claim of distinction to a doctrinal error.

positions.position: A name may denote the very essence or existent, not merely its spoken form; thus glorifying the Lord’s name addresses God Himself, and idolaters worshiped idols rather than their words.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): A name may denote the very essence or existent, not merely its spoken form; thus glorifying the Lord’s name addresses God Himself, and idolaters worshiped idols rather than their words. | mentions 87:1, 12:40

positions.position: Sibawayh’s account of verbs as forms of events made from the wording of nouns supports taking names as referents, since words themselves do not bring events into being.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (سيبويه): Sibawayh’s account of verbs as forms of events made from the wording of nouns supports taking names as referents, since words themselves do not bring events into being.

positions.position: Names identify realities because their existence or intelligibility distinguishes them from absence or confusion; spoken words serve as signs that let people communicate about what is absent.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Names identify realities because their existence or intelligibility distinguishes them from absence or confusion; spoken words serve as signs that let people communicate about what is absent.

positions.position: Al-Alusi disputes al-Bayḍawi’s objections: a proper name can refer to an essence conceived through an identifying aspect, and the cited verse permits other syntactic analyses.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Al-Alusi disputes al-Bayḍawi’s objections: a proper name can refer to an essence conceived through an identifying aspect, and the cited verse permits other syntactic analyses. | mentions 6:3

positions.position: In the Naqshbandi practice of heart remembrance, the worshiper attends to the incomparable essence signified by Allah; al-Alusi says Ibn Arabi developed this view in several works.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): In the Naqshbandi practice of heart remembrance, the worshiper attends to the incomparable essence signified by Allah; al-Alusi says Ibn Arabi developed this view in several works.

positions.position: Al-Alusi contrasts Companions, who experienced the divine essence, with later believers who know the names, and cites a report promising the latter fiftyfold reward.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Al-Alusi contrasts Companions, who experienced the divine essence, with later believers who know the names, and cites a report promising the latter fiftyfold reward.

positions.position: He further says the Prophet longs for later believers who are his brothers and would rejoice to meet one of them.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): He further says the Prophet longs for later believers who are his brothers and would rejoice to meet one of them.

positions.position: The pairing of Allah and Rahman is especially close, supporting the appositive reading and symbolizing the divine essence; al-Alusi links it to the report that Adam was created in God’s image.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): The pairing of Allah and Rahman is especially close, supporting the appositive reading and symbolizing the divine essence; al-Alusi links it to the report that Adam was created in God’s image. | mentions 17:110

positions.position: The spiritual progression passes from divine names to effects, from effects to attributes, and toward direct vision of the essence, culminating in longing for the divine encounter.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): The spiritual progression passes from divine names to effects, from effects to attributes, and toward direct vision of the essence, culminating in longing for the divine encounter. | mentions 89:27, 89:28, 75:22, 75:23

positions.position: He links this hoped-for encounter to the call for the tranquil soul to return to its Lord and to faces looking toward their Lord on Resurrection Day.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): He links this hoped-for encounter to the call for the tranquil soul to return to its Lord and to faces looking toward their Lord on Resurrection Day. | mentions 89:27, 89:28

positions.position: Human knowledge cannot encompass God’s essence or proper name, and Arabic has no comparable word from which its origin can be securely identified.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Human knowledge cannot encompass God’s essence or proper name, and Arabic has no comparable word from which its origin can be securely identified.

positions.position: Elmalılı says Abduh's deputyship reading amounts to acting as God's representative and self-effacement, appropriate only to special stations such as prophethood, sainthood, rule, and authority.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Elmalılı says Abduh's deputyship reading amounts to acting as God's representative and self-effacement, appropriate only to special stations such as prophethood, sainthood, rule, and authority.

positions.position: Bismillah says in the name of God, not by God, because it marks the deed as monotheistic practice and associates it with God’s name rather than invoking His essence.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): Bismillah says in the name of God, not by God, because it marks the deed as monotheistic practice and associates it with God’s name rather than invoking His essence.

positions.position: The wording is used for ritual slaughter and blessing or aid, as in verses 6:118–119 and “Read in the name of your Lord.”
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR-FULL (author): The wording is used for ritual slaughter and blessing or aid, as in verses 6:118–119 and “Read in the name of your Lord.” | mentions 6:118, 6:119, 96:1

positions.position: A name, linguistically, is an indicating word, from either the root for marking or the root for elevation.
positions.reasons: TABATABAI (author): A name, linguistically, is an indicating word, from either the root for marking or the root for elevation.

positions.position: Theoretical analysis distinguishes a spoken name from an attribute that indicates an external essence, sometimes calling the former the name of the latter; this distinction should not be imposed on ordinary language.
positions.reasons: TABATABAI (author): Theoretical analysis distinguishes a spoken name from an attribute that indicates an external essence, sometimes calling the former the name of the latter; this distinction should not be imposed on ordinary language.

question: What do God's names imply about His attributes?

positions.position: Al-Rahim shows mercy through provision in descendants and origin according to God's prior eternal knowledge.
positions.reasons: TUSTARI (author): Al-Rahim shows mercy through provision in descendants and origin according to God's prior eternal knowledge.

positions.position: Abu Bakr says God creates from breath of His spirit whatever He wills in His kingdom as mercy because He is merciful.
positions.reasons: TUSTARI (أبو بكر): Abu Bakr says God creates from breath of His spirit whatever He wills in His kingdom as mercy because He is merciful.

positions.position: Al-Ṭabarī says he treated the correct count elsewhere and will give full disagreement in another legal work, without resolving it here.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): Al-Ṭabarī says he treated the correct count elsewhere and will give full disagreement in another legal work, without resolving it here.

positions.position: Al-Ṭabarī says the prior books lack a miracle certifying their recipients, whereas the Qur'an's unmatched composition defeats all attempts to produce even a short surah and proves Muhammad's prophethood.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): Al-Ṭabarī says the prior books lack a miracle certifying their recipients, whereas the Qur'an's unmatched composition defeats all attempts to produce even a short surah and proves Muhammad's prophethood.

positions.position: Al-Fātiḥa's inimitable arrangement proves prophethood, while its praise and glorification direct people to recognize God's greatness, sovereignty, power, and dominion and to thank Him for His favors.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): Al-Fātiḥa's inimitable arrangement proves prophethood, while its praise and glorification direct people to recognize God's greatness, sovereignty, power, and dominion and to thank Him for His favors.

positions.position: The account of those favored through knowledge of God and His enabling teaches that every religious and worldly blessing comes from Him, directing requests to God rather than idols or rivals.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): The account of those favored through knowledge of God and His enabling teaches that every religious and worldly blessing comes from Him, directing requests to God rather than idols or rivals.

positions.position: Recounting punishments for disobedience warns people away from sin and from incurring God's anger, whose consequences lead to destruction.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): Recounting punishments for disobedience warns people away from sin and from incurring God's anger, whose consequences lead to destruction.

positions.position: The phrase means beginning by naming and remembering God, rather than claiming that the act itself is performed through God’s power.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): The phrase means beginning by naming and remembering God, rather than claiming that the act itself is performed through God’s power.

positions.position: Arabic can use a verbal noun in a form normally associated with a noun; thus bismillah can express beginning with the act of naming.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): Arabic can use a verbal noun in a form normally associated with a noun; thus bismillah can express beginning with the act of naming.

positions.position: The proposed derivation of Allāh from ilāh is an inference rather than an attested form heard directly from Arab speech.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): The proposed derivation of Allāh from ilāh is an inference rather than an attested form heard directly from Arab speech.

positions.position: Junayd checks that Nuri still observes prayer, then challenges whether God or Nuri himself says Allah; Nuri answers that it is love, and his ecstasy subsides.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (الجنيد): Junayd checks that Nuri still observes prayer, then challenges whether God or Nuri himself says Allah; Nuri answers that it is love, and his ecstasy subsides.

positions.position: Al-Shibli says Allah alone, rather than There is no god but God, because he will not use the latter to negate a rival.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (الشبلي): Al-Shibli says Allah alone, rather than There is no god but God, because he will not use the latter to negate a rival.

positions.position: Only God can name, see, or know God; before servant and creation there was only God, and all existence is through and for Him.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (أبو سعيد الخراز): Only God can name, see, or know God; before servant and creation there was only God, and all existence is through and for Him.

positions.position: Created beings are enraptured variously: their secret by divine majesty, heart by forms of gnosis, or tongue by constant remembrance.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (بعضهم): Created beings are enraptured variously: their secret by divine majesty, heart by forms of gnosis, or tongue by constant remembrance.

positions.position: Junayd tells Ibn Shibli that mentioning an absent God is backbiting; if one is absent it is such mention, while witnessing Him makes speech a breach of reverence.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (الجنيد): Junayd tells Ibn Shibli that mentioning an absent God is backbiting; if one is absent it is such mention, while witnessing Him makes speech a breach of reverence.

positions.position: A second report says God will join the one mercy to the other ninety-nine, completing one hundred for His servants on Judgment Day.
positions.reasons: THALABI (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): A second report says God will join the one mercy to the other ninety-nine, completing one hundred for His servants on Judgment Day.

positions.position: The basmala means that beings came into existence through God and creatures subsist through Him; ism distinguishes the one invoking blessing from its object.
positions.reasons: THALABI (author): The basmala means that beings came into existence through God and creatures subsist through Him; ism distinguishes the one invoking blessing from its object.

positions.position: The final mīm glosses are that God grants favor to all creation and forms His creation, supported by verses on divine favor and creation.
positions.reasons: THALABI (أبو بكر الوراق): The final mīm glosses are that God grants favor to all creation and forms His creation, supported by verses on divine favor and creation. | mentions 3:108, 59:24

positions.position: The Kummayt verse illustrates hearts becoming lovesick for God and yearning at His remembrance.
positions.reasons: THALABI (علي بن عبد الرحيم القناد): The Kummayt verse illustrates hearts becoming lovesick for God and yearning at His remembrance.

positions.position: Some derive ilāh from concealment: God is manifest through signs of lordship yet hidden from minds in His modality.
positions.reasons: THALABI (قوم): Some derive ilāh from concealment: God is manifest through signs of lordship yet hidden from minds in His modality.

positions.position: Al-Ḥārith says Allah comes from “made them needy”: servants need their Creator for benefits and harms like distressed, overpowered people.
positions.reasons: THALABI (الحارث بن أسد المجلسي): Al-Ḥārith says Allah comes from “made them needy”: servants need their Creator for benefits and harms like distressed, overpowered people.

positions.position: Shahr ibn Ḥawshab glosses Allah as the Creator of everything.
positions.reasons: THALABI (شهر بن حوشب): Shahr ibn Ḥawshab glosses Allah as the Creator of everything.

positions.position: Al-Rahim is a divine name derived from His attribute of mercy.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI-FULL (author): Al-Rahim is a divine name derived from His attribute of mercy.

positions.position: The formula begins or opens by naming God, seeking blessing and good auspices.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-QT (author): The formula begins or opens by naming God, seeking blessing and good auspices.

positions.position: The two divine names mean possessing mercy: mercy is God's abiding will of good, and the names differ in form, not meaning.
positions.reasons: WAHIDI-QT (author): The two divine names mean possessing mercy: mercy is God's abiding will of good, and the names differ in form, not meaning.

positions.position: The divine basmala and praise on worshippers' tongues teach them how to invoke, praise, glorify, and magnify God.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL (author): The divine basmala and praise on worshippers' tongues teach them how to invoke, praise, glorify, and magnify God.

positions.position: He also links Allah to aliha, to be bewildered: minds are dazed by trying to comprehend God, and lack of sound reflection lets error spread.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL (author): He also links Allah to aliha, to be bewildered: minds are dazed by trying to comprehend God, and lack of sound reflection lets error spread.

positions.position: He raises the question why the more emphatic attribute precedes the lesser when normal usage would progress from the lesser to the greater.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL (author): He raises the question why the more emphatic attribute precedes the lesser when normal usage would progress from the lesser to the greater.

positions.position: The Prophet says God has one hundred mercies, sent one to earth for mutual compassion and reserved ninety-nine to show mercy on Judgment Day.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (النبي): The Prophet says God has one hundred mercies, sent one to earth for mutual compassion and reserved ninety-nine to show mercy on Judgment Day.

positions.position: Another report says God will take the earthly mercy back and complete it to one hundred to show mercy to His servants on Judgment Day.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (author): Another report says God will take the earthly mercy back and complete it to one hundred to show mercy to His servants on Judgment Day.

positions.position: Knowing a divine name presupposes knowing its referent, arguments for the referent’s existence, and answers to objections against it; these inquiries alone exceed a thousand questions.
positions.reasons: RAZI (author): Knowing a divine name presupposes knowing its referent, arguments for the referent’s existence, and answers to objections against it; these inquiries alone exceed a thousand questions.

positions.position: Understanding the implied beginning requires surveying all obedience: true creeds and sincere deeds, their proofs, and answers to objections, a body of inquiry that may exceed ten thousand questions.
positions.reasons: RAZI (author): Understanding the implied beginning requires surveying all obedience: true creeds and sincere deeds, their proofs, and answers to objections, a body of inquiry that may exceed ten thousand questions.

positions.position: Razi says the Fātiḥa can yield ten thousand useful questions; he wrote the introduction to show that this claim is attainable, despite the scoffing of envious and ignorant opponents.
positions.reasons: RAZI (author): Razi says the Fātiḥa can yield ten thousand useful questions; he wrote the introduction to show that this claim is attainable, despite the scoffing of envious and ignorant opponents.

positions.position: Razi cites as a famous prophetic report that the community will divide into seventy-three sects, all in the Fire except one; he says this shows the other seventy-two hold false creeds.
positions.reasons: RAZI (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): Razi cites as a famous prophetic report that the community will divide into seventy-three sects, all in the Fire except one; he says this shows the other seventy-two hold false creeds.

positions.position: A prophetic report says, 'God was and there was no other thing'; al-Razi cites it to show that 'thing' can apply to God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (عمران بن الحصين): A prophetic report says, 'God was and there was no other thing'; al-Razi cites it to show that 'thing' can apply to God.

positions.position: Jahm says the Prophet and Companions never addressed God as 'thing,' a low term; instead they invoked Him as creator of things, earth, and heaven.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (جهم بن صفوان): Jahm says the Prophet and Companions never addressed God as 'thing,' a low term; instead they invoked Him as creator of things, earth, and heaven.

positions.position: A report collected by ʿAbd Allāh al-Anṣārī says the Prophet described nothing as more jealous than God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (عائشة): A report collected by ʿAbd Allāh al-Anṣārī says the Prophet described nothing as more jealous than God.

positions.position: Jahm objects that the Qur'an calls God creator of every thing and powerful over every thing, which would imply He is created and subject to power.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (جهم بن صفوان): Jahm objects that the Qur'an calls God creator of every thing and powerful over every thing, which would imply He is created and subject to power. | mentions 13:16, 5:120

positions.position: Al-Razi counters that excluding God from 'everything' is linguistically disfavored; custom permits exceptions only for a trivial minority, and God cannot be considered trivial.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Razi counters that excluding God from 'everything' is linguistically disfavored; custom permits exceptions only for a trivial minority, and God cannot be considered trivial. | mentions 13:16, 5:120

positions.position: Jahm reads 'nothing is like His likeness' to mean God is not a thing, since every thing resembles itself.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (جهم بن صفوان): Jahm reads 'nothing is like His likeness' to mean God is not a thing, since every thing resembles itself. | mentions 42:11

positions.position: Al-Razi says treating the kāf as extra makes part of God's speech vain and false; the verse must retain its force.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Razi says treating the kāf as extra makes part of God's speech vain and false; the verse must retain its force. | mentions 42:11

positions.position: Jahm argues that 'thing' is a common term including lowly entities and conveys no praise, whereas God's names must express praise and majesty.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (جهم بن صفوان): Jahm argues that 'thing' is a common term including lowly entities and conveys no praise, whereas God's names must express praise and majesty. | mentions 7:180

positions.position: Al-Razi explains that God's beautiful names denote lofty qualities; the command to invoke Him by them warns against calling Him by an unpraiseworthy term.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Razi explains that God's beautiful names denote lofty qualities; the command to invoke Him by them warns against calling Him by an unpraiseworthy term. | mentions 7:180

positions.position: 'Existence' has two meanings: awareness or discovery, and actual subsistence. Knowing that something exists requires it to exist, but it can exist without being known.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): 'Existence' has two meanings: awareness or discovery, and actual subsistence. Knowing that something exists requires it to exist, but it can exist without being known.

positions.position: Al-Razi thinks the word first meant awareness or discovery, since people perceive a thing before recognizing its actual existence; he treats the issue as lexical.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Razi thinks the word first meant awareness or discovery, since people perceive a thing before recognizing its actual existence; he treats the issue as lexical.

positions.position: The Qur'anic phrase 'they would have found God' uses existence to mean finding or recognizing Him; the Qur'an does not use the other sense, actual subsistence, here.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The Qur'anic phrase 'they would have found God' uses existence to mean finding or recognizing Him; the Qur'an does not use the other sense, actual subsistence, here. | mentions 4:64

positions.position: An objector's inference from recognized existence to actual existence fails: nonexistent things can be known, and a word used in one sense does not establish its use in another.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): An objector's inference from recognized existence to actual existence fails: nonexistent things can be known, and a word used in one sense does not establish its use in another.

positions.position: Muslim consensus permits calling God 'existent'; unlike 'thing,' this term cannot apply to what is nonexistent and therefore conveys praise, including that God's proofs are evident to every mind.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Muslim consensus permits calling God 'existent'; unlike 'thing,' this term cannot apply to what is nonexistent and therefore conveys praise, including that God's proofs are evident to every mind.

positions.position: God is unsurpassed in jealousy, love of excuse, and love of praise; His jealousy is why He forbids public and hidden indecencies and sends messengers.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النبي): God is unsurpassed in jealousy, love of excuse, and love of praise; His jealousy is why He forbids public and hidden indecencies and sends messengers.

positions.position: Calling God Light is sound because He illuminates, originates, and creates all lights.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Calling God Light is sound because He illuminates, originates, and creates all lights.

positions.position: God may be called the world's light because His wisdom orders worldly and afterlife benefits, as a town's organizer of welfare is called its light.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): God may be called the world's light because His wisdom orders worldly and afterlife benefits, as a town's organizer of welfare is called its light.

positions.position: God may be called Light because He grants faith, guidance, and knowledge, which belong to the kind of spiritual lights.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): God may be called Light because He grants faith, guidance, and knowledge, which belong to the kind of spiritual lights. | mentions 24:35

positions.position: The Prophet reports that God created creatures in darkness, then cast some of His light upon them; those touched by it were guided and others went astray.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النبي): The Prophet reports that God created creatures in darkness, then cast some of His light upon them; those touched by it were guided and others went astray.

positions.position: Literal light is opposed by darkness, but God is transcendent beyond having any opposite.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Literal light is opposed by darkness, but God is transcendent beyond having any opposite.

positions.position: Light disappears and undergoes setting, whereas God is beyond disappearance and passing away.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Light disappears and undergoes setting, whereas God is beyond disappearance and passing away.

positions.position: God says the religion He approves is repaired only through generosity and good character, and people should honor it through both.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النبي): God says the religion He approves is repaired only through generosity and good character, and people should honor it through both.

positions.position: In a divine report, one who insults God's friend is at war with God; God may destroy him, while He dislikes taking the believer's life though death is inevitable.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النبي): In a divine report, one who insults God's friend is at war with God; God may destroy him, while He dislikes taking the believer's life though death is inevitable.

positions.position: Ishaq ibn Rahawayh judges sound the report that God created Adam in the image of the Merciful.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (إسحاق بن راهويه): Ishaq ibn Rahawayh judges sound the report that God created Adam in the image of the Merciful.

positions.position: One interpretation makes the pronoun in Adam's image refer to the person struck, requiring care not to disfigure that person's face.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (العلماء): One interpretation makes the pronoun in Adam's image refer to the person struck, requiring care not to disfigure that person's face.

positions.position: A second interpretation says Adam was created in his final adult form at once, without passing through semen, embryo, or infancy.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (العلماء): A second interpretation says Adam was created in his final adult form at once, without passing through semen, embryo, or infancy.

positions.position: A third interpretation takes image as attribute: Adam was made God's earthly vicegerent, exercising control over earthly bodies as God exercises power over the world.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (العلماء): A third interpretation takes image as attribute: Adam was made God's earthly vicegerent, exercising control over earthly bodies as God exercises power over the world.

positions.position: God's eternal existence does not require an eternal time: if it needs time, that time is either eternal and requires another time without end, or originated after God already existed.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): God's eternal existence does not require an eternal time: if it needs time, that time is either eternal and requires another time without end, or originated after God already existed.

positions.position: Everything eternal is everlasting, but not everything everlasting is eternal; scripture calls the Lord's face enduring and says all perish except His face.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Everything eternal is everlasting, but not everything everlasting is eternal; scripture calls the Lord's face enduring and says all perish except His face. | mentions 55:27, 28:88

positions.position: Calling God first and last of all things means He has neither beginning nor end, since otherwise He could not be first and last with respect to all else.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Calling God first and last of all things means He has neither beginning nor end, since otherwise He could not be first and last with respect to all else. | mentions 57:3

positions.position: The world's creator cannot be originated, since an originated creator would require another creator and an impossible regress; whatever is eternal cannot cease.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The world's creator cannot be originated, since an originated creator would require another creator and an impossible regress; whatever is eternal cannot cease.

positions.position: Applied to a thing itself, true means really existent, since its opposite false means nonexistent; Labid's verse says everything apart from God is false.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Applied to a thing itself, true means really existent, since its opposite false means nonexistent; Labid's verse says everything apart from God is false.

positions.position: Applied to belief, true means a correct belief matching the thing as it is, and therefore deserving of affirmation and preservation.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Applied to belief, true means a correct belief matching the thing as it is, and therefore deserving of affirmation and preservation.

positions.position: Applied to speech or reports, true means truthful correspondence, making the statement worthy of affirmation and preservation.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Applied to speech or reports, true means truthful correspondence, making the statement worthy of affirmation and preservation.

positions.position: God deserves the name True in every sense: His existence cannot cease, belief in Him is correct and unchanging, and speaking of Him is the truest report.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): God deserves the name True in every sense: His existence cannot cease, belief in Him is correct and unchanging, and speaking of Him is the truest report.

positions.position: Azali means related to pre-eternity, but must not imply that God exists inside some pre-eternal thing; it means existence without any beginning.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Azali means related to pre-eternity, but must not imply that God exists inside some pre-eternal thing; it means existence without any beginning.

positions.position: Every eternal thing is enduring, but an enduring body or accident need not be eternal; ordinary usage also calls a person enduring, so baqi does not require eternity.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Every eternal thing is enduring, but an enduring body or accident need not be eternal; ordinary usage also calls a person enduring, so baqi does not require eternity. | mentions 55:27

positions.position: Some say baqi means everlasting and therefore cannot describe bodies, but Razi rejects that restriction because ordinary speakers say may God preserve you.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Some say baqi means everlasting and therefore cannot describe bodies, but Razi rejects that restriction because ordinary speakers say may God preserve you.

positions.position: A Prophetic supplication addresses God as existing before every existence, present with every existence, and remaining after every existence.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النبي): A Prophetic supplication addresses God as existing before every existence, present with every existence, and remaining after every existence.

positions.position: Grammarians call kana complete when it means happened or existed, and deficient when it has a subject and predicate, as in God was knowing and wise.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Grammarians call kana complete when it means happened or existed, and deficient when it has a subject and predicate, as in God was knowing and wise. | mentions 3:110, 4:11

positions.position: Razi challenges grammarians: if kana as a verb denotes an event in time, attaching one noun should express that event fully, making it complete rather than deficient.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi challenges grammarians: if kana as a verb denotes an event in time, attaching one noun should express that event fully, making it complete rather than deficient.

positions.position: Kana denotes occurrence or existence; for an entity's own occurrence one noun suffices, while occurrence of a quality requires both the subject and predicate.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Kana denotes occurrence or existence; for an entity's own occurrence one noun suffices, while occurrence of a quality requires both the subject and predicate.

positions.position: On this analysis, kain and existent have the same meaning, so kain may properly be applied to God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): On this analysis, kain and existent have the same meaning, so kain may properly be applied to God.

positions.position: Mu'tazilites and philosophers deny that real attributes distinct from existence and its modes subsist in God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (المعتزلة والفلاسفة): Mu'tazilites and philosophers deny that real attributes distinct from existence and its modes subsist in God.

positions.position: We can conceive God as existent while not attending to His power or knowledge, and conceive power without knowledge, showing distinct concepts.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): We can conceive God as existent while not attending to His power or knowledge, and conceive power without knowledge, showing distinct concepts.

positions.position: Knowledge concerns necessary, impossible, and possible things, while power concerns only possible things, proving their difference.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Knowledge concerns necessary, impossible, and possible things, while power concerns only possible things, proving their difference.

positions.position: Power brings the possible into existence but knowledge does not, so the two attributes differ.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Power brings the possible into existence but knowledge does not, so the two attributes differ.

positions.position: Not existent contradicts existent, whereas not knowing does not; what is negated by existence and knowledge claims is therefore distinct, likewise for power.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Not existent contradicts existent, whereas not knowing does not; what is negated by existence and knowledge claims is therefore distinct, likewise for power.

positions.position: The Quran calls God the Living and Sustainer; these names combine to provide the full praise.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The Quran calls God the Living and Sustainer; these names combine to provide the full praise. | mentions 2:255, 20:111, 40:65

positions.position: Hayy alone, meaning perceiving and acting or able to know and act, seems insufficiently praiseworthy; the praise lies in its combination with qayyum.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Hayy alone, meaning perceiving and acting or able to know and act, seems insufficiently praiseworthy; the praise lies in its combination with qayyum.

positions.position: Qayyum means sustaining and setting right everything else, which requires complete knowledge and power; thus Hayy qayyum means knowing every possible and acting on every originated thing.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Qayyum means sustaining and setting right everything else, which requires complete knowledge and power; thus Hayy qayyum means knowing every possible and acting on every originated thing.

positions.position: Knowledge and power are real attributes whose relations to known things and possible effects are concomitant; life alone is a real divine attribute without relation.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Knowledge and power are real attributes whose relations to known things and possible effects are concomitant; life alone is a real divine attribute without relation.

positions.position: Philosophers define living as perceiving and acting, but both are relational, so life on their account is not distinct from knowledge and power.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الفلاسفة): Philosophers define living as perceiving and acting, but both are relational, so life on their account is not distinct from knowledge and power.

positions.position: Theologians define life as an attribute that makes knowing and having power possible; they argue differing capacities among essences require an additional life attribute.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (المتكلمون): Theologians define life as an attribute that makes knowing and having power possible; they argue differing capacities among essences require an additional life attribute.

positions.position: Withholding or granting wealth yields Withholder and Expander, while lowering or raising status yields Abaser and Exalter.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Withholding or granting wealth yields Withholder and Expander, while lowering or raising status yields Abaser and Exalter.

positions.position: Some oppositions are contraries, such as exalting and humiliating or giving life and death; others are presence and absence, such as withholding versus extending or lowering versus raising.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Some oppositions are contraries, such as exalting and humiliating or giving life and death; others are presence and absence, such as withholding versus extending or lowering versus raising.

positions.position: Not honoring someone differs from actively humiliating them; the contrast between honor and abasement is a pair of opposites.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Not honoring someone differs from actively humiliating them; the contrast between honor and abasement is a pair of opposites.

positions.position: Khaliq means measuring or determining, which in God returns to knowledge; fatir derives from splitting and appears to mean originating at once.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Khaliq means measuring or determining, which in God returns to knowledge; fatir derives from splitting and appears to mean originating at once.

positions.position: Mu'tazilites and Ash'arites say God's act of bringing something into being is identical with the thing brought into being.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (المعتزلة والأشعرية): Mu'tazilites and Ash'arites say God's act of bringing something into being is identical with the thing brought into being.

positions.position: Those who deny a separate attribute of bringing into being argue that if it acts contingently it is simply power, while necessary effect would make God act by nature rather than choice.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Those who deny a separate attribute of bringing into being argue that if it acts contingently it is simply power, while necessary effect would make God act by nature rather than choice.

positions.position: They argue an eternal creating attribute entails eternal effects, while a created one needs another act of creation and an infinite regress.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): They argue an eternal creating attribute entails eternal effects, while a created one needs another act of creation and an infinite regress.

positions.position: They say power alone either suffices to produce effects once knowledge and will are present, making another attribute needless, or lacks efficacy and is not power.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): They say power alone either suffices to produce effects once knowledge and will are present, making another attribute needless, or lacks efficacy and is not power.

positions.position: Proponents of an eternal creating attribute point out that an able agent may act or refrain; God's ability to make a thousand suns does not mean He did so.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Proponents of an eternal creating attribute point out that an able agent may act or refrain; God's ability to make a thousand suns does not mean He did so.

positions.position: Being an agent who produces cannot mean merely that the effect exists, or explaining an effect by saying God produced it would explain it by itself; therefore producing differs from both power and effect.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Being an agent who produces cannot mean merely that the effect exists, or explaining an effect by saying God produced it would explain it by itself; therefore producing differs from both power and effect.

positions.position: Those identifying creation with its effect interpret Creator, Provider, Giver of life, and Giver of death as specific relations of God's power to outcomes.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Those identifying creation with its effect interpret Creator, Provider, Giver of life, and Giver of death as specific relations of God's power to outcomes.

positions.position: Those distinguishing the creative act from its effect say being Creator is a real attribute qualified by a relation, not a relation alone.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Those distinguishing the creative act from its effect say being Creator is a real attribute qualified by a relation, not a relation alone.

positions.position: Sabur does not punish an offender despite power to do so; Halim does likewise while continuing to bestow blessings.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Sabur does not punish an offender despite power to do so; Halim does likewise while continuing to bestow blessings.

positions.position: Among negations of divine acts: God creates neither falsehood nor play nor purposelessness, but creates in truth.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Among negations of divine acts: God creates neither falsehood nor play nor purposelessness, but creates in truth. | mentions 38:27, 3:191, 21:16, 23:115

positions.position: God is not pleased with unbelief, does not will injustice, and does not love corruption.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): God is not pleased with unbelief, does not will injustice, and does not love corruption. | mentions 39:7, 40:31, 2:205

positions.position: He does not punish without prior wrongdoing; believers' gratitude and faith leave no need for punishment.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): He does not punish without prior wrongdoing; believers' gratitude and faith leave no need for punishment. | mentions 4:147

positions.position: People's obedience benefits themselves and their wrongdoing harms themselves; God gains or loses nothing from them.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): People's obedience benefits themselves and their wrongdoing harms themselves; God gains or loses nothing from them. | mentions 17:7

positions.position: God does not break His word or promise and threat.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): God does not break His word or promise and threat. | mentions 50:29

positions.position: God neither begets nor is begotten.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): God neither begets nor is begotten. | mentions 112:3

positions.position: God neither sleeps nor forgets nor is ignorant, and knowledge of one thing never distracts Him from another.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): God neither sleeps nor forgets nor is ignorant, and knowledge of one thing never distracts Him from another. | mentions 2:255, 19:64, 34:3

positions.position: God's acts involve no fatigue, tools, material, or duration, and creating much or little takes no more time than an instant.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): God's acts involve no fatigue, tools, material, or duration, and creating much or little takes no more time than an instant. | mentions 38:38, 16:40, 16:77
