positions.position: God's power does not end and He is not impoverished, contrary to the claim that God is poor and humans rich.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): God's power does not end and He is not impoverished, contrary to the claim that God is poor and humans rich. | mentions 3:181

positions.position: The Quran affirms God's knowledge and uses forms including knower, all-knowing, most knowing, and past and future verbs of knowing.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The Quran affirms God's knowledge and uses forms including knower, all-knowing, most knowing, and past and future verbs of knowing. | mentions 2:255, 35:11, 65:12, 31:34, 13:9, 5:116, 6:124, 2:187, 2:197, 16:19

positions.position: Although the Quran says God teaches, do not call Him Teacher, because that name suggests deficiency.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Although the Quran says God teaches, do not call Him Teacher, because that name suggests deficiency. | mentions 2:31, 2:32, 4:113, 55:2

positions.position: Do not call God al-Allama: although intensive, the form suggests that knowledge was gained through effort and strain.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Do not call God al-Allama: although intensive, the form suggests that knowledge was gained through effort and strain.

positions.position: Khabar and khibra nearly mean knowledge; some define knowledge as report, and the frequent divine name Khabir also indicates knowledge.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Khabar and khibra nearly mean knowledge; some define knowledge as report, and the frequent divine name Khabir also indicates knowledge.

positions.position: Shahid means witness and knower when derived from seeing; if it means testimony, it belongs to speech instead.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Shahid means witness and knower when derived from seeing; if it means testimony, it belongs to speech instead.

positions.position: Hikma can mean knowledge or refraining from what is unsuitable and doing what is suitable.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Hikma can mean knowledge or refraining from what is unsuitable and doing what is suitable.

positions.position: Latif can mean knowledge of subtle matters or conveying benefits to people through a hidden, wondrous means.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Latif can mean knowledge of subtle matters or conveying benefits to people through a hidden, wondrous means.

positions.position: Razi treats will, pleasure, love, and aversion as divine qualities related to volition, citing Qur'anic examples.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi treats will, pleasure, love, and aversion as divine qualities related to volition, citing Qur'anic examples. | mentions 2:185

positions.position: The apparent is purely relational, meaning manifest through proofs, while the hidden is purely negative, meaning unknowable in essence.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The apparent is purely relational, meaning manifest through proofs, while the hidden is purely negative, meaning unknowable in essence.

positions.position: The name al-Qayyūm combines two features: absolute independence from anything else and the dependence of everything else on Him as its source.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The name al-Qayyūm combines two features: absolute independence from anything else and the dependence of everything else on Him as its source.

positions.position: Razi says the first feature is a negation and the second a relation; together they constitute al-Qayyūm.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi says the first feature is a negation and the second a relation; together they constitute al-Qayyūm.

positions.position: He cites divine approval both of gratitude and of believers, and also God's refusal to approve disbelief.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): He cites divine approval both of gratitude and of believers, and also God's refusal to approve disbelief. | mentions 39:7, 48:18, 58:22, 20:84

positions.position: Love is included among these qualities, with verses saying God loves His people and loves the purified.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Love is included among these qualities, with verses saying God loves His people and loves the purified. | mentions 5:54, 2:222

positions.position: The Ashʿarites define aversion as willing that an act not occur.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الأشعرية): The Ashʿarites define aversion as willing that an act not occur.

positions.position: The Muʿtazilites hold that aversion is a distinct quality besides will.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (المعتزلة): The Muʿtazilites hold that aversion is a distinct quality besides will.

positions.position: Razi gives no adjudication between these accounts, ending the report with “God knows best.”
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi gives no adjudication between these accounts, ending the report with “God knows best.”

positions.position: He establishes God's hearing and sight through verses that call Him the Hearing, the Seeing, and say He hears and sees.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): He establishes God's hearing and sight through verses that call Him the Hearing, the Seeing, and say He hears and sees. | mentions 42:11, 17:1, 20:46

positions.position: Other cited verses contrast God with an idol that neither hears nor sees and say that sight cannot encompass Him, though He encompasses sight.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Other cited verses contrast God with an idol that neither hears nor sees and say that sight cannot encompass Him, though He encompasses sight. | mentions 19:42, 6:103

positions.position: “First” and “last” each combine a relation with a negation: precedence without a predecessor, and persistence without a successor.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): “First” and “last” each combine a relation with a negation: precedence without a predecessor, and persistence without a successor.

positions.position: Razi groups divine speech under the noun kalām, citing the command to shelter a polytheist until he hears God's speech.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi groups divine speech under the noun kalām, citing the command to shelter a polytheist until he hears God's speech. | mentions 9:6

positions.position: He lists God's being grateful to His servants, supported by the promise that their efforts are appreciated and the description “grateful, knowing.”
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): He lists God's being grateful to His servants, supported by the promise that their efforts are appreciated and the description “grateful, knowing.” | mentions 17:19, 4:147

positions.position: He also counts past-tense forms of divine speech, citing God's direct address to Moses on two occasions.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): He also counts past-tense forms of divine speech, citing God's direct address to Moses on two occasions. | mentions 4:164, 7:143

positions.position: He records the future-tense form of speaking, in the statement that God speaks to a human only by revelation.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): He records the future-tense form of speaking, in the statement that God speaks to a human only by revelation. | mentions 42:51

positions.position: Razi lists divine saying in past, future, and verbal-noun forms, with Qur'anic examples for each.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi lists divine saying in past, future, and verbal-noun forms, with Qur'anic examples for each. | mentions 2:30

positions.position: The future form of saying is illustrated by God's instruction that the cow is such-and-such.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The future form of saying is illustrated by God's instruction that the cow is such-and-such. | mentions 2:68

positions.position: Razi includes both qīl and qawl among forms of divine saying, citing God's most truthful speech and His unalterable word.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi includes both qīl and qawl among forms of divine saying, citing God's most truthful speech and His unalterable word. | mentions 4:122, 50:29

positions.position: He cites command as a divine word, including God's ownership of command and His order to sacrifice a cow.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): He cites command as a divine word, including God's ownership of command and His order to sacrifice a cow. | mentions 30:4, 7:54, 2:67

positions.position: Promise is another divine word, attested as a binding promise in scripture and as God's promise to begin and restore creation.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Promise is another divine word, attested as a binding promise in scripture and as God's promise to begin and restore creation. | mentions 9:111, 10:4

positions.position: Razi includes revelation among divine words, citing revelation to God's servant and revelation as a mode of speaking.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi includes revelation among divine words, citing revelation to God's servant and revelation as a mode of speaking. | mentions 42:51, 53:10

positions.position: The transcendentists interpret divine greatness without corporeality: through eternal duration, knowledge and action, mercy and wisdom, and complete power.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أهل التنزيه والتقديس): The transcendentists interpret divine greatness without corporeality: through eternal duration, knowledge and action, mercy and wisdom, and complete power.

positions.position: Razi distinguishes al-kibriyāʾ from al-ʿaẓama: a divine report makes the former the cloak and the latter the waist-wrap, implying higher rank for the former.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi distinguishes al-kibriyāʾ from al-ʿaẓama: a divine report makes the former the cloak and the latter the waist-wrap, implying higher rank for the former.

positions.position: An unnamed poet captures the paradox of being absent yet present in the heart.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): An unnamed poet captures the paradox of being absent yet present in the heart.

positions.position: As al-Shiblī neared death, a bystander asked him to say the testimony; he answered with two verses addressing the ever-present beloved, not the requested formula.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الشبلي): As al-Shiblī neared death, a bystander asked him to say the testimony; he answered with two verses addressing the ever-present beloved, not the requested formula.

positions.position: Razi says the pronoun Hu has ineffable secrets; his written account feels paltry beside the joy and happiness he experiences in the heart when saying it.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi says the pronoun Hu has ineffable secrets; his written account feels paltry beside the joy and happiness he experiences in the heart when saying it.

positions.position: Calling “O He” acknowledges the servant's lowliness and the absence of any fitting relation between created humanity and the eternal Lord, hence the third-person address.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Calling “O He” acknowledges the servant's lowliness and the absence of any fitting relation between created humanity and the eternal Lord, hence the third-person address.

positions.position: “O He” also declares that everything besides God is sheer nonbeing; Razi links this annihilation to the verse that all things perish except His Face.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): “O He” also declares that everything besides God is sheer nonbeing; Razi links this annihilation to the verse that all things perish except His Face. | mentions 28:88

positions.position: The pronouns rank “I” highest, “you” midway, and “he” lowest: self-reference is most immediate, while direct address requires presence and third-person reference does not.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The pronouns rank “I” highest, “you” midway, and “he” lowest: self-reference is most immediate, while direct address requires presence and third-person reference does not.

positions.position: The Qur'an states the oneness formula with each pronoun: “I” in verses about God's warning and Moses, “you” in Jonah's prayer, and “He” in many passages.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The Qur'an states the oneness formula with each pronoun: “I” in verses about God's warning and Moses, “you” in Jonah's prayer, and “He” in many passages. | mentions 16:2, 20:14, 21:87, 2:163, 73:9

positions.position: Only God may say “There is no god but I” as a declaration, since it asserts divinity of its speaker; others may quote it, and full knowledge of “I” belongs only to God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Only God may say “There is no god but I” as a declaration, since it asserts divinity of its speaker; others may quote it, and full knowledge of “I” belongs only to God.

positions.position: A servant may say “There is no god but You” only while present; Jonah attained this when detached from every personal interest, a sign that witnessing requires such detachment.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A servant may say “There is no god but You” only while present; Jonah attained this when detached from every personal interest, a sign that witnessing requires such detachment. | mentions 21:87

positions.position: The third formula, “There is no god but He,” is appropriate for those who are absent.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The third formula, “There is no god but He,” is appropriate for those who are absent.

positions.position: Known divine descriptions fall into negative attributes that deny created defects and positive attributes that affirm the Creator's acts and ordering of creation.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Known divine descriptions fall into negative attributes that deny created defects and positive attributes that affirm the Creator's acts and ordering of creation.

positions.position: Negating defects in a ruler's presence can be insulting; likewise, describing God's perfection by created qualities is poor etiquette because creaturely perfection is infinitely lower.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Negating defects in a ruler's presence can be insulting; likewise, describing God's perfection by created qualities is poor etiquette because creaturely perfection is infinitely lower.

positions.position: Calling a sovereign great because he gave someone bread or water merits rebuke; created beings are even more negligible beside God's inexhaustible power.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Calling a sovereign great because he gave someone bread or water merits rebuke; created beings are even more negligible beside God's inexhaustible power.

positions.position: People nevertheless need negative and positive attributes at first, because sensual minds can be redirected toward holiness only through accessible descriptions of divine perfection.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): People nevertheless need negative and positive attributes at first, because sensual minds can be redirected toward holiness only through accessible descriptions of divine perfection.

positions.position: Once the soul turns from sense to holiness, it recognizes the shortcomings in both description types and leaves them for the name Hu.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Once the soul turns from sense to holiness, it recognizes the shortcomings in both description types and leaves them for the name Hu.

positions.position: The servant chooses Hu rather than “You” because it avoids claiming to have reached God's presence; it acknowledges that God is praised by and for Himself.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The servant chooses Hu rather than “You” because it avoids claiming to have reached God's presence; it acknowledges that God is praised by and for Himself.

positions.position: God cannot be defined through Himself, constituent parts, or external things: the first is circular, the second assumes composition, and creation is unlike the Creator.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): God cannot be defined through Himself, constituent parts, or external things: the first is circular, the second assumes composition, and creation is unlike the Creator.

positions.position: Razi's fifth benefit is that sustained recitation of Hu produces longing for God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi's fifth benefit is that sustained recitation of Hu produces longing for God.

positions.position: Awareness of divine perfections is partial because their degrees cannot be encompassed; this partial awareness generates endless longing, intensified by each advance.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Awareness of divine perfections is partial because their degrees cannot be encompassed; this partial awareness generates endless longing, intensified by each advance.

positions.position: Longing is the greatest station because it alternates pain at delay with pleasure in arrival, and relief from pain deepens joy.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Longing is the greatest station because it alternates pain at delay with pleasure in arrival, and relief from pain deepens joy.

positions.position: Razi concludes that persevering in Hu yields the highest stations, happiness, and bliss.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi concludes that persevering in Hu yields the highest stations, happiness, and bliss.

positions.position: He begins a sixth benefit by distinguishing conception, which forms an idea without judgment, from assent, which affirms existence or nonexistence.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): He begins a sixth benefit by distinguishing conception, which forms an idea without judgment, from assent, which affirms existence or nonexistence.

positions.position: Razi identifies conception with unity and assent with multiplicity.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi identifies conception with unity and assent with multiplicity.

positions.position: A report from the Prophet says that whoever makes his concerns one will be spared the concerns of this world and the next; Razi gives no grading.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): A report from the Prophet says that whoever makes his concerns one will be spared the concerns of this world and the next; Razi gives no grading.

positions.position: The servant's needs are endless, so only God, whose power, mercy, and wisdom are endless, can meet them; the servant should devote concern and speech to His remembrance.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The servant's needs are endless, so only God, whose power, mercy, and wisdom are endless, can meet them; the servant should devote concern and speech to His remembrance.

positions.position: The tenth benefit is that thought cannot attend to one thing while absorbed in another, so the worshipper should devote mind and tongue to the noblest object and remembrance: Hu.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The tenth benefit is that thought cannot attend to one thing while absorbed in another, so the worshipper should devote mind and tongue to the noblest object and remembrance: Hu.

positions.position: Razi calls remembrance one of the noblest stations and cites a divine report that God remembers a servant who remembers Him, privately or in a better gathering.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi calls remembrance one of the noblest stations and cites a divine report that God remembers a servant who remembers Him, privately or in a better gathering.

positions.position: Razi calls praise without asking the best form of remembrance.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi calls praise without asking the best form of remembrance.

positions.position: A report in which the Prophet speaks on God's authority promises the best gift to the one whom remembrance keeps from asking; Razi gives no grading.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): A report in which the Prophet speaks on God's authority promises the best gift to the one whom remembrance keeps from asking; Razi gives no grading.

positions.position: Because Hu carries no implication of asking or seeking, Razi concludes it is the greatest remembrance.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Because Hu carries no implication of asking or seeking, Razi concludes it is the greatest remembrance.

positions.position: Razi closes the chapter by recording a litany he saw in a book: “O He,” “O He beyond whom there is no He,” and other names.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi closes the chapter by recording a litany he saw in a book: “O He,” “O He beyond whom there is no He,” and other names.

positions.position: Al-Ghazālī calls “There is no god but God” the common people's monotheism and “There is no god but He” the elect's monotheism; Razi approves this distinction.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الغزالي): Al-Ghazālī calls “There is no god but God” the common people's monotheism and “There is no god but He” the elect's monotheism; Razi approves this distinction.

positions.position: Razi supports the elect's formula through the sequence in Qasas: the verse says “no god but He,” then “all things perish except His Face,” which he interprets as “except Him.”
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi supports the elect's formula through the sequence in Qasas: the verse says “no god but He,” then “all things perish except His Face,” which he interprets as “except Him.” | mentions 28:88

positions.position: He argues against denying that an efficient cause acts on essences: if it only bestows existence, existence itself is an essence, producing regress or denying causation altogether.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): He argues against denying that an efficient cause acts on essences: if it only bestows existence, existence itself is an essence, producing regress or denying causation altogether.

positions.position: The verse “rather, I wondered, while they scoff” assigns wonder to God according to a reading with ḍamma on the tāʾ; Razi explains wonder as an ignorant reaction.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The verse “rather, I wondered, while they scoff” assigns wonder to God according to a reading with ḍamma on the tāʾ; Razi explains wonder as an ignorant reaction. | mentions 37:12

positions.position: Razi's rule is to apply these words to their final effects in God's case, not to the initial bodily or emotional states that ordinarily cause them.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi's rule is to apply these words to their final effects in God's case, not to the initial bodily or emotional states that ordinarily cause them.

positions.position: He illustrates the rule with anger: its ordinary beginning is heated blood and temperament, while its final effect is harm to the one who incurs anger.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): He illustrates the rule with anger: its ordinary beginning is heated blood and temperament, while its final effect is harm to the one who incurs anger.

positions.position: “Jurist” entails understanding a speaker's purpose after ambiguity enters his speech, a condition impossible for God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): “Jurist” entails understanding a speaker's purpose after ambiguity enters his speech, a condition impossible for God.

positions.position: “Certain” derives from water settling in a basin and refers to knowledge reached after repeated indications; such acquisition is impossible for God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): “Certain” derives from water settling in a basin and refers to knowledge reached after repeated indications; such acquisition is impossible for God.

positions.position: “Clarifying” implies appearance after obscurity or separating confused things, which cannot apply to God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): “Clarifying” implies appearance after obscurity or separating confused things, which cannot apply to God.

positions.position: Razi lists scriptural terms whose literal senses imply defects: mockery, scheming, anger, wonder, arrogance, and modesty.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi lists scriptural terms whose literal senses imply defects: mockery, scheming, anger, wonder, arrogance, and modesty. | mentions 2:15, 3:54, 48:6, 37:12, 59:23, 2:26

positions.position: Galen says an angel visited in a dream after he withheld a discussion of the benefits of the eye, asking why he hid God's wisdom; Galen then wrote a separate, detailed treatise.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (جالينوس): Galen says an angel visited in a dream after he withheld a discussion of the benefits of the eye, asking why he hid God's wisdom; Galen then wrote a separate, detailed treatise.

positions.position: The question “Do you know of any namesake for Him?” concerns a proper namesake rather than a shared attribute; Razi says that name is Allah.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The question “Do you know of any namesake for Him?” concerns a proper namesake rather than a shared attribute; Razi says that name is Allah. | mentions 19:65

positions.position: A fourth derivation from lāha, “to rise,” means God transcends possible beings and created things, since only He is necessary, perfect, one, and the source of all.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A fourth derivation from lāha, “to rise,” means God transcends possible beings and created things, since only He is necessary, perfect, one, and the source of all.

positions.position: A third definition is one capable of acts that would make a worship-capable agent deserving of worship.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (بعض الناس): A third definition is one capable of acts that would make a worship-capable agent deserving of worship.

positions.position: Razi says the first two definitions fail to make God ilāh eternally, while the third preserves His eternal divinity.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi says the first two definitions fail to make God ilāh eternally, while the third preserves His eternal divinity.

positions.position: First proof: perfection is loved for itself; every other being is essentially contingent and deficient, while God is perfect in Himself, so He must be loved for Himself.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): First proof: perfection is loved for itself; every other being is essentially contingent and deficient, while God is perfect in Himself, so He must be loved for Himself.

positions.position: Second proof: possible beings cannot stand independently and need the Necessary Existent to exist; minds likewise depend on divine mercy and grace.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Second proof: possible beings cannot stand independently and need the Necessary Existent to exist; minds likewise depend on divine mercy and grace.

positions.position: A third etymology links ilāh with bewilderment: the deprived remain lost in ignorance, while those who attain knowledge become bewildered by divine oneness and majesty.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A third etymology links ilāh with bewilderment: the deprived remain lost in ignorance, while those who attain knowledge become bewildered by divine oneness and majesty.

positions.position: A fifth derivation connects ilāh with bewilderment: every imagined conception differs from God, yet denying Him is impossible because contingent things require a necessary source.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A fifth derivation connects ilāh with bewilderment: every imagined conception differs from God, yet denying Him is impossible because contingent things require a necessary source.

positions.position: The intellect can only affirm divine existence and perfection while admitting its inability to comprehend Him; this incapacity is itself insight and leaves the mind perplexed.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The intellect can only affirm divine existence and perfection while admitting its inability to comprehend Him; this incapacity is itself insight and leaves the mind perplexed.

positions.position: Razi compares divine existence to sunlight: if the sun never set, people would mistake its light on walls as inherent; because God cannot disappear, some mistakenly think creatures exist by themselves.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi compares divine existence to sunlight: if the sun never set, people would mistake its light on walls as inherent; because God cannot disappear, some mistakenly think creatures exist by themselves.

positions.position: People remember only God in severe distress, then credit weak causes after rescue; consistency requires turning to God in ease as well as hardship.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): People remember only God in severe distress, then credit weak causes after rescue; consistency requires turning to God in ease as well as hardship.

positions.position: Goodness and relief are sought from God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Goodness and relief are sought from God.

positions.position: Any apparent human benefactor can give only because God creates the impulse to give, so God is the true benefactor to whom people return.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Any apparent human benefactor can give only because God creates the impulse to give, so God is the true benefactor to whom people return.

positions.position: God alone is the true source of blessing, food, and existence, subduing nonexistence through creation; therefore He alone is truly God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): God alone is the true source of blessing, food, and existence, subduing nonexistence through creation; therefore He alone is truly God. | mentions 16:53, 6:14, 4:78

positions.position: God calls sinners His debtors but tells them to flee to Him, since He repays their debts and forgives them.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): God calls sinners His debtors but tells them to flee to Him, since He repays their debts and forgives them. | mentions 51:50

positions.position: Unlike kings who close their doors to the poor, God opens His door to them.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Unlike kings who close their doors to the poor, God opens His door to them.

positions.position: God asks sinners whether they hoped to meet Him; they say they hoped for pardon, and He promises them forgiveness.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): God asks sinners whether they hoped to meet Him; they say they hoped for pardon, and He promises them forgiveness.

positions.position: A report from Ibn ʿUmar describes ninety-nine huge records of sins outweighed by a card bearing the testimony of faith; nothing outweighs remembrance of God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): A report from Ibn ʿUmar describes ninety-nine huge records of sins outweighed by a card bearing the testimony of faith; nothing outweighs remembrance of God.

positions.position: Rāzī rejects foreign origin as an inference from resemblance alone, noting that Arabs identify God as creator and recognize no namesake for Him.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Rāzī rejects foreign origin as an inference from resemblance alone, noting that Arabs identify God as creator and recognize no namesake for Him. | mentions 31:25, 19:65

positions.position: Rāzī classifies things as useful and necessary, useful but unnecessary, necessary but harmful, or neither useful nor necessary, with worldly and afterlife examples.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Rāzī classifies things as useful and necessary, useful but unnecessary, necessary but harmful, or neither useful nor necessary, with worldly and afterlife examples.

positions.position: Rational objects are limitless: even endless study at the speed of lightning would yield finite knowledge beside the infinite unknown.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Rational objects are limitless: even endless study at the speed of lightning would yield finite knowledge beside the infinite unknown.

positions.position: Breath is useful and necessary in worldly life, while knowledge of God is necessary for the afterlife; losing it kills the heart and entails endless punishment.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Breath is useful and necessary in worldly life, while knowledge of God is necessary for the afterlife; losing it kills the heart and entails endless punishment.

positions.position: Money in this world and other kinds of knowledge in the afterlife are useful without being necessary.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Money in this world and other kinds of knowledge in the afterlife are useful without being necessary.

positions.position: Worldly illness, death, poverty, and aging are necessary harms, while the afterlife has no such necessary harm; worldly poverty and afterlife punishment are neither useful nor necessary.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Worldly illness, death, poverty, and aging are necessary harms, while the afterlife has no such necessary harm; worldly poverty and afterlife punishment are neither useful nor necessary.

positions.position: Loss of bodily life lasts only a moment, but loss of knowledge of God brings pain that endures forever.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Loss of bodily life lasts only a moment, but loss of knowledge of God brings pain that endures forever.

positions.position: Thought functions like breathing: proof preserves balanced faith and knowledge, while reflection expels corrupt doubts from the heart.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Thought functions like breathing: proof preserves balanced faith and knowledge, while reflection expels corrupt doubts from the heart.

positions.position: God knows every need and can fulfill every possible request, unlike human benefactors who may not know or meet a person’s needs.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): God knows every need and can fulfill every possible request, unlike human benefactors who may not know or meet a person’s needs.

positions.position: Receiving favor from God is preferable to accepting a human benefactor’s claim of favor.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Receiving favor from God is preferable to accepting a human benefactor’s claim of favor.

positions.position: Only God gives without compensation: all other givers seek material or spiritual return, while God is complete in Himself and gains no perfection from giving.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Only God gives without compensation: all other givers seek material or spiritual return, while God is complete in Himself and gains no perfection from giving.

positions.position: Anything contingent exists only through the Necessary Existent, so any mercy coming through another creature is created by God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Anything contingent exists only through the Necessary Existent, so any mercy coming through another creature is created by God.

positions.position: A human act of mercy occurs only when a decisive motive is present, and God creates that motive in the heart; He is the true merciful agent.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A human act of mercy occurs only when a decisive motive is present, and God creates that motive in the heart; He is the true merciful agent.

positions.position: A gift benefits its recipient only through God-given capacities and protection from harm, so God is the real giver and merciful benefactor.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A gift benefits its recipient only through God-given capacities and protection from harm, so God is the real giver and merciful benefactor.

positions.position: If creatures also show mercy, God’s gift is better because it humbles the recipient before God rather than before another creature.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): If creatures also show mercy, God’s gift is better because it humbles the recipient before God rather than before another creature.

positions.position: God’s gifts direct people toward earning eternal happiness, while a creature’s gift usually obliges the recipient to serve that creature’s aims.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): God’s gifts direct people toward earning eternal happiness, while a creature’s gift usually obliges the recipient to serve that creature’s aims.

positions.position: Servitude to God is preferable to becoming like a servant of a human benefactor.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Servitude to God is preferable to becoming like a servant of a human benefactor.

positions.position: A story tells of a Jewish neighbor who accepted Islam because he longed to see God; in a dream he says God forgave him for converting out of that longing.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A story tells of a Jewish neighbor who accepted Islam because he longed to see God; in a dream he says God forgave him for converting out of that longing.

positions.position: A person should keep company with remembrance of God so as not to be separated from Him in either world.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A person should keep company with remembrance of God so as not to be separated from Him in either world.

positions.position: A devotee says he will call on God throughout life, in the grave, at resurrection, while receiving the record, at the scales and bridge, in Paradise, and on seeing God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A devotee says he will call on God throughout life, in the grave, at resurrection, while receiving the record, at the scales and bridge, in Paradise, and on seeing God.

positions.position: God knows hidden faults that would alienate family, spouse, servant, or neighbor, yet conceals them through His generosity.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): God knows hidden faults that would alienate family, spouse, servant, or neighbor, yet conceals them through His generosity.

positions.position: A report says whoever is occupied with remembering God rather than asking receives more than those who ask; Abraham models praise followed by requests.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): A report says whoever is occupied with remembering God rather than asking receives more than those who ask; Abraham models praise followed by requests. | mentions 26:78, 26:83

positions.position: Concealment suits a defect, not the greatest honor of remembering God; reports praise dying with a tongue moist in remembrance and Ali’s saying that God’s mention ennobles those who remember Him.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Concealment suits a defect, not the greatest honor of remembering God; reports praise dying with a tongue moist in remembrance and Ali’s saying that God’s mention ennobles those who remember Him.

positions.position: He notes the widely held report that God has 1,001 sacred names found in the Qur’an and Sunna, and says studying each name is a noble discipline requiring knowledge of the named entity, proofs for its existence, and responses to
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): He notes the widely held report that God has 1,001 sacred names found in the Qur’an and Sunna, and says studying each name is a noble discipline requiring knowledge of the named entity, proofs for its existence, and responses to objections, collectively thousands of questions.

positions.position: The varied organs formed from similar semen show that a knowing, powerful Creator deliberately shapes them for human interests through mercy, making Him worthy of praise.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The varied organs formed from similar semen show that a knowing, powerful Creator deliberately shapes them for human interests through mercy, making Him worthy of praise.

positions.position: “Praise belongs to God” indicates the Creator's existence, knowledge, power, mercy, perfect wisdom, and entitlement to praise and glorification.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): “Praise belongs to God” indicates the Creator's existence, knowledge, power, mercy, perfect wisdom, and entitlement to praise and glorification.

positions.position: A prophetic report says God has seventy veils of light; if unveiled, the splendor of His face would burn everything perceived by sight, and only prophetic light reveals the number.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النبي): A prophetic report says God has seventy veils of light; if unveiled, the splendor of His face would burn everything perceived by sight, and only prophetic light reveals the number.

positions.position: Raising the hands signals leaving both worlds and directing all inner faculties toward God; “God is greatest” means He exceeds all beings, knowledge, comparison, and even the claim that He is simply greater.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Raising the hands signals leaving both worlds and directing all inner faculties toward God; “God is greatest” means He exceeds all beings, knowledge, comparison, and even the claim that He is simply greater.

positions.position: The opening glorification reveals the lights of divine majesty and moves from declaring God's transcendence to praising Him.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The opening glorification reveals the lights of divine majesty and moves from declaring God's transcendence to praising Him.

positions.position: “Blessed is Your name” unveils pre-eternity and eternity, since blessing here indicates abiding beyond extinction and nonexistence.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): “Blessed is Your name” unveils pre-eternity and eternity, since blessing here indicates abiding beyond extinction and nonexistence.

positions.position: “Exalted is Your majesty” signifies that God's knowledge and greatness exceed every stated measure.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): “Exalted is Your majesty” signifies that God's knowledge and greatness exceed every stated measure.

positions.position: “There is no god but You” means every attribute of majesty and perfection belongs only to God; ultimately reason, speech, understanding, and imagination fail before Him.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): “There is no god but You” means every attribute of majesty and perfection belongs only to God; ultimately reason, speech, understanding, and imagination fail before Him.

positions.position: Al-Razi prefers placing God's name first: God's existence precedes all else, so mention of Him should precede mention of other things.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Razi prefers placing God's name first: God's existence precedes all else, so mention of Him should precede mention of other things.

positions.position: He also invokes God's being First and Last and the ordering of affairs before and after Him as evidence for placing His name first.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): He also invokes God's being First and Last and the ordering of affairs before and after Him as evidence for placing His name first. | mentions 57:3, 30:4

positions.position: Putting the name first is more reverential; the following phrase also places the addressee before the verb, suggesting the implied wording is 'In God's name I begin.'
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Putting the name first is more reverential; the following phrase also places the addressee before the verb, suggesting the implied wording is 'In God's name I begin.' | mentions 1:5

positions.position: Al-Qushayri says realized knowers see God before anything; al-Razi explains that moving from creation to Creator is an inferior proof than descending from Creator to creation.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الأستاذ القشيري): Al-Qushayri says realized knowers see God before anything; al-Razi explains that moving from creation to Creator is an inferior proof than descending from Creator to creation.

positions.position: The implied action's position symbolizes spiritual attention: action-first moves from one's act toward need of God, while God's name first recognizes dependence on Him before considering oneself.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The implied action's position symbolizes spiritual attention: action-first moves from one's act toward need of God, while God's name first recognizes dependence on Him before considering oneself.

positions.position: Abu Ubayd treats 'name' as an extra word, so the phrase means 'by God'; he says it was added either for blessing or to distinguish it from an oath.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أبو عبيد): Abu Ubayd treats 'name' as an extra word, so the phrase means 'by God'; he says it was added either for blessing or to distinguish it from an oath.

positions.position: Al-Razi rejects Abu Ubayd's account: beginning concerns a human act, namely uttering and saying God's name, so 'begin with the name' means begin by mentioning God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Razi rejects Abu Ubayd's account: beginning concerns a human act, namely uttering and saying God's name, so 'begin with the name' means begin by mentioning God.

positions.position: Mentioning God and His name first mirrors their supreme rank: just as God precedes all beings in existence, His remembrance and name should precede all others.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Mentioning God and His name first mirrors their supreme rank: just as God precedes all beings in existence, His remembrance and name should precede all others.

positions.position: Readers agree that stopping after 'In the name' is deficient, after 'In the name of God' or through 'the Merciful' is sufficient, and after the full phrase is complete.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Readers agree that stopping after 'In the name' is deficient, after 'In the name of God' or through 'the Merciful' is sufficient, and after the full phrase is complete.

positions.position: A deficient stop leaves words unintelligible alone; a sufficient stop leaves intelligible words still connected to what follows; a complete stop leaves a finished clause unrelated to what follows.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A deficient stop leaves words unintelligible alone; a sufficient stop leaves intelligible words still connected to what follows; a complete stop leaves a finished clause unrelated to what follows.

positions.position: He distinguishes indirect from essential knowledge: inferring a builder from a building reveals no nature, just as inferring the Creator from contingent things gives only indirect knowledge of God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): He distinguishes indirect from essential knowledge: inferring a builder from a building reveals no nature, just as inferring the Creator from contingent things gives only indirect knowledge of God.

positions.position: In ordinary experience, essential apprehension comes through knowledge or sight; whether God could be essentially known through one or both, or through further modes, exceeds reason's ability to decide.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): In ordinary experience, essential apprehension comes through knowledge or sight; whether God could be essentially known through one or both, or through further modes, exceeds reason's ability to decide.

positions.position: Another derivation takes it from lāh, hidden and elevated: God is beyond sight and above all things; a cited poem uses lāh.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (author): Another derivation takes it from lāh, hidden and elevated: God is beyond sight and above all things; a cited poem uses lāh.

positions.position: Abū Yazīd al-Balkhī calls Allāh a foreign word, citing Jewish and Christian lāhā and saying Arabs adopted and changed it.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (أبو يزيد البلخي): Abū Yazīd al-Balkhī calls Allāh a foreign word, citing Jewish and Christian lāhā and saying Arabs adopted and changed it.

positions.position: A reported view treats Allāh as an attribute rather than a personal name because God is not sensed or immediately apprehended and is known through His attributes; Abū Ḥayyān calls this unusual.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (قيل): A reported view treats Allāh as an attribute rather than a personal name because God is not sensed or immediately apprehended and is known through His attributes; Abū Ḥayyān calls this unusual.

positions.position: Abū Ḥayyān distinguishes the word, its referent, and the act of naming; a judgment attributed literally to a name can instead use “name” metaphorically for its referent.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (author): Abū Ḥayyān distinguishes the word, its referent, and the act of naming; a judgment attributed literally to a name can instead use “name” metaphorically for its referent.

positions.position: Abū Ḥayyān holds that the names intensify mercy in different ways, so their combination is not mere repetition: faʿlān suggests fullness or dominance, while faʿīl suggests repeated occurrence at objects of mercy.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (author): Abū Ḥayyān holds that the names intensify mercy in different ways, so their combination is not mere repetition: faʿlān suggests fullness or dominance, while faʿīl suggests repeated occurrence at objects of mercy.

positions.position: Mujāhid distinguishes the names as mercy for this world and mercy for the next.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (مجاهد): Mujāhid distinguishes the names as mercy for this world and mercy for the next.

positions.position: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the two names concern the inhabitants of heaven and earth.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (الضحاك): Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the two names concern the inhabitants of heaven and earth.

positions.position: ʿIkrima distinguishes one mercy from one hundred mercies.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (عكرمة): ʿIkrima distinguishes one mercy from one hundred mercies.

positions.position: Al-Muḥāsibī distinguishes mercy toward souls from mercy toward hearts.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (المحاسبي): Al-Muḥāsibī distinguishes mercy toward souls from mercy toward hearts.

positions.position: Human mercy is defined either as tenderness in the heart or as intending good or averting harm, since one can help another without feeling tenderness.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (قيل): Human mercy is defined either as tenderness in the heart or as intending good or averting harm, since one can help another without feeling tenderness.

positions.position: If Allah derives from ilāh, its article is either dominant, like al-Najm for the Pleiades, or a necessary extra article under other derivations.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): If Allah derives from ilāh, its article is either dominant, like al-Najm for the Pleiades, or a necessary extra article under other derivations.

positions.position: God's mercy is metaphorical for His beneficence in one account; another makes it the will of good, a divine essential attribute, raising a debate over whether active attributes are originated.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): God's mercy is metaphorical for His beneficence in one account; another makes it the will of good, a divine essential attribute, raising a debate over whether active attributes are originated.

positions.position: Al-Khalil derives Allah from walah, because all creatures long for God; philosophers say all things love God, supported by the verse that everything glorifies Him.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (الخليل): Al-Khalil derives Allah from walah, because all creatures long for God; philosophers say all things love God, supported by the verse that everything glorifies Him. | mentions 17:44

positions.position: Al-Zamakhshari rejects treating Allah as an adjective: it is used as a noun, while adjectives require a noun they describe and cannot all remain without one.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (الزمخشري): Al-Zamakhshari rejects treating Allah as an adjective: it is used as a noun, while adjectives require a noun they describe and cannot all remain without one.

positions.position: The omitted alif in al-Rahman reflects that people know mercy’s effects but entrust knowledge of its full reality to God.
positions.reasons: BURHAN (author): The omitted alif in al-Rahman reflects that people know mercy’s effects but entrust knowledge of its full reality to God.

positions.position: Alif is also omitted from some active-participle forms such as qadara and ʿalima because it lies inside the word.
positions.reasons: BURHAN (author): Alif is also omitted from some active-participle forms such as qadara and ʿalima because it lies inside the word.

positions.position: Ibn Hibban reads the report comparing al-Fatiha with the Torah and Gospel as a difference in reward granted by God’s favor, not as intrinsic superiority within the Quran.
positions.reasons: BURHAN (ابن حبان): Ibn Hibban reads the report comparing al-Fatiha with the Torah and Gospel as a difference in reward granted by God’s favor, not as intrinsic superiority within the Quran.

positions.position: This purpose requires proving God's encompassing knowledge and His unique status as Creator, King, and Owner; prophets and revealed laws gather people to truth and teach them their Sovereign and what pleases Him, a purpose the Fātiḥa gathers in knowledge
positions.reasons: BIQAI (author): This purpose requires proving God's encompassing knowledge and His unique status as Creator, King, and Owner; prophets and revealed laws gather people to truth and teach them their Sovereign and what pleases Him, a purpose the Fātiḥa gathers in knowledge and action.

positions.position: The basmala stands to the Fātiḥa as the Fātiḥa stands to the Qur'an: by referring all things to God alone, it indicates that He alone is God and summarizes the Fātiḥa and the Qur'an's roots, branches, knowledge, and subtleties.
positions.reasons: BIQAI (author): The basmala stands to the Fātiḥa as the Fātiḥa stands to the Qur'an: by referring all things to God alone, it indicates that He alone is God and summarizes the Fātiḥa and the Qur'an's roots, branches, knowledge, and subtleties.

positions.position: The first creation is named in praise of God, since bringing creatures from nonexistence into existence is the greatest nurturing.
positions.reasons: BIQAI (العلامة سعد الدين مسعود ابن عمرو التفتازاني الشافعي): The first creation is named in praise of God, since bringing creatures from nonexistence into existence is the greatest nurturing.

positions.position: God is the ever-living witness whose knowledge misses nothing and whose permission governs all things; His universal mercy reaches creation and His special mercy favors His devoted servants.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (author): God is the ever-living witness whose knowledge misses nothing and whose permission governs all things; His universal mercy reaches creation and His special mercy favors His devoted servants.

positions.position: Ali reports that saying the basmala with a declaration of God's power in a crisis averts whatever calamity God wills.
positions.reasons: DURR (علي): Ali reports that saying the basmala with a declaration of God's power in a crisis averts whatever calamity God wills.

positions.position: Ata advises reading al-Fatiha to completion when seeking a need, which will be fulfilled by God's will.
positions.reasons: DURR (عطاء): Ata advises reading al-Fatiha to completion when seeking a need, which will be fulfilled by God's will.

positions.position: Ibn al-Arabi estimates Qur'anic sciences by multiplying its words by four—outer meaning, inner meaning, limit, and point of access—yielding vast totals, and says combinations and relations are beyond counting or human knowledge.
positions.reasons: ITQAN (ابن العربي): Ibn al-Arabi estimates Qur'anic sciences by multiplying its words by four—outer meaning, inner meaning, limit, and point of access—yielding vast totals, and says combinations and relations are beyond counting or human knowledge.

positions.position: Ibn al-Arabi divides Qur'anic knowledge into monotheism (creatures and God's names, attributes, and acts), reminder (promise, threat, afterlife, and purification), and rulings (duties, benefits, harms, commands, prohibitions, and recommendations).
positions.reasons: ITQAN (ابن العربي): Ibn al-Arabi divides Qur'anic knowledge into monotheism (creatures and God's names, attributes, and acts), reminder (promise, threat, afterlife, and purification), and rulings (duties, benefits, harms, commands, prohibitions, and recommendations).

positions.position: For Ibn al-Arabi, al-Fatiha is the Qur'an's mother because it contains all three domains, while al-Ikhlas is a third because it contains monotheism alone.
positions.reasons: ITQAN (ابن العربي): For Ibn al-Arabi, al-Fatiha is the Qur'an's mother because it contains all three domains, while al-Ikhlas is a third because it contains monotheism alone.

positions.position: Ali ibn Isa enumerates thirty Qur'anic subjects, including signs, analogy, commands and prohibitions, promise and threat, paradise and hell, divine names and acts, gratitude, argument, ethics, wisdom, praise, blame, and moral instruction.
positions.reasons: ITQAN (علي بن عيسى): Ali ibn Isa enumerates thirty Qur'anic subjects, including signs, analogy, commands and prohibitions, promise and threat, paradise and hell, divine names and acts, gratitude, argument, ethics, wisdom, praise, blame, and moral instruction.

positions.position: They reconcile the hadith calling the Fatiha two-thirds of the Qur’an by saying it indicates all Qur’anic aims through inclusion and implication, but not direct correspondence; those are two of three modes of indication.
positions.reasons: ITQAN (الزركشي وناصر الدين بن الميلق): They reconcile the hadith calling the Fatiha two-thirds of the Qur’an by saying it indicates all Qur’anic aims through inclusion and implication, but not direct correspondence; those are two of three modes of indication.

positions.position: A second explanation counts three kinds of rights—God’s claim on servants, servants’ claim on God, and people’s claims on one another—and says the Fatiha explicitly covers the first two, hence two-thirds.
positions.reasons: ITQAN (ناصر الدين بن الميلق): A second explanation counts three kinds of rights—God’s claim on servants, servants’ claim on God, and people’s claims on one another—and says the Fatiha explicitly covers the first two, hence two-thirds.

positions.position: There is no conflict between hadiths calling the Fatiha the greatest surah and al-Baqara the greatest: al-Baqara is greatest among surahs other than the Fatiha because of its detailed laws, parables, and arguments.
positions.reasons: ITQAN (author): There is no conflict between hadiths calling the Fatiha the greatest surah and al-Baqara the greatest: al-Baqara is greatest among surahs other than the Fatiha because of its detailed laws, parables, and arguments. | mentions 2:1

positions.position: Ibn al-Arabi quotes a teacher saying the Fatiha contains a thousand commands, prohibitions, rulings, and reports; Ibn Umar spent eight years teaching it because of its jurisprudential depth.
positions.reasons: ITQAN (ابن العربي): Ibn al-Arabi quotes a teacher saying the Fatiha contains a thousand commands, prohibitions, rulings, and reports; Ibn Umar spent eight years teaching it because of its jurisprudential depth.

positions.position: He distinguishes God’s eternal names in eternal speech from later names used of Him; the former follow the dispute about divine speech, while created designations are other than God.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): He distinguishes God’s eternal names in eternal speech from later names used of Him; the former follow the dispute about divine speech, while created designations are other than God.

positions.position: Al-Ālūsī says objections that identity would multiply or change the named apply only to names as created expressions, not names used for the essence.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Al-Ālūsī says objections that identity would multiply or change the named apply only to names as created expressions, not names used for the essence.

positions.position: Interpreters explain divine mercy as its effect, the will to do good, a king’s compassion by analogy, or a metaphorical attribute; some call it a revealed technical sense.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Interpreters explain divine mercy as its effect, the will to do good, a king’s compassion by analogy, or a metaphorical attribute; some call it a revealed technical sense.

positions.position: Al-Ālūsī rejects metaphorical reduction: mercy is truly God’s attribute in a manner befitting Him, without likening it to created emotion or specifying its modality.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Al-Ālūsī rejects metaphorical reduction: mercy is truly God’s attribute in a manner befitting Him, without likening it to created emotion or specifying its modality.

positions.position: Al-Bayḍāwī’s ordering moves from God’s universal outpouring of existence to each creature’s particular share and perfection; al-Ālūsī questions the distinction.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (البيضاوي): Al-Bayḍāwī’s ordering moves from God’s universal outpouring of existence to each creature’s particular share and perfection; al-Ālūsī questions the distinction.

positions.position: A second reason for opening with the basmala is to teach people how to begin: invoking God declares dependence on His power in every undertaking.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): A second reason for opening with the basmala is to teach people how to begin: invoking God declares dependence on His power in every undertaking.

positions.position: Reports urge asking God even for a sandal strap, and God tells Moses to ask for salt and a shoe strap; these support invocation in minor needs.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Reports urge asking God even for a sandal strap, and God tells Moses to ask for salt and a shoe strap; these support invocation in minor needs.

positions.position: He prefers seeking divine aid because it expresses humility, denies independent human power, and anticipates “You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help.”
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): He prefers seeking divine aid because it expresses humility, denies independent human power, and anticipates “You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help.” | mentions 1:5

positions.position: Razi's sixth argument says the basmala implies beginning with God's aid, reminds people that obedience depends on God's power, and makes audible recitation an act of commanding right.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (الفخر الرازي): Razi's sixth argument says the basmala implies beginning with God's aid, reminds people that obedience depends on God's power, and makes audible recitation an act of commanding right.

positions.position: Alusi argues that polytheists seek help from their gods as intermediaries, making the instrument analogy more apt for their practice than the accompaniment analogy.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi argues that polytheists seek help from their gods as intermediaries, making the instrument analogy more apt for their practice than the accompaniment analogy.

positions.position: An instrument must persist through every part of an action, but accompaniment need not; the report about God's naming better suits assistance because it teaches reliance on God's power.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): An instrument must persist through every part of an action, but accompaniment need not; the report about God's naming better suits assistance because it teaches reliance on God's power.

positions.position: Al-Baydawi's wording favors construing ba as seeking God's assistance, which makes His name seem essential to the act.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (البيضاوي): Al-Baydawi's wording favors construing ba as seeking God's assistance, which makes His name seem essential to the act.

positions.position: Al-Zamakhshari's wording favors accompaniment: this usage is more common, conveys blessing and reverence, rebuts idolaters' invocation, and implies God's name accompanies every part of the act.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (الزمخشري): Al-Zamakhshari's wording favors accompaniment: this usage is more common, conveys blessing and reverence, rebuts idolaters' invocation, and implies God's name accompanies every part of the act.

positions.position: Al-Zamakhshari also adduces the report that God's naming is in every Muslim's heart whether or not it is spoken, and the hadith about God's name protecting from harm.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (الزمخشري): Al-Zamakhshari also adduces the report that God's naming is in every Muslim's heart whether or not it is spoken, and the hadith about God's name protecting from harm.

positions.position: Alusi prefers assistance as nearly necessary: it expresses humility and dependence, rejects independent human power, opens mercy, and fits the Fatiha's appeal for help and the command to read in God's name.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi prefers assistance as nearly necessary: it expresses humility and dependence, rejects independent human power, opens mercy, and fits the Fatiha's appeal for help and the command to read in God's name. | mentions 1:5, 96:1

positions.position: He rejects the claim that assistance treats God's name as a debased tool: reliance on God is valid and Qur'an itself commands seeking His help.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): He rejects the claim that assistance treats God's name as a debased tool: reliance on God is valid and Qur'an itself commands seeking His help. | mentions 7:128

positions.position: Alusi calls the hidden imperative parsing awkward and unsupported; reflecting on the Fatiha's direct statement of worship and reliance conveys far more without that difficulty.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi calls the hidden imperative parsing awkward and unsupported; reflecting on the Fatiha's direct statement of worship and reliance conveys far more without that difficulty.

positions.position: Alusi offers a mystical reading: mentally the created act precedes its omission in speech, while only God's pre-eternal name appears, hinting at the fixed archetypes in divine knowledge and God's absolute priority.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi offers a mystical reading: mentally the created act precedes its omission in speech, while only God's pre-eternal name appears, hinting at the fixed archetypes in divine knowledge and God's absolute priority. | mentions 28:88

positions.position: Some gnostics say they see God in everything without believing in indwelling; Alusi calls this a higher rank than seeing God before things and mentions four spiritual ranks.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Some gnostics say they see God in everything without believing in indwelling; Alusi calls this a higher rank than seeing God before things and mentions four spiritual ranks.

positions.position: Every surah except Baraʾa opens with an allusion to Muhammad; Baraʾa omits it because divine majesty dominates, though the Muhammadan allusion is not wholly absent.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Every surah except Baraʾa opens with an allusion to Muhammad; Baraʾa omits it because divine majesty dominates, though the Muhammadan allusion is not wholly absent.

positions.position: Alusi limits this symbolism to the ba of the basmala and says it cannot be applied to every genitive ba.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi limits this symbolism to the ba of the basmala and says it cannot be applied to every genitive ba.

positions.position: Alusi's own symbolism makes ba the second rank after the simple alif, a sign of true existence; he recalls al-Shibli saying he was the point beneath ba and quotes Ibn Arabi on its secret of servitude.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi's own symbolism makes ba the second rank after the simple alif, a sign of true existence; he recalls al-Shibli saying he was the point beneath ba and quotes Ibn Arabi on its secret of servitude.

positions.position: The word name also denotes a signifier: an eternal divine designation in God’s eternal speech, or a created designation; the former debate follows the dispute about eternal speech.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): The word name also denotes a signifier: an eternal divine designation in God’s eternal speech, or a created designation; the former debate follows the dispute about eternal speech.

positions.position: Sunni scholars establish the eternal divine-name usage from transmitted evidence, while shifting disputes over created names toward the underlying question of divine speech.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (أهل السنة): Sunni scholars establish the eternal divine-name usage from transmitted evidence, while shifting disputes over created names toward the underlying question of divine speech.

positions.position: Because human mercy can mean tenderness of heart, commentators explain divine mercy figuratively as its effect, by a comparison, or as a metaphor for beneficence or will.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Because human mercy can mean tenderness of heart, commentators explain divine mercy figuratively as its effect, by a comparison, or as a metaphor for beneficence or will.

positions.position: In one explicit-metaphor account, beneficence is the referent for mercy according to Qadi Abu Bakr, while al-Ashʿari takes the referent to be the will to show beneficence.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (القاضي أبو بكر والأشعري): In one explicit-metaphor account, beneficence is the referent for mercy according to Qadi Abu Bakr, while al-Ashʿari takes the referent to be the will to show beneficence.

positions.position: Sunni authorities affirm scriptural attributes as transmitted, without asking how or resorting to figurative reinterpretation; al-Alusi cites al-Ashʿari’s al-Ibana as his final position.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (أهل السنة): Sunni authorities affirm scriptural attributes as transmitted, without asking how or resorting to figurative reinterpretation; al-Alusi cites al-Ashʿari’s al-Ibana as his final position.

positions.position: Al-Ashʿari says his creed is to adhere to scripture, the Prophet’s Sunna, reports from early Muslims, and what Ahmad ibn Hanbal taught.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (الأشعري): Al-Ashʿari says his creed is to adhere to scripture, the Prophet’s Sunna, reports from early Muslims, and what Ahmad ibn Hanbal taught.

positions.position: Al-Alusi says reports that al-Ashʿari interpreted mercy are unverified or later retracted; those claiming early Muslims endorsed such interpretation must provide clear proof.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Al-Alusi says reports that al-Ashʿari interpreted mercy are unverified or later retracted; those claiming early Muslims endorsed such interpretation must provide clear proof.

positions.position: He rejects the kingly-heart simile as an improper comparison about God, and says a softened heart does not itself benefit anyone; actual beneficence does.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): He rejects the kingly-heart simile as an improper comparison about God, and says a softened heart does not itself benefit anyone; actual beneficence does.

positions.position: Al-Alusi also rejects identifying divine mercy with will or beneficence: the proposed causal links are unproven for God, and analogy from visible causes is inappropriate.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Al-Alusi also rejects identifying divine mercy with will or beneficence: the proposed causal links are unproven for God, and analogy from visible causes is inappropriate.

positions.position: The puzzle about divine intensification concerns relations and recipients rather than an increase in God’s attribute; theologians answer differently depending on whether mercy is an essential or active attribute.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): The puzzle about divine intensification concerns relations and recipients rather than an increase in God’s attribute; theologians answer differently depending on whether mercy is an essential or active attribute.

positions.position: Rahim symbolizes Muhammad in his rank as messenger to all people, with its alif representing knowledge and divine support for his universal mission.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Rahim symbolizes Muhammad in his rank as messenger to all people, with its alif representing knowledge and divine support for his universal mission. | mentions 21:107

positions.position: Al-Sarmīnī enumerated 5,391,360 possible interpretations; al-Ālūsī says divine favor let him add roughly the square of that number, though only some possibilities occur.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Al-Sarmīnī enumerated 5,391,360 possible interpretations; al-Ālūsī says divine favor let him add roughly the square of that number, though only some possibilities occur.

positions.position: The universal reading magnifies God and teaches disavowal of independent power: carrying a straw is like carrying a mountain unless God helps.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): The universal reading magnifies God and teaches disavowal of independent power: carrying a straw is like carrying a mountain unless God helps.

positions.position: The Quran's whole discourse links Allah to all creatures, especially humans, and their return relation to Him; recitation permutations at completion, transmitted from Ali, are called hal-murtahil and signify no total break in existence.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): The Quran's whole discourse links Allah to all creatures, especially humans, and their return relation to Him; recitation permutations at completion, transmitted from Ali, are called hal-murtahil and signify no total break in existence.

positions.position: Trying to make the encompassing divine reality into a finite object of vision is impossible: imposing a bounded endpoint on it would cut off consciousness and existence rather than yield clear vision.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Trying to make the encompassing divine reality into a finite object of vision is impossible: imposing a bounded endpoint on it would cut off consciousness and existence rather than yield clear vision.

positions.position: The divine name is the highest organizing principle: without unity in existence, truth, and causality, the sciences remain fragmented and cannot establish even a partial truth.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): The divine name is the highest organizing principle: without unity in existence, truth, and causality, the sciences remain fragmented and cannot establish even a partial truth.

positions.position: The necessary existent is the first origin and ultimate cause of both knowledge and existence; nothing that acts upon or subdues a person can be conceived without God behind it.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): The necessary existent is the first origin and ultimate cause of both knowledge and existence; nothing that acts upon or subdues a person can be conceived without God behind it.

positions.position: A concise conceptual definition of Allah is the necessary existent comprising all attributes of perfection; saying only necessary existent is sufficient because that phrase implies the perfection-attributes.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): A concise conceptual definition of Allah is the necessary existent comprising all attributes of perfection; saying only necessary existent is sufficient because that phrase implies the perfection-attributes.

positions.position: By inductive reasoning proper names precede common nouns, which later arise from shared traits; therefore the claim that Allah’s name was transferred from a common noun or attribute is untenable.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): By inductive reasoning proper names precede common nouns, which later arise from shared traits; therefore the claim that Allah’s name was transferred from a common noun or attribute is untenable.

positions.position: Borrowing or derivation of Allah from another language cannot be determined; like its referent, the name remains veiled in eternity, and the most basic response to it is awe and greatness.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Borrowing or derivation of Allah from another language cannot be determined; like its referent, the name remains veiled in eternity, and the most basic response to it is awe and greatness.

positions.position: Older Turkish speakers used yarlığayıcı for mercy’s gracious result, but this remains an adjective; divine mercy itself is not an emotional inclination but the will of good or unlimited bestowal.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Older Turkish speakers used yarlığayıcı for mercy’s gracious result, but this remains an adjective; divine mercy itself is not an emotional inclination but the will of good or unlimited bestowal.

positions.position: Rahīm is a second divine attribute, best understood here as an intensive active participle meaning very merciful or much showing mercy.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Rahīm is a second divine attribute, best understood here as an intensive active participle meaning very merciful or much showing mercy.

positions.position: Rahman is a divine attribute exclusive to God whose relation is not a particular act; its primordial grace extends universally without condition.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Rahman is a divine attribute exclusive to God whose relation is not a particular act; its primordial grace extends universally without condition.

positions.position: God's wisdom requires that He display His own will and create creatures who possess will, rather than make all action compulsory.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): God's wisdom requires that He display His own will and create creatures who possess will, rather than make all action compulsory.

positions.position: The bayaniyya analysis treats the genitive inflection as distributed over three words to stress the divine proper name, a necessary inflection rather than ordinary narration grammar.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): The bayaniyya analysis treats the genitive inflection as distributed over three words to stress the divine proper name, a necessary inflection rather than ordinary narration grammar.

positions.position: The basmala's interpretive pivot is ba, which connects Allah's name, the first source and ultimate object of existence and progress, to the intended act.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): The basmala's interpretive pivot is ba, which connects Allah's name, the first source and ultimate object of existence and progress, to the intended act.

positions.position: Human acts are not their own complete cause: will is a moment in the stream of existence, and success depends on the outpouring between the First Cause and human will, first Rahmani and finally Rahimi.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Human acts are not their own complete cause: will is a moment in the stream of existence, and success depends on the outpouring between the First Cause and human will, first Rahmani and finally Rahimi.

positions.position: Because God is the true existent from whom every existence and beginning derives, every beginning, movement, and direction should start in His name.
positions.reasons: QUTB-ZILAL (author): Because God is the true existent from whom every existence and beginning derives, every beginning, movement, and direction should start in His name.

positions.position: A rajaz line by Abū Khālid al-Qanānī uses suman for name; Ibn Yaʿīsh doubts it proves the form, while ʿAbd al-Ḥakīm appeals to its written ya.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (أبو خالد القناني): A rajaz line by Abū Khālid al-Qanānī uses suman for name; Ibn Yaʿīsh doubts it proves the form, while ʿAbd al-Ḥakīm appeals to its written ya.

positions.position: In sacrifices and actions seeking blessing or aid, scripture uses the name of God and in the name of your Lord; the name accompanies the deed, while by God would imply appeal to divine power.
