positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): In sacrifices and actions seeking blessing or aid, scripture uses the name of God and in the name of your Lord; the name accompanies the deed, while by God would imply appeal to divine power. | mentions 6:118, 6:119, 96:1

positions.position: God’s name functions like a tribe’s identifying brand or an army’s recognized slogan, signaling affiliation with the one Lord.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): God’s name functions like a tribe’s identifying brand or an army’s recognized slogan, signaling affiliation with the one Lord.

positions.position: When requesting enablement or help, the verb may instead be attached to God's essential name as Creator; the basmala means that the recitation accompanies the blessing of His blessed name.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR-FULL (author): When requesting enablement or help, the verb may instead be attached to God's essential name as Creator; the basmala means that the recitation accompanies the blessing of His blessed name. | mentions 76:26

positions.position: The Basmala was probably prefixed to all suras from the middle Meccan period onward, retrospectively including suras already proclaimed.
positions.reasons: CORPUSCORANICUM (author): The Basmala was probably prefixed to all suras from the middle Meccan period onward, retrospectively including suras already proclaimed.

positions.position: The Basmala’s merciful divine attribute reflects the emotional dimension of divine and exemplary human conduct newly foregrounded in middle Meccan theology.
positions.reasons: CORPUSCORANICUM (author): The Basmala’s merciful divine attribute reflects the emotional dimension of divine and exemplary human conduct newly foregrounded in middle Meccan theology.

positions.position: Its use resembles the Christian Trinitarian formula placed before public and official messages, reformulated here as a statement about one God.
positions.reasons: CORPUSCORANICUM (author): Its use resembles the Christian Trinitarian formula placed before public and official messages, reformulated here as a statement about one God.

positions.position: Rahim means abundant mercy and may describe humans; for God it especially denotes limitless mercy, grace, and compassion creatures will merit in the future, of which protecting and forgiving are only facets.
positions.reasons: KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): Rahim means abundant mercy and may describe humans; for God it especially denotes limitless mercy, grace, and compassion creatures will merit in the future, of which protecting and forgiving are only facets.

positions.position: The Prophet says an important matter not begun in God’s Name will be cut off.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (Prophet Muhammad): The Prophet says an important matter not begun in God’s Name will be cut off.

positions.position: Another interpretation makes God’s opening in His Name an invitation for people to begin, unite, and commence through His Name as well.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (author): Another interpretation makes God’s opening in His Name an invitation for people to begin, unite, and commence through His Name as well.

positions.position: The Quran shows pre-Islamic Arabs knew the name Allāh as creator, although most idol worshippers denied His supreme sovereignty in the Age of Ignorance.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (author): The Quran shows pre-Islamic Arabs knew the name Allāh as creator, although most idol worshippers denied His supreme sovereignty in the Age of Ignorance. | mentions 43:87, 29:61, 29:63, 31:25, 39:38, 3:154, 5:50, 33:33, 48:26

question: Can God be a body or occupy a place?

positions.position: Ali reports the Prophet said al-Fatiha descended from a treasure beneath the Throne.
positions.reasons: DURR (النبي): Ali reports the Prophet said al-Fatiha descended from a treasure beneath the Throne. DURR (علي): Ali says al-Fatiha descended at Mecca from a treasure beneath the Throne.

positions.position: A name referring to a part of a referent's essence is impossible for God: every composite depends on other parts and is therefore contingent.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A name referring to a part of a referent's essence is impossible for God: every composite depends on other parts and is therefore contingent.

positions.position: Abū Hurayra reports a divine saying: God is with the servant who remembers Him, remembers the servant in return, and responds more generously to the servant's approach.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أبو هريرة): Abū Hurayra reports a divine saying: God is with the servant who remembers Him, remembers the servant in return, and responds more generously to the servant's approach.

positions.position: Abū Ṣāliḥ reports from Abū Hurayra a divine saying that God wrote above the Throne that His mercy overcomes His anger.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أبو صالح): Abū Ṣāliḥ reports from Abū Hurayra a divine saying that God wrote above the Throne that His mercy overcomes His anger.

positions.position: Abū Dharr reports a divine saying: God forbade injustice upon Himself and made it forbidden among people, commanding them not to wrong one another.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أبو ذر): Abū Dharr reports a divine saying: God forbade injustice upon Himself and made it forbidden among people, commanding them not to wrong one another.

positions.position: The divine term person does not mean a body with volume and individuation; it means a particular essence and determinate self.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The divine term person does not mean a body with volume and individuation; it means a particular essence and determinate self.

positions.position: God cannot literally be this light or a member of its kind: light is either a created body or an accident in a created body.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): God cannot literally be this light or a member of its kind: light is either a created body or an accident in a created body.

positions.position: He treats God as Light of the heavens and earth as an ambiguous verse whose interpretation is governed by rational proofs that God is not literally light.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): He treats God as Light of the heavens and earth as an ambiguous verse whose interpretation is governed by rational proofs that God is not literally light. | mentions 24:35

positions.position: A reading that says God owns the light of the heavens and earth removes the apparent difficulty of calling Him light.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A reading that says God owns the light of the heavens and earth removes the apparent difficulty of calling Him light. | mentions 24:35

positions.position: Divine self (nafs) means the thing's essence and identity, not a composite body: every body is composed, possible, and originated, which is impossible of God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Divine self (nafs) means the thing's essence and identity, not a composite body: every body is composed, possible, and originated, which is impossible of God.

positions.position: Haritha describes detachment, worship, and seeming to see the Throne, Paradise, and Hell; the Prophet tells him he has recognized faith, urges him to persist, and Haritha later dies a martyr.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النبي): Haritha describes detachment, worship, and seeming to see the Throne, Paradise, and Hell; the Prophet tells him he has recognized faith, urges him to persist, and Haritha later dies a martyr.

positions.position: Most Karramiyya call God a body but define this as a self-subsisting existent independent of a substrate, not as a composite of limbs; other groups reject the name.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الكرامية): Most Karramiyya call God a body but define this as a self-subsisting existent independent of a substrate, not as a composite of limbs; other groups reject the name.

positions.position: Razi denies that Karramiyya mean something other than length, breadth, and depth: their claim that God is above and greater than the Throne entails a spatially extended body.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi denies that Karramiyya mean something other than length, breadth, and depth: their claim that God is above and greater than the Throne entails a spatially extended body.

positions.position: The word body suggests a false meaning and is absent from Quran and hadith, so it should be avoided; theologians say it entails multiplicity of parts.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The word body suggests a false meaning and is absent from Quran and hadith, so it should be avoided; theologians say it entails multiplicity of parts.

positions.position: They say a God composed of essence and attributes would be divided and composite, hence possible rather than necessary.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (المعتزلة والفلاسفة): They say a God composed of essence and attributes would be divided and composite, hence possible rather than necessary.

positions.position: They argue eternal essence and eternal attributes would share eternity but differ in their specific natures, making each a composite of parts and generating an impossible infinite regress.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (المعتزلة والفلاسفة): They argue eternal essence and eternal attributes would share eternity but differ in their specific natures, making each a composite of parts and generating an impossible infinite regress.

positions.position: They argue an eternally receptive essence would have to be capable of receiving originated events in eternity, which they deem impossible.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (المعتزلة والفلاسفة): They argue an eternally receptive essence would have to be capable of receiving originated events in eternity, which they deem impossible.

positions.position: God feeds but is not fed and protects others while none can overrule Him.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): God feeds but is not fed and protects others while none can overrule Him. | mentions 6:14, 23:88

positions.position: Wahid means none shares God's unique essence or rivals Him in ordering the world and the affairs of the Throne.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Wahid means none shares God's unique essence or rivals Him in ordering the world and the affairs of the Throne.

positions.position: Ghani means free of needs and necessities.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Ghani means free of needs and necessities.

positions.position: God is not a substance, body, in a place or space, or an indwelling subject or substrate; He is unlike other essences by His own specific essence.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): God is not a substance, body, in a place or space, or an indwelling subject or substrate; He is unlike other essences by His own specific essence.

positions.position: The anthropomorphists argue that every existent is either spatially extended or inheres in something extended; what is neither, they say, is sheer nonexistence.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أهل التشبيه): The anthropomorphists argue that every existent is either spatially extended or inheres in something extended; what is neither, they say, is sheer nonexistence.

positions.position: Some who place God in space say He sits above the Throne.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أهل التشبيه): Some who place God in space say He sits above the Throne.

positions.position: Others among them say God is separated from the Throne by a finite distance.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أهل التشبيه): Others among them say God is separated from the Throne by a finite distance.

positions.position: A further group says God is separated from the Throne by an infinite distance.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أهل التشبيه): A further group says God is separated from the Throne by an infinite distance.

positions.position: They interpret divine exaltedness as God's purity from defects and needs.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أهل التنزيه والتقديس): They interpret divine exaltedness as God's purity from defects and needs.

positions.position: Razi summarizes that anthropomorphists treat great and greatest as names of the essence, while transcendence theologians treat them as attribute names.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi summarizes that anthropomorphists treat great and greatest as names of the essence, while transcendence theologians treat them as attribute names.

positions.position: Both camps count al-ʿAlī among the attribute names, but anthropomorphists mean spatial height and theologians of unity mean freedom from what is unbefitting to divinity.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Both camps count al-ʿAlī among the attribute names, but anthropomorphists mean spatial height and theologians of unity mean freedom from what is unbefitting to divinity.

positions.position: The theologians of transcendence argue that anything spatial is divisible and needy, and anything inhering in it is even more dependent; the Necessary Existent can be neither.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أهل التوحيد والتقديس): The theologians of transcendence argue that anything spatial is divisible and needy, and anything inhering in it is even more dependent; the Necessary Existent can be neither.

positions.position: Anthropomorphists read “great” as bodily size greater than the Throne and everything beneath it.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أهل التشبيه): Anthropomorphists read “great” as bodily size greater than the Throne and everything beneath it.

positions.position: Although the Qur'an uses “great” and “greatest” in parallel ways, Razi says earlier evidence suggests a distinction and seeks to resolve the tension.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Although the Qur'an uses “great” and “greatest” in parallel ways, Razi says earlier evidence suggests a distinction and seeks to resolve the tension. | mentions 2:255, 34:32

positions.position: Razi proposes that greatness is intrinsic whether or not anyone recognizes it, whereas magnificence means being regarded as great and is therefore accidental.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi proposes that greatness is intrinsic whether or not anyone recognizes it, whereas magnificence means being regarded as great and is therefore accidental.

positions.position: Those who place God in a location interpret His exaltedness as being above in space; some say He sits on the Throne, others posit a finite or infinite distance.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أهل التشبيه): Those who place God in a location interpret His exaltedness as being above in space; some say He sits on the Throne, others posit a finite or infinite distance.

positions.position: The pronoun “He” marks the speaker's distance from God through created defects and contingency, not through place; all contingent beings are absent from divine perfection.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The pronoun “He” marks the speaker's distance from God through created defects and contingency, not through place; all contingent beings are absent from divine perfection.

positions.position: Divine exaltedness cannot be spatial: a place-based elevation would belong essentially to the place and only incidentally to its occupant, making the place nobler than God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Divine exaltedness cannot be spatial: a place-based elevation would belong essentially to the place and only incidentally to its occupant, making the place nobler than God.

positions.position: The letter sīn is linked to God’s name al-Samīʿ, who hears every creature’s prayer from the Throne to beneath the earth.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The letter sīn is linked to God’s name al-Samīʿ, who hears every creature’s prayer from the Throne to beneath the earth.

positions.position: The mīm is associated with God’s dominion extending from the Throne to everything beneath the earth.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The mīm is associated with God’s dominion extending from the Throne to everything beneath the earth.

positions.position: God is neither body nor substance: these are negative concepts, whereas His unique essence is positive and real.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): God is neither body nor substance: these are negative concepts, whereas His unique essence is positive and real.

positions.position: A divine report calls the Fatiha a treasure from the treasures of God’s Throne, explaining its name Sura of the Treasure.
positions.reasons: NASAFI (الله تعالى): A divine report calls the Fatiha a treasure from the treasures of God’s Throne, explaining its name Sura of the Treasure.

positions.position: A Prophetic report calls the Fatiha a healing for every illness except al-sam; this grounds its names al-Shifa and al-Shafiya.
positions.reasons: NASAFI (النبي عليه السلام): A Prophetic report calls the Fatiha a healing for every illness except al-sam; this grounds its names al-Shifa and al-Shafiya.

positions.position: Anas reports God gave the Prophet al-Fatiha from the treasures of the Throne and divided it between them.
positions.reasons: DURR (النبي): Anas reports God gave the Prophet al-Fatiha from the treasures of the Throne and divided it between them.

positions.position: Al-Baqara came from earlier revelation, al-Fatiha and its closing verses from beneath the Throne, and the Mufassal as a gift.
positions.reasons: DURR (النبي): Al-Baqara came from earlier revelation, al-Fatiha and its closing verses from beneath the Throne, and the Mufassal as a gift. | mentions 2:285, 2:286

positions.position: Imran says al-Fatiha and the Throne Verse protect a household that day from the evil eye of humans and jinn.
positions.reasons: DURR (عمران بن حصين): Imran says al-Fatiha and the Throne Verse protect a household that day from the evil eye of humans and jinn. | mentions 2:255

question: What does inward remembrance of ٱللَّهِ involve?

positions.position: An unnamed authority in Arabic usage reads Lubayd’s “then the name of peace be upon you” as simply “then peace be upon you”; al-Ṭabarī rejects that reading as linguistically unsound.
positions.reasons: TAB (مقدم في العلم بلغة العرب): An unnamed authority in Arabic usage reads Lubayd’s “then the name of peace be upon you” as simply “then peace be upon you”; al-Ṭabarī rejects that reading as linguistically unsound.

positions.position: If “name” could simply mean its referent, Arabic would also permit “I ate the name of honey”; the unanimous rejection of such usage undermines that reading of Lubayd.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): If “name” could simply mean its referent, Arabic would also permit “I ate the name of honey”; the unanimous rejection of such usage undermines that reading of Lubayd.

positions.position: Al-Ṭabarī’s likelier reading of Lubayd is an exhortation to keep God’s name and remembrance after a delayed exhortative word, while leaving off remembering and grieving for the dead.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): Al-Ṭabarī’s likelier reading of Lubayd is an exhortation to keep God’s name and remembrance after a delayed exhortative word, while leaving off remembering and grieving for the dead.

positions.position: A second possible reading of Lubayd invokes God’s name for protection over the two people.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): A second possible reading of Lubayd invokes God’s name for protection over the two people.

positions.position: To support the delayed exhortation reading, al-Ṭabarī cites Arabic word order that places the thing urged before the delayed “take it” command.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): To support the delayed exhortation reading, al-Ṭabarī cites Arabic word order that places the thing urged before the delayed “take it” command.

positions.position: Ṭabarī rejects taking Labīd’s “name of peace” simply as “peace”; that reading would license impossible Arabic such as eating the name of honey.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): Ṭabarī rejects taking Labīd’s “name of peace” simply as “peace”; that reading would license impossible Arabic such as eating the name of honey.

positions.position: Of the two defensible readings of Labīd, the first—taking al-Salām as God’s name and an exhortation to keep His remembrance—is more apt.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): Of the two defensible readings of Labīd, the first—taking al-Salām as God’s name and an exhortation to keep His remembrance—is more apt.

positions.position: Abū ʿAmr explains Allah as the one whose essential greatness leaves minds bewildered.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (أبي عمرو بن العلاء): Abū ʿAmr explains Allah as the one whose essential greatness leaves minds bewildered.

positions.position: Al-Mubarrad explains Allah as the one whose remembrance creatures find repose in.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (المبرد): Al-Mubarrad explains Allah as the one whose remembrance creatures find repose in.

positions.position: Recognizing that sensible things are finite and eventually perish helps a person remain safe from harm and reach good outcomes.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Recognizing that sensible things are finite and eventually perish helps a person remain safe from harm and reach good outcomes.

positions.position: The human soul begins ignorant, as stated in the Qur’an, and can develop through its sensory, moving, perceptive, and rational powers.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The human soul begins ignorant, as stated in the Qur’an, and can develop through its sensory, moving, perceptive, and rational powers. | mentions 16:78

positions.position: One view says an oath by saying 'بله' does not take effect because that form means moisture.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (بعضهم): One view says an oath by saying 'بله' does not take effect because that form means moisture.

positions.position: Another view says an oath by 'بله' takes effect because the form is linguistically possible and the speaker intended an oath.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (آخرون): Another view says an oath by 'بله' takes effect because the form is linguistically possible and the speaker intended an oath.

positions.position: He leaves open whether invoking this form over a slaughter makes it lawful and whether saying 'Allah' this way in the prayer formula 'God is greatest' validates prayer.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): He leaves open whether invoking this form over a slaughter makes it lawful and whether saying 'Allah' this way in the prayer formula 'God is greatest' validates prayer.

positions.position: Al-Suhaylī reads “glorify the name of your Lord” as an insertion directing people to glorify the Lord and ensuring remembrance includes spoken utterance as well as inward recollection.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (السهيلي): Al-Suhaylī reads “glorify the name of your Lord” as an insertion directing people to glorify the Lord and ensuring remembrance includes spoken utterance as well as inward recollection. | mentions 87:1

positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (السهيلي): Al-Suhaylī compares this ellipsis with “God is greatest,” whose unstated completion lets the wording match the heart's intended exclusivity.

positions.reasons: MAWARDI (قوم): Some claim names of entities are the entities themselves and the spoken form is merely naming; al-Mawardi rejects this, since it would also make names of actions identical to the actions, which is untenable.

positions.position: A blessing is called mercy because it arises from mercy.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (author): A blessing is called mercy because it arises from mercy.

positions.position: One view derives both names from a single mercy, with al-Rahman as the more intensive form.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (unattributed): One view derives both names from a single mercy, with al-Rahman as the more intensive form.

positions.position: Another view derives the names from two distinct mercies so the names and attributes differ.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (unattributed): Another view derives the names from two distinct mercies so the names and attributes differ.

positions.position: Some derive the divine name from bewilderment: hearts are bewildered when contemplating God's greatness.

positions.position: Most scholars derive al-Raḥmān from mercy as an intensive form, meaning the possessor of unmatched mercy; faʿlān marks intensity.

positions.position: Al-Rahman means God's aid and victory.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (ابن عطاء): Al-Rahman means God's aid and victory.

positions.position: Thalab says al-Rahman is a Hebraicized non-Arabic word; Quraysh’s reported failure to recognize it in 25:60 is his evidence, as is Jarir’s verse mentioning Rahman as an offering.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (ثعلب): Thalab says al-Rahman is a Hebraicized non-Arabic word; Quraysh’s reported failure to recognize it in 25:60 is his evidence, as is Jarir’s verse mentioning Rahman as an offering. | mentions 25:60

positions.position: His poem is cited as evidence that al-Rahman is used in Arabic speech and poetry.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI-FULL (الشنفرى): His poem is cited as evidence that al-Rahman is used in Arabic speech and poetry.

positions.position: His verse is cited as linguistic evidence for al-Rahman as an established name.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI-FULL (جرير): His verse is cited as linguistic evidence for al-Rahman as an established name.

positions.position: Rahman is among dominant adjectival names that became proper names, like al-Dubaran and al-Ayyuq; Allah too is a dominant name.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF (author): Rahman is among dominant adjectival names that became proper names, like al-Dubaran and al-Ayyuq; Allah too is a dominant name.

positions.position: Al-Zamakhshari declines Rahman without tanwin, by analogy with ghadban, gharthan, and sakran.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF (author): Al-Zamakhshari declines Rahman without tanwin, by analogy with ghadban, gharthan, and sakran.

positions.position: Al-A'sha's use of kaf is cited as an example of a particle that can function as a noun, motivating a distinctive genitive mark for bi-.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (author): Al-A'sha's use of kaf is cited as an example of a particle that can function as a noun, motivating a distinctive genitive mark for bi-.

positions.position: Another account derives the word from walah, bewilderment: intellects are bewildered by the realities of God's attributes and by thought about knowing Him.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (قيل): Another account derives the word from walah, bewilderment: intellects are bewildered by the realities of God's attributes and by thought about knowing Him.

positions.position: Ibn Atiyya rejects that lexical claim: the Arabs objected to identifying the deity they were ordered to worship, not to the word al-Rahman itself.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (author): Ibn Atiyya rejects that lexical claim: the Arabs objected to identifying the deity they were ordered to worship, not to the word al-Rahman itself. | mentions 25:60

positions.position: The author says the Arabs' question showed ignorance of which deity was intended, not ignorance of the word Rahman itself.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): The author says the Arabs' question showed ignorance of which deity was intended, not ignorance of the word Rahman itself.

positions.position: Thaʿlab claims Rahman is non-Arabic, citing the Quraysh denial of the name in the Qur'an as evidence.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (تغلب): Thaʿlab claims Rahman is non-Arabic, citing the Quraysh denial of the name in the Qur'an as evidence. | mentions 25:60

positions.position: Al-Khaṭṭābī says al-Raḥmān's encompassing mercy covers creatures' provisions and interests and includes believers and unbelievers.
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD (الخطابي): Al-Khaṭṭābī says al-Raḥmān's encompassing mercy covers creatures' provisions and interests and includes believers and unbelievers.

positions.position: A tale says Zayd ibn Ḥāritha called on al-Raḥmān when a hypocrite bound him to kill him; successive warnings culminated in Gabriel freeing Zayd and killing the attacker.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A tale says Zayd ibn Ḥāritha called on al-Raḥmān when a hypocrite bound him to kill him; successive warnings culminated in Gabriel freeing Zayd and killing the attacker.

positions.position: All agree that al-Raḥmān is not read with imāla; grammarians differ on permissibility, with one view, perhaps Sībawayh's, allowing it because nūn is kasra-marked after the alif.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النحويون): All agree that al-Raḥmān is not read with imāla; grammarians differ on permissibility, with one view, perhaps Sībawayh's, allowing it because nūn is kasra-marked after the alif.

positions.position: The grammarians' more evident view disallows imāla of al-Raḥmān.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النحويون): The grammarians' more evident view disallows imāla of al-Raḥmān.

positions.position: Ibn al-Ḥaṣṣār counters that 13:30 explicitly says the disbelievers rejected al-Raḥmān.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (ابن الحصار): Ibn al-Ḥaṣṣār counters that 13:30 explicitly says the disbelievers rejected al-Raḥmān. | mentions 13:30

positions.position: Whether rahman declines depends on the proposed condition for non-declension: those requiring absence of fa‘lanah leave it indeclinable, while those requiring an existing fa‘la decline it; Nasafi prefers the first analysis.
positions.reasons: NASAFI (author): Whether rahman declines depends on the proposed condition for non-declension: those requiring absence of fa‘lanah leave it indeclinable, while those requiring an existing fa‘la decline it; Nasafi prefers the first analysis.

positions.position: The debate whether a name is identical to or distinct from its referent has a long scholarly history, with al-Ghazālī, Ibn al-Sayyid, and al-Suhaylī discussing both proofs.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): The debate whether a name is identical to or distinct from its referent has a long scholarly history, with al-Ghazālī, Ibn al-Sayyid, and al-Suhaylī discussing both proofs.

positions.position: Al-Suhaylī interprets glorifying the Lord's name as glorifying the Lord while also ensuring that remembrance includes spoken words as well as the heart.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (السهيلي): Al-Suhaylī interprets glorifying the Lord's name as glorifying the Lord while also ensuring that remembrance includes spoken words as well as the heart. | mentions 67:1, 87:1

positions.position: Al-Aʿlam treats raḥmān as a proper name, not an adjective, and parses it as apposition because a proper name cannot be an epithet.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الأعلم): Al-Aʿlam treats raḥmān as a proper name, not an adjective, and parses it as apposition because a proper name cannot be an epithet. | mentions 20:5, 55:1

positions.position: Al-Suhaylī rejects both apposition and explanatory apposition for raḥmān because Allah's name is already the clearest and most familiar of names.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (السهيلي): Al-Suhaylī rejects both apposition and explanatory apposition for raḥmān because Allah's name is already the clearest and most familiar of names.

positions.position: Al-Suhayli rejects the appositive analysis because Allah needs no clarification; Arabs ask what al-Rahman is but never what Allah is.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (السهيلي): Al-Suhayli rejects the appositive analysis because Allah needs no clarification; Arabs ask what al-Rahman is but never what Allah is. | mentions 25:60

positions.position: The author invokes the report that God has stored ninety-nine mercies for the Day of Resurrection to support Rahman's stronger intensity.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): The author invokes the report that God has stored ninety-nine mercies for the Day of Resurrection to support Rahman's stronger intensity.

positions.position: Al-Qurtubi says Arabs denied the name Rahman through ignorance of God and what is due to Him.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (القرطبي): Al-Qurtubi says Arabs denied the name Rahman through ignorance of God and what is due to Him.

positions.position: Quraysh's denial of Rahman at Hudaybiyya and in 25:60 was stubbornness: pre-Islamic poems already used Rahman for God.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): Quraysh's denial of Rahman at Hudaybiyya and in 25:60 was stubbornness: pre-Islamic poems already used Rahman for God. | mentions 25:60

positions.position: Al-Ḥarālī says the initial bāʾ manifests God's wisdom in causation, while ism makes what is hidden or obscure apparent to hearts through hearing and articulated individual forms.
positions.reasons: BIQAI (أبو الحسن الحرالي): Al-Ḥarālī says the initial bāʾ manifests God's wisdom in causation, while ism makes what is hidden or obscure apparent to hearts through hearing and articulated individual forms.

positions.position: For al-Ḥarālī, al-Raḥmān denotes mercy encompassing all that divine lordship covers.
positions.reasons: BIQAI (أبو الحسن الحرالي): For al-Ḥarālī, al-Raḥmān denotes mercy encompassing all that divine lordship covers.

positions.position: God deserves both attributes essentially; their repetition stresses their fitness for lordship and sovereignty and that mercy outweighs anger. All beautiful attributes follow, since encompassing mercy excludes deficiency; Biqāʿī promises further explanation at 3:8.
positions.reasons: BIQAI (author): God deserves both attributes essentially; their repetition stresses their fitness for lordship and sovereignty and that mercy outweighs anger. All beautiful attributes follow, since encompassing mercy excludes deficiency; Biqāʿī promises further explanation at 3:8. | mentions 3:8

positions.position: In a weak report, Abu Bakr taught Aisha a supplication against debt and distress invoking the Merciful of both worlds.
positions.reasons: DURR (أبو بكر): In a weak report, Abu Bakr taught Aisha a supplication against debt and distress invoking the Merciful of both worlds.

positions.position: Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit says the Prophet taught a supplication asking the Merciful of both worlds for relief and sufficiency from others.
positions.reasons: DURR (عبد الرحمن بن سابط): Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit says the Prophet taught a supplication asking the Merciful of both worlds for relief and sufficiency from others.

positions.position: In a weak report, Aisha's father taught her a prophetic supplication asking the Merciful of this world and the next to relieve grief and need.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (عائشة): In a weak report, Aisha's father taught her a prophetic supplication asking the Merciful of this world and the next to relieve grief and need.

positions.position: Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit says the Prophet taught a supplication seeking relief, response to the distressed, and mercy that makes one independent of others.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (عبد الرحمن بن سابط): Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit says the Prophet taught a supplication seeking relief, response to the distressed, and mercy that makes one independent of others.

positions.position: A report from Anas attributes to the Prophet an instruction to extend the writing of al-Rahman.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (أنس): A report from Anas attributes to the Prophet an instruction to extend the writing of al-Rahman.

positions.position: Al-Aʿlam and Ibn Malik say Rahman was originally a proper name, not an adjective or a name formed merely through prevailing usage.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (الأعلم وابن مالك): Al-Aʿlam and Ibn Malik say Rahman was originally a proper name, not an adjective or a name formed merely through prevailing usage.

positions.position: Al-Alusi argues that the alleged vowel shift need not be preceded by making the verb intransitive, since the shift itself makes it so.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Al-Alusi argues that the alleged vowel shift need not be preceded by making the verb intransitive, since the shift itself makes it so.

positions.position: Human mercy as tenderness does not force figurative interpretation when mercy is attributed to God; divine attributes are real in a manner befitting God, beyond creaturely comparison.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Human mercy as tenderness does not force figurative interpretation when mercy is attributed to God; divine attributes are real in a manner befitting God, beyond creaturely comparison.

positions.position: Al-Sukuti calls interpreting mercy as metaphor a Muʿtazilite tendency and says early Sunni authorities affirmed the revealed attribute without recasting it.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (السكوتي): Al-Sukuti calls interpreting mercy as metaphor a Muʿtazilite tendency and says early Sunni authorities affirmed the revealed attribute without recasting it.

positions.position: Al-Alusi says one cannot treat mercy as metaphor while affirming life, knowledge, will, power, speech, hearing, and sight literally on no principled distinction.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Al-Alusi says one cannot treat mercy as metaphor while affirming life, knowledge, will, power, speech, hearing, and sight literally on no principled distinction.

positions.position: Al-Alusi says Arabs’ question about Rahman reflected fear that they were being directed to another deity like themselves, not evidence that the word was non-Arabic.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Al-Alusi says Arabs’ question about Rahman reflected fear that they were being directed to another deity like themselves, not evidence that the word was non-Arabic. | mentions 25:60

positions.position: Rahmān can be explained as very merciful but cannot be translated as a proper divine name; esirgeyici wrongly suggests withholding or jealousy, while acıyıcı lacks the positive sense of mercy.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Rahmān can be explained as very merciful but cannot be translated as a proper divine name; esirgeyici wrongly suggests withholding or jealousy, while acıyıcı lacks the positive sense of mercy.

positions.position: Rahmān also cannot be translated as bağışlayıcı, since that confuses it with names such as Vehhāb or ʿAfūvv, which are not exclusive to God.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Rahmān also cannot be translated as bağışlayıcı, since that confuses it with names such as Vehhāb or ʿAfūvv, which are not exclusive to God.

positions.position: Every creature's original gifts and existence arise from Rahman's grace, received without anyone's earned choice.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Every creature's original gifts and existence arise from Rahman's grace, received without anyone's earned choice.

positions.position: All realms and beings, from obedient and believing to rebellious and idolatrous, are immersed in Rahman's mercy and freed from fear in that respect.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): All realms and beings, from obedient and believing to rebellious and idolatrous, are immersed in Rahman's mercy and freed from fear in that respect.

positions.position: Rahman is the instinctive grace seen in mother birds beating their wings over their young.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Rahman is the instinctive grace seen in mother birds beating their wings over their young.

positions.position: Gods mercy called Rahman reaches believers and disbelievers and supplies what they need for existence and life.
positions.reasons: TABATABAI (author): Gods mercy called Rahman reaches believers and disbelievers and supplies what they need for existence and life.

positions.position: Al-Raḥmān marks a middle Meccan usage that replaced the previously frequent rabb/rabbuka in a named group of suras.
positions.reasons: CORPUSCORANICUM (author): Al-Raḥmān marks a middle Meccan usage that replaced the previously frequent rabb/rabbuka in a named group of suras.

positions.position: Ammann reads the introduction of al-Raḥmān as softening frequent earlier threats of hell and emphasizing assurance of salvation.
positions.reasons: CORPUSCORANICUM (Ludwig Ammann): Ammann reads the introduction of al-Raḥmān as softening frequent earlier threats of hell and emphasizing assurance of salvation.

positions.position: Here al-Raḥmān joins Allāh, a divine name used only occasionally earlier and common from late Meccan times.
positions.reasons: CORPUSCORANICUM (author): Here al-Raḥmān joins Allāh, a divine name used only occasionally earlier and common from late Meccan times. | mentions 1:1

question: To whom and when does ٱلرَّحْمَٰنِ show mercy?

positions.position: Al-Rahman's mercy lets seekers detach from everything below Him; its worldly bounty reaches friend and enemy alike.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (author): Al-Rahman's mercy lets seekers detach from everything below Him; its worldly bounty reaches friend and enemy alike.

positions.position: Though rhetoric might progress from lesser to greater, al-Raḥmān comes first because worldly mercy precedes the afterlife.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (author): Though rhetoric might progress from lesser to greater, al-Raḥmān comes first because worldly mercy precedes the afterlife.

positions.position: Rahman's first mercy brings everyone into existence and sustains them regardless of effort.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Rahman's first mercy brings everyone into existence and sustains them regardless of effort.

positions.position: Rahman gives absolute hope and prevents universal despair; without it humans would lack existence and essential natural gifts.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Rahman gives absolute hope and prevents universal despair; without it humans would lack existence and essential natural gifts.

question: Was ٱلرَّحْمَٰنِ known to Arabs, and what is its origin?

positions.position: Pre-Islamic Arabs called God al-Rahman, but Musaylima the Liar later took the divine name for himself.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (author): Pre-Islamic Arabs called God al-Rahman, but Musaylima the Liar later took the divine name for himself. MAWARDI-FULL (author): Pre-Islamic Arabs called God al-Rahman, and Musaylima later appropriated that divine name for himself.

positions.position: Pre-Islamic verses by an unnamed poet and Salāma ibn Jandal use “al-Raḥmān,” demonstrating that the name was known among Arabs.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): Pre-Islamic verses by an unnamed poet and Salāma ibn Jandal use “al-Raḥmān,” demonstrating that the name was known among Arabs.

positions.position: He regards al-Rahman as a foreignized Hebrew word, not Arabic, since eloquent Quraysh did not know it until it was explained to them in 25:60.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI-FULL (ثعلب): He regards al-Rahman as a foreignized Hebrew word, not Arabic, since eloquent Quraysh did not know it until it was explained to them in 25:60. | mentions 25:60

positions.position: Banu Hanifa called Musaylima Rahman of Yamama and their poet called him Rahman; al-Zamakhshari condemns this as unbelief.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF (بنو حنيفة وشاعرهم): Banu Hanifa called Musaylima Rahman of Yamama and their poet called him Rahman; al-Zamakhshari condemns this as unbelief.

positions.position: Calling Musaylima Rahman of Yamama, including in his poet's praise, is presented as a facet of the Banu Hanifa's unbelieving perversity.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL (author): Calling Musaylima Rahman of Yamama, including in his poet's praise, is presented as a facet of the Banu Hanifa's unbelieving perversity.

positions.position: The author rejects Thaʿlab's claim that Rahman is foreign because Arabic poetry attests the word.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (author): The author rejects Thaʿlab's claim that Rahman is foreign because Arabic poetry attests the word.

positions.position: A hostile poet applied “Rahman” to Musaylima as a taunt in unbelief, not as a genuine divine description.
positions.reasons: NASAFI-FULL (author): A hostile poet applied “Rahman” to Musaylima as a taunt in unbelief, not as a genuine divine description.

positions.position: Thaʿlab reports the unusual claim that raḥmān is foreign, with its khāʾ adapted to Arabic ḥāʾ.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (ثعلب): Thaʿlab reports the unusual claim that raḥmān is foreign, with its khāʾ adapted to Arabic ḥāʾ.

positions.position: Thaʿlab gives a rare view that raḥmān is a foreign word with khāʾ, Arabized with ḥāʾ.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (ثعلب): Thaʿlab gives a rare view that raḥmān is a foreign word with khāʾ, Arabized with ḥāʾ.

positions.position: The poet's use of Rahman for Musaylima is dismissed as obstinate excess; the name normally occurs with the article or in annexation.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): The poet's use of Rahman for Musaylima is dismissed as obstinate excess; the name normally occurs with the article or in annexation.

positions.position: Tha'lab and al-Mubarrad transmit an unusual claim that the word is non-Arabic and pronounced with khā', citing a poem with rakhman.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (ثعلب والمبرد): Tha'lab and al-Mubarrad transmit an unusual claim that the word is non-Arabic and pronounced with khā', citing a poem with rakhman.

positions.position: Salama ibn Jundub's pre-Islamic verse calls God Rahman, showing the name was already known among Arabs.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (سلامة بن جندب): Salama ibn Jundub's pre-Islamic verse calls God Rahman, showing the name was already known among Arabs.

positions.position: The question whether Rahman is Arabic is longstanding; al-Alusi begins to explain the Arabs’ response by their fear of multiple gods rather than foreign origin.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): The question whether Rahman is Arabic is longstanding; al-Alusi begins to explain the Arabs’ response by their fear of multiple gods rather than foreign origin.

question: Is ٱلرَّحْمَٰنِ reserved for God?

positions.position: Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī calls al-Raḥmān a forbidden name for others; Ṭabarī says the community’s consensus already establishes the prohibition.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (الحسن البصري): Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī calls al-Raḥmān a forbidden name for others; Ṭabarī says the community’s consensus already establishes the prohibition.

positions.position: All enduring graces for believers issue through al-Rahman, and no creature can bear that name because creatures cannot give what lasts.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (author): All enduring graces for believers issue through al-Rahman, and no creature can bear that name because creatures cannot give what lasts.

positions.position: A flattering poet once called Musaylima rahmāna without the article, but the author says this was wrong even linguistically and all the more so religiously.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): A flattering poet once called Musaylima rahmāna without the article, but the author says this was wrong even linguistically and all the more so religiously.

question: What inward meanings does ٱلرَّحْمَٰنِ carry?

positions.position: Al-Rahman signifies the sweetness of benefaction, witnessed nearness, and careful service.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (بعضهم): Al-Rahman signifies the sweetness of benefaction, witnessed nearness, and careful service.

question: What is the form of ٱلرَّحِيمِ?

positions.position: Here “name” stands for “naming”: Arabic often uses a verbal noun in a form different from its regular pattern, as in karāmah for ikrām and kalām for taklīm.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): Here “name” stands for “naming”: Arabic often uses a verbal noun in a form different from its regular pattern, as in karāmah for ikrām and kalām for taklīm.

positions.position: Poetic examples use ʿaṭāʾ for iʿṭāʾ, ṭawl for iṭāla, and muṣāba for iṣāba, supporting the unusual verbal-noun form in the basmala.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): Poetic examples use ʿaṭāʾ for iʿṭāʾ, ṭawl for iṭāla, and muṣāba for iṣāba, supporting the unusual verbal-noun form in the basmala.

positions.position: “Raḥīm” follows faʿīl as a form of praise; Arabic uses faʿīl for praise or blame even when the verb’s vowel differs, as in ʿālim/ʿalīm and qādir/qadīr.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): “Raḥīm” follows faʿīl as a form of praise; Arabic uses faʿīl for praise or blame even when the verb’s vowel differs, as in ʿālim/ʿalīm and qādir/qadīr.

positions.position: Arabic normally names the subject first and follows it with attributes, so the sequence places the referent before its descriptions.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): Arabic normally names the subject first and follows it with attributes, so the sequence places the referent before its descriptions.

positions.position: Raḥīm is an intensive faʿīl form; faʿīl is one of the five standard intensive patterns, with some grammarians adding another faʿīl pattern.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (author): Raḥīm is an intensive faʿīl form; faʿīl is one of the five standard intensive patterns, with some grammarians adding another faʿīl pattern.

positions.position: Raḥīm is an intensive faʿīl derived from fāʿil; one cited line allows the sense of being shown mercy.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Raḥīm is an intensive faʿīl derived from fāʿil; one cited line allows the sense of being shown mercy.

positions.position: Al-Alusi rejects these explanations as disputed and argues that the forms are more plausibly intensive active forms from transitive verbs, especially clear in Rahim.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Al-Alusi rejects these explanations as disputed and argues that the forms are more plausibly intensive active forms from transitive verbs, especially clear in Rahim.

question: What does ٱلرَّحِيمِ mean?

positions.position: Some Kufans pause after raḥīm with its mīm quiescent, then begin al-ḥamdu with a cut hamza.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (قوم من الكوفيين): Some Kufans pause after raḥīm with its mīm quiescent, then begin al-ḥamdu with a cut hamza. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (قوم من الكوفيين): Some Kufans stop on raḥīm with a quiescent mīm, then begin al-ḥamdu with a hamza.

positions.position: Ibn Abbas glosses al-Rahim as gentle and caring toward those God wills to show mercy, and severe toward those He wills to chastise.
positions.reasons: IBNABIHATIM (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas glosses al-Rahim as gentle and caring toward those God wills to show mercy, and severe toward those He wills to chastise.

positions.position: Al-Rahim signifies God's affection and mercy.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (ابن عطاء): Al-Rahim signifies God's affection and mercy.

positions.position: Ibn al-Jarrāḥ’s first gloss is damaged in the text; he says al-Raḥīm provides protection and divine success.
positions.reasons: THALABI (عبد الله بن الجراح): Ibn al-Jarrāḥ’s first gloss is damaged in the text; he says al-Raḥīm provides protection and divine success.

positions.position: Ibn Abbas calls both names tender, with Rahim the more tender; the author interprets this as successive divine favor, not literal softness.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas calls both names tender, with Rahim the more tender; the author interprets this as successive divine favor, not literal softness.

positions.position: One class of relational names describes God as known, remembered, praised, and glorified; infinitely many such relations yield infinitely many possible names.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): One class of relational names describes God as known, remembered, praised, and glorified; infinitely many such relations yield infinitely many possible names.

positions.position: Because God's possible creations across kinds and species are limitless, the names derived from creating specific things are limitless too.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Because God's possible creations across kinds and species are limitless, the names derived from creating specific things are limitless too.

positions.position: Ra'uf and Rahim are close, but Ra'uf leans toward conferring benefit whereas Rahim leans toward removing harm.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Ra'uf and Rahim are close, but Ra'uf leans toward conferring benefit whereas Rahim leans toward removing harm.

positions.position: Fatih suggests creating the means of good; Wahib suggests conveying that good; Nafi suggests conveying benefit with the recipient's benefit in view.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Fatih suggests creating the means of good; Wahib suggests conveying that good; Nafi suggests conveying benefit with the recipient's benefit in view.

positions.position: If bringing things into being is not an additional attribute, acting is a purely relational attribute; names can describe creating in general or creating a specific kind for a wisdom.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): If bringing things into being is not an additional attribute, acting is a purely relational attribute; names can describe creating in general or creating a specific kind for a wisdom.

positions.position: Mujid means an agent affecting existence; muhdith more narrowly brings something into existence after nonexistence; mukawwin nearly means mujid.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Mujid means an agent affecting existence; muhdith more narrowly brings something into existence after nonexistence; mukawwin nearly means mujid.

positions.position: Munshi derives from growth and denotes gradual production, while mubdi denotes bringing something forth all at once; they are two kinds of general creation.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Munshi derives from growth and denotes gradual production, while mubdi denotes bringing something forth all at once; they are two kinds of general creation.

positions.position: Mukhtari is close to mubdi, while sani suggests effortful making.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Mukhtari is close to mubdi, while sani suggests effortful making.

positions.position: Bari means bringing into being in a way suited to benefit, like shaping a pen to suit its purpose.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Bari means bringing into being in a way suited to benefit, like shaping a pen to suit its purpose.

positions.position: Creating benefit or pain yields the names Benefiter or Harmful; creating life or death yields Giver of life or Giver of death.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Creating benefit or pain yields the names Benefiter or Harmful; creating life or death yields Giver of life or Giver of death.

positions.position: Granting honor yields Kind and Gentle, while imposing subjugation yields Overpowering and Compeller.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Granting honor yields Kind and Gentle, while imposing subjugation yields Overpowering and Compeller.

positions.position: A gloss says al-Raḥīm shows mercy in six fearful stages: the grave, resurrection, scales, record, bridge, and Hell.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A gloss says al-Raḥīm shows mercy in six fearful stages: the grave, resurrection, scales, record, bridge, and Hell.

positions.position: The formula’s nineteen letters are said to fend off the nineteen guardians of Hell.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The formula’s nineteen letters are said to fend off the nineteen guardians of Hell.

positions.position: A second claim says its nineteen letters expiate sins committed during the nineteen hours left after five daily prayer hours are subtracted from twenty-four.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A second claim says its nineteen letters expiate sins committed during the nineteen hours left after five daily prayer hours are subtracted from twenty-four.

positions.position: Sūrat al-Tawba lacks Bismillah because it commands fighting; slaughter uses a shorter formula because naming mercy is unsuitable to killing.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Sūrat al-Tawba lacks Bismillah because it commands fighting; slaughter uses a shorter formula because naming mercy is unsuitable to killing.

positions.position: Reciting the merciful formula seventeen times daily in obligatory prayers indicates that God created people for mercy, favor, and beneficence rather than killing and punishment.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Reciting the merciful formula seventeen times daily in obligatory prayers indicates that God created people for mercy, favor, and beneficence rather than killing and punishment.

positions.position: Another interpretation makes al-Raḥīm a description of Muḥammad, through whom people reach God’s favor by following his message.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (author): Another interpretation makes al-Raḥīm a description of Muḥammad, through whom people reach God’s favor by following his message.

positions.position: Grammarians assign al- uses including particular or generic reference, presence, evocation of a quality, predominance, relative meaning, and fixed or nonfixed augmentation.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (author): Grammarians assign al- uses including particular or generic reference, presence, evocation of a quality, predominance, relative meaning, and fixed or nonfixed augmentation.

positions.position: The poet al-ʿAmalas ibn ʿUqayl uses raḥīm to mean marḥūm, “one shown mercy.”
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (العملس بن عقيل): The poet al-ʿAmalas ibn ʿUqayl uses raḥīm to mean marḥūm, “one shown mercy.”

positions.position: The Kufans parse the bāʾ as instrumental and the phrase as accusative with an implied “I begin”; they posit that implied verb for acts begun with the formula.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (الكوفيون): The Kufans parse the bāʾ as instrumental and the phrase as accusative with an implied “I begin”; they posit that implied verb for acts begun with the formula.

positions.position: The majority connect raḥīm to al-ḥamdu, retaining the genitive ending and joining the following hamza.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (الجمهور): The majority connect raḥīm to al-ḥamdu, retaining the genitive ending and joining the following hamza. | mentions 1:2

positions.position: Al-ʿAmalas ibn ʿUqayl's verse uses raḥīm in the sense of one upon whom mercy is bestowed.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (العملس بن عقيل): Al-ʿAmalas ibn ʿUqayl's verse uses raḥīm in the sense of one upon whom mercy is bestowed.

positions.position: Al-Ṣādiq says the general wording concerns provision, while the specially worded raḥīm concerns forgiveness for believers.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الصادق): Al-Ṣādiq says the general wording concerns provision, while the specially worded raḥīm concerns forgiveness for believers.

positions.position: Al-Rahim describes God as especially gentle toward believers.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): Al-Rahim describes God as especially gentle toward believers.

positions.position: A report says al-Rahim is a name people cannot claim for themselves.
positions.reasons: DURR (author): A report says al-Rahim is a name people cannot claim for themselves.

positions.position: Al-Ālūsī’s allusive reading makes al-Raḥīm an epithet of Muḥammad from 9:128: Adam bears the names, while Muḥammad bears their meanings and completes creation.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Al-Ālūsī’s allusive reading makes al-Raḥīm an epithet of Muḥammad from 9:128: Adam bears the names, while Muḥammad bears their meanings and completes creation. | mentions 9:128, 2:31, 68:4

positions.position: Rahim is the grace through which ethical people compete in compassion and good works.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Rahim is the grace through which ethical people compete in compassion and good works.

positions.position: Rahim's further mercy grants the goals achieved by those who work.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Rahim's further mercy grants the goals achieved by those who work.

positions.position: Primordial creation is compelled and bestowed: stones, trees, and humans have their kinds through this unchosen mercy.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Primordial creation is compelled and bestowed: stones, trees, and humans have their kinds through this unchosen mercy.

positions.position: Without a further mercy enabling agency, people would be determinists and compelled beings, unable to act on what they know or desire.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Without a further mercy enabling agency, people would be determinists and compelled beings, unable to act on what they know or desire.

positions.position: God advances creatures according to good choices and grants enjoyment of mercy, while bad choices bring deprivation, pain, and punishment; this harmonizes their wills with His.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): God advances creatures according to good choices and grants enjoyment of mercy, while bad choices bring deprivation, pain, and punishment; this harmonizes their wills with His.

positions.position: The Jewish liturgical and epigraphic name ha-raḥamān probably entered north Arabian liturgical language through South Arabia.
positions.reasons: CORPUSCORANICUM (author): The Jewish liturgical and epigraphic name ha-raḥamān probably entered north Arabian liturgical language through South Arabia.

positions.position: The semantically related raḥīm renders the encountered name again in ordinary Arabic.
positions.reasons: CORPUSCORANICUM (author): The semantically related raḥīm renders the encountered name again in ordinary Arabic.

positions.position: The name’s dominance is not explained by its genealogy alone; liturgical experience likely shaped the focus on divine mercy, perhaps echoing kyrie eleēson and Christian salvation history.
positions.reasons: CORPUSCORANICUM (author): The name’s dominance is not explained by its genealogy alone; liturgical experience likely shaped the focus on divine mercy, perhaps echoing kyrie eleēson and Christian salvation history.

question: To whom and when does ٱلرَّحِيمِ show mercy?

positions.position: For al-Ḥarālī, al-Raḥīm denotes the particular mercy associated with what divinity approves.
positions.reasons: BIQAI (أبو الحسن الحرالي): For al-Ḥarālī, al-Raḥīm denotes the particular mercy associated with what divinity approves.

positions.position: Al-Zamakhshari and Abd al-Qahir say rhyme or verse endings should follow meanings and coherent ordering; sound alone cannot justify moving words, especially when the pattern is inconsistent.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (الزمخشري وعبد القاهر): Al-Zamakhshari and Abd al-Qahir say rhyme or verse endings should follow meanings and coherent ordering; sound alone cannot justify moving words, especially when the pattern is inconsistent.

positions.position: Al-Alusi offers a mystical reading of the order: Rahim points to Muhammad, whose completion of the basmala mirrors the completion of the created world.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Al-Alusi offers a mystical reading of the order: Rahim points to Muhammad, whose completion of the basmala mirrors the completion of the created world. | mentions 9:128

positions.position: In this symbolism Adam bears the names while Muhammad bears their meanings; Adam’s names are words, whereas Muhammad received comprehensive speech.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): In this symbolism Adam bears the names while Muhammad bears their meanings; Adam’s names are words, whereas Muhammad received comprehensive speech. | mentions 2:31

positions.position: Rahim answers particular despair, sustains specific aims and effort, and rewards responsibility.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Rahim answers particular despair, sustains specific aims and effort, and rewards responsibility.

positions.position: Rahim guides believers to Gods special mercy, their happiness in the afterlife and meeting their Lord.
positions.reasons: TABATABAI (author): Rahim guides believers to Gods special mercy, their happiness in the afterlife and meeting their Lord.

positions.position: God says His mercy encompasses everything, then promises a special share to those who are mindful.
positions.reasons: TABATABAI (author): God says His mercy encompasses everything, then promises a special share to those who are mindful. | mentions 7:156

question: What inward meanings does ٱلرَّحِيمِ carry?

positions.position: Mercy linguistically is tenderness of heart and an inclination entailing benefaction; a womb is named raḥim because it inclines over what it contains.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (author): Mercy linguistically is tenderness of heart and an inclination entailing benefaction; a womb is named raḥim because it inclines over what it contains.

positions.position: Divine names are understood by resultant acts and ends, not by the passive beginnings of human mercy.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (author): Divine names are understood by resultant acts and ends, not by the passive beginnings of human mercy.

question: How do ٱلرَّحْمَٰنِ and ٱلرَّحِيمِ differ?

positions.position: Al-Raḥmān extends mercy universally; al-Raḥīm specifies mercy for believers or selected recipients.
positions.reasons: TAB (العرزمي): Al-ʿArzami says al-Raḥmān extends mercy to all creation, while al-Raḥīm is mercy toward believers. TAB-FULL (العرزمي): Al-ʿAzramī distinguishes al-Raḥmān as mercy extending to all creation and al-Raḥīm as mercy toward believers. TAB-FULL (author): Ṭabarī reconciles both transmitted distinctions: al-Raḥmān denotes universal mercy and al-Raḥīm particular mercy, whether in this life, the next, or both. THALABI (قوم): One view makes al-Raḥmān merciful to all creation through creation and provision, while al-Raḥīm specially guides believers in this life and grants them Paradise and vision in the next. | mentions 7:156, 33:43 BAGHAWI (author): Those who distinguish them say Rahman is universal mercy, providing for all creatures in this world, while Rahim is particular mercy and forgiveness for believers in the hereafter. BAGHAWI-FULL (author): A distinction makes al-Rahman’s mercy universal in this world, like provision for all, while al-Rahim’s mercy is particular to believers in the hereafter. IBNATIYYA (العرزمي): Al-Arzami explains al-Rahman as mercy to all creation through rain, senses and general blessings, and al-Rahim as mercy to believers through guidance and kindness. IBNATIYYA-FULL (العرزمي): Al-ʿArzamī distinguishes Rahman as merciful to all creation through rain, senses, and universal favors, and Rahim as merciful to believers through guidance and kindness. TABRISI (بعض التابعين): Some Successors say Rahman embraces all creation while Rahim is especially for believers; the author explains this by creation and provision for all and guidance, Paradise, honor, and forgiveness for believers. QURTUBI (العرزمي): Al-ʿArzamī says al-Raḥmān’s mercy reaches all creation through rain and senses, while al-Raḥīm guides believers. QURTUBI (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): An esoteric report interprets basmala letters and says al-Raḥmān shows compassion to all creation, while al-Raḥīm is gentle toward believers. ABUHAYYAN (العزيزي): Al-ʿAzīzī assigns raḥmān to universal gifts such as rain and the senses, and raḥīm to believers through guidance and divine care. IBNKATHIR (العرزمي): Al-ʿArzami says Rahman covers all creation, while Rahim specifically describes mercy to believers. | mentions 25:59, 20:5, 33:43 DURR (الضحاك): Al-Dahhak says al-Rahman encompasses all creation while al-Rahim especially applies to believers. DURR-FULL (الضحاك): Al-Dahhak says al-Rahman applies to all creation, while al-Rahim is especially for believers.

positions.position: Al-Raḥmān concerns this world; al-Raḥīm concerns the next.
positions.reasons: THALABI (يحيى بن معاذ الرازي): Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh says al-Raḥmān provides for worldly livelihoods and al-Raḥīm for the afterlife. THALABI (مجاهد): Mujāhid says al-Raḥmān is for the people of this world and al-Raḥīm for the people of the afterlife. BAGHAWI (author): The invocation “Rahman of this world, Rahim of the hereafter” reflects universal Rahman but particular Rahim; people may call another merciful but not Rahman. TABRISI (عيسى ابن مريم): A prophetic report quotes Jesus as saying Rahman is merciful in this world and Rahim is merciful in the afterlife. BAYDAWI (author): By quantity, al-Raḥmān is worldly mercy shared by believers and unbelievers, while al-Raḥīm is afterlife mercy for believers. NASAFI (author): A supplication calls God Rahman of this world because mercy there reaches believer and unbeliever, and Rahim of the afterlife because there it is specific to believers. ALUSI (author): One distinction makes raḥmān’s worldly mercy encompass believers and unbelievers and raḥīm’s afterlife mercy favor believers; al-Ālūsī questions the allocation and its assumptions. ALUSI-FULL (بعضهم): Some say Rahman is more intensive by the number of recipients, covering believers and unbelievers in worldly life, while Rahim is reserved for believers in the afterlife. ELMALILI (author): A transmitted explanation calls God the Rahmān of this world and Rahīm of the afterlife, or the Rahmān of believers and unbelievers but Rahīm only of believers; the author clarifies that God is both names in both realms. | mentions 33:43

positions.position: Al-Raḥmān is more intensive or comprehensive than al-Raḥīm.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): Rahman marks mercy at its utmost limit, is used only of God, and is more emphatic than rahim, which is more emphatic than rāḥim. BAYDAWI (author): Al-Raḥmān is more emphatic than al-Raḥīm because the expanded form indicates greater meaning by quantity or quality. NASAFI-FULL (author): Rahman and Rahim are both derived from mercy, but Rahman is more emphatic because it has two augmentative patterns versus one in Rahim; added form signals added meaning. ABUHAYYAN (قيل): One view says the two names are synonymous; another distinguishes them, making raḥmān more emphatic and encompassing major blessings while raḥīm completes it with subtle blessings. ABUHAYYAN (ثعلب): Thaʿlab says raḥmān is more emphatic in praise and raḥīm is gentler. SAMIN-DURR (الزمخشري): Al-Zamakhshari and the author hold Rahman to be more intensive and exclusive to God; despite normal progression from weaker to stronger, Rahim follows to cover subtler blessings after Rahman covers great ones. ELMALILI (author): Rahman is more emphatic in encompassing every creature, while Rahim is more emphatic in actual beneficence, which also operates through servants.

positions.position: Abu ʿAli al-Farisi says Rahman covers all kinds of mercy and is unique to God, while Rahim concerns believers, as in 33:43; the author says these views reinforce one another.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (أبو علي الفارسي): Abu ʿAli al-Farisi says Rahman covers all kinds of mercy and is unique to God, while Rahim concerns believers, as in 33:43; the author says these views reinforce one another. | mentions 33:43 QURTUBI (أبو علي الفارسي): Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī says al-Raḥmān covers all mercy but is exclusive to God, while al-Raḥīm especially concerns believers. ABUHAYYAN (أبو علي الفارسي): Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī says raḥmān covers every kind of mercy and belongs uniquely to God, while raḥīm concerns believers, as in 33:43. | mentions 33:43 ABUHAYYAN-FULL (أبو علي الفارسي): Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī says raḥmān covers every kind of mercy and is exclusive to God, whereas raḥīm pertains to believers. | mentions 9:128

positions.position: Ibn ʿAbbas calls Rahman and Rahim two tender names, one more tender than the other.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbas calls Rahman and Rahim two tender names, one more tender than the other. BAGHAWI-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas calls al-Rahman and al-Rahim two tender names, one more tender than the other. DURR (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas glosses al-Rahman as gentle and al-Rahim as caring for creation through provision; both are tender names, one more tender. DURR (الله): A long report says al-Rahman and al-Rahim are tender names, with al-Rahim more tender.

positions.position: Ibn al-Mubārak says al-Raḥmān gives when asked, while al-Raḥīm is displeased when not asked.
positions.reasons: THALABI (ابن المبارك): Ibn al-Mubārak says al-Raḥmān gives when asked, while al-Raḥīm is displeased when not asked. QURTUBI (ابن المبارك): Ibn al-Mubārak says al-Raḥmān gives when asked while al-Raḥīm is angered when not asked; hadith supports this. ALUSI-FULL (ابن المبارك): Ibn al-Mubarak explains Rahman as the giver when asked and Rahim as the one who becomes angry when not asked.

positions.position: Abu Ubayda distinguishes them by saying al-Rahman is the possessor of mercy and al-Rahim is the merciful one.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (أبو عبيدة): Abu Ubayda distinguishes them by saying al-Rahman is the possessor of mercy and al-Rahim is the merciful one. MAWARDI-FULL (أبو عبيدة): He distinguishes the names by saying al-Rahman is the possessor of mercy and al-Rahim is the merciful one. TABRISI (author): Rahman and Rahim are intensive forms derived from mercy, and Rahman is more intensive; Abu Ubayda distinguishes the possessor of mercy from the merciful one.

positions.position: God’s universal worldly mercy includes provision, rain-bearing clouds, plants, bodily and mental health, and countless other blessings shared by believers and unbelievers.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): God’s universal worldly mercy includes provision, rain-bearing clouds, plants, bodily and mental health, and countless other blessings shared by believers and unbelievers. | mentions 14:34 TAB-FULL (author): Universal worldly mercy includes provision, rain, crops, bodily and intellectual health, and other blessings shared by believers and unbelievers. | mentions 16:18

positions.position: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses al-Raḥmān as tender toward those God wills to show mercy, and al-Raḥīm as gentle toward those He wills to treat gently, but severe toward those He wills to chastise.
positions.reasons: TAB (عبد الله بن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās glosses al-Raḥmān as tender toward those God wills to show mercy, and al-Raḥīm as gentle toward those He wills to treat gently, but severe toward those He wills to chastise. TAB-FULL (عبد الله بن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās glosses al-Raḥmān as tender toward those God wills to show mercy and severe toward those He wills to chastise; al-Raḥīm is the gentle toward those shown mercy.

positions.position: A report from the Prophet quotes Jesus distinguishing al-Raḥmān as merciful in this world and the next, and al-Raḥīm as merciful in the next.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (عيسى ابن مريم): A report from the Prophet quotes Jesus distinguishing al-Raḥmān as merciful in this world and the next, and al-Raḥīm as merciful in the next. IBNKATHIR (عيسى ابن مريم): A report attributed to Jesus distinguishes Rahman as merciful in this life and the next, and Rahim as merciful in the next life.

positions.position: Al-Rahman is more intensive than al-Rahim: its form and meaning extend, while al-Rahim’s meaning extends but its wording does not; people are named Rahim, but no one Rahman.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (author): Al-Rahman is more intensive than al-Rahim: its form and meaning extend, while al-Rahim’s meaning extends but its wording does not; people are named Rahim, but no one Rahman. MAWARDI-FULL (author): Al-Rahman is more emphatic than al-Rahim: its form and meaning extend mercy, whereas al-Rahim extends only in meaning; people may be named Rahim but not Rahman.

positions.position: A second distinction makes al-Rahman’s mercy for people of this world and the afterlife, and al-Rahim’s for people of this world only.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (unattributed): A second distinction makes al-Rahman’s mercy for people of this world and the afterlife, and al-Rahim’s for people of this world only. MAWARDI-FULL (author): A second account assigns al-Rahman to mercy for people of this world and the next, and al-Rahim to mercy for people of this world only.

positions.position: One view treats al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm as synonymous names for the merciful, like nadmān and nadīm.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (author): One view treats al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm as synonymous names for the merciful, like nadmān and nadīm. QURTUBI (أبو عبيدة): Abū ʿUbayda treats al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm as synonyms, like nadmān and nadīm.

positions.position: Some say al-Rahman and al-Rahim share the same meaning and root, like nadman and nadim, with one form more emphatic.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (بعض الناس): Some say al-Rahman and al-Rahim share the same meaning and root, like nadman and nadim, with one form more emphatic. IBNATIYYA-FULL (بعض الناس): Some say Rahman and Rahim have one meaning, like nadmān and nadīm, with one form more emphatic than the other.

positions.position: Abu Ali al-Farisi says al-Rahman names God's mercy in all its kinds and is exclusive to Him, while al-Rahim is for believers, as 33:43 says; Ibn Atiyya says the readings reinforce one another.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (أبو علي الفارسي): Abu Ali al-Farisi says al-Rahman names God's mercy in all its kinds and is exclusive to Him, while al-Rahim is for believers, as 33:43 says; Ibn Atiyya says the readings reinforce one another. | mentions 33:43 IBNKATHIR (أبو علي الفارسي): Abu ʿAli al-Farisi says Rahman encompasses every kind of mercy and is exclusive to God, while Rahim describes His mercy toward believers. | mentions 33:43

positions.position: Ikrima says Rahman signifies one mercy and Rahim a hundred mercies.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (عكرمة): Ikrima says Rahman signifies one mercy and Rahim a hundred mercies. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (عكرمة): ʿIkrima contrasts one mercy with a hundred mercies.

positions.position: A third account assigns al-Rahman to mercy exclusive to God and al-Rahim to mercy that creatures can share.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI-FULL (author): A third account assigns al-Rahman to mercy exclusive to God and al-Rahim to mercy that creatures can share. MAWARDI-FULL (author): One account of the two mercies assigns al-Rahman to mercy toward all creatures and al-Rahim to mercy toward the obedient.

positions.position: Ali says the two tender names differ in tenderness and remove despair from believing servants.
positions.reasons: TUSTARI (علي بن أبي طالب): Ali says the two tender names differ in tenderness and remove despair from believing servants.

positions.position: In Arabic, al-Raḥmān is farther from the ordinary faʿila yafʿalu pattern than al-Raḥīm, and that greater departure intensifies praise.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): In Arabic, al-Raḥmān is farther from the ordinary faʿila yafʿalu pattern than al-Raḥīm, and that greater departure intensifies praise.

positions.position: Al-Raḥmān covers this world and the next; al-Raḥīm focuses on the next.
positions.reasons: TAB (عيسى ابن مريم): A report says Jesus distinguished al-Raḥmān as mercy in this world and the next, and al-Raḥīm as mercy in the next world.

positions.position: Al-Ṭabarī accepts both transmitted distinctions: al-Raḥmān denotes God’s mercy to all creation, while al-Raḥīm denotes mercy specified for some, whether in this life, the next, or both.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): Al-Ṭabarī accepts both transmitted distinctions: al-Raḥmān denotes God’s mercy to all creation, while al-Raḥīm denotes mercy specified for some, whether in this life, the next, or both.

positions.position: In the hereafter, universal mercy means God’s just judgment: He wrongs no one even by an atom’s weight and repays each soul for what it earned.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): In the hereafter, universal mercy means God’s just judgment: He wrongs no one even by an atom’s weight and repays each soul for what it earned. | mentions 4:40

positions.position: God’s special mercy to believers in this life is the gracious aid that enables obedience, faith, following revelation, and avoiding sin, which He withholds from those He leaves astray.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): God’s special mercy to believers in this life is the gracious aid that enables obedience, faith, following revelation, and avoiding sin, which He withholds from those He leaves astray. | mentions 33:43

positions.position: In the next life, special mercy to believers is the lasting bliss, triumph, and honor prepared for them rather than unbelievers.
