positions.reasons: TAB (author): In the next life, special mercy to believers is the lasting bliss, triumph, and honor prepared for them rather than unbelievers.

positions.position: A second Abū Hurayra version gives the same recitation exchange but is not attributed to the Prophet.
positions.reasons: TAB (أبو هريرة): A second Abū Hurayra version gives the same recitation exchange but is not attributed to the Prophet.

positions.position: Al-Raḥmān follows the faʿlān pattern from raḥima, while al-Raḥīm follows faʿīl, a praise form that can occur despite the root’s vowel pattern.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): Al-Raḥmān follows the faʿlān pattern from raḥima, while al-Raḥīm follows faʿīl, a praise form that can occur despite the root’s vowel pattern.

positions.position: In Arabic, the more distant a praise name is from its ordinary verbal pattern, the stronger its commendation; thus al-Raḥmān adds intensity beyond al-Raḥīm.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): In Arabic, the more distant a praise name is from its ordinary verbal pattern, the stronger its commendation; thus al-Raḥmān adds intensity beyond al-Raḥīm.

positions.position: In the afterlife God’s universal mercy includes just treatment of everyone without the slightest wrong, while special mercy reserves guidance and the promised Garden for believers.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): In the afterlife God’s universal mercy includes just treatment of everyone without the slightest wrong, while special mercy reserves guidance and the promised Garden for believers. | mentions 33:43

positions.position: Ṭabarī finds the prophetic report and al-ʿAzramī’s distinction more apt than Ibn ʿAbbās’s wording, while agreeing the names carry distinguishable meanings.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): Ṭabarī finds the prophetic report and al-ʿAzramī’s distinction more apt than Ibn ʿAbbās’s wording, while agreeing the names carry distinguishable meanings.

positions.position: Ṭabarī explains that adding al-Raḥīm distinguishes God from Musaylima: no one else has ever combined al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm as names.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): Ṭabarī explains that adding al-Raḥīm distinguishes God from Musaylima: no one else has ever combined al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm as names.

positions.position: Ṭabarī rejects the gloss of al-Raḥmān as merely possessing mercy and al-Raḥīm as merciful: the latter need not assert that mercy is a settled attribute.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): Ṭabarī rejects the gloss of al-Raḥmān as merely possessing mercy and al-Raḥīm as merciful: the latter need not assert that mercy is a settled attribute.

positions.position: Ṭabarī rejects the gloss of al-Raḥmān as merely possessing mercy and al-Raḥīm as merciful: the latter need not assert that mercy is a settled attribute.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): Ṭabarī rejects the gloss of al-Raḥmān as merely possessing mercy and al-Raḥīm as merciful: the latter need not assert that mercy is a settled attribute.

positions.position: Allāh and al-Raḥmān are reserved for God, while al-Raḥīm may describe creatures; no one shares God’s divinity or deserves His exclusive names.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): Allāh and al-Raḥmān are reserved for God, while al-Raḥīm may describe creatures; no one shares God’s divinity or deserves His exclusive names. | mentions 27:60

positions.position: Some interpreters treat al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm as advanced in meaning before rabb al-ʿālamīn, making the apparent repetition part of reordered description rather than adjacent verses.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (جماعة من أهل التأويل): Some interpreters treat al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm as advanced in meaning before rabb al-ʿālamīn, making the apparent repetition part of reordered description rather than adjacent verses. | mentions 1:4

positions.position: He reads bism as divine awe, al-Rahman as aid, and al-Rahim as affection and love.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (الجنيد): He reads bism as divine awe, al-Rahman as aid, and al-Rahim as affection and love.

positions.position: One approaches al-Rahman only through His all-encompassing mercy, while al-Rahim is approached through obedience; the Prophet also bears the latter name (9:128).
positions.reasons: SULAMI (الواسطي): One approaches al-Rahman only through His all-encompassing mercy, while al-Rahim is approached through obedience; the Prophet also bears the latter name (9:128). | mentions 9:128

positions.position: Al-Rahim denotes mercy for creatures' livelihood and bodily welfare, so creatures may be called rahim, unlike the uniquely divine Rahman.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (بعضهم): Al-Rahim denotes mercy for creatures' livelihood and bodily welfare, so creatures may be called rahim, unlike the uniquely divine Rahman.

positions.position: The Prophet, called compassionate and merciful toward believers, is a means by which people reach God and the two divine names; the Merciful accepts the returning person despite faults and preserves even one who turns away.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (بعضهم): The Prophet, called compassionate and merciful toward believers, is a means by which people reach God and the two divine names; the Merciful accepts the returning person despite faults and preserves even one who turns away. | mentions 9:128

positions.position: Al-Rahman suits those sought by God, immersed in lights and realities; al-Rahim suits seekers remaining with themselves and tending outward practice.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (جعفر): Al-Rahman suits those sought by God, immersed in lights and realities; al-Rahim suits seekers remaining with themselves and tending outward practice.

positions.position: Al-Rahman's mercy reaches back into pre-eternity and has no endpoint, whereas al-Rahim connects mercy with worldly life, guidance, and provisions.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (جعفر): Al-Rahman's mercy reaches back into pre-eternity and has no endpoint, whereas al-Rahim connects mercy with worldly life, guidance, and provisions.

positions.position: Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl says al-Raḥmān removes harm and evil, while al-Raḥīm is compassionate but may be unable to remove them.
positions.reasons: THALABI (الحسين بن الفضل): Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl says al-Raḥmān removes harm and evil, while al-Raḥīm is compassionate but may be unable to remove them.

positions.position: Al-Warrāq says al-Raḥmān is merciful to deniers and unbelievers, while al-Raḥīm is merciful to monotheists and the grateful.
positions.reasons: THALABI (أبو بكر الوراق): Al-Warrāq says al-Raḥmān is merciful to deniers and unbelievers, while al-Raḥīm is merciful to monotheists and the grateful.

positions.position: The Prophet says whoever does not ask God makes Him angry; a poem contrasts God’s anger at unanswered supplication with people’s anger at being asked.
positions.reasons: THALABI (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): The Prophet says whoever does not ask God makes Him angry; a poem contrasts God’s anger at unanswered supplication with people’s anger at being asked.

positions.position: Al-Warrāq distinguishes al-Raḥmān as bestowed blessings and al-Raḥīm as benefits God has spared or withdrawn.
positions.reasons: THALABI (أبو بكر الوراق): Al-Warrāq distinguishes al-Raḥmān as bestowed blessings and al-Raḥīm as benefits God has spared or withdrawn.

positions.position: Al-Muzaydī says al-Raḥmān rescues people from the Fire and al-Raḥīm admits them to gardens.
positions.reasons: THALABI (محمد بن علي المزيدي): Al-Muzaydī says al-Raḥmān rescues people from the Fire and al-Raḥīm admits them to gardens. | mentions 3:103, 15:46

positions.position: Al-Muḥāsibī assigns al-Raḥmān mercy to souls and al-Raḥīm mercy to hearts.
positions.reasons: THALABI (المحاسبي): Al-Muḥāsibī assigns al-Raḥmān mercy to souls and al-Raḥīm mercy to hearts.

positions.position: Al-Sarī ibn Mughlis says al-Raḥmān removes distress and al-Raḥīm forgives sins.
positions.reasons: THALABI (السري بن مغلس): Al-Sarī ibn Mughlis says al-Raḥmān removes distress and al-Raḥīm forgives sins.

positions.position: Muṭahhar al-Warrāq says al-Raḥmān forgives even grave sins, while al-Raḥīm accepts even few acts of obedience.
positions.reasons: THALABI (مطهر بن الوراق): Muṭahhar al-Warrāq says al-Raḥmān forgives even grave sins, while al-Raḥīm accepts even few acts of obedience.

positions.position: Some say al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm are synonymous names for the merciful; mercy is either God’s will of good, an essential attribute, or withholding deserved punishment and doing good, an act-attribute.
positions.reasons: THALABI (قوم): Some say al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm are synonymous names for the merciful; mercy is either God’s will of good, an essential attribute, or withholding deserved punishment and doing good, an act-attribute.

positions.position: Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq summarizes the distinction as al-Raḥmān being a specific name with general scope and al-Raḥīm a general name with specific scope.
positions.reasons: THALABI (جعفر بن محمد الصادق): Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq summarizes the distinction as al-Raḥmān being a specific name with general scope and al-Raḥīm a general name with specific scope.

positions.position: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk assigns al-Raḥmān’s mercy to heaven’s inhabitants through their dwelling, obedience, and protection, and al-Raḥīm’s to earthly people through messengers, scriptures, counsel, and relief from calamities.
positions.reasons: THALABI (الضحاك): Al-Ḍaḥḥāk assigns al-Raḥmān’s mercy to heaven’s inhabitants through their dwelling, obedience, and protection, and al-Raḥīm’s to earthly people through messengers, scriptures, counsel, and relief from calamities.

positions.position: ʿIkrima says al-Raḥmān is associated with one mercy and al-Raḥīm with one hundred; he derives this from the Prophetic report that one mercy was sent to earth and ninety-nine are reserved for Judgment Day.
positions.reasons: THALABI (عكرمة): ʿIkrima says al-Raḥmān is associated with one mercy and al-Raḥīm with one hundred; he derives this from the Prophetic report that one mercy was sent to earth and ninety-nine are reserved for Judgment Day.

positions.position: The Prophet reports that God has one hundred mercies: one is shared among creation, while ninety-nine are reserved to show mercy to servants on the Resurrection Day.
positions.reasons: THALABI (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): The Prophet reports that God has one hundred mercies: one is shared among creation, while ninety-nine are reserved to show mercy to servants on the Resurrection Day.

positions.position: A name points to its referent, whereas an attribute conveys information about what is described; when an attribute is made a name it does both.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (author): A name points to its referent, whereas an attribute conveys information about what is described; when an attribute is made a name it does both.

positions.position: Al-Rahman and al-Rahim are divine names, and al-Rahim is a name derived from an attribute.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (author): Al-Rahman and al-Rahim are divine names, and al-Rahim is a name derived from an attribute.

positions.position: The other view says al-Rahman is Arabic like al-Rahim, with their similar letters reflected in Arabic usage and Shanfarā’s verse.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (unattributed): The other view says al-Rahman is Arabic like al-Rahim, with their similar letters reflected in Arabic usage and Shanfarā’s verse.

positions.position: Under the two-mercy view, al-Rahman denotes mercy to all creation, while al-Rahim denotes mercy to the obedient.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (unattributed): Under the two-mercy view, al-Rahman denotes mercy to all creation, while al-Rahim denotes mercy to the obedient.

positions.position: A third distinction reserves al-Rahman’s mercy to God alone and takes al-Rahim’s mercy as a kind also found among creatures.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (unattributed): A third distinction reserves al-Rahman’s mercy to God alone and takes al-Rahim’s mercy as a kind also found among creatures.

positions.position: The phrase mercy to the worlds in 21:107 means a benefit to them, linking the verse's usage to this definition.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI-FULL (author): The phrase mercy to the worlds in 21:107 means a benefit to them, linking the verse's usage to this definition. | mentions 21:107

positions.position: One view derives al-Rahman and al-Rahim from the same mercy, with al-Rahman simply more emphatic.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI-FULL (author): One view derives al-Rahman and al-Rahim from the same mercy, with al-Rahman simply more emphatic.

positions.position: Another view derives the names from two distinct mercies to distinguish the names and attributes.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI-FULL (author): Another view derives the names from two distinct mercies to distinguish the names and attributes.

positions.position: Al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm derive from mercy, whose basis is benefaction to the needy; both are intensive forms, with faʿlān more emphatic than faʿīl because it departs further from the base pattern.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (author): Al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm derive from mercy, whose basis is benefaction to the needy; both are intensive forms, with faʿlān more emphatic than faʿīl because it departs further from the base pattern.

positions.position: A further distinction assigns al-Raḥmān to creation and al-Raḥīm to provision.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (author): A further distinction assigns al-Raḥmān to creation and al-Raḥīm to provision.

positions.position: The pairing intensifies the attribution of mercy and teaches that all blessings come from God.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (author): The pairing intensifies the attribution of mercy and teaches that all blessings come from God.

positions.position: Another explanation says al-Raḥmān is more frequent in the Torah, al-Raḥīm in the Gospel, and Allah in the Qur’an, so the pairing shows all refer to God.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (author): Another explanation says al-Raḥmān is more frequent in the Torah, al-Raḥīm in the Gospel, and Allah in the Qur’an, so the pairing shows all refer to God.

positions.position: Another reported explanation is that God is seen but does not see.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (author): Another reported explanation is that God is seen but does not see.

positions.position: Another view distinguishes the names because other beings may be called raḥīm but not raḥmān.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (author): Another view distinguishes the names because other beings may be called raḥīm but not raḥmān.

positions.position: One distinction makes al-Raḥmān the provider for all creatures and al-Raḥīm the forgiver of all believers.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (author): One distinction makes al-Raḥmān the provider for all creatures and al-Raḥīm the forgiver of all believers.

positions.position: Another makes al-Raḥmān the giver of foundational blessings only God can create, while al-Raḥīm denotes one possessing mercy.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (author): Another makes al-Raḥmān the giver of foundational blessings only God can create, while al-Raḥīm denotes one possessing mercy.

positions.position: Some treat the two names as synonyms for merciful; al-Mubarrad describes them as favor upon favor, repeated to encourage hopeful hearts.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI-FULL (المبرد): Some treat the two names as synonyms for merciful; al-Mubarrad describes them as favor upon favor, repeated to encourage hopeful hearts.

positions.position: On this distinction, people may be called merciful (rahim) but not al-Rahman; the former is general in wording and particular in meaning, the latter opposite.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI-FULL (author): On this distinction, people may be called merciful (rahim) but not al-Rahman; the former is general in wording and particular in meaning, the latter opposite.

positions.position: Rahman follows faʿlan from rahima, like ghadban and sakran; rahim follows faʿil, like marid and saqim.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF (author): Rahman follows faʿlan from rahima, like ghadban and sakran; rahim follows faʿil, like marid and saqim.

positions.position: Rahman is more intensive than rahim; tradition calls God Rahman of this world and the next, but Rahim of this world.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF (author): Rahman is more intensive than rahim; tradition calls God Rahman of this world and the next, but Rahim of this world.

positions.position: Mercy suggests tenderness, as with a womb bending over its contents; of God it metaphorically means beneficence to servants, like a generous king.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF (author): Mercy suggests tenderness, as with a womb bending over its contents; of God it metaphorically means beneficence to servants, like a generous king.

positions.position: Rahman is the emphatic fa'lan form of mercy, while Rahim is fa'il; the former is more intensive, and added form signals added meaning.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL (author): Rahman is the emphatic fa'lan form of mercy, while Rahim is fa'il; the former is more intensive, and added form signals added meaning.

positions.position: God's mercy is figurative language for His beneficence: a kindly ruler does good to subjects, whereas harshness withholds favor.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL (author): God's mercy is figurative language for His beneficence: a kindly ruler does good to subjects, whereas harshness withholds favor.

positions.position: The ordering is complementary: Rahman covers great and foundational blessings, and Rahim completes it by covering blessings that are delicate and subtle.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL (author): The ordering is complementary: Rahman covers great and foundational blessings, and Rahim completes it by covering blessings that are delicate and subtle.

positions.position: Al-Rahman is an intensive form from mercy, reaching its utmost limit and belonging specifically to God; rahim exceeds rahim as a description of one who showed mercy once, while al-Rahman marks the utmost degree.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (author): Al-Rahman is an intensive form from mercy, reaching its utmost limit and belonging specifically to God; rahim exceeds rahim as a description of one who showed mercy once, while al-Rahman marks the utmost degree.

positions.position: Allah is genitive by annexation, and Rahman and Rahim are genitive as adjectives of Allah.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (author): Allah is genitive by annexation, and Rahman and Rahim are genitive as adjectives of Allah.

positions.position: Al-Sadiq formulates the distinction as a special name with a general attribute for Rahman, and a general name with a special attribute for Rahim.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (الصادق): Al-Sadiq formulates the distinction as a special name with a general attribute for Rahman, and a general name with a special attribute for Rahim.

positions.position: The Prophet says he was sent as mercy to the worlds and to break instruments and idols; an unrepentant drinker receives the pus of Hell, called clay of corruption.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النبي): The Prophet says he was sent as mercy to the worlds and to break instruments and idols; an unrepentant drinker receives the pus of Hell, called clay of corruption.

positions.position: Giving little or much yields Withholder or Expander; punishing sins yields Avenger, while foregoing punishment yields Pardoner, Forgiver, Merciful, or Compassionate.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Giving little or much yields Withholder or Expander; punishing sins yields Avenger, while foregoing punishment yields Pardoner, Forgiver, Merciful, or Compassionate.

positions.position: Aziz means God has no equal; Ghaffar removes punishment from sinners; Halim does not hasten punishment and still grants mercy.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Aziz means God has no equal; Ghaffar removes punishment from sinners; Halim does not hasten punishment and still grants mercy.

positions.position: A needy servant vocative signals a request: calling God generous, beneficent, or merciful implicitly asks for favor.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A needy servant vocative signals a request: calling God generous, beneficent, or merciful implicitly asks for favor.

positions.position: His fifth discussion says human rational souls differ in their natures, with some bright and noble, some low and dark, some compassionate, some harsh, and varied worldly desires.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): His fifth discussion says human rational souls differ in their natures, with some bright and noble, some low and dark, some compassionate, some harsh, and varied worldly desires.

positions.position: A report says God distributed one mercy among all earthly creatures and reserved ninety-nine mercies for His servants on Judgment Day.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): A report says God distributed one mercy among all earthly creatures and reserved ninety-nine mercies for His servants on Judgment Day.

positions.position: Rāzī says the report was for instruction: divine mercy is an unbounded sea and cannot literally be limited to a number.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Rāzī says the report was for instruction: divine mercy is an unbounded sea and cannot literally be limited to a number.

positions.position: Seeing a woman protect her child from heat, the Prophet tells the onlookers that God is more merciful to them than she is to her child.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): Seeing a woman protect her child from heat, the Prophet tells the onlookers that God is more merciful to them than she is to her child.

positions.position: Some say al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm are non-Arabic, perhaps Hebrew or Syriac forms later Arabized.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Some say al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm are non-Arabic, perhaps Hebrew or Syriac forms later Arabized.

positions.position: Everything attained is only a drop from God’s seas of mercy and a speck of His beneficence, revealing the meaning of al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Everything attained is only a drop from God’s seas of mercy and a speck of His beneficence, revealing the meaning of al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm.

positions.position: Inspecting the body’s four humors, organs, and benefits reveals God’s mercy in creating and guiding people and illuminates al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Inspecting the body’s four humors, organs, and benefits reveals God’s mercy in creating and guiding people and illuminates al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm. | mentions 14:34

positions.position: Rāzī’s primary position is that true mercy belongs only to God; even if others are called merciful, God’s mercy is more complete.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Rāzī’s primary position is that true mercy belongs only to God; even if others are called merciful, God’s mercy is more complete.

positions.position: A shepherd says wolves leave his flock alone since the shepherd reconciled himself with God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A shepherd says wolves leave his flock alone since the shepherd reconciled himself with God.

positions.position: Since God named Himself al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm, the author asks rhetorically how He could fail to show mercy.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Since God named Himself al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm, the author asks rhetorically how He could fail to show mercy.

positions.position: A beggar’s parable asks God to make His gift match His vast door of mercy, and not to deprive worshipers of that mercy.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A beggar’s parable asks God to make His gift match His vast door of mercy, and not to deprive worshipers of that mercy.

positions.position: Placing al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm after the name signifying power and exaltedness indicates that mercy is greater and more complete than wrath.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Placing al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm after the name signifying power and exaltedness indicates that mercy is greater and more complete than wrath.

positions.position: The three names correspond to three Qur’anic classes: Allah for those foremost in good, al-Raḥmān for the moderate, and al-Raḥīm for the self-wronging.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The three names correspond to three Qur’anic classes: Allah for those foremost in good, al-Raḥmān for the moderate, and al-Raḥīm for the self-wronging. | mentions 35:32

positions.position: Another gloss says Allah gives gifts, al-Raḥmān overlooks the slips of the saints, and al-Raḥīm overlooks their discourtesy.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Another gloss says Allah gives gifts, al-Raḥmān overlooks the slips of the saints, and al-Raḥīm overlooks their discourtesy.

positions.position: Anas reports that saying Bismillah al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm while undressing shields people from jinn; Rāzī asks whether it will not also shield them from hell’s guards.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أنس بن مالك): Anas reports that saying Bismillah al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm while undressing shields people from jinn; Rāzī asks whether it will not also shield them from hell’s guards.

positions.position: Repetition for emphasis is common in the Qur’an, and reaffirming that God is merciful is especially important.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Repetition for emphasis is common in the Qur’an, and reaffirming that God is merciful is especially important.

positions.position: He raises an unresolved issue: if 'the Merciful, the Compassionate' can stand as a verse despite modifying God, why cannot the first adjective and then the second each be a verse?
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): He raises an unresolved issue: if 'the Merciful, the Compassionate' can stand as a verse despite modifying God, why cannot the first adjective and then the second each be a verse?

positions.position: Mystics read assimilation of the two lām letters as a sign that when knowledge reaches the known, knowledge vanishes and only the eternal known remains unchanged.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أرباب الإشارات والمجاهدات): Mystics read assimilation of the two lām letters as a sign that when knowledge reaches the known, knowledge vanishes and only the eternal known remains unchanged.

positions.position: Readers agree that the rāʾ in al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm is doubled by assimilating the article lām; assimilation applies to thirteen nearby coronal letters, while distant articulation points require clarity.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (القراء): Readers agree that the rāʾ in al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm is doubled by assimilating the article lām; assimilation applies to thirteen nearby coronal letters, while distant articulation points require clarity. | mentions 9:112

positions.position: The alif before nūn in al-Raḥmān may be omitted for ease or written; the yāʾ in al-Raḥīm cannot be deleted because that would damage or confuse the word.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The alif before nūn in al-Raḥmān may be omitted for ease or written; the yāʾ in al-Raḥīm cannot be deleted because that would damage or confuse the word.

positions.position: Al-Khaṭṭābī argues the article belongs to Allah’s name because it accepts the vocative yā Allah, unlike al-Raḥmān or al-Raḥīm.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (الخطابي): Al-Khaṭṭābī argues the article belongs to Allah’s name because it accepts the vocative yā Allah, unlike al-Raḥmān or al-Raḥīm.

positions.position: A saying attributed to ʿAlī calls the basmala a cure and aid; al-Raḥmān aids believers and al-Raḥīm belongs to the repentant righteous.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (علي بن أبي طالب): A saying attributed to ʿAlī calls the basmala a cure and aid; al-Raḥmān aids believers and al-Raḥīm belongs to the repentant righteous.

positions.position: Al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm are intensive forms from raḥima, like ghaḍbān from ghaḍiba and ʿalīm from ʿalima.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (author): Al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm are intensive forms from raḥima, like ghaḍbān from ghaḍiba and ʿalīm from ʿalima.

positions.position: By quality, al-Raḥmān denotes mercy in both worlds and al-Raḥīm mercy in this world, since afterlife blessings are immense and worldly ones vary in size.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (author): By quality, al-Raḥmān denotes mercy in both worlds and al-Raḥīm mercy in this world, since afterlife blessings are immense and worldly ones vary in size.

positions.position: Alternatively, al-Raḥmān denotes great blessings and al-Raḥīm completes it by including blessings outside that category.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (author): Alternatively, al-Raḥmān denotes great blessings and al-Raḥīm completes it by including blessings outside that category.

positions.position: الرحمن and الرحيم are intensive forms of mercy; human mercy is tenderness, but divine names refer to the resulting beneficence rather than an emotional state.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL (author): الرحمن and الرحيم are intensive forms of mercy; human mercy is tenderness, but divine names refer to the resulting beneficence rather than an emotional state.

positions.position: الرحمن is stronger than الرحيم because the added form indicates added meaning; this difference can concern quantity or quality.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL (author): الرحمن is stronger than الرحيم because the added form indicates added meaning; this difference can concern quantity or quality.

positions.position: On a quantitative reading, God is “Merciful of this world” to believers and unbelievers alike, and “Compassionate in the next” specifically to believers.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL (author): On a quantitative reading, God is “Merciful of this world” to believers and unbelievers alike, and “Compassionate in the next” specifically to believers.

positions.position: Rahman is fa‘lan from mercy and denotes mercy encompassing everything, like ghadban denotes being filled with anger; rahim is fa‘il. Rahman is more intensive because its form has two augmentations rather than one, and greater length signals greater meaning.
positions.reasons: NASAFI (author): Rahman is fa‘lan from mercy and denotes mercy encompassing everything, like ghadban denotes being filled with anger; rahim is fa‘il. Rahman is more intensive because its form has two augmentations rather than one, and greater length signals greater meaning.

positions.position: Al-Zamakhsharī favors raḥmān for foundational blessings and raḥīm as a complement for finer, subtler blessings.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (الزمخشري): Al-Zamakhsharī favors raḥmān for foundational blessings and raḥīm as a complement for finer, subtler blessings.

positions.position: Al-Qurṭubī gives the reverse allocation: raḥmān for the next life and raḥīm for this life.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (القرطبي): Al-Qurṭubī gives the reverse allocation: raḥmān for the next life and raḥīm for this life.

positions.position: Al-Muzanī distinguishes blessings of worldly life from blessings of religion.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (المزني): Al-Muzanī distinguishes blessings of worldly life from blessings of religion.

positions.position: Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh relates the names to needs of the afterlife and worldly life.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (يحيى بن معاذ): Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh relates the names to needs of the afterlife and worldly life.

positions.position: Al-Ṣādiq says the generally framed name concerns provision broadly, while the specially framed name concerns forgiveness for believers.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (الصادق): Al-Ṣādiq says the generally framed name concerns provision broadly, while the specially framed name concerns forgiveness for believers.

positions.position: Another view says raḥmān gives blessings of kinds humans cannot provide, while raḥīm gives blessings of kinds humans can provide.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (قيل): Another view says raḥmān gives blessings of kinds humans cannot provide, while raḥīm gives blessings of kinds humans can provide.

positions.position: Al-Farrāʾ limits the dropped alif to bismillāh al-raḥmān al-raḥīm, where usage is especially frequent.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الفراء): Al-Farrāʾ limits the dropped alif to bismillāh al-raḥmān al-raḥīm, where usage is especially frequent.

positions.position: Human mercy is described either as tenderness arising in the heart or as intending good and averting harm, since people may help those for whom they feel no tenderness.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Human mercy is described either as tenderness arising in the heart or as intending good and averting harm, since people may help those for whom they feel no tenderness.

positions.position: Al-ʿAzīzī contrasts universal gifts such as rain and senses with guidance and loving care given to believers.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (العزيزي): Al-ʿAzīzī contrasts universal gifts such as rain and senses with guidance and loving care given to believers.

positions.position: Al-Muḥāsibī distinguishes mercy toward souls from mercy toward hearts.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (المحاسبي): Al-Muḥāsibī distinguishes mercy toward souls from mercy toward hearts.

positions.position: Thaʿlab calls raḥmān more laudatory and raḥīm more tender.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (ثعلب): Thaʿlab calls raḥmān more laudatory and raḥīm more tender.

positions.position: Some treat raḥmān and raḥīm as synonyms, while others distinguish them; al-Zamakhsharī makes raḥmān cover major blessings and raḥīm the finer ones.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Some treat raḥmān and raḥīm as synonyms, while others distinguish them; al-Zamakhsharī makes raḥmān cover major blessings and raḥīm the finer ones.

positions.position: Abū Ḥayyān says their intensification differs: raḥmān suggests fullness and dominance, while raḥīm signals repeated acts at sites of mercy, so their pairing is not mere emphasis.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Abū Ḥayyān says their intensification differs: raḥmān suggests fullness and dominance, while raḥīm signals repeated acts at sites of mercy, so their pairing is not mere emphasis.

positions.position: Mujāhid distinguishes them as mercy for this world and mercy for the next.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (مجاهد): Mujāhid distinguishes them as mercy for this world and mercy for the next.

positions.position: Al-Qurṭubī reverses the distinction, assigning raḥmān to the afterlife and raḥīm to this world.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (القرطبي): Al-Qurṭubī reverses the distinction, assigning raḥmān to the afterlife and raḥīm to this world.

positions.position: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the mercy encompasses the inhabitants of heaven and earth.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الضحاك): Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the mercy encompasses the inhabitants of heaven and earth.

positions.position: Al-Muzanī assigns raḥmān to worldly blessings and raḥīm to blessings of religion.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (المزني): Al-Muzanī assigns raḥmān to worldly blessings and raḥīm to blessings of religion.

positions.position: Al-Rahman and al-Rahim are derived adjectives from mercy, though some say al-Rahman is not derived because Arabs asked what al-Rahman is.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): Al-Rahman and al-Rahim are derived adjectives from mercy, though some say al-Rahman is not derived because Arabs asked what al-Rahman is. | mentions 25:60

positions.position: Ibn Abbas calls the two names tender, one more tender than the other, meaning more merciful; al-Khattabi says tenderness does not belong among divine attributes.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas calls the two names tender, one more tender than the other, meaning more merciful; al-Khattabi says tenderness does not belong among divine attributes.

positions.position: Some make Rahim more intensive and cite a report of worldly Rahim and afterlife Rahman, but the author says it instead confirms Rahman is stronger because afterlife mercy is greater.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): Some make Rahim more intensive and cite a report of worldly Rahim and afterlife Rahman, but the author says it instead confirms Rahman is stronger because afterlife mercy is greater.

positions.position: The patterns intensify differently: fa'lan conveys fullness and dominance, while fa'il conveys repeated occurrence at sites of mercy.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): The patterns intensify differently: fa'lan conveys fullness and dominance, while fa'il conveys repeated occurrence at sites of mercy.

positions.position: Abu Ubayda says fa'lan marks an intensified act, while fa'il can mean either agent or patient; his poem calls someone in war compassionate.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (أبو عبيدة): Abu Ubayda says fa'lan marks an intensified act, while fa'il can mean either agent or patient; his poem calls someone in war compassionate.

positions.position: Rahman is restricted in name but broad in action, whereas Rahim is broad in name but restricted in action; hence fa'lan is not transitive while fa'il is.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): Rahman is restricted in name but broad in action, whereas Rahim is broad in name but restricted in action; hence fa'lan is not transitive while fa'il is.

positions.position: The article in al-Rahman marks dominance; most scholars restrict it to God, unlike Rahim, which also describes the Prophet toward believers.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): The article in al-Rahman marks dominance; most scholars restrict it to God, unlike Rahim, which also describes the Prophet toward believers. | mentions 17:110, 9:128

positions.position: A report explains the letters as bāʾ for God's splendor, sīn for His glory, and mīm for His dominion; Rahman is merciful in both worlds and Rahim in the next. Ibn Kathir calls the report very strange and possibly Israelite
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (عيسى ابن مريم): A report explains the letters as bāʾ for God's splendor, sīn for His glory, and mīm for His dominion; Rahman is merciful in both worlds and Rahim in the next. Ibn Kathir calls the report very strange and possibly Israelite rather than Prophetic.

positions.position: Al-Razi rejects the claim that the name Allah is Hebrew rather than Arabic.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (فخر الدين الرازي): Al-Razi rejects the claim that the name Allah is Hebrew rather than Arabic.

positions.position: Al-Rahman and al-Rahim are intensive forms derived from mercy, with al-Rahman more emphatic; Ibn Jarir's discussion suggests agreement.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): Al-Rahman and al-Rahim are intensive forms derived from mercy, with al-Rahman more emphatic; Ibn Jarir's discussion suggests agreement.

positions.position: Some grammarians claim Rahman is not derived or is Hebrew while Rahim is Arabic; al-Zajjaj rejects this as an objectionable view.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (المبرد وأحمد بن يحيى): Some grammarians claim Rahman is not derived or is Hebrew while Rahim is Arabic; al-Zajjaj rejects this as an objectionable view.

positions.position: Abu ʿUbayd treats Rahman and Rahim as synonymous, like two parallel forms; others distinguish the intensive faʿlan form from faʿil.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (أبو عبيد): Abu ʿUbayd treats Rahman and Rahim as synonymous, like two parallel forms; others distinguish the intensive faʿlan form from faʿil.

positions.position: Ibn al-Mubarak says Rahman gives when asked, while Rahim becomes angry if not asked, linking the distinction to the hadith that God is angered by one who does not supplicate.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (ابن المبارك): Ibn al-Mubarak says Rahman gives when asked, while Rahim becomes angry if not asked, linking the distinction to the hadith that God is angered by one who does not supplicate.

positions.position: This distinction is supported by verses that name Rahman at God's establishing the Throne and Rahim for believers, although a traditional supplication calls Him Rahman and Rahim of both worlds.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): This distinction is supported by verses that name Rahman at God's establishing the Throne and Rahim for believers, although a traditional supplication calls Him Rahman and Rahim of both worlds. | mentions 25:59, 20:5, 33:43

positions.position: The claim that Rahim must intensify Rahman because it follows it is mistaken: the second word is another adjective, not emphatic repetition.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): The claim that Rahim must intensify Rahman because it follows it is mistaken: the second word is another adjective, not emphatic repetition.

positions.position: The naming sequence moves from the unique name Allah, to the exclusive Rahman, to Rahim, which also describes the Prophet and human beings; naming starts with the most honored and specific names.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): The naming sequence moves from the unique name Allah, to the exclusive Rahman, to Rahim, which also describes the Prophet and human beings; naming starts with the most honored and specific names. | mentions 17:110, 9:128, 76:2

positions.position: Al-Harali glosses the basmala: باء manifests causal wisdom; ism reveals what is hidden to hearts through hearing; Allah names the one hearts seek beyond reason; Rahman is universally merciful and Rahim grants mercy approved by divinity.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): Al-Harali glosses the basmala: باء manifests causal wisdom; ism reveals what is hidden to hearts through hearing; Allah names the one hearts seek beyond reason; Rahman is universally merciful and Rahim grants mercy approved by divinity.

positions.position: Ata al-Khurasani gives a terse account of the form al-Rahman al-Rahim.
positions.reasons: DURR (عطاء الخراساني): Ata al-Khurasani gives a terse account of the form al-Rahman al-Rahim.

positions.position: Anas describes the Prophet's recitation as measured, lengthening bismillah, al-Rahman, and al-Rahim.
positions.reasons: DURR (أنس): Anas describes the Prophet's recitation as measured, lengthening bismillah, al-Rahman, and al-Rahim.

positions.position: Ata al-Khurasani says that when the name al-Rahman was separated from God's name, it became “al-Rahman al-Rahim.”
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (عطاء الخراساني): Ata al-Khurasani says that when the name al-Rahman was separated from God's name, it became “al-Rahman al-Rahim.”

positions.position: Al-Rahman and al-Rahim describe mercy, with al-Rahim kind to those God wills to show mercy and severe toward those He wills to punish.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (ابن عباس): Al-Rahman and al-Rahim describe mercy, with al-Rahim kind to those God wills to show mercy and severe toward those He wills to punish.

positions.position: Ibn Abbas describes al-Rahman as gentle and al-Rahim as caring for creation through provision; both names are subtle, one more so than the other.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas describes al-Rahman as gentle and al-Rahim as caring for creation through provision; both names are subtle, one more so than the other.

positions.position: In the report that divides al-Fatiha between God and servants, God says the basmala invokes two gentle names, with al-Rahim gentler than al-Rahman.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (الله تعالى): In the report that divides al-Fatiha between God and servants, God says the basmala invokes two gentle names, with al-Rahim gentler than al-Rahman.

positions.position: A report gives Muawiya detailed calligraphic directions: shape the ba, distinguish the sin, form the mim, beautify Allah and al-Rahim, and extend al-Rahman.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (معاوية): A report gives Muawiya detailed calligraphic directions: shape the ba, distinguish the sin, form the mim, beautify Allah and al-Rahim, and extend al-Rahman.

positions.position: The conventional analysis makes al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm intensive adjectives from rahima, sometimes positing transfer to intransitive rahuma; al-Ālūsī disputes this derivation.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): The conventional analysis makes al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm intensive adjectives from rahima, sometimes positing transfer to intransitive rahuma; al-Ālūsī disputes this derivation.

positions.position: Al-Rāghib says raḥīm marks frequent action and raḥmān frequent, repeated action; Ibn al-Mubārak says the Merciful gives when asked, while the Compassionate is angered if not asked.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (الراغب وابن المبارك): Al-Rāghib says raḥīm marks frequent action and raḥmān frequent, repeated action; Ibn al-Mubārak says the Merciful gives when asked, while the Compassionate is angered if not asked.

positions.position: Al-Juwaynī treats the two names as equal in force, distinguishing repeated abundance in raḥmān from enduring action in raḥīm.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (الجويني): Al-Juwaynī treats the two names as equal in force, distinguishing repeated abundance in raḥmān from enduring action in raḥīm.

positions.position: Some distinguish raḥmān as the attribute of mercy and raḥīm as its relation to recipients, citing human use of raḥīm in 9:117 and 33:43 but not raḥmān.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Some distinguish raḥmān as the attribute of mercy and raḥīm as its relation to recipients, citing human use of raḥīm in 9:117 and 33:43 but not raḥmān. | mentions 9:117, 33:43

positions.position: Al-Ālūsī challenges the rule that greater form means greater intensity and disputes whether raḥmān is more abundant, more enduring, or simply equal to raḥīm.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Al-Ālūsī challenges the rule that greater form means greater intensity and disputes whether raḥmān is more abundant, more enduring, or simply equal to raḥīm.

positions.position: The Prophet’s intercession for all people at the gathering and reports of punishment relief complicate claims that afterlife mercy reaches only believers.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): The Prophet’s intercession for all people at the gathering and reports of punishment relief complicate claims that afterlife mercy reaches only believers. | mentions 17:79

positions.position: Ibn Hishām treats al-Raḥmān as a substitute, not adjective, with al-Raḥīm modifying it; Ibn Khurūf calls it a dominant adjective.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (ابن هشام وابن خروف): Ibn Hishām treats al-Raḥmān as a substitute, not adjective, with al-Raḥīm modifying it; Ibn Khurūf calls it a dominant adjective. | mentions 20:5, 55:1, 17:110, 25:60

positions.position: Ibn Kaysān, al-Sīrāfī, and others treat the part-to-whole addition as partitive, with some grammarians extending that analysis to all such constructions.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (ابن كيسان والسيرافي وجمع): Ibn Kaysān, al-Sīrāfī, and others treat the part-to-whole addition as partitive, with some grammarians extending that analysis to all such constructions.

positions.position: The basmala subtly honors Muhammad through the description of him as compassionate to believers; this early allusion anticipates his later praise and invites attention to God’s mercy.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): The basmala subtly honors Muhammad through the description of him as compassionate to believers; this early allusion anticipates his later praise and invites attention to God’s mercy. | mentions 9:128, 68:4

positions.position: Beginning with ba hastens glad tidings and signifies that mercy is central; a hadith says no one enters Paradise by deeds alone, but only through God's mercy, even the Prophet.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Beginning with ba hastens glad tidings and signifies that mercy is central; a hadith says no one enters Paradise by deeds alone, but only through God's mercy, even the Prophet.

positions.position: The Prophet's predominating quality was mercy, especially toward the believing community, as the Qur'an calls him a mercy to the worlds.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): The Prophet's predominating quality was mercy, especially toward the believing community, as the Qur'an calls him a mercy to the worlds. | mentions 21:107

positions.position: The familiar grammatical view is that al-Rahman and al-Rahim are intensive adjectives derived from rahima after a transitivity and vowel shift.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): The familiar grammatical view is that al-Rahman and al-Rahim are intensive adjectives derived from rahima after a transitivity and vowel shift.

positions.position: A concealed metaphor pictures God as a king whose heart softens toward subjects; the word mercy then stands for one of its supposed concomitants.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): A concealed metaphor pictures God as a king whose heart softens toward subjects; the word mercy then stands for one of its supposed concomitants.

positions.position: Others distinguish by quality: Rahman covers both worlds’ great blessings, while Rahim covers lesser worldly blessings; other explanations cite divine exclusivity, foundational favors, or rhyme.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (بعضهم): Others distinguish by quality: Rahman covers both worlds’ great blessings, while Rahim covers lesser worldly blessings; other explanations cite divine exclusivity, foundational favors, or rhyme.

positions.position: Another account treats mercy in this context as a technical religious meaning rather than a figurative use.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (بعضهم): Another account treats mercy in this context as a technical religious meaning rather than a figurative use.

positions.position: He challenges the claim that Rahman is more intensive than Rahim, beginning a broader critique of deriving comparative force solely from word length.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): He challenges the claim that Rahman is more intensive than Rahim, beginning a broader critique of deriving comparative force solely from word length.

positions.position: Al-Juwayni treats Rahman and Rahim as equal in force, citing a report that God is the Merciful of this world and the next and their two mercies.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (الجويني): Al-Juwayni treats Rahman and Rahim as equal in force, citing a report that God is the Merciful of this world and the next and their two mercies.

positions.position: Another distinction makes Rahman the attribute of mercy itself and Rahim the relation of that mercy to those who receive it.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (بعضهم): Another distinction makes Rahman the attribute of mercy itself and Rahim the relation of that mercy to those who receive it. | mentions 33:43, 9:117

positions.position: Al-Alusi says greater word length does not establish greater meaning in every case; the rule is general, and examples such as hadhir and hadhir show exceptions.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Al-Alusi says greater word length does not establish greater meaning in every case; the rule is general, and examples such as hadhir and hadhir show exceptions.

positions.position: The view assigning worldly mercy to believers and unbelievers but afterlife mercy only to believers falters because afterlife blessings are vastly more numerous and unbelievers may receive some relief.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): The view assigning worldly mercy to believers and unbelievers but afterlife mercy only to believers falters because afterlife blessings are vastly more numerous and unbelievers may receive some relief. | mentions 17:79

positions.position: Reports cited include the Prophet’s intercession for all people at the praised station and reduced punishment for some damned people in the afterlife.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Reports cited include the Prophet’s intercession for all people at the praised station and reduced punishment for some damned people in the afterlife. | mentions 17:79

positions.position: Al-Alusi argues that treating unbelievers’ worldly benefits as merely apparent would also defeat the claim that worldly mercy embraces both believers and unbelievers.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Al-Alusi argues that treating unbelievers’ worldly benefits as merely apparent would also defeat the claim that worldly mercy embraces both believers and unbelievers. | mentions 3:178, 9:55

positions.position: Even a partial reduction of punishment counts as mercy in some respect, since people in Hell ask its keepers for relief and any lesser evil is easier than a greater one.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Even a partial reduction of punishment counts as mercy in some respect, since people in Hell ask its keepers for relief and any lesser evil is easier than a greater one. | mentions 40:49

positions.position: The claim that Rahman covers both worlds while Rahim covers lesser worldly blessings lacks support and conflicts with the transmitted wording naming both mercies in both worlds.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): The claim that Rahman covers both worlds while Rahim covers lesser worldly blessings lacks support and conflicts with the transmitted wording naming both mercies in both worlds.

positions.position: Ibn Hisham says the ordering question is misplaced: Rahman is a substantivized appositive, not an adjective, and Rahim modifies it rather than Allah.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (ابن هشام): Ibn Hisham says the ordering question is misplaced: Rahman is a substantivized appositive, not an adjective, and Rahim modifies it rather than Allah.

positions.position: Al-Alusi objects that assigning general existence to Rahman and individualized existence to Rahim is arbitrary, since every existent thing is already a particular share.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Al-Alusi objects that assigning general existence to Rahman and individualized existence to Rahim is arbitrary, since every existent thing is already a particular share.

positions.position: Since Rahman is heard only definite, annexed, or vocative, rare poetic evidence cannot settle its declension; Rahim does not share this ambiguity.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Since Rahman is heard only definite, annexed, or vocative, rare poetic evidence cannot settle its declension; Rahim does not share this ambiguity.

positions.position: Stopping after only bism is defective; stopping after Bismillah or after Rahman is sufficient and sound, and the complete stop follows Rahim.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Stopping after only bism is defective; stopping after Bismillah or after Rahman is sufficient and sound, and the complete stop follows Rahim.

positions.position: Beginning other important, lawful affairs with Bismillah, with or without Rahman and Rahim, is recommended, sunnah, or obligatory according to circumstances.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Beginning other important, lawful affairs with Bismillah, with or without Rahman and Rahim, is recommended, sunnah, or obligatory according to circumstances.

positions.position: For slaughter or shooting game, saying Bismillah alone is obligatory; deliberate omission makes the animal unlawful, but forgetfulness is excused.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): For slaughter or shooting game, saying Bismillah alone is obligatory; deliberate omission makes the animal unlawful, but forgetfulness is excused. | mentions 6:121

positions.position: In slaughter and similar settings, omitting Rahman and Rahim is sunnah.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): In slaughter and similar settings, omitting Rahman and Rahim is sunnah.

positions.position: Commentators distinguish Rahmān as looking to pre-eternity and Rahīm to endless duration: creatures benefit from the former through an initial relation and from the latter through actual action at the end.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Commentators distinguish Rahmān as looking to pre-eternity and Rahīm to endless duration: creatures benefit from the former through an initial relation and from the latter through actual action at the end.

positions.position: Because Rahmān is God’s exclusive name, its kind of mercy and beneficence cannot issue from creatures; Rahīm is not exclusive and can describe mercy and generosity from creatures.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Because Rahmān is God’s exclusive name, its kind of mercy and beneficence cannot issue from creatures; Rahīm is not exclusive and can describe mercy and generosity from creatures.

positions.position: Unlike Rahmān, Rahīm is a pure adjective, requires a described noun, can be used of others, functions verbally, and has a definite article of reference.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Unlike Rahmān, Rahīm is a pure adjective, requires a described noun, can be used of others, functions verbally, and has a definite article of reference.

positions.position: Under Rahman's universal grace believers and unbelievers, and this world and the next, are equal; Rahim's grace sharply distinguishes them, as the two groups in 42:7 show.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Under Rahman's universal grace believers and unbelievers, and this world and the next, are equal; Rahim's grace sharply distinguishes them, as the two groups in 42:7 show. | mentions 42:7

positions.position: Thus the inherited formulations call God Rahman of this world and the next but Rahim of the next, or Rahman of believer and unbeliever but Rahim of the believer.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Thus the inherited formulations call God Rahman of this world and the next but Rahim of the next, or Rahman of believer and unbeliever but Rahim of the believer.

positions.position: Abduh neglects the inherited distinction because he assumes the lexicon does not support it; Elmalılı says this is mistaken.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (Şeyh Abduh): Abduh neglects the inherited distinction because he assumes the lexicon does not support it; Elmalılı says this is mistaken.

positions.position: Lexically Rahman is a predominant attribute specific to God, without an active relation and suggestive of eternity and the beginning; Rahim has an active relation and continues without end.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Lexically Rahman is a predominant attribute specific to God, without an active relation and suggestive of eternity and the beginning; Rahim has an active relation and continues without end.

positions.position: Rahman's mercy is an essential attribute of willing good at the outset, while Rahim's is an active attribute of doing good at the end.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Rahman's mercy is an essential attribute of willing good at the outset, while Rahim's is an active attribute of doing good at the end.

positions.position: Rahman and Rahim are not repeated merely for emphasis: each has its own foundational meaning and distinct mode of intensification.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Rahman and Rahim are not repeated merely for emphasis: each has its own foundational meaning and distinct mode of intensification.

positions.position: Some commentaries associate Rahman's mercy with great blessings and Rahim's with the subtleties of blessings.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (Bazı tefsirler): Some commentaries associate Rahman's mercy with great blessings and Rahim's with the subtleties of blessings.

positions.position: The grammatical pattern distinguishes them: Rahman's subject is restricted while its object is general; Rahim's subject is general while its object is restricted.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): The grammatical pattern distinguishes them: Rahman's subject is restricted while its object is general; Rahim's subject is general while its object is restricted.

positions.position: If this universal grace were all, distinctions between knowledge and ignorance, life and death, effort and idleness, obedience and disobedience, and faith and unbelief would disappear.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): If this universal grace were all, distinctions between knowledge and ignorance, life and death, effort and idleness, obedience and disobedience, and faith and unbelief would disappear.

positions.position: He proposes eight possible Turkish renderings, using both lamiyya and bayaniyya forms such as Allah's name with the two attributes or Allah, Rahman, Rahim as one name.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): He proposes eight possible Turkish renderings, using both lamiyya and bayaniyya forms such as Allah's name with the two attributes or Allah, Rahman, Rahim as one name.

positions.position: Most commentators prefer the lamiyya construction because its parsing is explicit and the meanings of the names and attributes are directly intended.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (Müfessirînin çoğu): Most commentators prefer the lamiyya construction because its parsing is explicit and the meanings of the names and attributes are directly intended.

positions.position: Combining Allah with Rahman and Rahim as one name foregrounds Allah but still fails to connect the act directly with mercy.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Combining Allah with Rahman and Rahim as one name foregrounds Allah but still fails to connect the act directly with mercy.

positions.position: Rahman and Rahim together encompass every meaning and condition of mercy; God alone bears both, and alone may be called Rahman, though a servant may be called Rahim.
positions.reasons: QUTB-ZILAL (author): Rahman and Rahim together encompass every meaning and condition of mercy; God alone bears both, and alone may be called Rahman, though a servant may be called Rahim.

positions.position: Quṭb leaves aside which mercy-name has broader scope and stresses that together they cover mercy in all its meanings, conditions, and domains.
positions.reasons: QUTB-ZILAL (author): Quṭb leaves aside which mercy-name has broader scope and stresses that together they cover mercy in all its meanings, conditions, and domains.

positions.position: The Prophet transmits God's division of al-Fatiha between Himself and the servant: each phrase receives divine acknowledgement and a tailored promise of blessing, mercy, ease of judgment, reward, help, and fulfillment of the servant's requests.
positions.reasons: TABATABAI (النبي): The Prophet transmits God's division of al-Fatiha between Himself and the servant: each phrase receives divine acknowledgement and a tailored promise of blessing, mercy, ease of judgment, reward, help, and fulfillment of the servant's requests.

positions.position: Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes rahman as God's inherent, inseparable abounding grace and rahim as that grace manifested in creation.
positions.reasons: ASAD-NOTES (Ibn al-Qayyim): Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes rahman as God's inherent, inseparable abounding grace and rahim as that grace manifested in creation.

positions.position: The common Turkish rendering is Rahman and Rahim Allah’s name; because an implicit verb depends on the activity intended, the author also proposes rendering it as invoking Allah’s name and seeking His help.
positions.reasons: KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): The common Turkish rendering is Rahman and Rahim Allah’s name; because an implicit verb depends on the activity intended, the author also proposes rendering it as invoking Allah’s name and seeking His help.

positions.position: الرحمن derives from mercy.
positions.reasons: SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT (author): الرحمن derives from mercy.

turns_on: The scope, time, intensity, or recipients of the two kinds of mercy.

question: Why are the divine names ordered and paired this way?

positions.position: ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī says God’s name was al-Raḥmān, then paired it with al-Raḥīm after the impostor Musaylima appropriated al-Raḥmān.
positions.reasons: TAB (عطاء الخراساني): ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī says God’s name was al-Raḥmān, then paired it with al-Raḥīm after the impostor Musaylima appropriated al-Raḥmān. IBNATIYYA (عطاء الخراساني): Ata al-Khurasani says God paired al-Rahman with al-Rahim after Musaylima adopted the name al-Rahman, making the combination exclusive to God. IBNATIYYA-FULL (عطاء الخراساني): ʿAta al-Khurasani claims Rahman was paired with Rahim after Musaylima adopted the name Rahman, making the pairing exclusive to God.

positions.position: Ata says al-Rahman is paired with al-Rahim to distinguish God’s name from anyone else’s, since no one bears both names.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (عطاء): Ata says al-Rahman is paired with al-Rahim to distinguish God’s name from anyone else’s, since no one bears both names. MAWARDI-FULL (عطاء): He says al-Rahman was paired with al-Rahim to distinguish God's name through its intensity, since no one else called himself both names.

positions.position: Repeating descriptive epithets can magnify the one described or reinforce the meaning until it settles in the mind.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (author): Repeating descriptive epithets can magnify the one described or reinforce the meaning until it settles in the mind. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Repeating an epithet can magnify the one described or reinforce the quality so it settles in the listener's mind.

positions.position: An unnamed, weakly informed interpreter equates al-Raḥmān with “possessor of mercy” and al-Raḥīm with “merciful,” then inconsistently treats the pair as equivalent forms like nadmān and nadīm.
positions.reasons: TAB (بعض من ضعفت معرفته بتأويل أهل التأويل): An unnamed, weakly informed interpreter equates al-Raḥmān with “possessor of mercy” and al-Raḥīm with “merciful,” then inconsistently treats the pair as equivalent forms like nadmān and nadīm.

positions.position: The order puts Allah first because worship belongs to Him alone, al-Raḥmān next because it is also reserved for Him, and al-Raḥīm last because creatures may share some quality of mercy.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): The order puts Allah first because worship belongs to Him alone, al-Raḥmān next because it is also reserved for Him, and al-Raḥīm last because creatures may share some quality of mercy. | mentions 27:60, 27:61, 27:62, 27:63, 27:64, 17:110

positions.position: Ṭabarī places Allāh first because no other being shares divine worship, then al-Raḥmān, which is also reserved for God, before the shared descriptor al-Raḥīm.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): Ṭabarī places Allāh first because no other being shares divine worship, then al-Raḥmān, which is also reserved for God, before the shared descriptor al-Raḥīm.

positions.position: On the non-Arabic-word view, al-Rahim would naturally precede al-Rahman as the Arabic name, but al-Rahman is placed first because it is more intensive and the pair removes ambiguity.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (ثعلب): On the non-Arabic-word view, al-Rahim would naturally precede al-Rahman as the Arabic name, but al-Rahman is placed first because it is more intensive and the pair removes ambiguity.

positions.position: Pairing al-Rahman with al-Rahim removes ambiguity; on his theory the Arabic al-Rahim would originally come first, but al-Rahman is placed first for greater intensity.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI-FULL (ثعلب): Pairing al-Rahman with al-Rahim removes ambiguity; on his theory the Arabic al-Rahim would originally come first, but al-Rahman is placed first for greater intensity.

positions.position: If both names are Arabic, they derive from mercy; mercy is a benefit to someone in need, and a benefit is called mercy because it arises from compassion.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI-FULL (author): If both names are Arabic, they derive from mercy; mercy is a benefit to someone in need, and a benefit is called mercy because it arises from compassion.

positions.position: Because Arabs commonly knew Allah but not al-Raḥmān, the names are paired to show that Allah, al-Raḥmān, and al-Raḥīm all name and describe Him.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (author): Because Arabs commonly knew Allah but not al-Raḥmān, the names are paired to show that Allah, al-Raḥmān, and al-Raḥīm all name and describe Him.

positions.position: Al-Raḥmān precedes al-Raḥīm because its stronger intensity and exclusive use make it like a proper name, and the more definite name comes first.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (author): Al-Raḥmān precedes al-Raḥīm because its stronger intensity and exclusive use make it like a proper name, and the more definite name comes first.

positions.position: Explanations for repeating al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm: the first occurrence is outside the sūra, it first seeks aid and the second assigns praise to God, or the repetition emphasizes mercy.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (author): Explanations for repeating al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm: the first occurrence is outside the sūra, it first seeks aid and the second assigns praise to God, or the repetition emphasizes mercy.

positions.position: ʿAlī b. ʿĪsā denies mere repetition: the first occurrence links servitude to blessings warranting worship, the second links praise to blessings warranting praise.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (علي بن عيسى): ʿAlī b. ʿĪsā denies mere repetition: the first occurrence links servitude to blessings warranting worship, the second links praise to blessings warranting praise.

positions.position: Though the usual diptote condition requires feminine faʿla, exclusivity does not remove the base pattern; faʿlana is also barred.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF (author): Though the usual diptote condition requires feminine faʿla, exclusivity does not remove the base pattern; faʿlana is also barred.

positions.position: Rahman precedes rahim though the usual order rises from lesser to greater: it covers great foundational blessings, then rahim adds subtle ones.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF (author): Rahman precedes rahim though the usual order rises from lesser to greater: it covers great foundational blessings, then rahim adds subtle ones.

positions.position: Rahman precedes Rahim because Rahman functions like a proper name exclusive to God, while Rahim can describe others too.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (author): Rahman precedes Rahim because Rahman functions like a proper name exclusive to God, while Rahim can describe others too.

positions.position: Al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm are genitive as adjectives of the first genitive noun; nominative is possible with an implied 'He is,' and accusative with an implied 'I mean.'
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm are genitive as adjectives of the first genitive noun; nominative is possible with an implied 'He is,' and accusative with an implied 'I mean.'

positions.position: Al-Mubarrad claims al-Raḥmān is Hebrew paired with Arabic al-Raḥīm; Qurṭubī rejects the claim.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (المبرد): Al-Mubarrad claims al-Raḥmān is Hebrew paired with Arabic al-Raḥīm; Qurṭubī rejects the claim.

positions.position: Qatāda says the basmala is God praising Himself; al-Zajjāj approves it as adjectival praise.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (قتادة): Qatāda says the basmala is God praising Himself; al-Zajjāj approves it as adjectival praise.

positions.position: Quṭrub says al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm are paired for emphasis; al-Zajjāj approves this rhetoric.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (قطرب): Quṭrub says al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm are paired for emphasis; al-Zajjāj approves this rhetoric.

positions.position: Al-Raḥīm can describe creatures; al-Raḥmān precedes it because it is more comprehensive, matching Qurʾānic order.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (author): Al-Raḥīm can describe creatures; al-Raḥmān precedes it because it is more comprehensive, matching Qurʾānic order.

positions.position: الرحمن points to the great blessings; الرحيم then includes the blessings left out and may also preserve the verse endings.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL (author): الرحمن points to the great blessings; الرحيم then includes the blessings left out and may also preserve the verse endings.

positions.position: Rahman is uniquely used as a name but broad in meaning; rahim can describe others but is specific to believers. Rahman therefore precedes the more intense form despite the usual progression from lesser to greater.
positions.reasons: NASAFI (author): Rahman is uniquely used as a name but broad in meaning; rahim can describe others but is specific to believers. Rahman therefore precedes the more intense form despite the usual progression from lesser to greater.

positions.position: Rahman describes mercy encompassing all creation, believer and unbeliever, especially in this world; Rahim describes mercy particular to believers in the hereafter, explaining the supplicatory usage and the order of the names.
positions.reasons: NASAFI-FULL (author): Rahman describes mercy encompassing all creation, believer and unbeliever, especially in this world; Rahim describes mercy particular to believers in the hereafter, explaining the supplicatory usage and the order of the names.

positions.position: Rahman is restricted as a name to God but universal in meaning, while Rahim can describe others and is particular in its referent; Rahman is nevertheless placed first despite its greater force.
positions.reasons: NASAFI-FULL (author): Rahman is restricted as a name to God but universal in meaning, while Rahim can describe others and is particular in its referent; Rahman is nevertheless placed first despite its greater force.

positions.position: Because Allah is the proper name encompassing the beautiful names, al-Raḥmān precedes al-Raḥīm: it is exclusive to Him and more intensive, so the stronger description comes first.
positions.reasons: BIQAI (author): Because Allah is the proper name encompassing the beautiful names, al-Raḥmān precedes al-Raḥīm: it is exclusive to Him and more intensive, so the stronger description comes first.

positions.position: Allah is a proper name encompassing all beautiful names; Rahman precedes Rahim because it is exclusive and more emphatic, following the order of existence, general mercy, then worship-specific mercy.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (author): Allah is a proper name encompassing all beautiful names; Rahman precedes Rahim because it is exclusive and more emphatic, following the order of existence, general mercy, then worship-specific mercy.

positions.position: Proposed reasons for placing al-Raḥmān first include its encompassing major blessings, al-Raḥīm completing lesser ones, or preserving verse-end rhyme; al-Ālūsī rejects rhyme alone.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Proposed reasons for placing al-Raḥmān first include its encompassing major blessings, al-Raḥīm completing lesser ones, or preserving verse-end rhyme; al-Ālūsī rejects rhyme alone.

positions.position: The scholar of al-Kashf says the sequence follows a descending order: Allah names the essence, Rahman universal mercy and existence, and Rahim each being’s particular share and perfections.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (العلامة المدقق في الكشف): The scholar of al-Kashf says the sequence follows a descending order: Allah names the essence, Rahman universal mercy and existence, and Rahim each being’s particular share and perfections.

positions.position: Humans cannot assign a direct proper name before experiencing a manifestation of the essence; the Qurʾān first introduces God through name-manifestations, and Rahmān and Rahīm initially unfold the name Allah.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Humans cannot assign a direct proper name before experiencing a manifestation of the essence; the Qurʾān first introduces God through name-manifestations, and Rahmān and Rahīm initially unfold the name Allah.

positions.position: The phrase moves from the pure name Allah to the name-and-attribute Rahmān and then the pure attribute Rahīm, gradually unfolding God’s name in the heart as the first manifestation of divine beauty.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): The phrase moves from the pure name Allah to the name-and-attribute Rahmān and then the pure attribute Rahīm, gradually unfolding God’s name in the heart as the first manifestation of divine beauty.

positions.position: Al-Bayḍāwī says the supplicant names God’s essence to show aid is sought from Him, then invokes al-Raḥmān for His favors and al-Raḥīm for further reasons discussed later.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (البيضاوي): Al-Bayḍāwī says the supplicant names God’s essence to show aid is sought from Him, then invokes al-Raḥmān for His favors and al-Raḥīm for further reasons discussed later.

positions.position: The order Allāh, al-Raḥmān, al-Raḥīm can symbolize Essence, unity of Attributes, and unity of divine acts, respectively.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (author): The order Allāh, al-Raḥmān, al-Raḥīm can symbolize Essence, unity of Attributes, and unity of divine acts, respectively.

question: Is the basmala a verse of al-Fātiḥa?

positions.position: The basmala is a verse of al-Fātiḥa.
positions.reasons: TAB (عظم أهل الكوفة): Most Kufan authorities count basmala as one of Fātiḥa’s seven verses; also transmitted from Companions and Successors. THALABI (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the seven oft-repeated verses as al-Fātiḥa and counts the basmala as its seventh verse. | mentions 15:87 IBNATIYYA (الشافعي): Al-Shafi'i counts the basmala as a verse of al-Fatiha. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): The Jabir and Abu Hurayra reports would imply that the basmala is a verse of al-Fatiha if sound. RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Tha‘labi transmits a version in which the Prophet counted the basmala as a complete verse of al-Fatiha; when reports conflict, affirmation outweighs omission. QURTUBI (الشافعي): Al-Shāfiʿī counts the basmala in al-Fātiḥa but has two positions about other sūras. BAYDAWI-FULL (أم سلمة): Umm Salama reports that the Prophet counted the basmala as a verse when reciting al-Fātiḥa. IBNKATHIR (أم سلمة): A report from Umm Salama says the Prophet recited and counted the basmala as a verse at the start of the Fatiha; Ibn Kathir notes the chain is weak because of ʿUmar ibn Harun. BURHAN (author): Al-Shafiʿi counts the basmala and makes the rest of 1:7 one verse; Abu Hanifa omits the basmala and divides its two phrases. Both count seven verses, but al-Shafiʿi's division better preserves the endings because anʿamta ʿalayhim does not match prior endings. DURR (النبي): The Prophet says to recite the basmala with al-Hamd, calls al-Fatiha the Mother of the Qur'an and seven oft-repeated verses, and counts the basmala as an ayah. DURR (علي): Ali identifies al-Hamd as the seven oft-repeated verses and counts the basmala as the seventh ayah. DURR (أم سلمة): Umm Salama says the Prophet recited al-Fatiha verse by verse and counted the basmala as an ayah. DURR-FULL (محمد بن كعب القرظي): Muhammad ibn Kab al-Qurazi counts the basmala as part of al-Fatiha's seven verses. ITQAN (أم سلمة): Umm Salama reports that the Prophet recited al-Fatiha verse by verse, counted the basmala as a verse, and did not count “ʿalayhim”; al-Suyuti says this supports the majority's seven-verse count. ITQAN (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): Umm Salama reports that the Prophet counted the basmala as a verse in his recitation of the opening sūra, but did not count عليهم as one. ALUSI (بعض الشافعية وحمزة): Some Shāfiʿīs and Ḥamza, with a view attributed to Aḥmad, count the basmala as a verse of al-Fātiḥa alone. ALUSI (أم سلمة): A report attributed to Umm Salama has the Prophet count the basmala as al-Fātiḥa’s first verse; al-Ālūsī questions the chain because Abū Mulayka’s hearing from her is unestablished. ALUSI (ابن خزيمة والحاكم): Their version has the Prophet count the basmala as a verse while reciting in prayer; al-Ālūsī reads it as the first Qurʾānic verse, not necessarily al-Fātiḥa’s. ALUSI-FULL (أم سلمة): A report attributed to Umm Salama has the Prophet count the basmala as the first Fatiha verse and the following phrases as the next verses. ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi presents Razi's eighth proof: Shafii counts the basmala, while Abu Hanifa counts sirat alladhina anamta alayhim; Razi calls the Hanafi count weak and says seven verses require the basmala.

positions.position: The basmala is not a verse of al-Fātiḥa.
