positions.reasons: TAB (عظم قرأة أهل المدينة ومتقنيهم): Most leading Medinan reciters exclude basmala from the seven and count those You favored as seventh verse. TAB-FULL (author): Ṭabarī argues the basmala is not a verse of the Opening: otherwise al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm would repeat immediately, word for word and sense for sense, without an intervening divider. KASHSHAF (قراء المدينة والبصرة والشام وفقهاؤها): Medina, Basra, and Syrian readers and jurists hold that the basmala is not a verse of al-Fatiha or any surah. QURTUBI (مالك): Mālik says the basmala is not a verse of al-Fātiḥa or other sūras, though it is Qurʾān in al-Naml. | mentions 27:30 QURTUBI (author): Since the basmala is not an al-Fātiḥa verse on the preferred view, prayer moves directly from takbīr to al-Fātiḥa without pause or opening supplication. NASAFI (author): Since the division report begins with al-hamdu lillah, Nasafi takes it as evidence that the basmala is not part of the Fatiha; he says it is not part of another sura either, by consensus. | mentions 1:2 NASAFI-FULL (author): The report begins God's response when the servant says “Praise belongs to God,” which indicates the basmala is not part of al-Fatiha; if it is outside al-Fatiha, consensus excludes it from other surahs too. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (مكي): Makkī argues that repeating raḥmān-raḥīm proves the basmala is not a Fātiḥa verse, since two adjacent verses with the same sense would lack a separating ending. IBNKATHIR (مالك وأبو حنيفة وأصحابهما): Malik, Abu Hanifa, and their followers say the basmala is not a verse of the Fatiha or any other surah. ELMALILI (author): The Shāfiʿī argument concludes that even if the basmala is not a whole verse of al-Fātiḥa, it is part of a verse, making its recitation obligatory and audible in prayer.

positions.position: The basmala is an independent Qurʾānic verse outside al-Fātiḥa.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (داود وأحمد): Dawud and one narration from Ahmad treat the basmala as an independent opening verse of each surah, not part of the surahs. IBNKATHIR (author): Scholars differ over whether the basmala is an independent opening verse, part of a verse, or not counted as part of the Fatiha. ALUSI (author): Al-Ālūsī says the Hanafi position treats the basmala as an independent Qurʾānic verse, not part of al-Fātiḥa, while many Hanafis require its recitation in prayer. ALUSI-FULL (ابن عباس): The statement identifying the Fatiha's seventh verse as the basmala is Ibn Abbas's own, not necessarily a Prophetic report; he may have reasoned that an independent Qur'anic verse belongs in the Fatiha. ELMALILI (author): The sound Ḥanafī position reconciles the other arguments: each opening basmala is an independent Qurʾānic verse, revealed to separate surahs and for blessing, and belongs to none of them. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): Since the Qur’an’s collection excluded non-Qur’anic material, each surah-opening basmala is a separate verse outside that surah’s verse count; the author says Hanafi jurists agree.

positions.position: The report says the Prophet recited the Fātiḥa verse by verse, counting seven, including the basmala.
positions.reasons: THALABI (مسلمة): The report says the Prophet recited the Fātiḥa verse by verse, counting seven, including the basmala. DURR (أم سلمة): Umm Salama reports the Prophet recited the full seven-verse al-Fatiha beginning with the basmala. DURR-FULL (أم سلمة): The Prophet recited al-Fatiha one verse at a time and counted the basmala among its verses.

positions.position: All agree al-Fatiha has seven verses: those counting the basmala begin the final verse at “the path of those”; those excluding it begin the first at “praise be to God” and the last at “not those angered.”
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI (author): All agree al-Fatiha has seven verses: those counting the basmala begin the final verse at “the path of those”; those excluding it begin the first at “praise be to God” and the last at “not those angered.” BAGHAWI-FULL (author): All agree the Fatiha has seven verses, but those counting the basmala begin the final verse at ‘those You favored’; others begin it at ‘not those under wrath.’

positions.position: Ibn ʿAbbas, through Saʿid ibn Jubayr, identifies the basmala as the seventh verse of the seven oft-repeated, saying God reserved it for this community; it supports counting it in al-Fatiha.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbas, through Saʿid ibn Jubayr, identifies the basmala as the seventh verse of the seven oft-repeated, saying God reserved it for this community; it supports counting it in al-Fatiha. | mentions 15:87 RAZI-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas identifies the seven oft-repeated verses as al-Fatiha and answers that its seventh verse is the basmala. | mentions 15:87

positions.position: Poetry by Jarīr and Qurʾān 18:2 illustrate fronting and delaying in Arabic; the apparent order can place the “upright” description before its intended antecedent.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): Poetry by Jarīr and Qurʾān 18:2 illustrate fronting and delaying in Arabic; the apparent order can place the “upright” description before its intended antecedent. | mentions 18:2

positions.position: These reorderings support the interpreters who deny that the basmala belongs to the Opening as a verse.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): These reorderings support the interpreters who deny that the basmala belongs to the Opening as a verse.

positions.position: Abū Hurayra says readers of the Mother of the Qurʾān should not leave the basmala because it is one of its verses and part of the seven oft-repeated.
positions.reasons: THALABI (أبو هريرة): Abū Hurayra says readers of the Mother of the Qurʾān should not leave the basmala because it is one of its verses and part of the seven oft-repeated.

positions.position: The Prophet tells a man who began reciting al-ḥamdu without the basmala that he cut off his prayer: leaving out this verse cuts off the Fātiḥa and invalidates the prayer.
positions.reasons: THALABI (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): The Prophet tells a man who began reciting al-ḥamdu without the basmala that he cut off his prayer: leaving out this verse cuts off the Fātiḥa and invalidates the prayer.

positions.position: Al-Zuhrī calls reciting the basmala in the Fātiḥa part of prayer’s sunnah and says one who omits it has not recited the sura; he names ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd as the first to abandon it in Medina.
positions.reasons: THALABI (الزهري): Al-Zuhrī calls reciting the basmala in the Fātiḥa part of prayer’s sunnah and says one who omits it has not recited the sura; he names ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd as the first to abandon it in Medina.

positions.position: Those counting the basmala cite its Quranic-script placement and a report from Ibn Abbas through Saʿid b. Jubayr: it is the seventh of the seven oft-repeated verses.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI-FULL (author): Those counting the basmala cite its Quranic-script placement and a report from Ibn Abbas through Saʿid b. Jubayr: it is the seventh of the seven oft-repeated verses. | mentions 15:87

positions.position: In the same report, Ibn Abbas says the basmala was reserved for this community and not disclosed to anyone before it.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI-FULL (ابن عباس): In the same report, Ibn Abbas says the basmala was reserved for this community and not disclosed to anyone before it. | mentions 15:87

positions.position: Ibn Atiyya says that, on their face, the Jabir and Abu Hurayra reports imply the basmala is an ayah of al-Fatiha.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (author): Ibn Atiyya says that, on their face, the Jabir and Abu Hurayra reports imply the basmala is an ayah of al-Fatiha.

positions.position: Many Meccan and Kufan reciters do not count an'amta alayhim as a verse.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (قراء مكة والكوفة): Many Meccan and Kufan reciters do not count an'amta alayhim as a verse.

positions.position: Jaʿfar calls the basmala the crowns of the suras.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (جعفر بن محمد الصادق): Jaʿfar calls the basmala the crowns of the suras.

positions.position: Seven verses is the agreed count; the six-verse count from Husayn al-Juʿfi and eight-verse count from ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd are anomalous, with 15:87 decisive.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): Seven verses is the agreed count; the six-verse count from Husayn al-Juʿfi and eight-verse count from ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd are anomalous, with 15:87 decisive. | mentions 15:87, 1:5

positions.position: ʿAli ibn al-Husayn explains mentioning God alone in 17:46 as saying the basmala.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (علي بن الحسين): ʿAli ibn al-Husayn explains mentioning God alone in 17:46 as saying the basmala. | mentions 17:46

positions.position: The sound report of Ubay ibn Kaʿb undermines counting the basmala as part of al-Fatiha: the Prophet elicited the sura beginning with al-hamdu.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): The sound report of Ubay ibn Kaʿb undermines counting the basmala as part of al-Fatiha: the Prophet elicited the sura beginning with al-hamdu.

positions.position: Razi calls the report from Umm Salama an explicit text supporting the basmala inclusion in al-Fatiha.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi calls the report from Umm Salama an explicit text supporting the basmala inclusion in al-Fatiha.

positions.position: Umm Salama reports that the Prophet recited al-Fatiha while counting the basmala as its first verse, followed by the rest of its verses.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أم سلمة عن النبي): Umm Salama reports that the Prophet recited al-Fatiha while counting the basmala as its first verse, followed by the rest of its verses.

positions.position: Razi argues that if reading the basmala at the start of al-Fatiha is obligatory, it must be one of its verses; Quran 96:1 commands reading in God's name and the letter has meaning.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi argues that if reading the basmala at the start of al-Fatiha is obligatory, it must be one of its verses; Quran 96:1 commands reading in God's name and the letter has meaning. | mentions 96:1

positions.position: The seven-verse count supports al-Shafi'i's division, with the basmala as one verse and the final phrase as one; Abu Hanifa denies the basmala verse and splits that final phrase, a weak view for Razi.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The seven-verse count supports al-Shafi'i's division, with the basmala as one verse and the final phrase as one; Abu Hanifa denies the basmala verse and splits that final phrase, a weak view for Razi.

positions.position: Because Abu Hanifa agrees the basmala is preferable and the Prophet likely recited it, following him makes it obligatory; with no accepted distinction, it must be part of al-Fatiha.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Because Abu Hanifa agrees the basmala is preferable and the Prophet likely recited it, following him makes it obligatory; with no accepted distinction, it must be part of al-Fatiha. | mentions 7:158

positions.position: Another report says the Prophet rebuked a worshipper who began al-Fatiha without the basmala: omitting a verse cuts the prayer, which is invalid without the whole surah.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أبو هريرة عن النبي): Another report says the Prophet rebuked a worshipper who began al-Fatiha without the basmala: omitting a verse cuts the prayer, which is invalid without the whole surah.

positions.position: Since inclusion settles disputed ritual rules more cautiously, he favors it under the Prophetic maxim to leave doubtful matters for secure ones.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Since inclusion settles disputed ritual rules more cautiously, he favors it under the Prophetic maxim to leave doubtful matters for secure ones.

positions.position: The verse-count objection disappears if the basmala and the words after it form one verse; a complete verse in al-Fatiha can be part of a longer verse elsewhere, and al-Kawthar’s count covers its distinctive content.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The verse-count objection disappears if the basmala and the words after it form one verse; a complete verse in al-Fatiha can be part of a longer verse elsewhere, and al-Kawthar’s count covers its distinctive content. | mentions 10:10

positions.position: Mālik’s practice is al-Fātiḥa plus a sūra in the first two units and al-Fātiḥa alone in the final units.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (مالك): Mālik’s practice is al-Fātiḥa plus a sūra in the first two units and al-Fātiḥa alone in the final units.

positions.position: Other authorities require some additional Qurʾān with al-Fātiḥa, setting one verse, two verses, or no minimum.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (عمران بن حصين وأبو سعيد الخدري وخوات بن جبير): Other authorities require some additional Qurʾān with al-Fātiḥa, setting one verse, two verses, or no minimum.

positions.position: Al-Shāfiʿī cites a report from Abū Hurayra explicitly calling the basmala one of al-Fātiḥa’s verses.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (أبو هريرة): Al-Shāfiʿī cites a report from Abū Hurayra explicitly calling the basmala one of al-Fātiḥa’s verses.

positions.position: Al-Shāfiʿī preferred ʿAlī’s report that the Prophet said “I have turned my face” after the opening takbīr; Muslim records it.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (علي): Al-Shāfiʿī preferred ʿAlī’s report that the Prophet said “I have turned my face” after the opening takbīr; Muslim records it.

positions.position: Abū Ḥayyān rejects Makkī's rearrangement argument as flawed and says the Qur'anic order is eloquent, linking lordship to judgment and mercy to worship.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Abū Ḥayyān rejects Makkī's rearrangement argument as flawed and says the Qur'anic order is eloquent, linking lordship to judgment and mercy to worship.

positions.position: The opening is especially elegant whether the basmala is counted as the first verse or “Praise be to God” is; both begin the discourse fittingly.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): The opening is especially elegant whether the basmala is counted as the first verse or “Praise be to God” is; both begin the discourse fittingly.

positions.position: One Shafiʿi position makes the basmala a verse of the Fatiha alone; another makes it part of the first verse of every surah, and Ibn Kathir calls both views unusual.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (الشافعي): One Shafiʿi position makes the basmala a verse of the Fatiha alone; another makes it part of the first verse of every surah, and Ibn Kathir calls both views unusual.

positions.position: Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna calls the surah al-Waqiya, the protecting one.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (سفيان بن عيينة): Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna calls the surah al-Waqiya, the protecting one.

positions.position: Umm Salama says the Prophet paused phrase by phrase in recitation, and al-Daraqutni calls the report's chain sound.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (أم سلمة): Umm Salama says the Prophet paused phrase by phrase in recitation, and al-Daraqutni calls the report's chain sound.

positions.position: Yahya ibn Abi Kathir calls it al-Kafiya: it suffices in place of other surahs, while none can replace it; this is also stated in a mursal report.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (يحيى بن أبي كثير): Yahya ibn Abi Kathir calls it al-Kafiya: it suffices in place of other surahs, while none can replace it; this is also stated in a mursal report.

positions.position: Al-Bayhaqi reports that ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, and Abu Hurayra interpret the seven oft-repeated in 15:87 as the Fatiha, with the basmala its seventh verse.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (علي وابن عباس وأبو هريرة): Al-Bayhaqi reports that ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, and Abu Hurayra interpret the seven oft-repeated in 15:87 as the Fatiha, with the basmala its seventh verse. | mentions 15:87

positions.position: The basmala is counted differently because it came as part of a verse in some readings; readers of those modes count it, while others omit it and count a replacement after اهدنا to keep al-Fatiha seven verses.
positions.reasons: BURHAN (author): The basmala is counted differently because it came as part of a verse in some readings; readers of those modes count it, while others omit it and count a replacement after اهدنا to keep al-Fatiha seven verses. | mentions 27:30, 1:6

positions.position: Abu Sa'id recited al-Fatiha seven times over a scorpion-stung chief who recovered; the Prophet approved the healing and allowed the sheep payment.
positions.reasons: DURR (النبي): Abu Sa'id recited al-Fatiha seven times over a scorpion-stung chief who recovered; the Prophet approved the healing and allowed the sheep payment.

positions.position: Al-Hasan counts al-Fatiha as eight verses by including both the basmala and “anʿamta ʿalayhim.”
positions.reasons: ITQAN (الحسن): Al-Hasan counts al-Fatiha as eight verses by including both the basmala and “anʿamta ʿalayhim.”

positions.position: Some count al-Fatiha as six verses by counting neither the basmala nor “anʿamta ʿalayhim.”
positions.reasons: ITQAN (بعضهم): Some count al-Fatiha as six verses by counting neither the basmala nor “anʿamta ʿalayhim.”

positions.position: Another view counts al-Fatiha as nine verses, including both the basmala and “iyyāka naʿbud.”
positions.reasons: ITQAN (آخر): Another view counts al-Fatiha as nine verses, including both the basmala and “iyyāka naʿbud.”

positions.position: Treating the basmala merely as a separator between sūras is an unsafe claim; if that were its sole function, it would not appear between al-Anfal and Bara'a.
positions.reasons: ITQAN (author): Treating the basmala merely as a separator between sūras is an unsafe claim; if that were its sole function, it would not appear between al-Anfal and Bara'a.

positions.position: A weak report through Burayda has the Prophet identify the basmala as the verse given to him after Solomon and recited at the opening of prayer.
positions.reasons: ITQAN (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): A weak report through Burayda has the Prophet identify the basmala as the verse given to him after Solomon and recited at the opening of prayer.

positions.position: A report says al-Fātiḥa equals two-thirds of the Qurʾān; al-Ālūsī disputes al-Shihāb’s reward-based explanation that the summary’s concision supplies a third.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): A report says al-Fātiḥa equals two-thirds of the Qurʾān; al-Ālūsī disputes al-Shihāb’s reward-based explanation that the summary’s concision supplies a third.

positions.position: Al-Dailamī’s report from Abū al-Dardāʾ says al-Fātiḥa outweighs the Qurʾān sevenfold on the scale; al-Ālūsī says its apparent reward claim challenges that explanation.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (أبو الدرداء): Al-Dailamī’s report from Abū al-Dardāʾ says al-Fātiḥa outweighs the Qurʾān sevenfold on the scale; al-Ālūsī says its apparent reward claim challenges that explanation.

positions.position: He suggests reconciling the virtue reports through increased later reward, differing circumstances, an inclusive use of equals, or Qurʾān meaning prayer as in 17:78.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): He suggests reconciling the virtue reports through increased later reward, differing circumstances, an inclusive use of equals, or Qurʾān meaning prayer as in 17:78. | mentions 17:78

positions.position: Al-Zaylaʿī and al-Zāhidī report the sound Hanafi view as obligation, including each rakʿa with obligatory recitation; Ibn Wahbān prescribes prostration for forgetful omission.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (الزيلعي والزهيدي وابن وهبان): Al-Zaylaʿī and al-Zāhidī report the sound Hanafi view as obligation, including each rakʿa with obligatory recitation; Ibn Wahbān prescribes prostration for forgetful omission.

positions.position: They transmit Umm Salama’s report that the Prophet paused verse by verse, beginning with the basmala; al-Ālūsī says this proves its Qurʾānic status, not its membership in al-Fātiḥa.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (أبو عبيد وأحمد وأبو داود): They transmit Umm Salama’s report that the Prophet paused verse by verse, beginning with the basmala; al-Ālūsī says this proves its Qurʾānic status, not its membership in al-Fātiḥa.

positions.position: Abū Hurayra reports that the Prophet asked Ubayy the Qurʾān’s greatest verse; Ubayy answered the basmala and the Prophet affirmed it, proving a verse but not its place in al-Fātiḥa.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (أبي بن كعب): Abū Hurayra reports that the Prophet asked Ubayy the Qurʾān’s greatest verse; Ubayy answered the basmala and the Prophet affirmed it, proving a verse but not its place in al-Fātiḥa.

positions.position: Al-Ālūsī’s central reply to al-Rāzī is that obligation, Qurʾānic writing, and being an independent verse do not entail that the basmala is part of al-Fātiḥa.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Al-Ālūsī’s central reply to al-Rāzī is that obligation, Qurʾānic writing, and being an independent verse do not entail that the basmala is part of al-Fātiḥa.

positions.position: The command “read in your Lord’s name” does not prove the basmala is part of al-Fātiḥa; the verse’s context concerns reading itself, and obligation does not entail inclusion.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): The command “read in your Lord’s name” does not prove the basmala is part of al-Fātiḥa; the verse’s context concerns reading itself, and obligation does not entail inclusion. | mentions 96:1

positions.position: Its appearance in Qurʾānic script is al-Rāzī’s strongest evidence that it is Qurʾān, but it still does not show that it is part of al-Fātiḥa.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Its appearance in Qurʾānic script is al-Rāzī’s strongest evidence that it is Qurʾān, but it still does not show that it is part of al-Fātiḥa.

positions.position: The verse about following earlier prophets does not establish a binding basmala formula for Muhammad or prove that formula’s membership in al-Fātiḥa.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): The verse about following earlier prophets does not establish a binding basmala formula for Muhammad or prove that formula’s membership in al-Fātiḥa. | mentions 6:90, 7:158

positions.position: Some Shafi'is, Hamza, and a view attributed to Ahmad count it as a verse of the Fatiha alone.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Some Shafi'is, Hamza, and a view attributed to Ahmad count it as a verse of the Fatiha alone.

positions.position: Medinese including Malik, Syrians including al-Awza'i, and Basrans including Abu Amr and Ya'qub follow the fifth position.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Medinese including Malik, Syrians including al-Awza'i, and Basrans including Abu Amr and Ya'qub follow the fifth position.

positions.position: Alusi explains his shift from Shafi'i sympathies to Hanafi doctrine and undertakes to defend his school against Fakhr al-Razi's sixteen proofs that the basmala is a Fatiha verse.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi explains his shift from Shafi'i sympathies to Hanafi doctrine and undertakes to defend his school against Fakhr al-Razi's sixteen proofs that the basmala is a Fatiha verse.

positions.position: Abu Musa, through his son Abu Burda, reports the Prophet identifying the basmala as the special verse not given to anyone after Solomon and asking about the prayer's opening.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (النبي): Abu Musa, through his son Abu Burda, reports the Prophet identifying the basmala as the special verse not given to anyone after Solomon and asking about the prayer's opening. | mentions 27:30

positions.position: Razi argues that the command to read in God's name and the meaningful ba make reciting the basmala obligatory, hence part of the Fatiha.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (الفخر الرازي): Razi argues that the command to read in God's name and the meaningful ba make reciting the basmala obligatory, hence part of the Fatiha. | mentions 96:1

positions.position: Razi argues that obligatory basmala recitation before the Fatiha, following the Prophet, makes it part of the sura.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (الفخر الرازي): Razi argues that obligatory basmala recitation before the Fatiha, following the Prophet, makes it part of the sura. | mentions 7:158

positions.position: Alusi says Razi's proofs do not establish Fatiha membership: the Hanafi position accepts the basmala as an independent Qur'anic verse, and many Hanafis require its prayer recitation.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi says Razi's proofs do not establish Fatiha membership: the Hanafi position accepts the basmala as an independent Qur'anic verse, and many Hanafis require its prayer recitation.

positions.position: Razi argues that the Prophet called the basmala the Qur'an's greatest verse, so it must be a complete verse in the Fatiha rather than only in al-Naml.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (الفخر الرازي): Razi argues that the Prophet called the basmala the Qur'an's greatest verse, so it must be a complete verse in the Fatiha rather than only in al-Naml. | mentions 27:30

positions.position: Razi argues that earlier prophets began good works with God's name, so Muhammad and his followers should do likewise, citing the commands to follow their guidance and the Prophet.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (الفخر الرازي): Razi argues that earlier prophets began good works with God's name, so Muhammad and his followers should do likewise, citing the commands to follow their guidance and the Prophet. | mentions 11:41, 27:30, 6:90, 7:158

positions.position: Razi reasons that God, being eternal, should be mentioned before created beings; the required precedence supports reciting the basmala as a Fatiha verse.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (الفخر الرازي): Razi reasons that God, being eternal, should be mentioned before created beings; the required precedence supports reciting the basmala as a Fatiha verse.

positions.position: Razi says repeated revelation and the Prophet's instruction to write the formula in the muṣḥaf, together with precautionary hadith, require accepting its recitation and handling rulings.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (الفخر الرازي): Razi says repeated revelation and the Prophet's instruction to write the formula in the muṣḥaf, together with precautionary hadith, require accepting its recitation and handling rulings.

positions.position: Alusi interprets the first Abu Hurayra wording as seven verses from al-Hamdu lillah to the end, while the basmala is one Qur'anic verse; his reading preserves the Hanafi view.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi interprets the first Abu Hurayra wording as seven verses from al-Hamdu lillah to the end, while the basmala is one Qur'anic verse; his reading preserves the Hanafi view.

positions.position: Ibn Khuzayma and al-Hakim transmit a count that treats the basmala as one verse and al-Hamdu lillah as the next; Alusi says it still does not prove Fatiha membership.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Ibn Khuzayma and al-Hakim transmit a count that treats the basmala as one verse and al-Hamdu lillah as the next; Alusi says it still does not prove Fatiha membership.

positions.position: Alusi says the first two pause reports illustrate recitation practice and prove only that the basmala is a Qur'anic verse, not that it belongs to the Fatiha.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi says the first two pause reports illustrate recitation practice and prove only that the basmala is a Qur'anic verse, not that it belongs to the Fatiha.

positions.position: The Ibn Khuzayma version counts the basmala as the Qur'an's first verse and al-Hamdu lillah as its second, without specifying the Fatiha.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): The Ibn Khuzayma version counts the basmala as the Qur'an's first verse and al-Hamdu lillah as its second, without specifying the Fatiha.

positions.position: Alusi says matching verse lengths and end-rhymes is desirable but not required, and separating a described word from its qualification across verses has precedent.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi says matching verse lengths and end-rhymes is desirable but not required, and separating a described word from its qualification across verses has precedent.

positions.position: Alusi construes Abu Hurayra's wording as a rhetorical clarification that the basmala is one Qur'anic verse, not one of the Fatiha's verses; the report's opening can retain its literal sense on this reading.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi construes Abu Hurayra's wording as a rhetorical clarification that the basmala is one Qur'anic verse, not one of the Fatiha's verses; the report's opening can retain its literal sense on this reading.

positions.position: Alusi calls inscription in Qur'anic script the strongest proof that the basmala is Qur'an, but says it does not prove that it is part of the Fatiha.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi calls inscription in Qur'anic script the strongest proof that the basmala is Qur'an, but says it does not prove that it is part of the Fatiha.

positions.position: Alusi says Razi's seventh proof works for Hanafis, since they too accept that the text between the covers includes the basmala as Qur'an.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi says Razi's seventh proof works for Hanafis, since they too accept that the text between the covers includes the basmala as Qur'an.

positions.position: He says Razi's eighth proof depends on first proving Abu Hanifa's verse division weak, a claim Alusi regards as formidable to establish.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): He says Razi's eighth proof depends on first proving Abu Hanifa's verse division weak, a claim Alusi regards as formidable to establish.

positions.position: Alusi accepts Razi's third proof only for the basmala's Qur'anic status, a point Hanafis do not dispute.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi accepts Razi's third proof only for the basmala's Qur'anic status, a point Hanafis do not dispute.

positions.position: Alusi says several reports in Razi's fourth argument are weak and in any case do not establish that the basmala is part of the Fatiha.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi says several reports in Razi's fourth argument are weak and in any case do not establish that the basmala is part of the Fatiha.

positions.position: Alusi calls the seventh prayer-interruption report fabricated in style and says its missing chain and absence from Shafi'i's leading proofs further undermine it.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi calls the seventh prayer-interruption report fabricated in style and says its missing chain and absence from Shafi'i's leading proofs further undermine it.

positions.position: Alusi says Razi's fifth argument wrongly infers Fatiha membership from the obligation to recite the basmala and misuses the command in al-Alaq.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi says Razi's fifth argument wrongly infers Fatiha membership from the obligation to recite the basmala and misuses the command in al-Alaq. | mentions 96:1

positions.position: Razi's tenth argument does not establish a Fatiha verse against Hanafis, since Alusi has already explained their doctrine.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Razi's tenth argument does not establish a Fatiha verse against Hanafis, since Alusi has already explained their doctrine.

positions.position: Alusi says Razi's appeal to following earlier prophets misreads Qur'anic exegesis and Prophetic reports, and obligation still would not prove that the basmala is part of the Fatiha.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi says Razi's appeal to following earlier prophets misreads Qur'anic exegesis and Prophetic reports, and obligation still would not prove that the basmala is part of the Fatiha. | mentions 6:90

positions.position: Alusi dismisses Razi's thirteenth proof and says the remaining arguments cannot establish the disputed point.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi dismisses Razi's thirteenth proof and says the remaining arguments cannot establish the disputed point.

positions.position: Alusi prefers this stronger Muslim report over al-Thalabi's versions: its seven-verse count starts with al-Hamdu lillah and leaves the basmala outside the Fatiha, while not denying its Qur'anic status.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi prefers this stronger Muslim report over al-Thalabi's versions: its seven-verse count starts with al-Hamdu lillah and leaves the basmala outside the Fatiha, while not denying its Qur'anic status.

positions.position: Blessing does not uniquely follow from accompaniment: if inferred from context it can equally attend instrumental reliance, and Alusi denies that blessing is the inherent meaning of accompaniment.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Blessing does not uniquely follow from accompaniment: if inferred from context it can equally attend instrumental reliance, and Alusi denies that blessing is the inherent meaning of accompaniment.

positions.position: Alusi denies that God's name cannot be an instrument if the basmala is part of a sura; opening a work does not prevent a phrase from being its part.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi denies that God's name cannot be an instrument if the basmala is part of a sura; opening a work does not prevent a phrase from being its part.

positions.position: He reads the hadith about God's name preventing harm as invoking God's aid and protection; even alternative readings about accompanying benefit are only supporting indications, and many indications also favor assistance.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): He reads the hadith about God's name preventing harm as invoking God's aid and protection; even alternative readings about accompanying benefit are only supporting indications, and many indications also favor assistance.

positions.position: The basmala summarizes the Quran's subject and aim; al-Fatiha and the successive surahs unfold its inexhaustible detail and wise ordering, beyond merely measurable length or poetic feeling.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): The basmala summarizes the Quran's subject and aim; al-Fatiha and the successive surahs unfold its inexhaustible detail and wise ordering, beyond merely measurable length or poetic feeling. | mentions 18:109

positions.position: The basmala in 27:30 is plainly part of that verse and certainly Qurʾān by explicit, unanimously established transmission; surah-opening basmalas raise a separate question.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): The basmala in 27:30 is plainly part of that verse and certainly Qurʾān by explicit, unanimously established transmission; surah-opening basmalas raise a separate question. | mentions 27:30

positions.position: Like al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal has two transmitted positions, reflecting uncertainty between the two hadith reports.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (Ahmed b. Hanbel): Like al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal has two transmitted positions, reflecting uncertainty between the two hadith reports.

positions.position: Because the basmala is independent rather than part of al-Fātiḥa, reciting it in every prayer is not obligatory like al-Fātiḥa, though beginning each recitation and important undertaking with it is sunnah.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Because the basmala is independent rather than part of al-Fātiḥa, reciting it in every prayer is not obligatory like al-Fātiḥa, though beginning each recitation and important undertaking with it is sunnah.

positions.position: Outwardly the basmala has four words, but in reality and legal reckoning it has seven because bāʾ and the two definite articles count as words, while bāʾ also implies a verb and its agent.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Outwardly the basmala has four words, but in reality and legal reckoning it has seven because bāʾ and the two definite articles count as words, while bāʾ also implies a verb and its agent.

positions.position: These early authorities hold that every surah-opening basmala is one verse of that surah, yielding 113 such verses in the Qurʾān.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (Saîd b. Cübeyr, Zührî, Atâ, İbn Mübârek): These early authorities hold that every surah-opening basmala is one verse of that surah, yielding 113 such verses in the Qurʾān.

positions.position: In his later position al-Shāfiʿī and his followers adopt the view that each surah-opening basmala is a verse.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (İmam Şâfiî ve ashâbı): In his later position al-Shāfiʿī and his followers adopt the view that each surah-opening basmala is a verse.

positions.position: Their argument is that the early community wrote the basmalas in the muṣḥafs while preserving the Qurʾān’s purity and excluding even Āmīn.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Their argument is that the early community wrote the basmalas in the muṣḥafs while preserving the Qurʾān’s purity and excluding even Āmīn.

positions.position: Against disagreement over the basmala's status, Quṭb prefers counting it as a verse of al-Fatiha, making the surah seven verses.
positions.reasons: QUTB-ZILAL (author): Against disagreement over the basmala's status, Quṭb prefers counting it as a verse of al-Fatiha, making the surah seven verses.

positions.position: ʿAbd al-Wahhāb argues the Prophet conveyed Qur’an uniformly and publicly; had the basmala belonged to Fātiha he would have made that clear, excluding secret or missing Qur’an.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (عبد الوهاب): ʿAbd al-Wahhāb argues the Prophet conveyed Qur’an uniformly and publicly; had the basmala belonged to Fātiha he would have made that clear, excluding secret or missing Qur’an.

positions.position: An Arabic-style argument against making the basmala a Fātiha verse is the close repetition of al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm in a short passage, which weakens eloquence.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): An Arabic-style argument against making the basmala a Fātiha verse is the close repetition of al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm in a short passage, which weakens eloquence.

positions.position: A report says the Prophet recited Fātiha and counted the basmala with al-ḥamdu lillāh as a verse; al-Ṭaḥāwī objects that Ibn Abī Mulayka did not hear Umm Salama, and another report from him conflicts.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (أم سلمة): A report says the Prophet recited Fātiha and counted the basmala with al-ḥamdu lillāh as a verse; al-Ṭaḥāwī objects that Ibn Abī Mulayka did not hear Umm Salama, and another report from him conflicts. | mentions 1:2

positions.position: Zakariyyāʾ notes the cited wording is not the transmitted wording; other versions only show that the basmala is a verse by itself, not that it belongs to Fātiha.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (زكرياء شيخ الإسلام): Zakariyyāʾ notes the cited wording is not the transmitted wording; other versions only show that the basmala is a verse by itself, not that it belongs to Fātiha.

positions.position: Ibn al-Mubārak and al-Shāfiʿī cite Muslim’s report that the Prophet recited the basmala before Sūrat al-Kawthar after God revealed it.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (أنس بن مالك): Ibn al-Mubārak and al-Shāfiʿī cite Muslim’s report that the Prophet recited the basmala before Sūrat al-Kawthar after God revealed it. | mentions 108:1

positions.position: Al-Mazari, citing Makki ibn Abi Talib, says the regional counters did not count the opening basmala as a verse in each surah; they differed only for al-Fatiha.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR-FULL (المازري): Al-Mazari, citing Makki ibn Abi Talib, says the regional counters did not count the opening basmala as a verse in each surah; they differed only for al-Fatiha.

positions.position: Ali reports that the basmala is part of al-Fatiha, which the Prophet recited and counted as one of its verses; similar Sunni reports exist.
positions.reasons: TABATABAI (علي): Ali reports that the basmala is part of al-Fatiha, which the Prophet recited and counted as one of its verses; similar Sunni reports exist.

positions.position: Counting the Basmala as a verse derives from Q 15:87’s seven repeated elements; seven is a round number below ten, so the identification does not require exactly seven verses.
positions.reasons: CORPUSCORANICUM (author): Counting the Basmala as a verse derives from Q 15:87’s seven repeated elements; seven is a round number below ten, so the identification does not require exactly seven verses. | mentions 15:87

positions.position: Rubin interprets seven in Q 15:87 as a round number under ten rather than an exact count.
positions.reasons: CORPUSCORANICUM (Rubin): Rubin interprets seven in Q 15:87 as a round number under ten rather than an exact count. | mentions 15:87

turns_on: Whether a Qurʾānic opening verse belongs to al-Fātiḥa itself or stands outside its verse count.

question: Is the basmala a verse of each other sūra?

positions.position: Ibn al-Mubarak says the basmala is a verse in every sura; the author calls this anomalous and rejected.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (ابن المبارك): Ibn al-Mubarak says the basmala is a verse in every sura; the author calls this anomalous and rejected. QURTUBI (عبد الله بن المبارك): Ibn al-Mubārak holds that the basmala is a verse at the beginning of every sūra.

positions.position: They count the basmala as part of al-Fātiḥa and every sura.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL (قراء مكة والكوفة وفقهاؤهما وابن المبارك والشافعي): They count the basmala as part of al-Fātiḥa and every sura. BAYDAWI-FULL (قراء المدينة والبصرة والشام ومالك والأوزاعي): They disagree that the basmala is part of every sura.

positions.position: The Prophet calls the basmala the unique verse revealed after Solomon; the author takes his recitation of the full formula to show it is a complete verse of al-Fātiḥa and the sura openings, whereas Naml contains it within a longer
positions.reasons: THALABI (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): The Prophet calls the basmala the unique verse revealed after Solomon; the author takes his recitation of the full formula to show it is a complete verse of al-Fātiḥa and the sura openings, whereas Naml contains it within a longer verse. | mentions 27:30

positions.position: Al-Shafi‘i and a group affirm the basmala as part of the Fatiha and sura openings.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (الشافعي): Al-Shafi‘i and a group affirm the basmala as part of the Fatiha and sura openings.

positions.position: Abu Hanifa and others deny that the basmala is part of the Fatiha and sura openings.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (أبو حنيفة): Abu Hanifa and others deny that the basmala is part of the Fatiha and sura openings.

positions.position: The author's companions hold that the basmala is a verse of al-Fatiha and every sura; omitting it invalidates obligatory and supererogatory prayer, and they favor audible recitation.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (أصحابنا): The author's companions hold that the basmala is a verse of al-Fatiha and every sura; omitting it invalidates obligatory and supererogatory prayer, and they favor audible recitation.

positions.position: These readers do not use the basmala to separate suras; the other readers do, except between al-Anfal and al-Tawba.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (حمزة وخلف ويعقوب واليزيدي): These readers do not use the basmala to separate suras; the other readers do, except between al-Anfal and al-Tawba.

positions.position: The leading authorities among al-Shafi‘i’s followers agree the basmala is Qur’an in every sura; their two opinions concern whether it is a full verse alone or joined to what follows.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The leading authorities among al-Shafi‘i’s followers agree the basmala is Qur’an in every sura; their two opinions concern whether it is a full verse alone or joined to what follows.

positions.position: Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls numerical parallels involving the basmala and angels witty interpretation rather than firm knowledge.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (ابن عطية): Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls numerical parallels involving the basmala and angels witty interpretation rather than firm knowledge. | mentions 97:1

positions.position: Abū Yūsuf requires three verses or one long verse; Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan also permits one verse or a meaningful phrase.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (أبو يوسف ومحمد بن الحسن): Abū Yūsuf requires three verses or one long verse; Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan also permits one verse or a meaningful phrase.

positions.position: A report says that any significant matter begun without the basmala is cut off or incomplete.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): A report says that any significant matter begun without the basmala is cut off or incomplete.

positions.position: Abū Ḥanīfa stated no position here, so al-Bayḍāwī infers he did not regard it as part of the sura; Muḥammad al-Ḥasan says all text between the covers is God's speech.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL (author): Abū Ḥanīfa stated no position here, so al-Bayḍāwī infers he did not regard it as part of the sura; Muḥammad al-Ḥasan says all text between the covers is God's speech.

positions.position: All deny that the basmala at each sūra’s opening is a verse, except Ibn al-Mubārak, who says it is a verse in every sūra.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (ابن المبارك): All deny that the basmala at each sūra’s opening is a verse, except Ibn al-Mubārak, who says it is a verse in every sūra.

positions.position: The Companions opened God's Book with the basmala; scholars agree it is part of the verse in Surat al-Naml, while disputing its status at surah openings.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): The Companions opened God's Book with the basmala; scholars agree it is part of the verse in Surat al-Naml, while disputing its status at surah openings. | mentions 27:30

positions.position: Malikis and others who deny the basmala’s Quranic status argue that it was not mutawatir at surah openings and therefore is not Quran.
positions.reasons: ITQAN (المالكية): Malikis and others who deny the basmala’s Quranic status argue that it was not mutawatir at surah openings and therefore is not Quran.

positions.position: Al-Thalabi reports that Ali began each sura in prayer with the basmala and said omitting it meant losing a verse.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (علي): Al-Thalabi reports that Ali began each sura in prayer with the basmala and said omitting it meant losing a verse.

positions.position: A third position counts it as a verse of the Fatiha alone.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): A third position counts it as a verse of the Fatiha alone.

positions.position: A fourth position treats it only as a portion of a verse in the Fatiha.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): A fourth position treats it only as a portion of a verse in the Fatiha.

positions.position: A tenth position counts it as a distinct verse repeatedly revealed.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): A tenth position counts it as a distinct verse repeatedly revealed.

positions.position: Ibn Abbas, Ibn al-Mubarak, Meccans including Ibn Kathir, Kufans including Asim and al-Kisa'i, most Shafi'is, and Imamis hold it is a verse in all suras except Bara'a.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Ibn Abbas, Ibn al-Mubarak, Meccans including Ibn Kathir, Kufans including Asim and al-Kisa'i, most Shafi'is, and Imamis hold it is a verse in all suras except Bara'a. | mentions 9:1

positions.position: A second position counts the basmala as a verse of every sura except Bara'a.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): A second position counts the basmala as a verse of every sura except Bara'a. | mentions 9:1

positions.position: Mālik, al-Awzāʿī, and jurists of Medina, Syria, and Basra hold that the basmala is not a verse at sura openings, though it is part of the verse in Sūrat al-Naml.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (مالك والأوزاعي وفقهاء المدينة والشام والبصرة): Mālik, al-Awzāʿī, and jurists of Medina, Syria, and Basra hold that the basmala is not a verse at sura openings, though it is part of the verse in Sūrat al-Naml. | mentions 27:30

positions.position: Ibn al-Mubārak and al-Shāfiʿī’s view judged more authentic by Ibn ʿĀshūr count it as a verse at the beginning of every sura.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (عبد الله بن المبارك والشافعي): Ibn al-Mubārak and al-Shāfiʿī’s view judged more authentic by Ibn ʿĀshūr count it as a verse at the beginning of every sura.

positions.position: No direct statement is transmitted from Abū Ḥanīfa; al-Zamakhsharī inferred that he did not regard it as part of the suras, an inference Ibn ʿĀshūr accepts.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (أبو حنيفة): No direct statement is transmitted from Abū Ḥanīfa; al-Zamakhsharī inferred that he did not regard it as part of the suras, an inference Ibn ʿĀshūr accepts.

positions.position: For the view that the basmala opens every sura as a verse, Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers the argument that identical openings everywhere violate the rhetorical art of varying openings.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): For the view that the basmala opens every sura as a verse, Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers the argument that identical openings everywhere violate the rhetorical art of varying openings.

positions.position: Numerous reports from the Imams of the Prophet's household and Sunni reports indicate that the basmala is part of every sura except al-Bara'a.
positions.reasons: TABATABAI (author): Numerous reports from the Imams of the Prophet's household and Sunni reports indicate that the basmala is part of every sura except al-Bara'a.

positions.position: Every sūrah except one opens with the basmalah, also found in 27:30.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (author): Every sūrah except one opens with the basmalah, also found in 27:30. | mentions 27:30

positions.position: Scholars disagree whether the basmalah is a verse of each sūrah or a marker beginning a new sūrah.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (author): Scholars disagree whether the basmalah is a verse of each sūrah or a marker beginning a new sūrah.

question: Is the basmala Qurʾānic text?

positions.position: A report from Ṭalḥa ibn ʿUbayd Allāh says that whoever omits the basmala has omitted a verse from God’s Book.
positions.reasons: THALABI (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): A report from Ṭalḥa ibn ʿUbayd Allāh says that whoever omits the basmala has omitted a verse from God’s Book. RAZI-FULL (طلحة بن عبيد الله عن النبي): The Prophet says that whoever omits the basmala has omitted a verse from God's Book. DURR (النبي): The Prophet says whoever omits the basmala has omitted a verse from God's Book.

positions.position: The basmala outside Sūrat al-Naml is not Qurʾānic text.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): A sixth position says repeated revelation made the basmala both a verse and, on other occasions, not a verse. ALUSI-FULL (author): One reported position says the basmala is not a verse of any sura. ALUSI-FULL (author): Many suras were revealed without a basmala and received it later; the sound report about the beginning of revelation supports that it is not a verse of those suras. IBNASHUR (author): Although Ibn ʿĀshūr follows Mālik’s view that the basmala is not a verse at the start of al-Baqara, he explains it here because earlier commentators made this customary. | mentions 27:30

positions.position: Malik, Abu Hanifa and the majority of jurists and reciters do not count the basmala as a verse.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (مالك، وأبو حنيفة، وجمهور الفقهاء والقراء): Malik, Abu Hanifa and the majority of jurists and reciters do not count the basmala as a verse. IBNATIYYA-FULL (مالك وأبو حنيفة وجمهور الفقهاء والقراء): Malik, Abu Hanifa, and most jurists and readers do not count the basmala as a verse.

positions.position: Ibn Abbas explicitly counts the basmala as a verse.
positions.reasons: DURR (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas explicitly counts the basmala as a verse. DURR-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas identifies the basmala as a verse.

positions.position: The basmala is Qurʾānic text.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (يعلى): The narrator reports asking Muhammad b. al-Hasan whether the basmala is Quran, introducing a discussion of its legal status. RAZI-FULL (author): Since Muslims agree that everything between the two covers is God's speech and the basmala is there, Razi counts it as divine speech; he notes this does not refute Abu Bakr al-Razi's view that it is Quran only as a surah divider. RAZI-FULL (author): Because the basmala unquestionably appears in Quran 27:30 and recurs in Quranic script, Razi argues every occurrence is Quran, by analogy with repeated Quranic refrains. | mentions 27:30, 55:13, 77:15

positions.position: Scholars disagree whether the basmala is a complete verse; Aḥmad has two transmitted positions.
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD (العلماء): Scholars disagree whether the basmala is a complete verse; Aḥmad has two transmitted positions. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (العلماء): Scholars also disagree whether it is part of al-Fātiḥa; two positions are transmitted from Aḥmad.

positions.position: One group counts the basmala but not “those upon whom You bestowed favor” as a verse.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (author): One group counts the basmala but not “those upon whom You bestowed favor” as a verse. BAYDAWI (author): Another group excludes the basmala and counts “those upon whom You bestowed favor.”

positions.position: Ibn al-Anbari and al-Bayhaqi report that the Prophet paused verse by verse, beginning with the basmala.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Ibn al-Anbari and al-Bayhaqi report that the Prophet paused verse by verse, beginning with the basmala. ALUSI-FULL (author): Ibn al-Anbari and al-Bayhaqi also report the Prophet pausing verse by verse, beginning with the basmala.

positions.position: Ibn ʿAbbās says that when a basmala verse was revealed, the Prophet knew the previous sura had ended and another had begun.
positions.reasons: THALABI (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās says that when a basmala verse was revealed, the Prophet knew the previous sura had ended and another had begun.

positions.position: In the divine report dividing prayer between God and the servant, the basmala glorifies God, al-ḥamdu praises Him, al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm extols Him, Mālik delegates the matter, the worship-and-help verse is shared, and guidance is granted to the servant.
positions.reasons: THALABI (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): In the divine report dividing prayer between God and the servant, the basmala glorifies God, al-ḥamdu praises Him, al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm extols Him, Mālik delegates the matter, the worship-and-help verse is shared, and guidance is granted to the servant.

positions.position: The author argues from the arrangement of verse endings and the basmala’s placement that it was written where revealed, rather than inserted merely to divide suras.
positions.reasons: THALABI (author): The author argues from the arrangement of verse endings and the basmala’s placement that it was written where revealed, rather than inserted merely to divide suras.

positions.position: The author adds that scribes used black ink for the basmala, unlike non-Qurʾānic marginal material, which supports its status as Qurʾān.
positions.reasons: THALABI (author): The author adds that scribes used black ink for the basmala, unlike non-Qurʾānic marginal material, which supports its status as Qurʾān.

positions.position: Since the basmala recurs at the beginning of each surah and is established as part of it, Qushayri gives distinct, non-repeated allusions in each surah and treats this one at length here.
positions.reasons: QUSHAYRI (author): Since the basmala recurs at the beginning of each surah and is established as part of it, Qushayri gives distinct, non-repeated allusions in each surah and treats this one at length here.

positions.position: The lover finds blame for loving the beloved pleasurable; Qushayri reads the command in 15:97 as listening to what is said with praise of God.
positions.reasons: QUSHAYRI (author): The lover finds blame for loving the beloved pleasurable; Qushayri reads the command in 15:97 as listening to what is said with praise of God. | mentions 15:97

positions.position: Al-Thawri, Ibn al-Mubarak, and al-Shafiʿi count the basmala in every surah except al-Tawba, since it is written in the codex in Quranic script.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI-FULL (الثوري وابن المبارك والشافعي): Al-Thawri, Ibn al-Mubarak, and al-Shafiʿi count the basmala in every surah except al-Tawba, since it is written in the codex in Quranic script.

positions.position: Ja'far al-Sadiq calls the basmala the crowns of the surahs.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (جعفر بن محمد الصادق): Ja'far al-Sadiq calls the basmala the crowns of the surahs.

positions.position: Ali b. al-Husayn interprets the turning away in 17:46 when the Lord is mentioned alone as occurring when one says the basmala.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (علي بن الحسين): Ali b. al-Husayn interprets the turning away in 17:46 when the Lord is mentioned alone as occurring when one says the basmala. | mentions 17:46

positions.position: Amr b. Ubayd makes iyyaka na'budu a separate verse, yielding eight; Ibn Atiyya also calls this anomalous.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (عمرو بن عبيد): Amr b. Ubayd makes iyyaka na'budu a separate verse, yielding eight; Ibn Atiyya also calls this anomalous.

positions.position: If sound, the Jabir and Abu Hurayra reports can be understood as lessons: the Prophet saw them rehearsing prayer outside prayer and taught the basmala for that reason, not because it was a verse.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (author): If sound, the Jabir and Abu Hurayra reports can be understood as lessons: the Prophet saw them rehearsing prayer outside prayer and taught the basmala for that reason, not because it was a verse.

positions.position: Ibn al-Mubarak holds that the basmala is a verse in every surah; Ibn Atiyya calls this an anomalous view rejected by others.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (ابن المبارك): Ibn al-Mubarak holds that the basmala is a verse in every surah; Ibn Atiyya calls this an anomalous view rejected by others.

positions.position: Some say the nineteen letters of the basmala correspond one by one to the nineteen keepers of Hell in 74:30, whose repeated basmala gives them strength.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (بعض الناس): Some say the nineteen letters of the basmala correspond one by one to the nineteen keepers of Hell in 74:30, whose repeated basmala gives them strength. | mentions 74:30

positions.position: He compares that numerology with claims that the Night of Decree is the twenty-seventh night because of a word in its surah, and that thirty-some angels rushed to record a thirty-some-letter praise formula.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (author): He compares that numerology with claims that the Night of Decree is the twenty-seventh night because of a word in its surah, and that thirty-some angels rushed to record a thirty-some-letter praise formula. | mentions 97:3

positions.position: A similar letter-count claim says thirty-some angels competed to record “Our Lord, to You belongs praise, abundant, good and blessed praise”; Ibn Atiyya presents it as the same sort of numerology.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (author): A similar letter-count claim says thirty-some angels competed to record “Our Lord, to You belongs praise, abundant, good and blessed praise”; Ibn Atiyya presents it as the same sort of numerology.

positions.position: Ibn Atiyya rejects Ata's account as weak: the basmala preceded Musaylima's rise, and Musaylima's use of the name did not become established.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (author): Ibn Atiyya rejects Ata's account as weak: the basmala preceded Musaylima's rise, and Musaylima's use of the name did not become established.

positions.position: Abu Ubayda treats the word ism as an extra connective and takes the basmala to mean Allah Himself, as in Labid's verse.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (أبو عبيدة): Abu Ubayda treats the word ism as an extra connective and takes the basmala to mean Allah Himself, as in Labid's verse.

positions.position: Al-Qadi Abu Bakr calls the basmala's Quranic status categorical: error is at least sinful, since its inclusion must be proved by mass transmission, not a solitary report.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (القاضي أبو بكر): Al-Qadi Abu Bakr calls the basmala's Quranic status categorical: error is at least sinful, since its inclusion must be proved by mass transmission, not a solitary report.

positions.position: Al-Ghazali counters that denying the basmala's Quranic status faces the same proof dilemma; although absence is the default, its Quranic-script inscription requires separate evidence.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الغزالي): Al-Ghazali counters that denying the basmala's Quranic status faces the same proof dilemma; although absence is the default, its Quranic-script inscription requires separate evidence.

positions.position: Razi says transmission establishes that the basmala was revealed to Muhammad and written in Quranic script; inclusion matters only for legal rulings such as prayer, recitation in impurity, and touching the codex, which are ijtihadi, so the issue is not
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi says transmission establishes that the basmala was revealed to Muhammad and written in Quranic script; inclusion matters only for legal rulings such as prayer, recitation in impurity, and touching the codex, which are ijtihadi, so the issue is not categorical.

positions.position: In al-Tha'labi's report, the Prophet tells Abu Burda that he alone after Solomon received an ayah, then links it to the basmala used to begin Quran recitation and prayer.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أبو بريدة عن أبيه عن النبي): In al-Tha'labi's report, the Prophet tells Abu Burda that he alone after Solomon received an ayah, then links it to the basmala used to begin Quran recitation and prayer.

positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Because the basmala is written in Quranic script, while headings and division marks were kept out to prevent mixing non-Quranic text, its inscription marks it as Quran.

positions.position: The severity of abtar is shown by Quran 108:3, where God calls the Prophet's enemy cut off; thus prayer without the basmala is gravely defective and invalid.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The severity of abtar is shown by Quran 108:3, where God calls the Prophet's enemy cut off; thus prayer without the basmala is gravely defective and invalid. | mentions 108:3

positions.position: Opponents argue that counting the basmala as a verse repeats الرحمن الرحيم within the sura, contrary to the evidence.

positions.position: A variant transmitted by Abu Dawud al-Sijistani says God calls Malik yawm al-din a point between Himself and the servant, which supports three verses on either side when the basmala is counted.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أبو هريرة): A variant transmitted by Abu Dawud al-Sijistani says God calls Malik yawm al-din a point between Himself and the servant, which supports three verses on either side when the basmala is counted.

positions.position: Half can describe a division of meaning rather than an exact count, as in calling inheritance law half of knowledge or saying half the people are angry.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Half can describe a division of meaning rather than an exact count, as in calling inheritance law half of knowledge or saying half the people are angry.

positions.position: A report traces the written invocation from Quraysh’s باسمك اللهم through successive revealed forms until the full basmala was written after the verse in al-Naml.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A report traces the written invocation from Quraysh’s باسمك اللهم through successive revealed forms until the full basmala was written after the verse in al-Naml. | mentions 11:41, 17:110, 27:30

positions.position: Because every component and the complete formula occur in Qur’anic revelation, its established fame and many proofs make exclusion an attack on the reliability of the rest of the Qur’an.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Because every component and the complete formula occur in Qur’anic revelation, its established fame and many proofs make exclusion an attack on the reliability of the rest of the Qur’an.

positions.position: Razi opens the objection concerning basmala verse status by citing Abu Hurayra’s report about the verse count of al-Mulk.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أبو هريرة): Razi opens the objection concerning basmala verse status by citing Abu Hurayra’s report about the verse count of al-Mulk.

positions.position: Those counting the basmala treat the final phrase from sirat alladhina through the end as one verse; Abu Hanifa, omitting the basmala, splits that ending into two verses.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Those counting the basmala treat the final phrase from sirat alladhina through the end as one verse; Abu Hanifa, omitting the basmala, splits that ending into two verses.

positions.position: Starting a verse with ghayr separates a modifier or exception from what it qualifies, though each belongs syntactically with the preceding phrase.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Starting a verse with ghayr separates a modifier or exception from what it qualifies, though each belongs syntactically with the preceding phrase.

positions.position: The request to guide us to the path of the blessed is incomplete without excluding those under anger or astray; the whole qualified phrase should therefore be one verse.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The request to guide us to the path of the blessed is incomplete without excluding those under anger or astray; the whole qualified phrase should therefore be one verse. | mentions 14:28

positions.position: Umm Salama reports that the Prophet counted the basmala as a verse marking the separation between suras.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أم سلمة): Umm Salama reports that the Prophet counted the basmala as a verse marking the separation between suras.

positions.position: Mālik’s school has three positions on the additional sūra: sunnah, meritorious, or obligatory.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (أصحاب مالك): Mālik’s school has three positions on the additional sūra: sunnah, meritorious, or obligatory.

positions.position: Medinan, Syrian, and Basran counters count “Anʿamta ʿalayhim”; Kūfan readers and jurists count the basmala instead.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (أهل الكوفة): Medinan, Syrian, and Basran counters count “Anʿamta ʿalayhim”; Kūfan readers and jurists count the basmala instead.

positions.position: Writing the basmala in muṣḥafs may mark a sūra boundary or blessing, rather than prove verse status.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (author): Writing the basmala in muṣḥafs may mark a sūra boundary or blessing, rather than prove verse status.

positions.position: Mālik’s well-known school does not count the basmala as a verse and omits it in obligatory prayer, but permits voluntary recitation.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (مالك): Mālik’s well-known school does not count the basmala as a verse and omits it in obligatory prayer, but permits voluntary recitation.

positions.position: Umm Salama reports the Prophet counted the basmala and “Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds” as one verse.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (النبي): Umm Salama reports the Prophet counted the basmala and “Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds” as one verse.

positions.position: The reports explain the disagreement whether the basmala is a separate verse or part of the following verse.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (author): The reports explain the disagreement whether the basmala is a separate verse or part of the following verse.

positions.position: There is consensus that the muṣḥaf text is God's speech and agreement to include the basmala in muṣḥafs despite rigorous exclusion of non-Qur'anic matter.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (author): There is consensus that the muṣḥaf text is God's speech and agreement to include the basmala in muṣḥafs despite rigorous exclusion of non-Qur'anic matter.

positions.position: The order may also preserve the sūra's verse-end rhyme.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (author): The order may also preserve the sūra's verse-end rhyme.

positions.position: The disagreement concerns whether the basmala is an independent verse or counted with what follows; Muslims agree it is Qur'an and is written in the codices, which were carefully kept free of additions such as آمين.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL (author): The disagreement concerns whether the basmala is an independent verse or counted with what follows; Muslims agree it is Qur'an and is written in the codices, which were carefully kept free of additions such as آمين.

positions.position: Nasafi answers that the basmala is still Qur’an, revealed to separate the suras; its Qur’anic status does not require it to belong to a sura’s verse count.
positions.reasons: NASAFI (author): Nasafi answers that the basmala is still Qur’an, revealed to separate the suras; its Qur’anic status does not require it to belong to a sura’s verse count.

positions.position: In the Hanafi account the basmala remains a Qur'anic verse revealed to separate surahs; this does not contradict its exclusion from the surahs themselves.
positions.reasons: NASAFI-FULL (author): In the Hanafi account the basmala remains a Qur'anic verse revealed to separate surahs; this does not contradict its exclusion from the surahs themselves.

positions.position: The basmala has eighteen pronounced letters and nineteen written letters; when words are separated, the count becomes twenty-two.
positions.reasons: QASHANI (author): The basmala has eighteen pronounced letters and nineteen written letters; when words are separated, the count becomes twenty-two.

positions.position: Eighteen signifies eighteen thousand worlds, whose principal realms are the dominion, kingdom, Throne, Footstool, heavens, elements, and three genera of offspring.
positions.reasons: QASHANI (author): Eighteen signifies eighteen thousand worlds, whose principal realms are the dominion, kingdom, Throne, Footstool, heavens, elements, and three genera of offspring.

positions.position: The Meccan and Kufan majority count the basmala as a verse and do not count “whom You favored” separately; other counters reverse those choices.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الجمهور المكيون والكوفيون): The Meccan and Kufan majority count the basmala as a verse and do not count “whom You favored” separately; other counters reverse those choices.

positions.position: Al-Mawardi calls the person who says bismillah mubasmil and labels that usage a later coinage.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (الماوردي): Al-Mawardi calls the person who says bismillah mubasmil and labels that usage a later coinage.

positions.position: Ibn Abi Rabi'a's verse attests basmala as established poetic usage, while Tha'lab and al-Mutarriz transmit it without calling it a late coinage.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (عمر بن أبي ربيعة): Ibn Abi Rabi'a's verse attests basmala as established poetic usage, while Tha'lab and al-Mutarriz transmit it without calling it a late coinage.

positions.position: These Companions are cited as holding that the basmala is a verse at the start of every surah except al-Tawba; several Successors and a group of later authorities agree.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (ابن عباس وابن عمر وابن الزبير وأبو هريرة وعلي): These Companions are cited as holding that the basmala is a verse at the start of every surah except al-Tawba; several Successors and a group of later authorities agree. | mentions 9:1

positions.position: A weak version adds that saying the basmala is God's remembrance.
positions.reasons: DURR (الله): A weak version adds that saying the basmala is God's remembrance.

positions.position: A weak report says the basmala is the verse the Prophet promised had not been given to another prophet after Solomon.
positions.reasons: DURR (بريدة): A weak report says the basmala is the verse the Prophet promised had not been given to another prophet after Solomon.

positions.position: Ibn Abbas says people neglected an ayah revealed only to the Prophet, unless Solomon also received it: the basmala.
positions.reasons: DURR (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas says people neglected an ayah revealed only to the Prophet, unless Solomon also received it: the basmala.

positions.position: The Prophet called prayer incomplete when a man omitted the basmala, which he counted as part of al-Hamd and a necessary verse.
positions.reasons: DURR (النبي): The Prophet called prayer incomplete when a man omitted the basmala, which he counted as part of al-Hamd and a necessary verse.

positions.position: A very weak report gives symbolic expansions of the basmala's letters and distinguishes mercy in this world from the next.
positions.reasons: DURR (أبو سعيد الخدري): A very weak report gives symbolic expansions of the basmala's letters and distinguishes mercy in this world from the next.

positions.position: Abū Hurayra reports that the Prophet opened congregational recitation with the basmala and identifies it as a verse of God's Book.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (أبو هريرة): Abū Hurayra reports that the Prophet opened congregational recitation with the basmala and identifies it as a verse of God's Book.

positions.position: In a weak report, the Prophet promised Burayda a unique revealed verse or surah and identified the basmala when asked how to begin Quran recitation in prayer.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): In a weak report, the Prophet promised Burayda a unique revealed verse or surah and identified the basmala when asked how to begin Quran recitation in prayer.

positions.position: Ibn Abbas says the basmala was revealed only to the Prophet, apart from its revelation to Solomon.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas says the basmala was revealed only to the Prophet, apart from its revelation to Solomon.

positions.position: In a weak report, Gabriel began delivering revelation to the Prophet with the basmala.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (ابن عمر): In a weak report, Gabriel began delivering revelation to the Prophet with the basmala.

positions.position: The report says leaving the basmala means leaving a verse and thereby invalidating one's prayer.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): The report says leaving the basmala means leaving a verse and thereby invalidating one's prayer.

positions.position: Talha reports the Prophet saying that whoever leaves the basmala has left a verse of God's Book.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): Talha reports the Prophet saying that whoever leaves the basmala has left a verse of God's Book.

positions.position: Aisha reports that the Prophet counted the basmala as verse one, al-hamd as two, al-Rahman al-Rahim as three, Malik yawm al-din as four, then indicated five for the next verse.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (أم سلمة): Aisha reports that the Prophet counted the basmala as verse one, al-hamd as two, al-Rahman al-Rahim as three, Malik yawm al-din as four, then indicated five for the next verse.

positions.position: The author denies that the basmala lacked tawatur: its unmarked inclusion in Companion and later codices proves its Quranic status, since they prohibited writing non-Quranic material there and would not mislead Muslims.
positions.reasons: ITQAN (author): The author denies that the basmala lacked tawatur: its unmarked inclusion in Companion and later codices proves its Quranic status, since they prohibited writing non-Quranic material there and would not mislead Muslims.

positions.position: In a report through Mujahid, Ibn Abbas says people neglected a verse revealed only to Muhammad, perhaps also Solomon: the basmala.
positions.reasons: ITQAN (ابن عباس): In a report through Mujahid, Ibn Abbas says people neglected a verse revealed only to Muhammad, perhaps also Solomon: the basmala.

positions.position: Outside the sūra context of 27:30, scholars held ten positions: from nowhere a Qurʾānic verse to a verse or verse-part in all or selected sūras.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Outside the sūra context of 27:30, scholars held ten positions: from nowhere a Qurʾānic verse to a verse or verse-part in all or selected sūras. | mentions 27:30

positions.position: A report attributed to Ṭalḥa says whoever leaves the basmala has left a verse of God’s Book; al-Ālūsī says such reports establish its Qurʾānic status only.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (طلحة بن عبيد الله): A report attributed to Ṭalḥa says whoever leaves the basmala has left a verse of God’s Book; al-Ālūsī says such reports establish its Qurʾānic status only.

positions.position: Repeated Qurʾānic phrases in other sūras do not prove the basmala is a constituent verse there; the comparison with repeated refrains is invalid.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Repeated Qurʾānic phrases in other sūras do not prove the basmala is a constituent verse there; the comparison with repeated refrains is invalid. | mentions 77:15, 55:13

positions.position: Alusi says the fifth position, that the basmala is an independent verse marking sura beginnings, is the well-known Hanafi doctrine.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi says the fifth position, that the basmala is an independent verse marking sura beginnings, is the well-known Hanafi doctrine.

positions.position: Al-Tunisi transmits a consensus among every religious community's scholars that God began each revealed book with the basmala.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (أبو بكر التونسي): Al-Tunisi transmits a consensus among every religious community's scholars that God began each revealed book with the basmala.

positions.position: A fifth position makes it an independent verse revealed to mark sura openings and separate suras, for blessing.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): A fifth position makes it an independent verse revealed to mark sura openings and separate suras, for blessing.

positions.position: A seventh position treats it as part of a verse in every sura.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): A seventh position treats it as part of a verse in every sura.

positions.position: An eighth position makes it a full verse in the Fatiha but only part of verses in other suras.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): An eighth position makes it a full verse in the Fatiha but only part of verses in other suras.

positions.position: A ninth position reverses the eighth: it is part of a Fatiha verse and a full verse elsewhere.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): A ninth position reverses the eighth: it is part of a Fatiha verse and a full verse elsewhere.

positions.position: Talha's report says omitting the basmala is equivalent to leaving a verse of the Qur'an.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (طلحة بن عبيدالله): Talha's report says omitting the basmala is equivalent to leaving a verse of the Qur'an.

positions.position: Razi argues that its inscription in Qur'anic script, unlike sura names and divisions, proves it is Qur'an.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (الفخر الرازي): Razi argues that its inscription in Qur'anic script, unlike sura names and divisions, proves it is Qur'an.

positions.position: Razi argues that the basmala must be God's speech because it occurs between the covers of the Qur'an, which Muslims agree contains God's speech.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (الفخر الرازي): Razi argues that the basmala must be God's speech because it occurs between the covers of the Qur'an, which Muslims agree contains God's speech.

positions.position: Al-Daraqutni reports that the Prophet counted verse by verse, counted the basmala, but did not count alayhim separately.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Al-Daraqutni reports that the Prophet counted verse by verse, counted the basmala, but did not count alayhim separately.
