positions.position: Alusi challenges proponents to explain why an independent basmala would not add to these counts, or why a basmala counted as part of a sura was not counted.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi challenges proponents to explain why an independent basmala would not add to these counts, or why a basmala counted as part of a sura was not counted.

positions.position: He rejects Razi's analogy to a phrase that is a verse in one place and part of a verse elsewhere: that other phrase has a reason to be partial, while this basmala does not.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): He rejects Razi's analogy to a phrase that is a verse in one place and part of a verse elsewhere: that other phrase has a reason to be partial, while this basmala does not.

positions.position: Alusi's conclusion is that the basmala is an independent Qur'anic verse, not a part of any sura, and its recitation is obligatory rather than merely recommended.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi's conclusion is that the basmala is an independent Qur'anic verse, not a part of any sura, and its recitation is obligatory rather than merely recommended.

positions.position: He regards it as implausible that Abu Hanifa would leave this major prayer issue without an explicit ruling; the valid report from him supports obligation.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): He regards it as implausible that Abu Hanifa would leave this major prayer issue without an explicit ruling; the valid report from him supports obligation.

positions.position: A symbolic interpreter says the kasra of the basmala's ba teaches that divine knowledge is reached through humility and servitude; Ibn al-Farid's verse makes lowering a cause of elevation by God's gift, not human stratagem.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): A symbolic interpreter says the kasra of the basmala's ba teaches that divine knowledge is reached through humility and servitude; Ibn al-Farid's verse makes lowering a cause of elevation by God's gift, not human stratagem.

positions.position: Ibn al-Farid's poem says that a lowered point of ba can raise the seeker beyond what effort could attain, provided one recognizes one's own humility and dependence.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (ابن الفارض): Ibn al-Farid's poem says that a lowered point of ba can raise the seeker beyond what effort could attain, provided one recognizes one's own humility and dependence.

positions.position: The basmala begins God’s speech because it summarizes what follows and is a magnificent verse whose benefits are immense; investigating it requires a wide range of disciplines.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): The basmala begins God’s speech because it summarizes what follows and is a magnificent verse whose benefits are immense; investigating it requires a wide range of disciplines.

positions.position: Al-Alusi illustrates the range of required learning, from grammar, morphology, rhetoric and language to theology, law, hadith, philosophy, letters, natural sciences, and ethics.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Al-Alusi illustrates the range of required learning, from grammar, morphology, rhetoric and language to theology, law, hadith, philosophy, letters, natural sciences, and ethics.

positions.position: Al-Ālūsī reads the hadith universally: every matter that comes to mind, important or trivial, should begin with the basmala, as the verse says every bird flies with its wings.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Al-Ālūsī reads the hadith universally: every matter that comes to mind, important or trivial, should begin with the basmala, as the verse says every bird flies with its wings. | mentions 6:38

positions.position: The hadith concerns matters not recognized as complete in religious law: they may be materially finished yet deficient in meaning, since the basmala completes their meanings.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): The hadith concerns matters not recognized as complete in religious law: they may be materially finished yet deficient in meaning, since the basmala completes their meanings.

positions.position: The Quran is not a chance or merely poetic anthology but a coherent true discourse like a single comprehensive sentence, beginning with basmala and ending with al-Nas.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): The Quran is not a chance or merely poetic anthology but a coherent true discourse like a single comprehensive sentence, beginning with basmala and ending with al-Nas.

positions.position: Abduh's explanation is sound for the Quran's revelation, recitation, and writing because of the basmala's position at their beginnings, and it matters in special settings too.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Abduh's explanation is sound for the Quran's revelation, recitation, and writing because of the basmala's position at their beginnings, and it matters in special settings too.

positions.position: The basmala's words, composition, rhetoric, sound, and even its sweet pattern of letters cannot be fully carried into Turkish, so it should be recited in Arabic and understood through explanation.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): The basmala's words, composition, rhetoric, sound, and even its sweet pattern of letters cannot be fully carried into Turkish, so it should be recited in Arabic and understood through explanation.

positions.position: Whether the basmala written before surahs is a verse within them, a verse-part, or an independent Qurʾānic unit is a scholarly issue tied to faith, prayer, and recitation.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Whether the basmala written before surahs is a verse within them, a verse-part, or an independent Qurʾānic unit is a scholarly issue tied to faith, prayer, and recitation.

positions.position: The Qurʾānic wisdom concerns the relation of God to the world, especially people and their acts; the basmala’s bāʾ expresses this relation of divinity and servitude.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): The Qurʾānic wisdom concerns the relation of God to the world, especially people and their acts; the basmala’s bāʾ expresses this relation of divinity and servitude.

positions.position: A report from Umm Salama says the Prophet counted the basmala together with al-ḥamdu lillāh as one verse.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (Ümmü Seleme): A report from Umm Salama says the Prophet counted the basmala together with al-ḥamdu lillāh as one verse.

positions.position: An unspecified group is reported to count nine verses; that count requires excluding the basmala and combining two other verse units.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (بعض الناس): An unspecified group is reported to count nine verses; that count requires excluding the basmala and combining two other verse units.

positions.position: Medinan verse-counting does not count the basmala and treats anʿamta ʿalayhim as a separate verse.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (أهل المدينة): Medinan verse-counting does not count the basmala and treats anʿamta ʿalayhim as a separate verse.

positions.position: Meccan and Kufan counting treats the basmala as a verse and anʿamta ʿalayhim as part of the following verse.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (أهل مكة وأهل الكوفة): Meccan and Kufan counting treats the basmala as a verse and anʿamta ʿalayhim as part of the following verse.

positions.position: Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī counts both the basmala and anʿamta ʿalayhim as separate verses.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (الحسن البصري): Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī counts both the basmala and anʿamta ʿalayhim as separate verses.

positions.position: Anas’s report in al-Bukhārī that the Prophet elongated the basmala does not establish verse status: the reciting and elongating pronouns refer to Anas, who gives it as a familiar example.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (أنس بن مالك): Anas’s report in al-Bukhārī that the Prophet elongated the basmala does not establish verse status: the reciting and elongating pronouns refer to Anas, who gives it as a familiar example.

positions.position: Readers agree to say the basmala when beginning any sura except Barāʾa, regardless of whether their juristic school counts it as a verse.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): Readers agree to say the basmala when beginning any sura except Barāʾa, regardless of whether their juristic school counts it as a verse.

positions.position: Al-Jāḥiẓ tells of al-Muʾarrij al-Sadūsī restoring the basmala before Barāʾa after hearing a phrase about the Commander returning rights; if true, Ibn ʿĀshūr treats it as a joke.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (مؤرج السدوسي): Al-Jāḥiẓ tells of al-Muʾarrij al-Sadūsī restoring the basmala before Barāʾa after hearing a phrase about the Commander returning rights; if true, Ibn ʿĀshūr treats it as a joke.

positions.position: Arabic may use “name” for the named thing itself, as al-Nabigha's verse uses it for foolishness, but this is not the sense of “name” in the basmala.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR-FULL (author): Arabic may use “name” for the named thing itself, as al-Nabigha's verse uses it for foolishness, but this is not the sense of “name” in the basmala.

positions.position: “Name them” can serve as a challenge to establish that supposed partners exist, using a name metonymically for the named one's existence; Ibn Ashur says this is likewise not the basmala's usage.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR-FULL (author): “Name them” can serve as a challenge to establish that supposed partners exist, using a name metonymically for the named one's existence; Ibn Ashur says this is likewise not the basmala's usage. | mentions 13:33

question: How are al-Fātiḥa's seven verses divided?

positions.position: Abu Huraira reports the Prophet saying that al-Fatiha has seven verses and the first is the basmala.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أبو هريرة عن النبي): Abu Huraira reports the Prophet saying that al-Fatiha has seven verses and the first is the basmala. BAYDAWI (النبي): Abū Hurayra reports the Prophet saying al-Fatiha has seven verses and its first is the basmala. BAYDAWI-FULL (أبو هريرة): The Prophet reportedly called the basmala the first of al-Fātiḥa's seven verses. ALUSI-FULL (أبو هريرة): Abu Hurayra reports the Prophet saying that the Fatiha has seven verses, beginning with the basmala. ELMALILI (Ebû Hüreyre): A report from Abū Hurayra says the Prophet counted al-Fātiḥa as seven verses and named the basmala as its first.

positions.position: The Fatiha is called the seven oft-repeated because everyone agrees it has seven verses.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (author): The Fatiha is called the seven oft-repeated because everyone agrees it has seven verses. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): An authentic hadith calls al-Fatiha the seven oft-repeated, meaning its seven verses.

positions.position: All Qurʾān readers and scholars agree that al-Fātiḥa has seven verses; they disagree over which words make the count seven.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): All Qurʾān readers and scholars agree that al-Fātiḥa has seven verses; they disagree over which words make the count seven.

positions.position: Critics ask why al-Fātiḥa has seven verses when, they argue, the meaning of its remaining verses is already contained in “Master of Judgment Day” and “You alone we worship and ask for help.”
positions.reasons: TAB (أهل الإلحاد الطاعنون في القرآن): Critics ask why al-Fātiḥa has seven verses when, they argue, the meaning of its remaining verses is already contained in “Master of Judgment Day” and “You alone we worship and ask for help.”

positions.position: Gabriel says the seven verses overlay Hell’s seven gates, so reciters pass them safely; he had feared punishment before the Fātiḥa was revealed.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (جبريل): Gabriel says the seven verses overlay Hell’s seven gates, so reciters pass them safely; he had feared punishment before the Fātiḥa was revealed. | mentions 15:43

positions.position: Al-Shafi‘i’s count is preferable: the pause after an‘amta ‘alayhim does not match the sura’s verse endings, and verse endings elsewhere are either near-rhyming or matching.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Shafi‘i’s count is preferable: the pause after an‘amta ‘alayhim does not match the sura’s verse endings, and verse endings elsewhere are either near-rhyming or matching.

positions.position: Muslim’s report adds “and more” after al-Fātiḥa, distinguishing the prescribed opening from additional verses.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (عبادة بن الصامت): Muslim’s report adds “and more” after al-Fātiḥa, distinguishing the prescribed opening from additional verses.

positions.position: Al-Bustī explains al-Fātiḥa’s superiority over Torah and Gospel as greater reward for this community, not intrinsic superiority in God’s speech.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (البستي): Al-Bustī explains al-Fātiḥa’s superiority over Torah and Gospel as greater reward for this community, not intrinsic superiority in God’s speech.

positions.position: Al-Bustī interprets “greatest sūra” as greatest in reward.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (البستي): Al-Bustī interprets “greatest sūra” as greatest in reward.

positions.position: The Prophet asks Ubayy which verse is greatest; Ubayy answers the Throne Verse, and the Prophet praises his knowledge.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (أبي بن كعب): The Prophet asks Ubayy which verse is greatest; Ubayy answers the Throne Verse, and the Prophet praises his knowledge.

positions.position: Ibn al-ʿArabī argues that Torah, Gospel, and Qurʾān are the best scriptures, so superiority over the best entails superiority over all.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (ابن العربي): Ibn al-ʿArabī argues that Torah, Gospel, and Qurʾān are the best scriptures, so superiority over the best entails superiority over all.

positions.position: The community agrees al-Fātiḥa has seven verses; reports of six or eight are anomalous.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (الأمة): The community agrees al-Fātiḥa has seven verses; reports of six or eight are anomalous.

positions.position: The Prophet is quoted saying every important matter not begun with the basmala is deficient.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (النبي): The Prophet is quoted saying every important matter not begun with the basmala is deficient.

positions.position: The Prophet is quoted saying al-Fatiha is a cure for every illness, explaining its names al-Shāfiya and al-Shifāʾ.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (النبي): The Prophet is quoted saying al-Fatiha is a cure for every illness, explaining its names al-Shāfiya and al-Shifāʾ.

positions.position: Putting the governed phrase first gives emphasis, exclusivity, and reverence; the name precedes recitation and makes an act religiously complete, as in the cited verses.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL (author): Putting the governed phrase first gives emphasis, exclusivity, and reverence; the name precedes recitation and makes an act religiously complete, as in the cited verses. | mentions 11:41, 1:5

positions.position: The Fatiha has seven verses by consensus.
positions.reasons: NASAFI (author): The Fatiha has seven verses by consensus.

positions.position: Other reports say al-Fatiha descended with eighty thousand angels, the Throne Verse and Yunus with thirty thousand each, and “Ask those We sent before you” with twenty thousand.
positions.reasons: BURHAN (author): Other reports say al-Fatiha descended with eighty thousand angels, the Throne Verse and Yunus with thirty thousand each, and “Ask those We sent before you” with twenty thousand. | mentions 1:1, 2:255, 10:1, 43:45

positions.position: Ibn al-Arabi cites reports that al-Fatiha has seven verses and al-Mulk thirty, and that the Prophet recited Aal Imran's final ten; verse counts should follow early Muslims' practice.
positions.reasons: BURHAN (ابن العربي): Ibn al-Arabi cites reports that al-Fatiha has seven verses and al-Mulk thirty, and that the Prophet recited Aal Imran's final ten; verse counts should follow early Muslims' practice.

positions.position: An ayah may descend twice to magnify its importance and recall it when a new cause arises; the Fatiha is said to have descended once in Mecca and once in Medina, and this resolves the report about the Makkan Hūd
positions.reasons: BURHAN (author): An ayah may descend twice to magnify its importance and recall it when a new cause arises; the Fatiha is said to have descended once in Mecca and once in Medina, and this resolves the report about the Makkan Hūd verse.

positions.position: A report from Umm Salama says the Prophet divided his recitation verse by verse; some later scholars therefore objected to stopping mid-verse for meaning.
positions.reasons: BURHAN (أم سلمة): A report from Umm Salama says the Prophet divided his recitation verse by verse; some later scholars therefore objected to stopping mid-verse for meaning.

positions.position: Ibn Hibban says calling al-Fatiha the greatest surah means greatest in reward, not that one part of the Quran is intrinsically superior.
positions.reasons: BURHAN (ابن حبان): Ibn Hibban says calling al-Fatiha the greatest surah means greatest in reward, not that one part of the Quran is intrinsically superior.

positions.position: Abu Said reports the Prophet calling al-Fatiha the greatest surah in a Bukhari narration; al-Zarkashi says this does not conflict with Ayat al-Kursi’s rank among verses, since the comparisons concern surahs and verses respectively.
positions.reasons: BURHAN (author): Abu Said reports the Prophet calling al-Fatiha the greatest surah in a Bukhari narration; al-Zarkashi says this does not conflict with Ayat al-Kursi’s rank among verses, since the comparisons concern surahs and verses respectively.

positions.position: The Basrans analyze بسم الله as part of a nominal sentence, meaning my beginning is in God's name.
positions.reasons: BURHAN (البصريون): The Basrans analyze بسم الله as part of a nominal sentence, meaning my beginning is in God's name.

positions.position: The Kufans analyze بسم الله as part of a verbal sentence.
positions.reasons: BURHAN (الكوفيون): The Kufans analyze بسم الله as part of a verbal sentence.

positions.position: Al-Zamakhshari follows the Kufans but puts the implied verb after God's name and varies it by context; the author prefers this for contextual fit and foregrounding God's name.
positions.reasons: BURHAN (author): Al-Zamakhshari follows the Kufans but puts the implied verb after God's name and varies it by context; the author prefers this for contextual fit and foregrounding God's name.

positions.position: The Prophet says al-Fatiha has seven verses, one of them the basmala, and is the seven oft-repeated verses and Great Qur'an.
positions.reasons: DURR (النبي): The Prophet says al-Fatiha has seven verses, one of them the basmala, and is the seven oft-repeated verses and Great Qur'an.

positions.position: Ibrahim asked al-Aswad whether al-Fatiha belongs to the Qur'an; al-Aswad affirmed that it does.
positions.reasons: DURR (إبراهيم): Ibrahim asked al-Aswad whether al-Fatiha belongs to the Qur'an; al-Aswad affirmed that it does.

positions.position: Before the Hijra, Amr ibn al-Jamuh heard al-Fatiha, admired it, and asked whether Muhammad's other speech was like it.
positions.reasons: DURR (رجل من بني سلمة): Before the Hijra, Amr ibn al-Jamuh heard al-Fatiha, admired it, and asked whether Muhammad's other speech was like it.

positions.position: Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi counts al-Fatiha as seven verses including the basmala.
positions.reasons: DURR (محمد بن كعب القرظي): Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi counts al-Fatiha as seven verses including the basmala.

positions.position: Umm Salama reports that the Prophet recited the Fātiḥa including the basmala and called it seven verses.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (أم سلمة): Umm Salama reports that the Prophet recited the Fātiḥa including the basmala and called it seven verses.

positions.position: It is the seven mathānī by agreement on seven verses; disputes over counting the basmala or “those You favored” are governed by transmitted reports.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): It is the seven mathānī by agreement on seven verses; disputes over counting the basmala or “those You favored” are governed by transmitted reports. | mentions 1:1, 1:7

positions.position: Al-Ālūsī replies that lack of an earlier command does not prove earlier absence, and only the Qurʾān’s Arabic wording and arrangement may be distinctive.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Al-Ālūsī replies that lack of an earlier command does not prove earlier absence, and only the Qurʾān’s Arabic wording and arrangement may be distinctive.

positions.position: Al-Dāraquṭnī’s version says the Prophet counted the basmala but did not pause after “those You favored”; al-Ālūsī says it is not explicit that it belongs to al-Fātiḥa.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (الدارقطني): Al-Dāraquṭnī’s version says the Prophet counted the basmala but did not pause after “those You favored”; al-Ālūsī says it is not explicit that it belongs to al-Fātiḥa. | mentions 1:7

positions.position: A report from Abū Hurayra says the seven verses of al-Fātiḥa begin with the basmala; al-Ālūsī reads the wording as counting seven al-Ḥamd verses and separately affirming the basmala as Qurʾān.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (أبو هريرة): A report from Abū Hurayra says the seven verses of al-Fātiḥa begin with the basmala; al-Ālūsī reads the wording as counting seven al-Ḥamd verses and separately affirming the basmala as Qurʾān.

positions.position: The argument from seven verses assumes that Abū Ḥanīfa’s count is wrong; al-Ālūsī says that premise is difficult to establish.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): The argument from seven verses assumes that Abū Ḥanīfa’s count is wrong; al-Ālūsī says that premise is difficult to establish.

positions.position: Razi begins his eighth proof by noting that most count the Fatiha as seven verses, then introduces disagreement over the count.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (الفخر الرازي): Razi begins his eighth proof by noting that most count the Fatiha as seven verses, then introduces disagreement over the count.

positions.position: Al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi transmit Abu Hurayra's report that the Fatiha has seven verses, with the basmala one of them.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (أبو هريرة): Al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi transmit Abu Hurayra's report that the Fatiha has seven verses, with the basmala one of them.

positions.position: Alusi reads the stopping after an'amta alayhim as a complete meaning; stopping before ghayri'l-maghdubi would leave a phrase syntactically incomplete, and no separate count of alayhim is required.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi reads the stopping after an'amta alayhim as a complete meaning; stopping before ghayri'l-maghdubi would leave a phrase syntactically incomplete, and no separate count of alayhim is required.

positions.position: A report from Ibn ʿAbbās says that omitting the basmala omits 114 verses from God’s Book.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (İbn Abbas): A report from Ibn ʿAbbās says that omitting the basmala omits 114 verses from God’s Book.

positions.position: An unnamed view takes the seven oft-repeated verses in 15:87 to be al-Fatiha, seven verses repeated in prayer.
positions.reasons: QUTB-ZILAL (author): An unnamed view takes the seven oft-repeated verses in 15:87 to be al-Fatiha, seven verses repeated in prayer. | mentions 15:87

positions.position: Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī dissents from the seven-verse count and says Fātiha has eight verses.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (الحسن البصري): Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī dissents from the seven-verse count and says Fātiha has eight verses.

positions.position: Al-Ḥusayn al-Juʿfī is reported to count six verses in Fātiha.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (الحسين الجعفي): Al-Ḥusayn al-Juʿfī is reported to count six verses in Fātiha.

positions.position: This report confirms seven verses arranged as three, one, and three.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): This report confirms seven verses arranged as three, one, and three. | mentions 1:2, 1:3, 1:4, 1:5, 1:6, 1:7

positions.position: A report that Fātiha has seven verses, the first being the basmala, is cited for the Shāfiʿī position; it appears in al-Ṭabarānī, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqī, below Ṣaḥīḥ status.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (أبو هريرة): A report that Fātiha has seven verses, the first being the basmala, is cited for the Shāfiʿī position; it appears in al-Ṭabarānī, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqī, below Ṣaḥīḥ status.

turns_on: Which opening and final phrases are counted separately among the seven.

question: Why is al-Fātiḥa called the seven oft-repeated?

positions.position: Abu Hurayra reports the Prophet naming the sura Umm al-Qur’an, Fatiha al-Kitab, and the seven oft-repeated verses; no grading is given.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (أبو هريرة): Abu Hurayra reports the Prophet naming the sura Umm al-Qur’an, Fatiha al-Kitab, and the seven oft-repeated verses; no grading is given. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): Abū Hurayra reports that the Prophet said no comparable sūra was revealed in the Torah, Gospel, Psalms, or Qur'an; al-Fātiḥa is the seven oft-repeated verses and the great Qur'an given to him. QURTUBI (أبو هريرة): Abū Hurayra transmits the names Umm al-Qurʾān, Umm al-Kitāb, and the seven oft-repeated verses; al-Tirmidhī grades the report ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ.

positions.position: Seven are oft-repeated because Fātiḥa is recited in every prayer, obligatory or voluntary; 15:87.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): Seven are oft-repeated because Fātiḥa is recited in every prayer, obligatory or voluntary; 15:87. TAB (الحسن البصري): Al-Ḥasan identifies seven oft-repeated verses as Fātiḥa, repeated in every recitation or perhaps prayer; 15:87. MAWARDI (author): It is oft-repeated because it is recited in every obligatory and voluntary prayer.

positions.position: Prophet names Fātiḥa Mother of Qurʾān, Opening of Book and seven oft-repeated verses; Ṭabarī calls report sound.
positions.reasons: TAB (رسول الله): Prophet names Fātiḥa Mother of Qurʾān, Opening of Book and seven oft-repeated verses; Ṭabarī calls report sound. DURR (النبي): The Prophet identifies al-Hamd as the Mother of the Qur'an and Book, seven oft-repeated verses, al-Fatiha, and the Great Qur'an.

positions.position: ʿAlī recited the basmala when opening a sura in prayer, said omitting it diminishes the prayer, and called it the completion of the seven oft-repeated verses and the Great Qurʾān.
positions.reasons: THALABI (علي بن أبي طالب): ʿAlī recited the basmala when opening a sura in prayer, said omitting it diminishes the prayer, and called it the completion of the seven oft-repeated verses and the Great Qurʾān. DURR-FULL (علي): Ali recited the basmala when beginning a surah in prayer and said omitting it diminishes the prayer; it completes the seven oft-repeated verses.

positions.position: Ubayy reports that the Prophet called the Fātiḥa the unmatched Mother of the Qur’an and seven oft-repeated verses, divided between God and servant, with the servant receiving what he asks.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (أبى بن كعب): Ubayy reports that the Prophet called the Fātiḥa the unmatched Mother of the Qur’an and seven oft-repeated verses, divided between God and servant, with the servant receiving what he asks. QURTUBI (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): The Prophet tells Ubayy ibn Kaʿb that no Torah or Gospel passage matches the Mother of the Qurʾān, the seven oft-repeated verses divided between God and servant.

positions.position: It is the seven oft-repeated because scholars agree that it consists of seven verses.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI (author): It is the seven oft-repeated because scholars agree that it consists of seven verses. BAYDAWI (author): It is called the Seven Oft-Repeated because it comprises seven verses by agreement.

positions.position: It is called oft-repeated because it is recited in every prayer cycle.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI (author): It is called oft-repeated because it is recited in every prayer cycle. RAZI-FULL (author): It is called the oft-repeated because it is recited in prayer and then followed by another sura. | mentions 15:87

positions.position: One explanation of al-Mathani is that the surah is repeated in every prayer cycle.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (author): One explanation of al-Mathani is that the surah is repeated in every prayer cycle. RAZI-FULL (author): Another explanation is that it is repeated in every prayer cycle. | mentions 15:87

positions.position: Abu Saʿid ibn al-Muʿalla reports that the Prophet promised to teach him the Qur'an's greatest surah and identified it as al-Hamd, the seven oft-repeated and the great Qur'an.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): Abu Saʿid ibn al-Muʿalla reports that the Prophet promised to teach him the Qur'an's greatest surah and identified it as al-Hamd, the seven oft-repeated and the great Qur'an. DURR (النبي): The Prophet told Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mualla that al-Hamd is the greatest sura, the seven oft-repeated verses, and Great Qur'an given to him.

positions.position: Fatiha is the seven oft-repeated and Mother of the Book, its greatest and earliest part; Mecca is Mother of Villages because oldest; 3:96.
positions.reasons: IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL (author): Fatiha is the seven oft-repeated and Mother of the Book, its greatest and earliest part; Mecca is Mother of Villages because oldest; 3:96.

positions.position: Abū al-Najm’s verse pairs Fātiḥa’s praise with Qurʾān and oft-repeated, supporting the name’s association with Fātiḥa.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): Abū al-Najm’s verse pairs Fātiḥa’s praise with Qurʾān and oft-repeated, supporting the name’s association with Fātiḥa.

positions.position: An anonymous rajaz calls Mother of Book seven oft-repeated verses, doubled from Qurʾān’s verses.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): An anonymous rajaz calls Mother of Book seven oft-repeated verses, doubled from Qurʾān’s verses.

positions.position: Calling Fātiḥa seven oft-repeated does not prevent whole Qurʾān or later sūras also being mathānī for another understood reason.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): Calling Fātiḥa seven oft-repeated does not prevent whole Qurʾān or later sūras also being mathānī for another understood reason.

positions.position: God taught the Prophet to put His beautiful names before all actions and made this instruction a practice for everyone beginning speech, letters, books, or needs.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): God taught the Prophet to put His beautiful names before all actions and made this instruction a practice for everyone beginning speech, letters, books, or needs.

positions.position: Before reciting, standing, sitting, or another action, the phrase means beginning that act by naming and remembering God.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): Before reciting, standing, sitting, or another action, the phrase means beginning that act by naming and remembering God.

positions.position: Al-Ṭabarī rejects construing the phrase as “by God” in every act: it means beginning with God’s naming and remembrance, not claiming that an action is performed by God.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): Al-Ṭabarī rejects construing the phrase as “by God” in every act: it means beginning with God’s naming and remembrance, not claiming that an action is performed by God.

positions.position: Al-Ṭabarī objects that “possessor of mercy” asserts an established attribute, whereas “merciful” can describe past, present, or future action; the terms therefore do not simply mean the same thing.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): Al-Ṭabarī objects that “possessor of mercy” asserts an established attribute, whereas “merciful” can describe past, present, or future action; the terms therefore do not simply mean the same thing.

positions.position: Calling it al-mathani does not preclude applying that name to other passages; al-A‘sha of Hamdan’s verse calls other passages al-mathani and the long suras.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (author): Calling it al-mathani does not preclude applying that name to other passages; al-A‘sha of Hamdan’s verse calls other passages al-mathani and the long suras.

positions.position: Al-Fatiha is known by three names: Fatiḥat al-Kitāb, Umm al-Qurʾān, and al-Sabʿ al-Mathānī.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI (author): Al-Fatiha is known by three names: Fatiḥat al-Kitāb, Umm al-Qurʾān, and al-Sabʿ al-Mathānī.

positions.position: Another view says it was revealed twice, once in Mecca and once in Medina, which explains the name al-Mathānī.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI (author): Another view says it was revealed twice, once in Mecca and once in Medina, which explains the name al-Mathānī.

positions.position: It is called Fatiḥat al-Kitāb because God began the Qur'an with it.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI (author): It is called Fatiḥat al-Kitāb because God began the Qur'an with it.

positions.position: Mujahid says God reserved the seven oft-repeated for this community and stored it for them.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI (مجاهد): Mujahid says God reserved the seven oft-repeated for this community and stored it for them.

positions.position: The reported equivalence may reflect the surah's meanings or be a divine preference not rationally explained; similar equivalences are reported for al-Ikhlas and al-Zalzala.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (author): The reported equivalence may reflect the surah's meanings or be a divine preference not rationally explained; similar equivalences are reported for al-Ikhlas and al-Zalzala. | mentions 112:1, 99:1

positions.position: The surah is counted as seven verses by consensus, apart from the anomalous report that al-Husayn al-Ju'fi counted six.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (author): The surah is counted as seven verses by consensus, apart from the anomalous report that al-Husayn al-Ju'fi counted six.

positions.position: Al-Husayn al-Ju'fi reportedly counts six verses in al-Fatiha; Ibn Atiyya calls this anomalous and unreliable.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (حسين الجعفي): Al-Husayn al-Ju'fi reportedly counts six verses in al-Fatiha; Ibn Atiyya calls this anomalous and unreliable.

positions.position: The statement that God gave the Prophet seven oft-repeated verses in 15:87 settles the verse-count question.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (author): The statement that God gave the Prophet seven oft-repeated verses in 15:87 settles the verse-count question. | mentions 15:87

positions.position: Ibn Atiyya calls the letter-count explanation a playful exegetical conceit, not sound scholarship.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (author): Ibn Atiyya calls the letter-count explanation a playful exegetical conceit, not sound scholarship.

positions.position: These authorities say the sura was revealed in Mecca; its linkage with Meccan al-Hijr and the identification of the seven oft-repeated verses support that view.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (ابن عباس وموسى بن جعفر عن أبيه وعلي بن الحسين وقتادة وأبو العالية ومحمد بن يحيى بن حبان): These authorities say the sura was revealed in Mecca; its linkage with Meccan al-Hijr and the identification of the seven oft-repeated verses support that view. | mentions 15:87

positions.position: The author adds that prayer was prescribed in Mecca and no prayer in Islam is known to have been performed without al-hamdu.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): The author adds that prayer was prescribed in Mecca and no prayer in Islam is known to have been performed without al-hamdu.

positions.position: The name al-Mathani is explained either by its repetition in every prayer cycle or because this sura was reserved as a treasure for this community.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): The name al-Mathani is explained either by its repetition in every prayer cycle or because this sura was reserved as a treasure for this community.

positions.position: Al-Fātiḥa is so named because the book begins with it in recitation and writing; Umm al-Qur'an and Umm al-Kitāb because it leads the book; al-sabʿ al-mathānī is explained later in 15:87.
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD (author): Al-Fātiḥa is so named because the book begins with it in recitation and writing; Umm al-Qur'an and Umm al-Kitāb because it leads the book; al-sabʿ al-mathānī is explained later in 15:87. | mentions 15:87

positions.position: Ibn Durayd says umm can mean a banner; the Fātiḥa is the believers’ rallying point as a banner is an army’s, while earth is called mother because all return to it and umm can mean a destination.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (ابن دريد): Ibn Durayd says umm can mean a banner; the Fātiḥa is the believers’ rallying point as a banner is an army’s, while earth is called mother because all return to it and umm can mean a destination.

positions.position: One explanation of al-sabʿ al-mathānī is that half the sura is the servant’s praise and half God’s gift to the servant.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): One explanation of al-sabʿ al-mathānī is that half the sura is the servant’s praise and half God’s gift to the servant. | mentions 15:87

positions.position: A Prophetic report says no comparable sura occurs in the Torah, Gospel, Psalms, or Qur’an, and identifies it as the seven oft-repeated verses and the great Qur’an.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): A Prophetic report says no comparable sura occurs in the Torah, Gospel, Psalms, or Qur’an, and identifies it as the seven oft-repeated verses and the great Qur’an. | mentions 15:87

positions.position: A further explanation says each of its seven verses equals the recitation of seven portions of the Qur’an, so reciting it earns the reward of reciting all of it.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A further explanation says each of its seven verses equals the recitation of seven portions of the Qur’an, so reciting it earns the reward of reciting all of it. | mentions 15:87

positions.position: Another explanation takes mathānī as praises and commendations of God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Another explanation takes mathānī as praises and commendations of God. | mentions 15:87

positions.position: A final explanation says God revealed the sura twice, which is why it is called oft-repeated.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A final explanation says God revealed the sura twice, which is why it is called oft-repeated. | mentions 15:87

positions.position: A third view holds that the sura descended once in Mecca and again in Medina, its double revelation explaining its honorific name al-mathānī.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A third view holds that the sura descended once in Mecca and again in Medina, its double revelation explaining its honorific name al-mathānī.

positions.position: A rare report has al-Hasan al-Basri count al-Fatiha as eight verses, while the well-known view accepted by most counts seven and identifies them with the seven oft-repeated verses.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الحسن البصري): A rare report has al-Hasan al-Basri count al-Fatiha as eight verses, while the well-known view accepted by most counts seven and identifies them with the seven oft-repeated verses. | mentions 15:87

positions.position: In al-Bukhārī’s report, the Prophet calls al-Fātiḥa the greatest sūra, the seven oft-repeated verses, and the magnificent Qurʾān.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (أبو سعيد بن المعلى): In al-Bukhārī’s report, the Prophet calls al-Fātiḥa the greatest sūra, the seven oft-repeated verses, and the magnificent Qurʾān.

positions.position: The preferred view allows gradation by remarkable meanings and density of teaching, not by the Qurʾān’s shared status as God’s speech.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (إسحاق بن راهويه وابن العربي وابن الحصار): The preferred view allows gradation by remarkable meanings and density of teaching, not by the Qurʾān’s shared status as God’s speech.

positions.position: Qurṭubī counts twelve names for al-Fātiḥa.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (author): Qurṭubī counts twelve names for al-Fātiḥa.

positions.position: Al-Fātiḥa is called al-Mathānī because it repeats in every prayer unit; another explanation says it was reserved for this community.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (الجمهور): Al-Fātiḥa is called al-Mathānī because it repeats in every prayer unit; another explanation says it was reserved for this community.

positions.position: Al-Shaʿbī recommends al-Fātiḥa for flank pain and transmits Ibn ʿAbbās’s account naming it the basis of the Qurʾān.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (الشعبي وابن عباس): Al-Shaʿbī recommends al-Fātiḥa for flank pain and transmits Ibn ʿAbbās’s account naming it the basis of the Qurʾān.

positions.position: Calling al-Fātiḥa Umm al-Kitāb or al-Mathānī does not exclude other uses; the Qurʾān itself is called a repeated book.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (author): Calling al-Fātiḥa Umm al-Kitāb or al-Mathānī does not exclude other uses; the Qurʾān itself is called a repeated book. | mentions 39:23

positions.position: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the seven mathānī as the seven long sūras; scholars differ whether the seventh is Yūnus or al-Anfāl with al-Tawba.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the seven mathānī as the seven long sūras; scholars differ whether the seventh is Yūnus or al-Anfāl with al-Tawba. | mentions 2:1, 7:1, 10:1

positions.position: Mathānī may denote sūras after the first and before short sūras; al-Anfāl follows the long ones in size, while miʾūn exceed one hundred verses.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (author): Mathānī may denote sūras after the first and before short sūras; al-Anfāl follows the long ones in size, while miʾūn exceed one hundred verses.

positions.position: Qurṭubī prefers the Meccan view: al-Ḥijr is Meccan and names seven oft-repeated verses; prayer was prescribed in Mecca.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (author): Qurṭubī prefers the Meccan view: al-Ḥijr is Meccan and names seven oft-repeated verses; prayer was prescribed in Mecca. | mentions 15:87

positions.position: It is repeated in prayer, or—if the report is sound—was revealed in Mecca when prayer was imposed and in Medina when the qibla changed.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (author): It is repeated in prayer, or—if the report is sound—was revealed in Mecca when prayer was imposed and in Medina when the qibla changed.

positions.position: Bayḍāwī confirms it is Meccan, citing the Meccan verse that says God gave the Prophet the seven oft-repeated verses.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (author): Bayḍāwī confirms it is Meccan, citing the Meccan verse that says God gave the Prophet the seven oft-repeated verses. | mentions 15:87

positions.position: It is called al-Mathani because it is repeated in every prayer; it is also called the Prayer based on reports and its obligatory status, and al-Hamd and al-Asas because it grounds the Qur’an.
positions.reasons: NASAFI (author): It is called al-Mathani because it is repeated in every prayer; it is also called the Prayer based on reports and its obligatory status, and al-Hamd and al-Asas because it grounds the Qur’an.

positions.position: A report from Ubay identifies al-Fātiḥa as the seven oft-repeated verses and one of the seven long sūras, revealed some time after al-Ḥijr.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (أبي): A report from Ubay identifies al-Fātiḥa as the seven oft-repeated verses and one of the seven long sūras, revealed some time after al-Ḥijr.

positions.position: A third report says it was revealed twice, but Ibn Kathir prefers the Meccan account, connecting it with the seven oft-repeated in 15:87.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): A third report says it was revealed twice, but Ibn Kathir prefers the Meccan account, connecting it with the seven oft-repeated in 15:87. | mentions 15:87

positions.position: The title al-Sabʿ al-Mathani is explained by its repetition in every prayer unit, though Ibn Kathir notes another meaning will follow.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): The title al-Sabʿ al-Mathani is explained by its repetition in every prayer unit, though Ibn Kathir notes another meaning will follow.

positions.position: Reports from Abu Hurayra identify Umm al-Qur'an as the Fatiha and the seven oft-repeated; al-Daraqutni says its transmitters are trustworthy.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): Reports from Abu Hurayra identify Umm al-Qur'an as the Fatiha and the seven oft-repeated; al-Daraqutni says its transmitters are trustworthy. | mentions 15:87

positions.position: Another report from Ubayy calls Umm al-Qur'an the seven oft-repeated, divided between God and His servant; al-Tirmidhi grades it hasan gharib.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): Another report from Ubayy calls Umm al-Qur'an the seven oft-repeated, divided between God and His servant; al-Tirmidhi grades it hasan gharib.

positions.position: In a hadith graded sound by al-Tirmidhi, the Prophet calls it Umm al-Qur'an, Umm al-Kitab, the seven oft-repeated, and the great Qur'an.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): In a hadith graded sound by al-Tirmidhi, the Prophet calls it Umm al-Qur'an, Umm al-Kitab, the seven oft-repeated, and the great Qur'an.

positions.position: Al-Fātiḥa is also called the Mother of the Book, Foundation, Oft-Repeated, Treasure, Healer, Sufficient, Fulfilling, Protector, Incantation, Praise, Gratitude, Supplication, and Prayer.
positions.reasons: BIQAI (author): Al-Fātiḥa is also called the Mother of the Book, Foundation, Oft-Repeated, Treasure, Healer, Sufficient, Fulfilling, Protector, Incantation, Praise, Gratitude, Supplication, and Prayer.

positions.position: Supplication is the very act of turning to the One invoked, and prayer is the greatest encompassing expression of that turn.
positions.reasons: BIQAI (author): Supplication is the very act of turning to the One invoked, and prayer is the greatest encompassing expression of that turn.

positions.position: The Fatiha's many titles converge on مراقبة: it is the Mother of the Book, foundation, oft-repeated, treasure, healing, sufficing, complete, protecting, incantation, praise, thanks, supplication and prayer.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (author): The Fatiha's many titles converge on مراقبة: it is the Mother of the Book, foundation, oft-repeated, treasure, healing, sufficing, complete, protecting, incantation, praise, thanks, supplication and prayer.

positions.position: Ali recited the basmala at a sura's start in prayer, saying its omission reduces the seven oft-repeated verses.
positions.reasons: DURR (علي): Ali recited the basmala at a sura's start in prayer, saying its omission reduces the seven oft-repeated verses.

positions.position: Reports from ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, and most Companions support its Meccan origin.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (علي وابن عباس وقتادة وأكثر الصحابة): Reports from ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, and most Companions support its Meccan origin.

positions.position: Mathānī may refer to repeated recitation, repetition with another sūra, two revelation occasions, its combination of praise and prayer, or God’s response to each verse.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Mathānī may refer to repeated recitation, repetition with another sūra, two revelation occasions, its combination of praise and prayer, or God’s response to each verse.

positions.position: Other derivations connect mathānī to praise of God or its reciter, or to God’s special bestowal of it on this community.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Other derivations connect mathānī to praise of God or its reciter, or to God’s special bestowal of it on this community.

positions.position: Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn al-Mubārak, Meccan and most Kufan readers, most Shāfiʿīs, and Imāmīs hold it is a verse in every sūra except al-Tawba.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (ابن عباس وابن المبارك وأهل مكة وأهل الكوفة وغالب أصحاب الشافعي والإمامية): Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn al-Mubārak, Meccan and most Kufan readers, most Shāfiʿīs, and Imāmīs hold it is a verse in every sūra except al-Tawba.

positions.position: Ibn ʿAbbās and others also explained the seven mathānī as the seven long sūras, weakening the dating argument from 15:87.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Ibn ʿAbbās and others also explained the seven mathānī as the seven long sūras, weakening the dating argument from 15:87. | mentions 15:87

positions.position: Ibn Abbas identifies the seventh of the seven oft-repeated verses as the basmala.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas identifies the seventh of the seven oft-repeated verses as the basmala. | mentions 15:87

positions.position: He reads the second wording as telling readers to recite the basmala before the Fatiha; its description of the Fatiha as the seven oft-repeated verses motivates reciting it.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): He reads the second wording as telling readers to recite the basmala before the Fatiha; its description of the Fatiha as the seven oft-repeated verses motivates reciting it.

positions.position: Al-Fatiha has many circulating names, but reliable Sunnah establishes only Fātihat al-Kitāb, al-Sabʿ al-Mathānī, and Umm al-Qurʾān/Umm al-Kitāb; Ibn ʿĀshūr limits discussion to these.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): Al-Fatiha has many circulating names, but reliable Sunnah establishes only Fātihat al-Kitāb, al-Sabʿ al-Mathānī, and Umm al-Qurʾān/Umm al-Kitāb; Ibn ʿĀshūr limits discussion to these.

positions.position: In Sūrat Fātiḥat al-Kitāb, general-to-specific annexation is acceptable when both terms are generic nouns and the broader term is shortened by adding the narrower one; convention makes it idiomatic.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): In Sūrat Fātiḥat al-Kitāb, general-to-specific annexation is acceptable when both terms are generic nouns and the broader term is shortened by adding the narrower one; convention makes it idiomatic.

positions.position: He also allows Sūrat Fātiḥat al-Kitāb as an annexation of a described noun to its adjective: a sura characterized as the opener of the Book.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): He also allows Sūrat Fātiḥat al-Kitāb as an annexation of a described noun to its adjective: a sura characterized as the opener of the Book.

positions.position: In al-Bukhari, the Prophet identifies al-Ḥamdu lillāh as the seven oft-repeated verses and the mighty Qur’an given to him.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (أبو سعيد ابن المعلى): In al-Bukhari, the Prophet identifies al-Ḥamdu lillāh as the seven oft-repeated verses and the mighty Qur’an given to him. | mentions 1:2

positions.position: Mathānī has several possible morphological analyses; all derive from pairing a second with a first, and the verse is called repeated because it is recited in every rakʿa.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): Mathānī has several possible morphological analyses; all derive from pairing a second with a first, and the verse is called repeated because it is recited in every rakʿa.

positions.position: Another view takes mathānī as repetition in prayer generally, supported by Arabic use of dual forms for repeated action and by the Qur’an’s recurrent stories and themes.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): Another view takes mathānī as repetition in prayer generally, supported by Arabic use of dual forms for repeated action and by the Qur’an’s recurrent stories and themes. | mentions 67:4, 39:23

positions.position: A report from Abu Hurayra says to recite the basmala with al-Fatiha, since it is the Mother of the Qur'an, the seven oft-repeated verses, and one of its verses.
positions.reasons: TABATABAI (النبي): A report from Abu Hurayra says to recite the basmala with al-Fatiha, since it is the Mother of the Qur'an, the seven oft-repeated verses, and one of its verses.

positions.position: Muslims recite the Fātiḥah at diverse life events; funeral services are called fātiḥah in some lands as an opening from one life to another.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (author): Muslims recite the Fātiḥah at diverse life events; funeral services are called fātiḥah in some lands as an opening from one life to another.

positions.position: The Prophet identifies the Fātiḥah as the greatest sūrah, calling it Praise be to God and the seven oft-repeated, and linking it to 15:87.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (Prophet Muhammad): The Prophet identifies the Fātiḥah as the greatest sūrah, calling it Praise be to God and the seven oft-repeated, and linking it to 15:87. | mentions 15:87

positions.position: In a hadith qudsī, God responds to the servant’s praise, magnification, and glorification during the prayer, which is divided between them.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (God): In a hadith qudsī, God responds to the servant’s praise, magnification, and glorification during the prayer, which is divided between them.

positions.position: Another title, The Seven Oft-Repeated, is linked to 15:87.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (author): Another title, The Seven Oft-Repeated, is linked to 15:87. | mentions 15:87

question: What does the divided prayer report say about al-Fātiḥa?

positions.position: Abū Hurayra reports that the Prophet said God answers the worshipper's recitation: He calls al-ḥamdu praise, al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm commendation, Mālik Yawm al-Dīn glorification, and the rest of the surah the servant's share.
positions.reasons: TAB (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): Abū Hurayra reports that the Prophet said God answers the worshipper's recitation: He calls al-ḥamdu praise, al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm commendation, Mālik Yawm al-Dīn glorification, and the rest of the surah the servant's share.

positions.position: Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh reports the divine saying that the prayer is divided between God and His servant, with the servant receiving what he asks; the first three praises are God's, and what follows is for the servant.
positions.reasons: TAB (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh reports the divine saying that the prayer is divided between God and His servant, with the servant receiving what he asks; the first three praises are God's, and what follows is for the servant.

positions.position: The Prophet says the prayer is divided between God and the servant: the opening praise, mercy, and judgment belong to God, and the remainder is the servant’s request.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (جابر بن عبد الله الأنصاري عن رسول الله): The Prophet says the prayer is divided between God and the servant: the opening praise, mercy, and judgment belong to God, and the remainder is the servant’s request. | mentions 1:2, 1:1, 1:4

positions.position: The Fatiha is called the Mother of the Book because it commands servanthood and praises God's lordship; the report of prayer divided between God and servant refers to reciting it, making it the basis of subtle gifts and nearness.
positions.reasons: QUSHAYRI (author): The Fatiha is called the Mother of the Book because it commands servanthood and praises God's lordship; the report of prayer divided between God and servant refers to reciting it, making it the basis of subtle gifts and nearness.

positions.position: It is called prayer because God says He divided the prayer between Himself and His servant in two halves, meaning this sura.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): It is called prayer because God says He divided the prayer between Himself and His servant in two halves, meaning this sura.

positions.position: In the divided-prayer report, God calls the basmala glorification, al-Hamd praise, the two mercy names extolling, the Master of Judgment entrustment, and the remaining response a sharing and a request granted.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أبو هريرة عن النبي): In the divided-prayer report, God calls the basmala glorification, al-Hamd praise, the two mercy names extolling, the Master of Judgment entrustment, and the remaining response a sharing and a request granted.

positions.position: The report of prayer divided between God and the servant omits the basmala; opponents infer that it is not a verse of al-Fatiha.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أبو هريرة): The report of prayer divided between God and the servant omits the basmala; opponents infer that it is not a verse of al-Fatiha.

positions.position: Opponents identify the divided prayer with al-Fatiha: without the basmala its seven verses divide three-and-a-half to each side, whereas counting it gives God four-and-a-half and the servant two-and-a-half.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (المخالف): Opponents identify the divided prayer with al-Fatiha: without the basmala its seven verses divide three-and-a-half to each side, whereas counting it gives God four-and-a-half and the servant two-and-a-half.

positions.position: The divided-prayer report makes al-Fatiha’s recitation integral to both solitary and congregational prayer because the division occurs through recitation.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أبو هريرة): The divided-prayer report makes al-Fatiha’s recitation integral to both solitary and congregational prayer because the division occurs through recitation.

positions.position: In the divided-prayer report, God responds to al-Fātiḥa’s opening and names its middle and last portions without mentioning the basmala.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (أبو هريرة): In the divided-prayer report, God responds to al-Fātiḥa’s opening and names its middle and last portions without mentioning the basmala.

positions.position: Al-Harali explains the sound report that God divided prayer between Himself and His servant: the first three verses are God's praise, which He accepts from the reciting servant as praise and glorification.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): Al-Harali explains the sound report that God divided prayer between Himself and His servant: the first three verses are God's praise, which He accepts from the reciting servant as praise and glorification.

positions.position: In the divided-prayer hadith, God answers al-Fatiha's phrases with praise and says the servant receives what he asks.
positions.reasons: DURR (الله): In the divided-prayer hadith, God answers al-Fatiha's phrases with praise and says the servant receives what he asks.

positions.position: Calling the sūra al-Ṣalāh is supported by the report “I divided the prayer”; prayer may stand for the sūra by whole-part relation or convention.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Calling the sūra al-Ṣalāh is supported by the report “I divided the prayer”; prayer may stand for the sūra by whole-part relation or convention.

positions.position: Abu Hurayra reports in Sahih Muslim that God calls al-Fatiha a prayer divided between Himself and His servant: praise, mercy, and glorification are the Lord's; worship and aid are shared; guidance and the servant's request belong to the servant, who
positions.reasons: QUTB-ZILAL (رسول الله): Abu Hurayra reports in Sahih Muslim that God calls al-Fatiha a prayer divided between Himself and His servant: praise, mercy, and glorification are the Lord's; worship and aid are shared; guidance and the servant's request belong to the servant, who receives what he asks.

positions.position: Abu Hurayra reports a divine hadith, transmitted by Muslim and the four Sunan collections, in which God answers the servant's phrases in al-Fatiha and shares the central petition between them.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR-FULL (أبو هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): Abu Hurayra reports a divine hadith, transmitted by Muslim and the four Sunan collections, in which God answers the servant's phrases in al-Fatiha and shares the central petition between them.

question: Why does al-Fātiḥa have its different titles?

positions.position: It is called the Opening of the Book because it begins written Qurʾāns and is recited in prayers, opening the following sūras in writing and recitation.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): It is called the Opening of the Book because it begins written Qurʾāns and is recited in prayers, opening the following sūras in writing and recitation. QURTUBI (author): It is called the Opening of the Book because it begins Qurʾānic recitation, muṣḥaf writing, and prayer. IBNKATHIR (author): The surah is called al-Fatiha because it opens the written Book and begins recitation in prayer.

positions.position: Al-Fātiḥa is Umm al-Kitāb because it is written first in codices and recited before every other surah in prayer.
positions.reasons: MAJAZ (author): Al-Fātiḥa is Umm al-Kitāb because it is written first in codices and recited before every other surah in prayer. BAGHAWI (author): Another explanation of Umm al-Kitāb is that it precedes and leads the following surahs, being first written in codices and read in prayer.

positions.position: Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī reports from the Prophet that the Fātiḥa heals poison.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أبو سعيد الخدري): Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī reports from the Prophet that the Fātiḥa heals poison. IBNKATHIR (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): A report from Abu Saʿid calls the Fatiha a healing from every poison.

positions.position: The author's father thought regular qunut supplication was Quran because he saw the Prophet repeat it in prayer, and held this despite Companions’ disagreement.
positions.reasons: IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL (أبي): The author's father thought regular qunut supplication was Quran because he saw the Prophet repeat it in prayer, and held this despite Companions’ disagreement.

positions.position: The Prophet’s statement no prayer except with Sūrat al-Ḥamd supports Fatiha’s indispensable place in prayer.
positions.reasons: IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL (النبي): The Prophet’s statement no prayer except with Sūrat al-Ḥamd supports Fatiha’s indispensable place in prayer.

positions.position: It is the Mother of the Qurʾān because it precedes the other sūras in reading and writing, while they follow it.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): It is the Mother of the Qurʾān because it precedes the other sūras in reading and writing, while they follow it.

positions.position: Two explanations are reported for Mecca as “Mother of the Towns”: it precedes and gathers the towns, or the earth was spread out from it.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): Two explanations are reported for Mecca as “Mother of the Towns”: it precedes and gathers the towns, or the earth was spread out from it.

positions.position: One unnamed view says al-Fātiḥa is named for opening the delight of intimate address, making it an opening to every good.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (قيل): One unnamed view says al-Fātiḥa is named for opening the delight of intimate address, making it an opening to every good.

positions.position: Another view treats the title as God's first opening of discourse: proper conduct grants access to later subtleties, while failure bars them.
positions.reasons: SULAMI (قيل): Another view treats the title as God's first opening of discourse: proper conduct grants access to later subtleties, while failure bars them.

positions.position: The author notes that ʿAlī included the basmala among the verses he counted as the Mother of the Book.
positions.reasons: THALABI (علي بن أبي طالب): The author notes that ʿAlī included the basmala among the verses he counted as the Mother of the Book.

positions.position: Ibn ʿAbbās says the Prophet voiced the basmala in Mecca, prompting pagans to mock the mention of the “god of al-Yamāma,” meaning Musaylima; the author connects this to the command for moderate volume.
positions.reasons: THALABI (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās says the Prophet voiced the basmala in Mecca, prompting pagans to mock the mention of the “god of al-Yamāma,” meaning Musaylima; the author connects this to the command for moderate volume. | mentions 17:110

positions.position: Anas says the Prophet, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar opened recitation with al-ḥamdu lillāh; the author interprets this as opening prayer with the sura called al-Ḥamd, not beginning at verse two.
positions.reasons: THALABI (أنس بن مالك): Anas says the Prophet, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar opened recitation with al-ḥamdu lillāh; the author interprets this as opening prayer with the sura called al-Ḥamd, not beginning at verse two.

positions.position: It is called Fatiha al-Kitab because the written Qur’an begins with it and it is first in recitation.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (author): It is called Fatiha al-Kitab because the written Qur’an begins with it and it is first in recitation.

positions.position: It is called Umm al-Qur’an because it precedes the rest, which follow it; an army’s banner is also called umm because the army follows it, as Labid’s verse illustrates.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (author): It is called Umm al-Qur’an because it precedes the rest, which follow it; an army’s banner is also called umm because the army follows it, as Labid’s verse illustrates.

positions.position: The years already lived are also called umm because they precede a person’s present, supported by the cited verse about fifty years.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (author): The years already lived are also called umm because they precede a person’s present, supported by the cited verse about fifty years.

positions.position: Most scholars allow calling the Fatiha Umm al-Kitab because al-Kitab means the Qur’an.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (الأكثرون): Most scholars allow calling the Fatiha Umm al-Kitab because al-Kitab means the Qur’an.

positions.position: Hasan and Ibn Sirin reject calling it Umm al-Kitab, reserving that title for the Preserved Tablet in 43:4.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (الحسن وابن سيرين): Hasan and Ibn Sirin reject calling it Umm al-Kitab, reserving that title for the Preserved Tablet in 43:4. | mentions 43:4

positions.position: Makka is called Umm al-Qura because it precedes the other towns.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (unattributed): Makka is called Umm al-Qura because it precedes the other towns.

positions.position: Alternatively, Makkah is Umm al-Qura because the earth was spread out from it and originated there, like children originating from a mother.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (unattributed): Alternatively, Makkah is Umm al-Qura because the earth was spread out from it and originated there, like children originating from a mother.

positions.position: Saying bismillah is called basmala, a coined usage that also occurs in poetry by Umar ibn Abi Rabi‘a.
positions.reasons: MAWARDI (author): Saying bismillah is called basmala, a coined usage that also occurs in poetry by Umar ibn Abi Rabi‘a.

positions.position: It is Umm al-Kitāb because it is the Qur'an's origin; umm means origin, as Mecca is Umm al-Qura, where the land was spread out from beneath it.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI (author): It is Umm al-Kitāb because it is the Qur'an's origin; umm means origin, as Mecca is Umm al-Qura, where the land was spread out from beneath it.

positions.position: The majority of scholars permit the title Umm al-Quran, contrary to Ibn Sirin's dislike.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (جمهور العلماء): The majority of scholars permit the title Umm al-Quran, contrary to Ibn Sirin's dislike.

positions.position: Yahya b. Ya'mar analogizes Umm al-Quran to Umm al-Qura for Mecca and Umm Khurasan for Merv.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (يحيى بن يعمر): Yahya b. Ya'mar analogizes Umm al-Quran to Umm al-Qura for Mecca and Umm Khurasan for Merv.

positions.position: Hasan b. Abi al-Hasan also gives al-Fatiha the name Umm al-Quran.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (الحسن بن أبي الحسن): Hasan b. Abi al-Hasan also gives al-Fatiha the name Umm al-Quran.

positions.position: There is no disagreement that the surah is called Fatihat al-Kitab because its position makes it the opening of the Book.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (author): There is no disagreement that the surah is called Fatihat al-Kitab because its position makes it the opening of the Book.

positions.position: Hasan b. Abi al-Hasan objects to the title Umm al-Kitab, reserving that name for the lawful and unlawful, as in 3:7.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (الحسن بن أبي الحسن): Hasan b. Abi al-Hasan objects to the title Umm al-Kitab, reserving that name for the lawful and unlawful, as in 3:7. | mentions 3:7

positions.position: Ibn Abbas and others accept Umm al-Kitab as a name for al-Fatiha.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (ابن عباس وغيره): Ibn Abbas and others accept Umm al-Kitab as a name for al-Fatiha.

positions.position: A report from Umm Salama says the Prophet paused on the sukun of rahim, stopped there, and began al-hamd with a hamzat al-qat'; some Kufans recited this way.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (أم سلمة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): A report from Umm Salama says the Prophet paused on the sukun of rahim, stopped there, and began al-hamd with a hamzat al-qat'; some Kufans recited this way.

positions.position: Most reciters read al-rahimi l-hamdu with the genitive ending and connect the alif of al-hamd.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (جمهور الناس): Most reciters read al-rahimi l-hamdu with the genitive ending and connect the alif of al-hamd.

positions.position: Ibn Sirin disliked calling al-Fatiha Umm al-Quran.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (ابن سيرين): Ibn Sirin disliked calling al-Fatiha Umm al-Quran.

positions.position: The sura is uncontroversially called the Opening of the Book because of its position at the start.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): The sura is uncontroversially called the Opening of the Book because of its position at the start.

positions.position: Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan dislikes calling it the Mother of the Book, reserving that designation for the decisive verses that contain lawful and unlawful rulings.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (الحسن بن أبي الحسن): Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan dislikes calling it the Mother of the Book, reserving that designation for the decisive verses that contain lawful and unlawful rulings. | mentions 3:7

positions.position: Ibn ʿAbbas and others do call al-Fatiha the Mother of the Book.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (ابن عباس وغيره): Ibn ʿAbbas and others do call al-Fatiha the Mother of the Book.

positions.position: Al-Bukhari explains “Mother of the Book” by its being written first in the codex and recited first in prayer.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (البخاري): Al-Bukhari explains “Mother of the Book” by its being written first in the codex and recited first in prayer.

positions.position: Ibn Sirin dislikes the title Mother of the Qur'an, while most scholars allow it.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (ابن سيرين): Ibn Sirin dislikes the title Mother of the Qur'an, while most scholars allow it.

positions.position: Yahya ibn Yaʿmar gives geographic analogies for “mother” and says al-hamdu is the Mother of the Qur'an.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (يحيى بن يعمر): Yahya ibn Yaʿmar gives geographic analogies for “mother” and says al-hamdu is the Mother of the Qur'an.

positions.position: Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan also calls the sura the Mother of the Qur'an.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (الحسن بن أبي الحسن): Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan also calls the sura the Mother of the Qur'an.

positions.position: The Prophet warns that a believer's discernment looks by God's light.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النبي): The Prophet warns that a believer's discernment looks by God's light.

positions.position: The most prudent person remembers death and prepares for it; turning from the deluding world toward the eternal home lets light expand the heart for preparation.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النبي): The most prudent person remembers death and prepares for it; turning from the deluding world toward the eternal home lets light expand the heart for preparation.

positions.position: Explaining 39:22, the Prophet says light entering the heart expands it; its signs are turning to the lasting home, leaving delusion, and preparing for death.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النبي): Explaining 39:22, the Prophet says light entering the heart expands it; its signs are turning to the lasting home, leaving delusion, and preparing for death. | mentions 39:22

positions.position: An angel tells the Prophet that two lights never granted to anyone before him are the Opening of the Book and the closing verses of al-Baqara.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النبي): An angel tells the Prophet that two lights never granted to anyone before him are the Opening of the Book and the closing verses of al-Baqara.

positions.position: Ibn Umar's prayer asks God to make him share in each day's guidance-light, mercy, provision, relief from harm, protection from trials, and removal of evil.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النبي): Ibn Umar's prayer asks God to make him share in each day's guidance-light, mercy, provision, relief from harm, protection from trials, and removal of evil.

positions.position: Asked about Paradise's people, the Prophet says that though unkempt and poorly clothed, one person's light would suffice for all the earth.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النبي): Asked about Paradise's people, the Prophet says that though unkempt and poorly clothed, one person's light would suffice for all the earth.

positions.position: A second report describes humble, ragged people overlooked by rulers and suitors; their inward need is hidden, and one person's light would suffice for the earth.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النبي): A second report describes humble, ragged people overlooked by rulers and suitors; their inward need is hidden, and one person's light would suffice for the earth.

positions.position: In a divine report, God says His light is His guidance and that whoever professes His word of divine unity enters His fortress and is safe.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النبي): In a divine report, God says His light is His guidance and that whoever professes His word of divine unity enters His fortress and is safe.

positions.position: The Prophet seeks protection in God's complete words and His light, by which earth was brightened and darkness illuminated, from lost blessing and sudden calamity.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النبي): The Prophet seeks protection in God's complete words and His light, by which earth was brightened and darkness illuminated, from lost blessing and sudden calamity.

positions.position: The Prophet's well-known prayer asks for light in his heart, hearing, and sight.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النبي): The Prophet's well-known prayer asks for light in his heart, hearing, and sight.

positions.position: The Prophet says God created Adam in His image.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النبي): The Prophet says God created Adam in His image.

positions.position: The Prophet forbids disfiguring faces, saying God created Adam in the image of the Merciful.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (النبي): The Prophet forbids disfiguring faces, saying God created Adam in the image of the Merciful.

positions.position: Jesus sees a sinner’s punishment replaced by mercy after the man’s child learns Bismillah; God says He is ashamed to punish below ground while His name is remembered above.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Jesus sees a sinner’s punishment replaced by mercy after the man’s child learns Bismillah; God says He is ashamed to punish below ground while His name is remembered above.

positions.position: ʿUmra al-Farghāniyya explains that menstruating women and the ritually impure may be barred from Qur’an recitation but not from Bismillah, since a beloved is not barred from remembering the beloved.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (عمرة الفرغانية): ʿUmra al-Farghāniyya explains that menstruating women and the ritually impure may be barred from Qur’an recitation but not from Bismillah, since a beloved is not barred from remembering the beloved.

positions.position: A knower puts Bismillah in his shroud so he can ask God to treat him according to the title of His book.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A knower puts Bismillah in his shroud so he can ask God to treat him according to the title of His book.

positions.position: It is called the Foundation because it is the first sura, contains the noblest aims, and is indispensable to prayer, the greatest worship after faith.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): It is called the Foundation because it is the first sura, contains the noblest aims, and is indispensable to prayer, the greatest worship after faith.

positions.position: The Prophet calls the Fātiḥa healing from every poison; a companion’s recitation cured an epileptic, and the Prophet also calls it healing from every disease.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): The Prophet calls the Fātiḥa healing from every poison; a companion’s recitation cured an epileptic, and the Prophet also calls it healing from every disease.

positions.position: Rāzī explains the healing spiritually and physically: since unbelief is called a disease, the sura’s theology, duties, and spiritual unveilings heal all three domains.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Rāzī explains the healing spiritually and physically: since unbelief is called a disease, the sura’s theology, duties, and spiritual unveilings heal all three domains. | mentions 2:10

positions.position: Because the sura moves from praise to worship to a request for guidance, it teaches that religious guidance is the highest aim and the garden of knowledge surpasses the garden of pleasure.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Because the sura moves from praise to worship to a request for guidance, it teaches that religious guidance is the highest aim and the garden of knowledge surpasses the garden of pleasure.

positions.position: It is called the Sura of Gratitude because it praises God for His favor, generosity, and beneficence.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): It is called the Sura of Gratitude because it praises God for His favor, generosity, and beneficence.

positions.position: It is called the Sura of Supplication because it includes the request for the straight path.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): It is called the Sura of Supplication because it includes the request for the straight path.

positions.position: Ḥudhayfa ibn al-Yamān reports that a child’s recitation of al-Ḥamd lillāh during a destined calamity leads God to lift it for forty years.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (حذيفة بن اليمان): Ḥudhayfa ibn al-Yamān reports that a child’s recitation of al-Ḥamd lillāh during a destined calamity leads God to lift it for forty years.

positions.position: Al-Ḥusayn says knowledge flowed from 104 heavenly books through the four major books and the Qur’an until it was concentrated in the Fātiḥa, whose interpretation equals knowledge of all revelation.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الحسين): Al-Ḥusayn says knowledge flowed from 104 heavenly books through the four major books and the Qur’an until it was concentrated in the Fātiḥa, whose interpretation equals knowledge of all revelation.

positions.position: Rāzī explains that the Fātiḥa contains all divine aims because it fully treats theology, religious practice, and spiritual unveiling.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Rāzī explains that the Fātiḥa contains all divine aims because it fully treats theology, religious practice, and spiritual unveiling.

positions.position: A report from Abu Huraira says the Prophet told believers not to omit the basmala when reciting the Mother of the Book because it is one of its verses.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أبو هريرة عن النبي): A report from Abu Huraira says the Prophet told believers not to omit the basmala when reciting the Mother of the Book because it is one of its verses.

positions.position: Unlike the incomplete guidance request, al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin is a complete sentence by itself, so it can be a verse before الرحمن الرحيم.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Unlike the incomplete guidance request, al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin is a complete sentence by itself, so it can be a verse before الرحمن الرحيم.
