positions.position: Al-Shafi‘i explains Aisha’s phrase al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin as a title for the entire sura, not only its opening words.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الشافعي): Al-Shafi‘i explains Aisha’s phrase al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin as a title for the entire sura, not only its opening words.

positions.position: The Prophet’s instruction to a Bedouin to read whatever Qur’an is easy applies equally to the follower and the solitary worshipper.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The Prophet’s instruction to a Bedouin to read whatever Qur’an is easy applies equally to the follower and the solitary worshipper.

positions.position: A Tirmidhi report says that after worshippers admitted reading behind the imam, the Prophet told them to read Umm al-Qur’an, since prayer is invalid without it; al-Tirmidhi grades the report hasan.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (عبادة بن الصامت): A Tirmidhi report says that after worshippers admitted reading behind the imam, the Prophet told them to read Umm al-Qur’an, since prayer is invalid without it; al-Tirmidhi grades the report hasan.

positions.position: Al-Shafi‘i requires recitation in every rak‘a, which Razi supports by the Prophet’s consistent practice and the command to follow him.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الشافعي): Al-Shafi‘i requires recitation in every rak‘a, which Razi supports by the Prophet’s consistent practice and the command to follow him. | mentions 7:158

positions.position: The Prophet told the Bedouin to read Umm al-Qur’an and then to do likewise in every rak‘a; the command includes verbal recitation because speech is an action of the tongue.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الشافعي): The Prophet told the Bedouin to read Umm al-Qur’an and then to do likewise in every rak‘a; the command includes verbal recitation because speech is an action of the tongue.

positions.position: Razi supports obligatory Fatiha recitation because the Prophet consistently recited it and commands require following him.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi supports obligatory Fatiha recitation because the Prophet consistently recited it and commands require following him. | mentions 6:153

positions.position: The rightly guided caliphs also consistently recited it, and the Prophet commanded Muslims to follow their sunna.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The rightly guided caliphs also consistently recited it, and the Prophet commanded Muslims to follow their sunna.

positions.position: Muslims everywhere recite it in prayer, and the Qur'an commands following the path of believers.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Muslims everywhere recite it in prayer, and the Qur'an commands following the path of believers. | mentions 4:115

positions.position: The prophetic statement “no prayer without the Opening of the Book” directly supports the requirement.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The prophetic statement “no prayer without the Opening of the Book” directly supports the requirement.

positions.position: The command to recite what is easy from the Qur'an is obligatory; because reciting other passages is not, the obligatory recitation must be the Fatiha.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The command to recite what is easy from the Qur'an is obligatory; because reciting other passages is not, the obligatory recitation must be the Fatiha. | mentions 73:20

positions.position: Reciting the Fatiha is the safer course, following the prophetic instruction to leave what causes doubt for what does not.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Reciting the Fatiha is the safer course, following the prophetic instruction to leave what causes doubt for what does not.

positions.position: The Prophet's constant practice makes abandoning his command forbidden, and Muslims agree that the Fatiha is better and more complete than another recitation.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The Prophet's constant practice makes abandoning his command forbidden, and Muslims agree that the Fatiha is better and more complete than another recitation. | mentions 24:63

positions.position: Prayer seeks remembrance of the heart, and this concise surah gathers lordship and servitude and is equated with the mighty Qur'an; nothing else can replace it.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Prayer seeks remembrance of the heart, and this concise surah gathers lordship and servitude and is equated with the mighty Qur'an; nothing else can replace it. | mentions 20:14, 15:87

positions.position: Al-Suddī reports that Medina’s people began recitation with the basmala.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (أهل المدينة): Al-Suddī reports that Medina’s people began recitation with the basmala.

positions.position: Mālik transmits the Prophet’s complaint about contested recitation through Ibn Akīma; al-Zuhrī says people stopped reciting al-Ḥamd aloud.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (ابن أكيمة الليثي): Mālik transmits the Prophet’s complaint about contested recitation through Ibn Akīma; al-Zuhrī says people stopped reciting al-Ḥamd aloud.

positions.position: Muslim’s reports say the Prophet, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar began with al-Ḥamd and did not mention the basmala in recitation.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (عائشة وأنس بن مالك): Muslim’s reports say the Prophet, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar began with al-Ḥamd and did not mention the basmala in recitation.

positions.position: Most scholars reserve al-Raḥmān for God, citing 17:110 and 43:45; Musaylima’s self-title became attached to him as “the liar.”
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (أكثر العلماء): Most scholars reserve al-Raḥmān for God, citing 17:110 and 43:45; Musaylima’s self-title became attached to him as “the liar.” | mentions 17:110, 43:45

positions.position: A report from Umm Salama pauses after al-Raḥīm with a cut hamza at al-Ḥamd; some Kūfans read this way.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (أم سلمة): A report from Umm Salama pauses after al-Raḥīm with a cut hamza at al-Ḥamd; some Kūfans read this way.

positions.position: Most readers connect al-Raḥīm to al-Ḥamd, using the genitive and connecting hamza.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (جمهور الناس): Most readers connect al-Raḥīm to al-Ḥamd, using the genitive and connecting hamza.

positions.position: Ibn ʿAṭiyya attributes the final analogy to Yaḥyā ibn Ziyād’s analysis of alif-lām-mīm.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (يحيى بن زياد): Ibn ʿAṭiyya attributes the final analogy to Yaḥyā ibn Ziyād’s analysis of alif-lām-mīm.

positions.position: Any rebellious being among jinn, humans, or animals may be called a shayṭān, marking distance from truth and insolence.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (author): Any rebellious being among jinn, humans, or animals may be called a shayṭān, marking distance from truth and insolence.

positions.position: Yaḥyā ibn Yaḥyā calls ranking Qurʾānic parts erroneous and says Mālik disliked repeatedly reciting one sūra to the exclusion of others.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (يحيى بن يحيى): Yaḥyā ibn Yaḥyā calls ranking Qurʾānic parts erroneous and says Mālik disliked repeatedly reciting one sūra to the exclusion of others.

positions.position: It is called Sūrat al-Ḥamd because it contains praise.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (author): It is called Sūrat al-Ḥamd because it contains praise.

positions.position: The majority permit Umm al-Kitāb, while al-Ḥasan, Anas, and Ibn Sīrīn reserve it for the whole Qurʾān or Preserved Tablet.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (الحسن وأنس وابن سيرين): The majority permit Umm al-Kitāb, while al-Ḥasan, Anas, and Ibn Sīrīn reserve it for the whole Qurʾān or Preserved Tablet. | mentions 3:7, 43:4

positions.position: Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar explains Umm al-Qurʾān by analogy with Mecca and Merv as regional “mothers.”
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (يحيى بن يعمر): Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar explains Umm al-Qurʾān by analogy with Mecca and Merv as regional “mothers.”

positions.position: Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr calls it al-Kāfiya because it suffices in place of other sūras, while none replaces it.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (يحيى بن أبي كثير): Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr calls it al-Kāfiya because it suffices in place of other sūras, while none replaces it.

positions.position: A report attributed to the Prophet says Umm al-Qurʾān replaces other passages, but nothing else replaces it.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (محمد بن خلاد الإسكندراني): A report attributed to the Prophet says Umm al-Qurʾān replaces other passages, but nothing else replaces it.

positions.position: Al-Fatiha is Umm al-Qur'an because it opens the Qur'an and is like its root and origin, hence al-Asās.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (author): Al-Fatiha is Umm al-Qur'an because it opens the Qur'an and is like its root and origin, hence al-Asās.

positions.position: It is also Umm al-Qur'an because it gathers praise, worship of commands and prohibitions, promise and threat, theoretical wisdom, practical guidance, and knowledge of the blessed and wretched.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (author): It is also Umm al-Qur'an because it gathers praise, worship of commands and prohibitions, promise and threat, theoretical wisdom, practical guidance, and knowledge of the blessed and wretched.

positions.position: Its other names include al-Kanz, al-Wāfiya, al-Kāfiya, al-Ḥamd, al-Shukr, al-Duʿāʾ, Taʿlīm al-Masʾala, and al-Ṣalāt; the latter names reflect its supplication and prayer recitation.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (author): Its other names include al-Kanz, al-Wāfiya, al-Kāfiya, al-Ḥamd, al-Shukr, al-Duʿāʾ, Taʿlīm al-Masʾala, and al-Ṣalāt; the latter names reflect its supplication and prayer recitation.

positions.position: The Fatiha is called Umm al-Qur’an on the basis of the Prophet’s statement that prayer is invalid without reciting Umm al-Qur’an.
positions.reasons: NASAFI (النبي عليه السلام): The Fatiha is called Umm al-Qur’an on the basis of the Prophet’s statement that prayer is invalid without reciting Umm al-Qur’an.

positions.position: Because the Fatiha contains the meanings found throughout the Qur’an, it is also called al-Wafiya and al-Kafiya.
positions.reasons: NASAFI (author): Because the Fatiha contains the meanings found throughout the Qur’an, it is also called al-Wafiya and al-Kafiya.

positions.position: Ibn Abbas advises a person who falls ill or complains of pain to turn to the Fatiha, calling it al-Asas.
positions.reasons: NASAFI (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas advises a person who falls ill or complains of pain to turn to the Fatiha, calling it al-Asas.

positions.position: Raḥmān follows the intensive faʿlān pattern, unusually from a transitive root; its article marks dominance, and the title is used only for God.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Raḥmān follows the intensive faʿlān pattern, unusually from a transitive root; its article marks dominance, and the title is used only for God.

positions.position: Some treat Rahman and Rahim as synonyms like nadman and nadim, with one view saying the pair is emphatic; another says Rahman is paired with Rahim because Musaylima claimed the former title.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): Some treat Rahman and Rahim as synonyms like nadman and nadim, with one view saying the pair is emphatic; another says Rahman is paired with Rahim because Musaylima claimed the former title.

positions.position: The Musaylima explanation is very weak because his claim is irrelevant and the basmala predates his rise.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): The Musaylima explanation is very weak because his claim is irrelevant and the basmala predates his rise.

positions.position: Most connect al-Rahim to al-hamd with kasra on mīm, normally as an inflectional ending; a second explanation treats it as a pause form restored with kasra before a consonant.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): Most connect al-Rahim to al-hamd with kasra on mīm, normally as an inflectional ending; a second explanation treats it as a pause form restored with kasra before a consonant.

positions.position: Umm Salama transmits stopping after al-Rahim and beginning al-hamd with a cut hamza.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (أم سلمة): Umm Salama transmits stopping after al-Rahim and beginning al-hamd with a cut hamza.

positions.position: Al-Kisa'i reports a dialectal reading fathing mīm and connecting al-hamd by transferring the hamza's vowel; Ibn Atiyya says it is not established as a reading, and the author prefers parsing the fathah as an accusative cut-off construction.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (الكسائي): Al-Kisa'i reports a dialectal reading fathing mīm and connecting al-hamd by transferring the hamza's vowel; Ibn Atiyya says it is not established as a reading, and the author prefers parsing the fathah as an accusative cut-off construction. | mentions 3:1

positions.position: Scholars dispute whether a name is identical with its named referent; this creates an apparent problem of a thing being annexed to itself.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): Scholars dispute whether a name is identical with its named referent; this creates an apparent problem of a thing being annexed to itself.

positions.position: Abu al-Baqa's best answer is that name here means naming, which differs from the name itself and its referent.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (أبو البقاء): Abu al-Baqa's best answer is that name here means naming, which differs from the name itself and its referent.

positions.position: The author reports Abu al-Baqa's second answer: supply an omitted annex, yielding in the name of the named God.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): The author reports Abu al-Baqa's second answer: supply an omitted annex, yielding in the name of the named God.

positions.position: The author reports Abu al-Baqa's third solution, treating ism as superfluous, like the poetic phrase meaning peace be upon you.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): The author reports Abu al-Baqa's third solution, treating ism as superfluous, like the poetic phrase meaning peace be upon you.

positions.position: Abu Ubayda, al-Akhfash, and Qutrub also adopt the analysis that ism is superfluous; poems by the cited poets illustrate it.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (أبو عبيدة والأخفش وقطرب): Abu Ubayda, al-Akhfash, and Qutrub also adopt the analysis that ism is superfluous; poems by the cited poets illustrate it.

positions.position: Al-Akhfash says the alleged extra word shifts the phrase from an oath to an invocation of blessing.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (الأخفش): Al-Akhfash says the alleged extra word shifts the phrase from an oath to an invocation of blessing.

positions.position: Qutrub says the added word serves honor and exaltation.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (قطرب): Qutrub says the added word serves honor and exaltation.

positions.position: Apparent self-annexation also occurs in name-plus-title and noun-plus-description phrases; grammarians explain these by meaning-name shifts or omitted annexes.
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR (author): Apparent self-annexation also occurs in name-plus-title and noun-plus-description phrases; grammarians explain these by meaning-name shifts or omitted annexes.

positions.position: Ibn ʿAbbas calls the surah the foundation of the Qur'an and says its foundation is the basmala.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbas calls the surah the foundation of the Qur'an and says its foundation is the basmala.

positions.position: Al-Dahhak is said to have transmitted a similar explanation of the basmala.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (الضحاك): Al-Dahhak is said to have transmitted a similar explanation of the basmala.

positions.position: Jabir's report describes clouds fleeing, winds and sea becoming still, animals listening, devils pelted, and God's promise of blessing when His name is said over something.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (جابر بن عبد الله): Jabir's report describes clouds fleeing, winds and sea becoming still, animals listening, devils pelted, and God's promise of blessing when His name is said over something.

positions.position: The basmala is recommended on entering the toilet, based on reports transmitted on that practice.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): The basmala is recommended on entering the toilet, based on reports transmitted on that practice.

positions.position: Al-Zamakhshari also records the names Surat al-Salah and al-Kanz.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (الزمخشري): Al-Zamakhshari also records the names Surat al-Salah and al-Kanz.

positions.position: Allah is a name not used for anyone else, and Arabic does not clearly derive it from an ordinary verb.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): Allah is a name not used for anyone else, and Arabic does not clearly derive it from an ordinary verb.

positions.position: Rahman is a name specific to God; Musaylima's self-title Rahman of Yamama became a byword for lying.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): Rahman is a name specific to God; Musaylima's self-title Rahman of Yamama became a byword for lying. | mentions 17:110, 21:26

positions.position: ʿAta al-Khurasani explains that Rahim follows Rahman to prevent anyone claiming the exclusive title Rahman, since only God is described as both.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (عطاء الخراساني): ʿAta al-Khurasani explains that Rahim follows Rahman to prevent anyone claiming the exclusive title Rahman, since only God is described as both.

positions.position: Umm Salama's report says the Prophet paused between the basmala, al-Hamd, Rahman al-Rahim, and Malik yawm al-din; some Kufans pause at the basmala while most connect it to al-Hamd.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): Umm Salama's report says the Prophet paused between the basmala, al-Hamd, Rahman al-Rahim, and Malik yawm al-din; some Kufans pause at the basmala while most connect it to al-Hamd. | mentions 1:2, 1:3, 1:4

positions.position: There is no disagreement that the surah has seven verses; reports of eight from ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd and six from Husayn al-Juʿfi are aberrant.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): There is no disagreement that the surah has seven verses; reports of eight from ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd and six from Husayn al-Juʿfi are aberrant.

positions.position: Al-Kisaʾi says some Arabs connect the basmala to al-Hamd by transferring the vowel of the connecting hamza to the mīm; Ibn ʿAtiyya says he knew of no transmitted canonical reading for it.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (الكسائي): Al-Kisaʾi says some Arabs connect the basmala to al-Hamd by transferring the vowel of the connecting hamza to the mīm; Ibn ʿAtiyya says he knew of no transmitted canonical reading for it. | mentions 2:1, 2:2

positions.position: The majority call it Umm al-Kitab; Anas is cited for this name.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (الجمهور): The majority call it Umm al-Kitab; Anas is cited for this name.

positions.position: The surah has twenty-five words and one hundred thirteen letters.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): The surah has twenty-five words and one hundred thirteen letters.

positions.position: Al-Bukhari explains Umm al-Kutub by its being written first in Qur'anic codices and recited first in prayer.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (البخاري): Al-Bukhari explains Umm al-Kutub by its being written first in Qur'anic codices and recited first in prayer.

positions.position: Another explanation of Umm al-Kitab is that the meanings of the whole Qur'an return to what the Fatiha contains.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): Another explanation of Umm al-Kitab is that the meanings of the whole Qur'an return to what the Fatiha contains.

positions.position: Ibn Jarir says Arabs call a comprehensive or leading thing with dependent parts an umm, such as the head's covering or an army's banner.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (ابن جرير): Ibn Jarir says Arabs call a comprehensive or leading thing with dependent parts an umm, such as the head's covering or an army's banner.

positions.position: Ibn Jarir cites Dhu al-Rumma's verse calling a spear an umm, a focal point followed in affairs.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (ذو الرمة): Ibn Jarir cites Dhu al-Rumma's verse calling a spear an umm, a focal point followed in affairs.

positions.position: Mecca is called Umm al-Qura because it precedes and gathers the other settlements, or because the earth was spread from it.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): Mecca is called Umm al-Qura because it precedes and gathers the other settlements, or because the earth was spread from it.

positions.position: Hasan and Ibn Sirin dislike the name Umm al-Kitab, taking it to refer to the Preserved Tablet; Hasan also calls the clear verses Umm al-Kitab.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (الحسن وابن سيرين): Hasan and Ibn Sirin dislike the name Umm al-Kitab, taking it to refer to the Preserved Tablet; Hasan also calls the clear verses Umm al-Kitab.

positions.position: A report through Abu Hurayra from Ubayy repeats that the Fatiha has no equal in the Torah, Gospel, Psalms, or Qur'an; al-Tirmidhi calls it hasan sahih.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): A report through Abu Hurayra from Ubayy repeats that the Fatiha has no equal in the Torah, Gospel, Psalms, or Qur'an; al-Tirmidhi calls it hasan sahih.

positions.position: The report that the Prophet called the Fatiha the best surah has a good chain according to Ibn Kathir; the Companion's identity is uncertain between al-ʿAbdi and al-Ansari al-Bayyadi.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (عبد الله بن جابر): The report that the Prophet called the Fatiha the best surah has a good chain according to Ibn Kathir; the Companion's identity is uncertain between al-ʿAbdi and al-Ansari al-Bayyadi.

positions.position: These scholars infer that some verses and surahs are superior to others from the superiority reports.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (إسحاق بن راهويه وأبو بكر بن العربي وابن الحصار): These scholars infer that some verses and surahs are superior to others from the superiority reports.

positions.position: Hasan also objects to calling the surah Umm al-Qur'an.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (الحسن): Hasan also objects to calling the surah Umm al-Qur'an.

positions.position: Another group denies ranking Qur'anic passages, since all are God's speech and ranking could imply deficiency in what is less preferred; a report from Malik agrees.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (الأشعري وأبو بكر الباقلاني وابن حبان ويحيى بن يحيى): Another group denies ranking Qur'anic passages, since all are God's speech and ranking could imply deficiency in what is less preferred; a report from Malik agrees.

positions.position: The Prophet says prayer without Umm al-Qur'an is deficient, and the divine hadith answers the servant's praise verse by verse as the Fatiha is divided between God and servant.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): The Prophet says prayer without Umm al-Qur'an is deficient, and the divine hadith answers the servant's praise verse by verse as the Fatiha is divided between God and servant. | mentions 1:2, 1:3, 1:4, 1:5, 1:6, 1:7

positions.position: A report that each prayer unit needs al-Hamd and another surah is questionable in authenticity.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): A report that each prayer unit needs al-Hamd and another surah is questionable in authenticity.

positions.position: Al-Hamd is another name for the surah.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): Al-Hamd is another name for the surah.

positions.position: It is also called al-Salah because the divine hadith names recitation of al-Hamd as the servant's praise, and the surah is a condition of prayer.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): It is also called al-Salah because the divine hadith names recitation of al-Hamd as the servant's praise, and the surah is a condition of prayer.

positions.position: Al-Ḥarālī says people stop at apparent causes or trace causes back only as far as reason allows; the basmala folds away those intermediaries and declares everything to be through God's name, with no other ultimate cause.
positions.reasons: BIQAI (أبو الحسن الحرالي): Al-Ḥarālī says people stop at apparent causes or trace causes back only as far as reason allows; the basmala folds away those intermediaries and declares everything to be through God's name, with no other ultimate cause.

positions.position: Al-Ḥarālī says the basmala begins the Mother of the Qur'an because it folds up the causal order as the Mother of the Qur'an gathers earlier scriptures; it also holds the secret of acts appearing through divine care in 1:5, and
positions.reasons: BIQAI (أبو الحسن الحرالي): Al-Ḥarālī says the basmala begins the Mother of the Qur'an because it folds up the causal order as the Mother of the Qur'an gathers earlier scriptures; it also holds the secret of acts appearing through divine care in 1:5, and should open people's words and deeds, outwardly and inwardly. | mentions 1:5

positions.position: The Fātiḥa is mother and foundation of every good, repeated continually, a treasure, cure, sufficiency for worries, fulfillment of aims, protection from evil, and remedy for every affliction.
positions.reasons: BIQAI (author): The Fātiḥa is mother and foundation of every good, repeated continually, a treasure, cure, sufficiency for worries, fulfillment of aims, protection from evil, and remedy for every affliction.

positions.position: Al-Mashdali's method for Qur'anic coherence is to identify a surah's purpose, its prerequisites and their distance from the goal, then answer expectations raised as the discourse unfolds.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (أبو الفضل محمد المشدالي المغربي): Al-Mashdali's method for Qur'anic coherence is to identify a surah's purpose, its prerequisites and their distance from the goal, then answer expectations raised as the discourse unfolds.

positions.position: A surah's name summarizes its purpose, as a title signals the details within; Adam demonstrated this naming principle when he named things before the angels.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (author): A surah's name summarizes its purpose, as a title signals the details within; Adam demonstrated this naming principle when he named things before the angels.

positions.position: Since the basmala is a kind of praise, it naturally leads to comprehensive al-hamd: begin affairs by praising God as the one deserving every praise, with hope and awe guiding the way.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (author): Since the basmala is a kind of praise, it naturally leads to comprehensive al-hamd: begin affairs by praising God as the one deserving every praise, with hope and awe guiding the way.

positions.position: Al-Harali says all Qur'an is God's speech, but some verses voice what creatures at different levels ought to say yet cannot express; God teaches them words that fulfill their duty.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): Al-Harali says all Qur'an is God's speech, but some verses voice what creatures at different levels ought to say yet cannot express; God teaches them words that fulfill their duty.

positions.position: Al-Harali says the Qur'an's sevenfold gathering in Muhammad's heart relates to the Mother of Qur'an's universals as the Qur'an's gathering in his heart relates to the Mother.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): Al-Harali says the Qur'an's sevenfold gathering in Muhammad's heart relates to the Mother of Qur'an's universals as the Qur'an's gathering in his heart relates to the Mother.

positions.position: Al-Harali says the Qur'an reached the Prophet on his tongue over the span of the prophetic mission, after its descent to the lowest heaven.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): Al-Harali says the Qur'an reached the Prophet on his tongue over the span of the prophetic mission, after its descent to the lowest heaven.

positions.position: Aisha reports that Muhammad's character was the Qur'an, making his conduct the visible form of its inner reality.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (عائشة): Aisha reports that Muhammad's character was the Qur'an, making his conduct the visible form of its inner reality.

positions.position: Al-Harali says the Fatiha is the Qur'an's mother: its first three verses encompass the divine names and attributes, while its last three cover the creature's way to God, mercy or failure.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): Al-Harali says the Fatiha is the Qur'an's mother: its first three verses encompass the divine names and attributes, while its last three cover the creature's way to God, mercy or failure. | mentions 2:281, 75:17, 33:50, 33:52

positions.position: Al-Baqara aims to prove the Book is guidance to follow; belief in the unseen, especially resurrection and the afterlife, is its greatest guidance and organizing theme.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (author): Al-Baqara aims to prove the Book is guidance to follow; belief in the unseen, especially resurrection and the afterlife, is its greatest guidance and organizing theme.

positions.position: The cow story makes the surah's title apt because resurrection occurs through an apparently slight human cause; it is a clearer sign of divine power than Abraham's story or earlier Israelite resurrections.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (author): The cow story makes the surah's title apt because resurrection occurs through an apparently slight human cause; it is a clearer sign of divine power than Abraham's story or earlier Israelite resurrections.

positions.position: The following comparison of hearts and stones shows the guided and astray: hearts become hard and wretched, while stones display fear and yield benefit that reaches God's servants.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (author): The following comparison of hearts and stones shows the guided and astray: hearts become hard and wretched, while stones display fear and yield benefit that reaches God's servants.

positions.position: Al-Baqara is also called the Radiant and the Hump: it illuminates guidance and sufficiency, brightens believers' faces at judgment, and exalts belief in the afterlife above every other good after monotheism.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (author): Al-Baqara is also called the Radiant and the Hump: it illuminates guidance and sufficiency, brightens believers' faces at judgment, and exalts belief in the afterlife above every other good after monotheism.

positions.position: Al-Bayhaqi transmits an alternative mursal route through al-Layth, Uqayl, Ibn Shihab, Umm Salama and Abu Salama; he calls the mursal report good because Abu Salama did not meet Ibn Masud.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (البيهقي): Al-Bayhaqi transmits an alternative mursal route through al-Layth, Uqayl, Ibn Shihab, Umm Salama and Abu Salama; he calls the mursal report good because Abu Salama did not meet Ibn Masud.

positions.position: Abu Shama says that if sound, seven letters means seven forms or categories of Qur'anic content, not the dialects in which recitation was permitted.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (أبو شامة): Abu Shama says that if sound, seven letters means seven forms or categories of Qur'anic content, not the dialects in which recitation was permitted.

positions.position: Ibn al-Jazari cites the Prophet's report to Ibn Masud from al-Tabarani: the Qur'an's seven categories include lawful, forbidden, clear, ambiguous, parables, commands and warnings, each with its proper response.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (ابن الجزري): Ibn al-Jazari cites the Prophet's report to Ibn Masud from al-Tabarani: the Qur'an's seven categories include lawful, forbidden, clear, ambiguous, parables, commands and warnings, each with its proper response.

positions.position: Al-Bayhaqi also reports from Abu Huraira a version that describes five Qur'anic forms: lawful, forbidden, clear, ambiguous and parables.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (أبو هريرة): Al-Bayhaqi also reports from Abu Huraira a version that describes five Qur'anic forms: lawful, forbidden, clear, ambiguous and parables.

positions.position: Al-Harali reads the seven letters as a completion of creation and religious, worldly and afterlife well-being: Muhammad is the comprehensive final prophet and his book seals the scriptures; he cites the report I was sent to complete noble character.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): Al-Harali reads the seven letters as a completion of creation and religious, worldly and afterlife well-being: Muhammad is the comprehensive final prophet and his book seals the scriptures; he cites the report I was sent to complete noble character.

positions.position: The quoted supplication asks God to set right religion as the safeguard of one's affairs, worldly livelihood and the afterlife to which one returns.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (author): The quoted supplication asks God to set right religion as the safeguard of one's affairs, worldly livelihood and the afterlife to which one returns.

positions.position: Al-Harali divides the three domains of well-being into action and restraint, yielding six letters; God then grants Muhammad a seventh, inclusive letter, so the Qur'an descends in seven letters.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): Al-Harali divides the three domains of well-being into action and restraint, yielding six letters; God then grants Muhammad a seventh, inclusive letter, so the Qur'an descends in seven letters.

positions.position: The worldly pair is halal and haram: lawful things cultivate body and soul, forbidden things must be purified away; the pair originates in the Torah and is completed in the Qur'an.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): The worldly pair is halal and haram: lawful things cultivate body and soul, forbidden things must be purified away; the pair originates in the Torah and is completed in the Qur'an.

positions.position: The afterlife pair is warning and command; avoiding prohibitions purifies and obeying commands advances the next life, even when it sacrifices temporary worldly benefits for enduring whole good.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): The afterlife pair is warning and command; avoiding prohibitions purifies and obeying commands advances the next life, even when it sacrifices temporary worldly benefits for enduring whole good.

positions.position: The religious pair is clear guidance about heart, character and bodily duties, and ambiguous matters beyond limited reason that require declaring God incomparable; five letters are for practice and the sixth for restraint.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): The religious pair is clear guidance about heart, character and bodily duties, and ambiguous matters beyond limited reason that require declaring God incomparable; five letters are for practice and the sixth for restraint.

positions.position: The six letters are shared with prior scriptures but perfected in the Qur'an; its unique seventh is the inclusive letter of praise, gifted directly to Muhammad and embodied in his heart, recitation and character.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): The six letters are shared with prior scriptures but perfected in the Qur'an; its unique seventh is the inclusive letter of praise, gifted directly to Muhammad and embodied in his heart, recitation and character.

positions.position: Ibn Sirin disliked the name Umm al-Qur'an, citing Umm al-Kitab in 13:39, and preferred Fatihat al-Kitab.
positions.reasons: DURR (محمد بن سيرين): Ibn Sirin disliked the name Umm al-Qur'an, citing Umm al-Kitab in 13:39, and preferred Fatihat al-Kitab. | mentions 13:39

positions.position: Sufyan ibn Uyayna called al-Fatiha al-Wafiya, the Complete.
positions.reasons: DURR (سفيان بن عيينة): Sufyan ibn Uyayna called al-Fatiha al-Wafiya, the Complete.

positions.position: Al-Sha'bi prescribed al-Fatiha, the foundation of the Qur'an, to a man with flank pain.
positions.reasons: DURR (الشعبي): Al-Sha'bi prescribed al-Fatiha, the foundation of the Qur'an, to a man with flank pain.

positions.position: The Prophet says scripture is the most rightful basis for taking a fee after companions cured a bitten man with al-Fatiha.
positions.reasons: DURR (النبي): The Prophet says scripture is the most rightful basis for taking a fee after companions cured a bitten man with al-Fatiha.

positions.position: Abu Salman recounts companions cured a man suffering a seizure with al-Fatiha; the Prophet called it the Mother of the Qur'an and healing.
positions.reasons: DURR (أبو سلمان): Abu Salman recounts companions cured a man suffering a seizure with al-Fatiha; the Prophet called it the Mother of the Qur'an and healing.

positions.position: The Prophet called al-Hamd the best part of the Qur'an in a report authenticated by al-Hakim.
positions.reasons: DURR (أنس): The Prophet called al-Hamd the best part of the Qur'an in a report authenticated by al-Hakim.

positions.position: The Prophet names four revelations from beneath the Throne: Mother of the Book, Throne Verse, endings of al-Baqara, and al-Kawthar.
positions.reasons: DURR (النبي): The Prophet names four revelations from beneath the Throne: Mother of the Book, Throne Verse, endings of al-Baqara, and al-Kawthar. | mentions 2:255, 2:285, 2:286, 108:1

positions.position: Abu Umama also transmits the four-revelations report as a Companion statement.
positions.reasons: DURR (أبو أمامة): Abu Umama also transmits the four-revelations report as a Companion statement.

positions.position: A report from Abu al-Darda says al-Fatiha suffices beyond any other Qur'anic passage and would outweigh the Qur'an sevenfold.
positions.reasons: DURR (النبي): A report from Abu al-Darda says al-Fatiha suffices beyond any other Qur'anic passage and would outweigh the Qur'an sevenfold.

positions.position: Makhul characterizes the Mother of the Qur'an as recitation, request, and supplication.
positions.reasons: DURR (مكحول): Makhul characterizes the Mother of the Qur'an as recitation, request, and supplication.

positions.position: Raja al-Ghanawi transmits the instruction to seek healing through God's own praise, identified as al-Hamd and al-Ikhlas.
positions.reasons: DURR (رجاء الغنوي): Raja al-Ghanawi transmits the instruction to seek healing through God's own praise, identified as al-Hamd and al-Ikhlas. | mentions 112:1

positions.position: Ibn al-Salah says Qur'an recitation is a human privilege; angels eagerly listen to people reciting.
positions.reasons: DURR (ابن الصلاح): Ibn al-Salah says Qur'an recitation is a human privilege; angels eagerly listen to people reciting.

positions.position: Umm al-Qur'an replaces any other sura, but no other sura can replace it.
positions.reasons: DURR (عبادة بن الصامت): Umm al-Qur'an replaces any other sura, but no other sura can replace it.

positions.position: Jabir's report says al-Hamd and the mercy names are praise, then the remaining portion belongs to the servant.
positions.reasons: DURR (الله): Jabir's report says al-Hamd and the mercy names are praise, then the remaining portion belongs to the servant.

positions.position: Ali says the Prophet instructed him to begin prayer with the basmala when he said he recited al-Hamd.
positions.reasons: DURR (النبي): Ali says the Prophet instructed him to begin prayer with the basmala when he said he recited al-Hamd.

positions.position: The Prophet told Ali to say the basmala when beginning prayer instead of beginning directly with al-hamd.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (علي): The Prophet told Ali to say the basmala when beginning prayer instead of beginning directly with al-hamd.

positions.position: Al-Fātiḥa was originally an adjective for the first part because it opens the whole; alternatively it is a verbal noun used for the object, as with al-Khātima.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Al-Fātiḥa was originally an adjective for the first part because it opens the whole; alternatively it is a verbal noun used for the object, as with al-Khātima.

positions.position: He finds an instrumental reading of fātiḥa unsuitable: the instrument need not share the action, and it could wrongly imply that the opening part is incidental.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): He finds an instrumental reading of fātiḥa unsuitable: the instrument need not share the action, and it could wrongly imply that the opening part is incidental.

positions.position: Abū al-Suʿūd explains the title’s first addition as the name of the named sūra and its second as possessive, meaning the opening of the Book.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (أبو السعود): Abū al-Suʿūd explains the title’s first addition as the name of the named sūra and its second as possessive, meaning the opening of the Book.

positions.position: Reciting the basmala over forbidden acts is itself forbidden without being disbelief according to the sound view; over disliked acts it is disliked, unless contempt makes it disbelief.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Reciting the basmala over forbidden acts is itself forbidden without being disbelief according to the sound view; over disliked acts it is disliked, unless contempt makes it disbelief.

positions.position: Since the basmala is a kind of praise, it fittingly precedes the comprehensive praise that follows.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Since the basmala is a kind of praise, it fittingly precedes the comprehensive praise that follows. | mentions 1:2

positions.position: Al-Mursī says it was named because it was the first sūra written on the Preserved Tablet; al-Ālūsī says this needs transmission and sequence of writing is uncertain.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (المرسي): Al-Mursī says it was named because it was the first sūra written on the Preserved Tablet; al-Ālūsī says this needs transmission and sequence of writing is uncertain.

positions.position: Umm al-Kitāb and Umm al-Qurʾān reflect its priority, like a mother preceding what follows, a banner leading an army, or its encompassing the Qurʾān’s aims.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Umm al-Kitāb and Umm al-Qurʾān reflect its priority, like a mother preceding what follows, a banner leading an army, or its encompassing the Qurʾān’s aims.

positions.position: The alleged prophetic prohibition on calling it Umm al-Kitāb has no basis; sound reports establish that title, and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī also used it.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (الحسن البصري): The alleged prophetic prohibition on calling it Umm al-Kitāb has no basis; sound reports establish that title, and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī also used it.

positions.position: He answers the Muʿtazilī objection that worship has no prior command: monotheism is worship’s foundation, and Muhammad’s prior charge to proclaim it suffices.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): He answers the Muʿtazilī objection that worship has no prior command: monotheism is worship’s foundation, and Muhammad’s prior charge to proclaim it suffices. | mentions 1:1

positions.position: Other titles include al-Kanz, al-Wāfiya, al-Kāfiya, and al-Asās, associated with its gathered treasures, sufficiency, indivisibility in prayer, and status as Qurʾānic foundation.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Other titles include al-Kanz, al-Wāfiya, al-Kāfiya, and al-Asās, associated with its gathered treasures, sufficiency, indivisibility in prayer, and status as Qurʾānic foundation.

positions.position: Names such as al-Ḥamd, al-Shukr, al-Duʿāʾ, Taʿlīm al-Masʾala, and al-Suʾāl describe its praise, gratitude, supplication, and instruction in asking.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Names such as al-Ḥamd, al-Shukr, al-Duʿāʾ, Taʿlīm al-Masʾala, and al-Suʾāl describe its praise, gratitude, supplication, and instruction in asking.

positions.position: Al-Nūr refers to its prominence, its illumination of hearts, or its embodiment of Qurʾānic meaning; al-Qurʾān al-ʿAẓīm is another title.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Al-Nūr refers to its prominence, its illumination of hearts, or its embodiment of Qurʾānic meaning; al-Qurʾān al-ʿAẓīm is another title.

positions.position: Al-Dāraquṭnī’s report urges reciting the basmala before al-Ḥamd and calls it one of its verses; al-Ālūsī offers a figurative reading that preserves seven verses without it.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (أبو هريرة): Al-Dāraquṭnī’s report urges reciting the basmala before al-Ḥamd and calls it one of its verses; al-Ālūsī offers a figurative reading that preserves seven verses without it.

positions.position: A report says the Prophet rebuked a worshipper for beginning al-Ḥamd without the basmala and called omission a broken prayer; al-Ālūsī questions its wording and evidentiary force.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (أبو هريرة): A report says the Prophet rebuked a worshipper for beginning al-Ḥamd without the basmala and called omission a broken prayer; al-Ālūsī questions its wording and evidentiary force.

positions.position: Al-Daraqutni's version commands reciting the basmala before al-Hamd and calls the basmala one of the Fatiha's verses.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (أبو هريرة): Al-Daraqutni's version commands reciting the basmala before al-Hamd and calls the basmala one of the Fatiha's verses.

positions.position: A second proof is that all realities needing expression have a name, so the creator must have a name that can bear divine attributes rather than only a generic title.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): A second proof is that all realities needing expression have a name, so the creator must have a name that can bear divine attributes rather than only a generic title.

positions.position: A third proof is that if Allah were merely a descriptive title or common noun, the confession of divine oneness would not exclude partners as it does with a proper name.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): A third proof is that if Allah were merely a descriptive title or common noun, the confession of divine oneness would not exclude partners as it does with a proper name.

positions.position: The basmala’s hidden indications are inexhaustible; it is the Qur’an’s title and a gateway to secrets beyond the formal scholars’ semantic discussions.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): The basmala’s hidden indications are inexhaustible; it is the Qur’an’s title and a gateway to secrets beyond the formal scholars’ semantic discussions.

positions.position: The opening and ending letters, alif forms, and nine groups of triads invite mystical reflection: articulation points, omitted letters, written/spoken forms, vowel states, word classes, genitives, divine names, agency, and connection patterns.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): The opening and ending letters, alif forms, and nine groups of triads invite mystical reflection: articulation points, omitted letters, written/spoken forms, vowel states, word classes, genitives, divine names, agency, and connection patterns.

positions.position: He also asks about the four elements, nineteen letters, letter connections and spellings, and other graphic details, while saying formal scholars generally stop at meanings and possibilities.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): He also asks about the four elements, nineteen letters, letter connections and spellings, and other graphic details, while saying formal scholars generally stop at meanings and possibilities.

positions.position: The Prophet says prayer is invalid without reciting the Opening of the Book; the report is in both Sahih collections.
positions.reasons: QUTB-ZILAL (رسول الله [ ص ]): The Prophet says prayer is invalid without reciting the Opening of the Book; the report is in both Sahih collections.

positions.position: The short surah gathers core Islamic creed, worldview, feelings, and guidance, explaining its repetition in every rakʿa and why prayer without it is invalid.
positions.reasons: QUTB-ZILAL (author): The short surah gathers core Islamic creed, worldview, feelings, and guidance, explaining its repetition in every rakʿa and why prayer without it is invalid.

positions.position: Annexing Fātiha to the Book is a true relation: here the Book means the rest of the Qur’an apart from this sura, like a preface belonging to a work.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): Annexing Fātiha to the Book is a true relation: here the Book means the rest of the Qur’an apart from this sura, like a preface belonging to a work.

positions.position: Al-Bukhari’s Book of Medicine reports that Abu Saʿid al-Khudri used Umm al-Qurʾān in a cure for a stung person; the account includes a fuller story.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (أبو سعيد الخدري): Al-Bukhari’s Book of Medicine reports that Abu Saʿid al-Khudri used Umm al-Qurʾān in a cure for a stung person; the account includes a fuller story.

positions.position: A sound hadith calls a prayer deficient when Umm al-Qurʾān is not recited.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): A sound hadith calls a prayer deficient when Umm al-Qurʾān is not recited.

positions.position: Umm means the origin or source of a thing, which explains the title Umm al-Qurʾān.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): Umm means the origin or source of a thing, which explains the title Umm al-Qurʾān.

positions.position: One explanation of Umm al-Qurʾān is that Fātiha begins the Qur’an and is therefore like a mother as origin and source of what follows.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): One explanation of Umm al-Qurʾān is that Fātiha begins the Qur’an and is therefore like a mother as origin and source of what follows.

positions.position: A third explanation is that Fātiha compresses all Qur’anic theoretical knowledge and practical rulings, including creed, prophecy, admonition, stories, worship, transactions, ethics, and legal manners.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): A third explanation is that Fātiha compresses all Qur’anic theoretical knowledge and practical rulings, including creed, prophecy, admonition, stories, worship, transactions, ethics, and legal manners.

positions.position: The name Fātihat al-Kitāb is established in several hadith, including the Prophet’s rule that prayer is invalid without reciting it.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): The name Fātihat al-Kitāb is established in several hadith, including the Prophet’s rule that prayer is invalid without reciting it.

positions.position: A view attributed to ʿUmar says the verses are repeated because another sura is joined to them in each rakʿa; Ibn ʿĀshūr considers this sound.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (عمر بن الخطاب): A view attributed to ʿUmar says the verses are repeated because another sura is joined to them in each rakʿa; Ibn ʿĀshūr considers this sound.

positions.position: Fātiha derives from fatḥ, opening by removing an obstruction to an intended place; figuratively it means the first thing, by analogy with the first person entering through a door.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): Fātiha derives from fatḥ, opening by removing an obstruction to an intended place; figuratively it means the first thing, by analogy with the first person entering through a door.

positions.position: A sound hadith from ʿĀʾisha says prayers were first prescribed as two rakʿas, then travel prayer remained so while resident prayer was lengthened; Ibn ʿĀshūr uses this to explain the title.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (عائشة): A sound hadith from ʿĀʾisha says prayers were first prescribed as two rakʿas, then travel prayer remained so while resident prayer was lengthened; Ibn ʿĀshūr uses this to explain the title.

positions.position: Fātiha opens the suras as a preface to a speech or book, while its summary of Qur’anic aims makes it a rhetorically apt introduction.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): Fātiha opens the suras as a preface to a speech or book, while its summary of Qur’anic aims makes it a rhetorically apt introduction.

positions.position: Other accounts place Sūrat Nūn wa-l-Qalam and al-Muzzammil before Fātiha.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): Other accounts place Sūrat Nūn wa-l-Qalam and al-Muzzammil before Fātiha.

positions.position: Some say Fātiha was the first complete sura revealed, in contrast to al-Qalam, which they regard as having come in fragments.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (بعضهم): Some say Fātiha was the first complete sura revealed, in contrast to al-Qalam, which they regard as having come in fragments.

positions.position: A report attributed to Jābir ibn Zayd places Fātiha fifth in the order of sura revelation.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (جابر بن زيد): A report attributed to Jābir ibn Zayd places Fātiha fifth in the order of sura revelation.

positions.position: Its later revelation does not conflict with its first position: once enough Qur’an existed to form a Book, Fātiha was revealed as its preface.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): Its later revelation does not conflict with its first position: once enough Qur’an existed to form a Book, Fātiha was revealed as its preface.

positions.position: Fātiha is not used here in its literal sense of opening; it names the beginning, either as a verbal noun or as an opener that initiates the whole.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): Fātiha is not used here in its literal sense of opening; it names the beginning, either as a verbal noun or as an opener that initiates the whole.

positions.position: The first thing may be called Fātiha as the object of opening, where the action first appears, or as an active participle converted into a name for the beginning.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): The first thing may be called Fātiha as the object of opening, where the action first appears, or as an active participle converted into a name for the beginning.

positions.position: Al-Taftazani says the feminine suffix shifts Fātiha from a description to a noun; Fātiha and Khātima can stand independently of any feminine noun.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (التفتزاني): Al-Taftazani says the feminine suffix shifts Fātiha from a description to a noun; Fātiha and Khātima can stand independently of any feminine noun.

positions.position: Al-Rāzī answers that Qur’anic repetition can emphasize meaning and that affirming God’s mercy is especially important.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (الرازي): Al-Rāzī answers that Qur’anic repetition can emphasize meaning and that affirming God’s mercy is especially important.

positions.position: By frequent use, Fātihat al-Kitāb became the conventional proper name of this sura.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): By frequent use, Fātihat al-Kitāb became the conventional proper name of this sura.

positions.position: As Sūrat al-Ḥamd and Sūrat al-Ṣalāh, the Fātiḥah begins each prayer cycle for Sunnis and many Shiites.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (author): As Sūrat al-Ḥamd and Sūrat al-Ṣalāh, the Fātiḥah begins each prayer cycle for Sunnis and many Shiites.

positions.position: Shiite law permits reciting the Fātiḥah in the third and fourth cycles or an alternative formula praising God.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (author): Shiite law permits reciting the Fātiḥah in the third and fourth cycles or an alternative formula praising God.

positions.position: The Fātiḥah is a prayer encapsulating metaphysical and eschatological realities and teaches the proper human disposition toward God.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (author): The Fātiḥah is a prayer encapsulating metaphysical and eschatological realities and teaches the proper human disposition toward God.

positions.position: Its structure moves from God’s nature in the first three verses, through the God-human relationship, to human states in the final three.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (author): Its structure moves from God’s nature in the first three verses, through the God-human relationship, to human states in the final three.

positions.position: The Fātiḥah’s exalted status generated many independent commentaries, often showing how the Quran as a whole is contained in it.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (author): The Fātiḥah’s exalted status generated many independent commentaries, often showing how the Quran as a whole is contained in it.

positions.position: The sūrah is seen as a synthesis and the Quran’s most important chapter, hence Umm al-kitāb; the title also refers to 3:7 and the celestial archetype of scripture.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (author): The sūrah is seen as a synthesis and the Quran’s most important chapter, hence Umm al-kitāb; the title also refers to 3:7 and the celestial archetype of scripture. | mentions 3:7, 13:39, 43:4

positions.position: It is called the Mother of the Quran because it contains the meaning of the entire Quran.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (author): It is called the Mother of the Quran because it contains the meaning of the entire Quran.

positions.position: The title The Cure reflects its reputed healing power for body and soul.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (author): The title The Cure reflects its reputed healing power for body and soul.

positions.position: The title The Foundation reflects the Fātiḥah’s role as a foundation for the whole Quran.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (author): The title The Foundation reflects the Fātiḥah’s role as a foundation for the whole Quran.

question: When and where was al-Fātiḥa revealed?

positions.position: Al-Fātiḥa was revealed in Mecca.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): Al-Ṭabarī identifies Fātiḥa as a Meccan sūra of seven verses. THALABI (سعيد بن المسيب): Another group, reporting from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib and followed by Meccan and many Hijazi reciters, counts the basmala as a verse of the Fātiḥa and does not count “those You favored” separately. MAWARDI (قتادة): Qatada holds that the Fatiha is Meccan. BAGHAWI (author): Meccan and Kufan readers and most Hijazi jurists count it as part of al-Fatiha only, written to separate surahs. BAGHAWI (author): Most scholars call the surah Meccan, and Baghawi prefers this because al-Hijr is Meccan, so its seven oft-repeated could not have been promised before its revelation. | mentions 15:87 BAGHAWI-FULL (قرّاء مكة والكوفة وأكثر فقهاء الحجاز): Meccan and Kufan readers and most Hijazi jurists count the basmala as part of the Fatiha only; it is written to separate surahs. KASHSHAF (قراء مكة والكوفة وفقهاؤهما): Meccan and Kufan readers and jurists, with al-Shafii and followers, count it as a verse of al-Fatiha and every surah. IBNATIYYA (ابن عباس، وموسى بن جعفر عن أبيه، وعلي بن الحسين، وقتادة، وأبو العالية، ومحمد بن يحيى بن حبان): Ibn Abbas, Musa b. Ja'far from his father, Ali b. al-Husayn, Qatada, Abu al-Aliya and Muhammad b. Yahya b. Habban hold that al-Fatiha is Meccan; 15:87 supports this because al-Hijr is unanimously Meccan. | mentions 15:87 IBNATIYYA (أبي بن كعب): Ubayy's report identifies al-Fatiha as the seven oft-repeated; the seven long surahs were revealed some time after al-Hijr, supporting a Meccan dating. | mentions 15:87 IBNATIYYA (author): Prayer became obligatory in Mecca, and no report preserves a Muslim prayer without reciting al-Fatiha; this supports its Meccan origin. IBNATIYYA-FULL (الشافعي): Al-Shafiʿi counts the basmala as a verse of al-Fatiha; many Meccan and Kufan readers do not count “those whom You favored.” | mentions 1:7 IBNJAWZI-ZAD (علي بن أبي طالب والحسن وأبو العالية وقتادة وأبو ميسرة): One view holds that al-Fātiḥa was revealed in Mecca. RAZI-FULL (علي بن أبي طالب): ʿAlī reports that the Fātiḥa descended in Mecca from a treasure beneath the Throne; al-Thaʿlabī says most scholars agree. RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Rāzī identifies Sūrat al-Fātiḥa as Meccan and says it has seven verses. QURTUBI (ابن عباس وقتادة وأبو العالية): Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, and Abū al-ʿĀliya call al-Fātiḥa Meccan; other authorities call it Medinan; some split its revelation. | mentions 15:87 QURTUBI (author): Qurṭubī says another angel brought the gifts while Gabriel brought Qurʾānic recitation in Mecca. | mentions 26:193 BAYDAWI (قراء مكة والكوفة وفقهاؤهما وابن المبارك والشافعي): Meccan and Kufan reciters and jurists, Ibn al-Mubārak, and al-Shāfiʿī hold that the basmala is part of al-Fatiha and every sūra. ABUHAYYAN (علي وابن عباس وعلي بن الحسين وقتادة وأبو العالية وعطاء وابن جبير ومحمد بن يحيى بن حبان وجعفر الصادق): These authorities hold that al-Fātiḥa is Meccan; Abū Ḥayyān says the claim is supported by the seven oft-repeated verses being mentioned in a Meccan sūra. | mentions 15:87 ABUHAYYAN (أبو هريرة وعطاء بن يسار ومجاهد وسواد بن زياد والزهري وعبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير): These authorities hold that al-Fātiḥa is Medinan, contrary to the Meccan attribution. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (علي، وابن عباس، وعلي بن الحسين، وقتادة، وأبو العالية، وعطاء، وابن جبير، ومحمد بن يحيى بن حبان، وجعفر الصادق): These authorities hold that the Fātiḥa is Meccan; Abū Ḥayyān cites the seven oft-repeated verses and the Meccan status of al-Ḥijr in support. | mentions 15:87 IBNKATHIR (ابن عباس وقتادة وأبو العالية): Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatada, and Abu al-ʿAliya hold that the surah was revealed in Mecca. IBNKATHIR (أبو الليث السمرقندي): Abu al-Layth al-Samarqandi says half the surah was revealed in Mecca and half in Medina; Ibn Kathir calls this very strange, as transmitted by al-Qurtubi. BURHAN (ابن عباس والضحاك ومقاتل وعطاء): Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, Muqatil, and Ata classify al-Fatiha as Meccan, while Mujahid classifies it as Medinan. DURR (author): Al-Suyuti identifies al-Fatiha as Meccan and consisting of seven verses. DURR (قتادة): Qatada holds that al-Fatiha was revealed at Mecca, contrary to the Medina reports. ITQAN (الجمهور): The majority count al-Fatiha as seven verses, with Kufan and Meccan counters counting the basmala but not “anʿamta ʿalayhim,” and others doing the reverse. ITQAN (author): Most authorities consider al-Fātiḥa Meccan. Its identification with the seven oft-repeated verses in a Meccan sūra implies it was already revealed, and prayer was obligatory in Mecca with no known prayer omitting it. ITQAN (علي بن أبي طالب): A report transmitted by al-Wāḥidī and al-Thaʿlabī says al-Fātiḥa descended in Mecca from a treasure beneath the Throne. ALUSI (author): Al-Ālūsī says most authorities classify al-Fātiḥa as Meccan, even counting it among the earliest revealed passages. ALUSI (author): The Meccan setting of 15:87 is often used to date al-Fātiḥa, but the argument depends on identifying the seven mathānī with it and on denying prior divine endowment. | mentions 15:87 ALUSI (أبو ميسرة): An author-cited report from Abū Maysara says the Prophet first heard the call in Mecca, then recited al-Fātiḥa; al-Ālūsī says it would strongly prove Meccan origin if sound. QUTB-ZILAL (author): Al-Fatiha is Meccan and has seven verses; Muslims recite it at least seventeen times daily, more with voluntary prayers, and may repeat it without limit. IBNASHUR (author): The majority agree Fātiha is Meccan; the author’s preferred chronology is al-ʿAlaq, then al-Muddaththir, then Fātiha. | mentions 96:1 IBNASHUR (الشافعي وأحمد وإسحاق وأبو ثور): One view of al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, Abū Thawr, and most Meccan and Kufan jurists counts it as a verse at the start of Fātiha only. IBNASHUR-FULL (author): For al-Fatiha, the Kufan and Meccan counters counted the basmala as a verse, while the Basran, Syrian, and Medinan counters did not.

positions.position: Al-Fātiḥa was revealed in Medina.
positions.reasons: THALABI (قراء المدينة والبصرة والكوفة، مالك، الأوزاعي، أبو حنيفة): The Medinan, Basran, and Kufan reciters, with Mālik, al-Awzāʿī, and Abū Ḥanīfa, treat the basmala as an opening blessing, not a verse of this or other suras, and say it need not be recited; on this count “those You favored” is verse six. MAWARDI (مجاهد): Mujahid holds that the Fatiha is Medinan, contrary to Qatada’s view. BAGHAWI (author): The Medinan and Basran readers and Kufan jurists say the basmala is not part of any surah; it opens them for blessing. BAGHAWI (مجاهد): Mujahid considers the surah Medinan. BAGHAWI-FULL (قرّاء المدينة والبصرة وفقهاء الكوفة): Medinan and Basran readers and Kufan jurists hold that the basmala is not part of the Fatiha or other surahs, but opens them for blessing. IBNATIYYA (عطاء بن يسار، وسوادة بن زياد، والزهري محمد بن مسلم، وعبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير): Ata b. Yasar, Sawada b. Ziyad, al-Zuhri and Abd Allah b. Ubayd b. Umayr instead regard al-Fatiha as Medinan. IBNATIYYA-FULL (عطاء بن يسار وسوادة بن زياد والزهري وعبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير): ʿAta ibn Yasar, Sawada ibn Ziyad, al-Zuhri, and ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr say al-Fatiha was revealed in Medina. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (أبو هريرة ومجاهد وعبيد بن عمير وعطاء الخراساني): A second view holds that al-Fātiḥa was revealed in Medina; Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have held both views. RAZI-FULL (مجاهد): Mujāhid says it descended in Medina, but Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl rejects this as a lapse against scholarly consensus. BAYDAWI (قراء المدينة والبصرة والشام وفقهاؤها ومالك والأوزاعي): The reciters and jurists of Medina, Basra, and Syria, Mālik, and al-Awzāʿī reject its being part of every sūra. IBNKATHIR (أبو هريرة ومجاهد وعطاء بن يسار والزهري): Abu Hurayra, Mujahid, ʿAta ibn Yasar, and al-Zuhri hold that the surah was revealed in Medina. ITQAN (مجاهد): Mujāhid is reliably reported by al-Firyābī and Abū ʿUbayd to consider al-Fātiḥa Medinan; al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl calls this a slip, and Ibn ʿAṭiyya also names several who held it. ALUSI (مجاهد): Mujāhid calls the sūra Medinan; al-Ālūsī treats this solitary view as an error, noting it would mean years of prayer without al-Fātiḥa. STUDYQURAN (author): Most scholars reject a Medinan origin because Muslims needed the sūrah to perform obligatory prayers.

positions.position: Al-Fātiḥa was revealed in both Mecca and Medina.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (قيل): The name al-mathānī is explained by the Fātiḥa having been revealed twice. QURTUBI (الثعلبي): Some say al-Fātiḥa is both Meccan and Medinan because Gabriel brought it twice; Qurṭubī prefers his reconciliation. ABUHAYYAN (قيل): A further view calls al-Fātiḥa both Meccan and Medinan. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (أبو هريرة، وعطاء بن يسار، ومجاهد، وسواد بن زياد، والزهري، وعبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير): These authorities say the Fātiḥa is Medinan, while another reported position calls it both Meccan and Medinan. ITQAN (بعضهم): Some say al-Fātiḥa was revealed twice, once in Mecca and once in Medina, to magnify its honor; a fourth view divides it between the two cities.

positions.position: Another explanation is that al-Fatiha was reserved as a treasure for this community and had not been revealed to anyone before it.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (author): Another explanation is that al-Fatiha was reserved as a treasure for this community and had not been revealed to anyone before it.

positions.position: The Prophet told Ubayy that no comparable surah had been revealed in the Torah, Gospel or Qur'an.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عن أبي بن كعب): The Prophet told Ubayy that no comparable surah had been revealed in the Torah, Gospel or Qur'an.

positions.position: An unnamed report says al-Fatiha is equivalent to two-thirds of the Qur'an.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (غير مسمى): An unnamed report says al-Fatiha is equivalent to two-thirds of the Qur'an.

positions.position: Anas reports that the Prophet assigned al-Fatiha thirty more merits than other speech.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (أنس بن مالك عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): Anas reports that the Prophet assigned al-Fatiha thirty more merits than other speech.

positions.position: A further Prophetic report assigns twenty merits to saying la ilaha illa Allah and thirty to saying al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): A further Prophetic report assigns twenty merits to saying la ilaha illa Allah and thirty to saying al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin.

positions.position: The merit comparison concerns believers seeking reward: al-hamdu combines praise with the monotheism contained in la ilaha illa Allah, while the latter contains monotheism alone.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (author): The merit comparison concerns believers seeking reward: al-hamdu combines praise with the monotheism contained in la ilaha illa Allah, while the latter contains monotheism alone.

positions.position: In their role of warding off unbelief and association, la ilaha illa Allah is superior; the Prophet called it the best statement he and earlier prophets had uttered.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (author): In their role of warding off unbelief and association, la ilaha illa Allah is superior; the Prophet called it the best statement he and earlier prophets had uttered.

positions.position: The Prophet says no equivalent to al-Fatiha was revealed in the Torah, Gospel, or Qur'an.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (رسول الله): The Prophet says no equivalent to al-Fatiha was revealed in the Torah, Gospel, or Qur'an.

positions.position: A report says al-Fatiha equals two-thirds of the Qur'an; this may reflect its meanings or an unreasoned divine preference, like the reported merit of al-Ikhlas and al-Zalzala.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): A report says al-Fatiha equals two-thirds of the Qur'an; this may reflect its meanings or an unreasoned divine preference, like the reported merit of al-Ikhlas and al-Zalzala. | mentions 112:1, 99:1

positions.position: Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl argues that the Meccan Sūrat al-Ḥijr already refers to the seven oft-repeated verses and that it is implausible for the Prophet to live in Mecca over a decade without the Fātiḥa.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (حسين بن الفضل): Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl argues that the Meccan Sūrat al-Ḥijr already refers to the seven oft-repeated verses and that it is implausible for the Prophet to live in Mecca over a decade without the Fātiḥa. | mentions 15:87

positions.position: A report from Abū Saʿīd calls al-Fātiḥa a cure for every poison; al-Dārimī transmits it.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (أبو سعيد الخدري): A report from Abū Saʿīd calls al-Fātiḥa a cure for every poison; al-Dārimī transmits it.

positions.position: The ruqya name is established by Abū Saʿīd’s report of the man who recited al-Fātiḥa over a sick chief.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (أبو سعيد الخدري): The ruqya name is established by Abū Saʿīd’s report of the man who recited al-Fātiḥa over a sick chief.

positions.position: Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects the inference that Gabriel never brought al-Fātiḥa; the report about another angel may mean Gabriel announced him.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (ابن عطية): Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects the inference that Gabriel never brought al-Fātiḥa; the report about another angel may mean Gabriel announced him.

positions.position: Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan said that everything between the two covers is God's speech.
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI (محمد بن الحسن): Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan said that everything between the two covers is God's speech.

positions.position: Al-Zamakhsharī supplies a delayed verb such as “I read” or “I recite,” and claims fronting yields exclusivity; Abū Ḥayyān disputes the latter claim.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (الزمخشري): Al-Zamakhsharī supplies a delayed verb such as “I read” or “I recite,” and claims fronting yields exclusivity; Abū Ḥayyān disputes the latter claim.

positions.position: Sībawayh says fronting an object is good Arabic just as ordinary order is; Abū Ḥayyān cites this against the claim that fronting necessarily entails exclusivity.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (سيبويه): Sībawayh says fronting an object is good Arabic just as ordinary order is; Abū Ḥayyān cites this against the claim that fronting necessarily entails exclusivity.

positions.position: Abū Ḥayyān rejects al-Zamakhsharī's claim that fronting necessarily restricts meaning, citing Sībawayh's example of ordinary good Arabic word order.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Abū Ḥayyān rejects al-Zamakhsharī's claim that fronting necessarily restricts meaning, citing Sībawayh's example of ordinary good Arabic word order.

positions.position: Between the two parses, Abū Ḥayyān says the verbal estimate is preferable because verbs are the basic governors, though the alternative preserves a clause's second constituent.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Between the two parses, Abū Ḥayyān says the verbal estimate is preferable because verbs are the basic governors, though the alternative preserves a clause's second constituent.

positions.position: Al-Zamakhsharī supplies a delayed verb such as I read or recite, since what follows the basmala is recitation, and says fronting implies restriction.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الزمخشري): Al-Zamakhsharī supplies a delayed verb such as I read or recite, since what follows the basmala is recitation, and says fronting implies restriction.

positions.position: One position identifies a name with the named object; Abu ʿUbayda and Sibawayh hold this view, as do al-Baqillani and Ibn Furak.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (أبو عبيدة وسيبويه): One position identifies a name with the named object; Abu ʿUbayda and Sibawayh hold this view, as do al-Baqillani and Ibn Furak.

positions.position: Some authorities include al-Fātiḥa among verses revealed repeatedly.
positions.reasons: ITQAN (قوم): Some authorities include al-Fātiḥa among verses revealed repeatedly.

positions.position: Among the material granted to Muhammad but not to any earlier prophet are al-Fatiha, Ayat al-Kursi, and the conclusion of al-Baqara.
positions.reasons: ITQAN (author): Among the material granted to Muhammad but not to any earlier prophet are al-Fatiha, Ayat al-Kursi, and the conclusion of al-Baqara.

positions.position: Banū Ḥanīfa called Musaylima “the Merciful of Yamāma”; al-Ālūsī treats this as blasphemous excess, not evidence that the sacred name is ordinarily shared.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Banū Ḥanīfa called Musaylima “the Merciful of Yamāma”; al-Ālūsī treats this as blasphemous excess, not evidence that the sacred name is ordinarily shared.

positions.position: Sūra may derive, with hamza, from the remnant of something, or without hamza from a building tier, an enclosing city wall, or elevation.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Sūra may derive, with hamza, from the remnant of something, or without hamza from a building tier, an enclosing city wall, or elevation.

positions.position: The claim that Fātiha is called mathānī because it descended twice, in Mecca and Medina, is very remote: the sura is agreed to be Meccan, making a second descent pointless.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): The claim that Fātiha is called mathānī because it descended twice, in Mecca and Medina, is very remote: the sura is agreed to be Meccan, making a second descent pointless.

positions.position: If early Muslims also wrote sura names and Meccan or Medinan labels, writing is no proof that the basmala belongs at each opening; the single-color ink evidence defeats a colored-ink theory.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): If early Muslims also wrote sura names and Meccan or Medinan labels, writing is no proof that the basmala belongs at each opening; the single-color ink evidence defeats a colored-ink theory.

turns_on: Which reports locate its descent in Mecca, Medina, or both.

question: What explains the reported absence of al-Fātiḥa from Ibn Masʿūd's codex?

positions.position: Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Ibn Mas'ud report the Prophet explaining al-Rahman as merciful in this world and the next, al-Rahim as merciful in the next world.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (أبو سعيد الخدري وابن مسعود عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Ibn Mas'ud report the Prophet explaining al-Rahman as merciful in this world and the next, al-Rahim as merciful in the next world. IBNATIYYA-FULL (أبو سعيد الخدري وابن مسعود): Abu Saʿid al-Khudri and Ibn Masʿud report the Prophet's distinction: Rahman is merciful in this world and the next, while Rahim is merciful in the next.

positions.position: Critics say Ibn Masʿūd's codex differed from others, omitted the Opening, and erased the two protective sūras, which he denied belonged in the Book.
positions.reasons: IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL (ابن مسعود): Critics say Ibn Masʿūd's codex differed from others, omitted the Opening, and erased the two protective sūras, which he denied belonged in the Book.

positions.position: Ibn Qutayba doubts that Abdullah omitted Fatiha from his codex and rejects inferring this learned Companion did not know it was Quran.
positions.reasons: IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL (author): Ibn Qutayba doubts that Abdullah omitted Fatiha from his codex and rejects inferring this learned Companion did not know it was Quran.

positions.position: The Prophet praised Abdullah's recitation, telling people who wanted Quran fresh as revealed to follow Ibn Umm ʿAbd's reading.
positions.reasons: IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL (النبي): The Prophet praised Abdullah's recitation, telling people who wanted Quran fresh as revealed to follow Ibn Umm ʿAbd's reading.

positions.position: Umar called Abdullah a container filled with knowledge, supporting Ibn Qutayba’s case for his learning.
positions.reasons: IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL (عمر): Umar called Abdullah a container filled with knowledge, supporting Ibn Qutayba’s case for his learning.

positions.position: The theorists say Abdullah did not write Fatiha because compilation guards against doubt, forgetting, additions and omissions, but it is short and repeated every prayer and rakʿa.
positions.reasons: IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL (أهل النظر): The theorists say Abdullah did not write Fatiha because compilation guards against doubt, forgetting, additions and omissions, but it is short and repeated every prayer and rakʿa.

positions.position: Ibn Qutayba concludes Abdullah knew Fatiha was Quran but had no need to write it, since no Muslim could neglect learning or praying with it.
positions.reasons: IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL (author): Ibn Qutayba concludes Abdullah knew Fatiha was Quran but had no need to write it, since no Muslim could neglect learning or praying with it.

positions.position: Another position, held by al-Thawri, Ibn al-Mubarak, and al-Shafiʿi in one view, counts it in al-Fatiha and every surah except al-Tawba because it is written like the Qur'an in the codex.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI (author): Another position, held by al-Thawri, Ibn al-Mubarak, and al-Shafiʿi in one view, counts it in al-Fatiha and every surah except al-Tawba because it is written like the Qur'an in the codex.

positions.position: Those who count the basmala as part of al-Fatiha and the surahs cite its writing in the codex in the same script as Qur'anic text.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI (author): Those who count the basmala as part of al-Fatiha and the surahs cite its writing in the codex in the same script as Qur'anic text.

positions.position: Al-Bukhari explains the title Umm al-Kitab by al-Fatiha being written first in the codex and recited first in prayer.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (البخاري): Al-Bukhari explains the title Umm al-Kitab by al-Fatiha being written first in the codex and recited first in prayer.

positions.position: Ibn Masʿūd reports that no one loves praise more than God, who praises Himself, and no one is more jealous, so God forbids indecency and sends scripture and messengers to excuse people.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (عبد الله بن مسعود): Ibn Masʿūd reports that no one loves praise more than God, who praises Himself, and no one is more jealous, so God forbids indecency and sends scripture and messengers to excuse people.

positions.position: Some Hanafis accuse al-Shafi‘i of dissenting from consensus on the basmala at every sura’s opening; Razi answers that its Qur’anic-script placement in the codex proves it is Qur’an.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Some Hanafis accuse al-Shafi‘i of dissenting from consensus on the basmala at every sura’s opening; Razi answers that its Qur’anic-script placement in the codex proves it is Qur’an.

positions.position: Those denying that the basmala is part of each sura offer two explanations for its codex placement: it separates suras, or it is Qur’an as an independent verse revealed at each opening or once for insertion throughout.
