positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (المخالف): Those denying that the basmala is part of each sura offer two explanations for its codex placement: it separates suras, or it is Qur’an as an independent verse revealed at each opening or once for insertion throughout.

positions.position: Opponents cite Ibn Mas‘ud teaching an Ajami to replace al-athim with al-yatim, then saying Quranic error is replacing a mercy verse with a punishment verse rather than using a synonym.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (عبد الله بن مسعود): Opponents cite Ibn Mas‘ud teaching an Ajami to replace al-athim with al-yatim, then saying Quranic error is replacing a mercy verse with a punishment verse rather than using a synonym. | mentions 44:43

positions.position: Opponents argue that the Qur’an was in earlier scriptures, whose wording was Hebrew or Syriac rather than the Arabic wording, so meaning can be Qur’an in another language.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (المخالف): Opponents argue that the Qur’an was in earlier scriptures, whose wording was Hebrew or Syriac rather than the Arabic wording, so meaning can be Qur’an in another language. | mentions 26:196, 87:19

positions.position: Opponents cite God’s statement that this Qur’an was revealed to warn people who do not understand Arabic, arguing that communicated meaning in their language is still Qur’an.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (المخالف): Opponents cite God’s statement that this Qur’an was revealed to warn people who do not understand Arabic, arguing that communicated meaning in their language is still Qur’an. | mentions 6:19

positions.position: Razi objects that Hanafis selectively invoke Ibn Mas‘ud: they reject his reported uncertainty about faith, though they rely on him here; reports that he omitted al-Fatiha and the protective suras likely reflect views he later abandoned.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi objects that Hanafis selectively invoke Ibn Mas‘ud: they reject his reported uncertainty about faith, though they rely on him here; reports that he omitted al-Fatiha and the protective suras likely reflect views he later abandoned.

positions.position: Being in earlier scriptures means the Qur’an’s stories are found there, while warning people means warning them of its meaning; this limited figurative reading is warranted by decisive proofs.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Being in earlier scriptures means the Qur’an’s stories are found there, while warning people means warning them of its meaning; this limited figurative reading is warranted by decisive proofs. | mentions 26:196, 6:19

positions.position: Qur’an 73:20 commands recitation for both a solitary worshipper and a follower behind an imam.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Qur’an 73:20 commands recitation for both a solitary worshipper and a follower behind an imam. | mentions 73:20

positions.position: Al-Shafi‘i’s position is said to be agreed upon by Companions including Abu Bakr, Umar, Ali, and Ibn Mas‘ud.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Shafi‘i’s position is said to be agreed upon by Companions including Abu Bakr, Umar, Ali, and Ibn Mas‘ud.

positions.position: Rifa‘a ibn Malik reports the Prophet instructing an uninformed worshipper to praise and magnify God if he has memorized no Qur’an; for one unable to recite even Arabic remembrance, Razi recommends invoking God in any language one can manage.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (رفاعة بن مالك): Rifa‘a ibn Malik reports the Prophet instructing an uninformed worshipper to praise and magnify God if he has memorized no Qur’an; for one unable to recite even Arabic remembrance, Razi recommends invoking God in any language one can manage.

positions.position: For the remaining case of knowing no al-Fatiha, Qur’an, or Arabic remembrance, Razi requires whatever remembrance of God is possible in any language, following the command to do as much as one can.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): For the remaining case of knowing no al-Fatiha, Qur’an, or Arabic remembrance, Razi requires whatever remembrance of God is possible in any language, following the command to do as much as one can.

positions.position: Reports say Ibn Mas‘ud denied that al-Fatiha and the two protective suras belonged to the Qur’an, creating a dilemma for the status of transmission and his own knowledge.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (ابن مسعود): Reports say Ibn Mas‘ud denied that al-Fatiha and the two protective suras belonged to the Qur’an, creating a dilemma for the status of transmission and his own knowledge.

positions.position: If transmission was mass-transmitted in the Companions’ time, Ibn Mas‘ud’s denial would imply disbelief or deficient reason; if not, Qur’an’s transmission would lack certain proof, so Razi judges the attribution false.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): If transmission was mass-transmitted in the Companions’ time, Ibn Mas‘ud’s denial would imply disbelief or deficient reason; if not, Qur’an’s transmission would lack certain proof, so Razi judges the attribution false.

positions.position: Ibn Masʿūd says the basmala’s nineteen letters protect the reader from each of Hell’s nineteen guardians.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (عبد الله بن مسعود): Ibn Masʿūd says the basmala’s nineteen letters protect the reader from each of Hell’s nineteen guardians. | mentions 74:30

positions.position: Al-Muhallab locates al-Fātiḥa’s ruqya specifically in “You alone we worship and ask for help.”
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (المهلب): Al-Muhallab locates al-Fātiḥa’s ruqya specifically in “You alone we worship and ask for help.”

positions.position: Qurṭubī says the whole sūra is ruqya: the Prophet asked how it was a ruqya, not how it contained one.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (author): Qurṭubī says the whole sūra is ruqya: the Prophet asked how it was a ruqya, not how it contained one.

positions.position: Al-Fātiḥa is Qurʾān by consensus; Ibn Masʿūd explained its omission from his muṣḥaf as shorthand.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (author): Al-Fātiḥa is Qurʾān by consensus; Ibn Masʿūd explained its omission from his muṣḥaf as shorthand.

positions.position: Asked why he omitted al-Fātiḥa from his muṣḥaf, Ibn Masʿūd said he would have written it before every sūra.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (عبد الله بن مسعود): Asked why he omitted al-Fātiḥa from his muṣḥaf, Ibn Masʿūd said he would have written it before every sūra.

positions.position: ʿUmar and Ibn Masʿūd opened prayer with “Glory and praise to You, O God”; Sufyān, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, and Ḥanafīs followed.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (عمر وابن مسعود): ʿUmar and Ibn Masʿūd opened prayer with “Glory and praise to You, O God”; Sufyān, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, and Ḥanafīs followed.

positions.position: Ibn Masʿūd reports adding “the All-Hearing, All-Knowing”; the Prophet says Gabriel taught the shorter formula.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (ابن مسعود): Ibn Masʿūd reports adding “the All-Hearing, All-Knowing”; the Prophet says Gabriel taught the shorter formula.

positions.position: A report through Ibn Masʿūd and Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī attributes to the Prophet the same distinction; Abū Ḥayyān says it must be accepted if sound.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): A report through Ibn Masʿūd and Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī attributes to the Prophet the same distinction; Abū Ḥayyān says it must be accepted if sound.

positions.position: Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh says the names concern the interests of the afterlife and worldly life.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (يحيى بن معاذ): Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh says the names concern the interests of the afterlife and worldly life.

positions.position: A report from Ibn Masʿūd and Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī attributes to the Prophet the interpretation raḥmān for this world and raḥīm for the afterlife; if sound, Abū Ḥayyān says it must be followed.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL (ابن مسعود، وأبو سعيد الخدري): A report from Ibn Masʿūd and Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī attributes to the Prophet the interpretation raḥmān for this world and raḥīm for the afterlife; if sound, Abū Ḥayyān says it must be followed.

positions.position: Ibn Masʿud reportedly says reciting the basmala shields a person from each of the nineteen keepers of Hell; Ibn ʿAtiyya supports this with a report of more than thirty angels hastening to record praise.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (ابن مسعود): Ibn Masʿud reportedly says reciting the basmala shields a person from each of the nineteen keepers of Hell; Ibn ʿAtiyya supports this with a report of more than thirty angels hastening to record praise.

positions.position: The Fatiha opens recitation and was placed first when the Companions wrote the master codex.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): The Fatiha opens recitation and was placed first when the Companions wrote the master codex.

positions.position: Ibn Masʿud explains that he omitted the Fatiha from his codex because he would have written it at the start of every surah where it is recited in prayer; Muslims' memorization sufficed.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (ابن مسعود): Ibn Masʿud explains that he omitted the Fatiha from his codex because he would have written it at the start of every surah where it is recited in prayer; Muslims' memorization sufficed.

positions.position: In a report judged by the Prophet, a companion recited the Fatiha as ruqya over a stung man who recovered; the Prophet approved the reward of thirty sheep and asked how he knew it was ruqya.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (أبو سعيد الخدري): In a report judged by the Prophet, a companion recited the Fatiha as ruqya over a stung man who recovered; the Prophet approved the reward of thirty sheep and asked how he knew it was ruqya.

positions.position: Al-Bazzar reports that reciting the Fatiha and Surat al-Ikhlas before sleep protects from everything except death.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): Al-Bazzar reports that reciting the Fatiha and Surat al-Ikhlas before sleep protects from everything except death. | mentions 112:1

positions.position: The surah is called a ruqya because the Prophet affirmed its use in healing a stung man and asked how the companion knew it was a ruqya.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): The surah is called a ruqya because the Prophet affirmed its use in healing a stung man and asked how the companion knew it was a ruqya.

positions.position: Ibn Masud omitted al-Fatiha from his codex, reasoning that if written it would be placed at the beginning of everything.
positions.reasons: DURR (إبراهيم): Ibn Masud omitted al-Fatiha from his codex, reasoning that if written it would be placed at the beginning of everything.

positions.position: Alusi lists many authorities for silent recitation, including al-Thawri, Ibn al-Mubarak, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn al-Zubayr, Ammar, major Successors, and Ahmad.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi lists many authorities for silent recitation, including al-Thawri, Ibn al-Mubarak, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn al-Zubayr, Ammar, major Successors, and Ahmad.

question: What does al-Fātiḥa teach as a whole?

positions.position: Earlier scriptures each contain some meanings found together in the Qur'an: the Torah gives admonitions and detail, the Psalms praise and glorify, and the Gospel admonishes and reminds; the Qur'an gathers these and adds more.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): Earlier scriptures each contain some meanings found together in the Qur'an: the Torah gives admonitions and detail, the Psalms praise and glorify, and the Gospel admonishes and reminds; the Qur'an gathers these and adds more.

positions.position: The Qur'an's varied contents—encouragement, warning, commands, prohibitions, stories, argument, and parables—also make its extended expression purposeful.
positions.reasons: TAB (author): The Qur'an's varied contents—encouragement, warning, commands, prohibitions, stories, argument, and parables—also make its extended expression purposeful.

positions.position: The sura omits seven letters associated with torment: thāʾ with ruin, jīm with Hell, khāʾ with disgrace, zāy and shīn with breath, the tree or misery, ẓāʾ with shade and blazing fire, and fāʾ with separation or falsehood.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The sura omits seven letters associated with torment: thāʾ with ruin, jīm with Hell, khāʾ with disgrace, zāy and shīn with breath, the tree or misery, ẓāʾ with shade and blazing fire, and fāʾ with separation or falsehood. | mentions 25:14, 15:43, 7:179, 66:8, 16:27, 11:106, 44:43, 77:30, 70:15, 30:14, 20:61

positions.position: Rāzī answers that, although all letters can occur in words about punishment, these seven omitted initials correspond to Hell’s seven gates; understanding the sura protects readers from them.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Rāzī answers that, although all letters can occur in words about punishment, these seven omitted initials correspond to Hell’s seven gates; understanding the sura protects readers from them. | mentions 15:44

positions.position: The explicit proofs that the basmala is in al-Fatiha outweigh a report whose purpose is another point; caution also favors his position.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The explicit proofs that the basmala is in al-Fatiha outweigh a report whose purpose is another point; caution also favors his position.

positions.position: Someone who knows part of al-Fatiha reads that portion plus six other verses; one who knows no part must read whatever Qur’an they know, or glorify and praise God if they know none.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Someone who knows part of al-Fatiha reads that portion plus six other verses; one who knows no part must read whatever Qur’an they know, or glorify and praise God if they know none. | mentions 73:20

positions.position: The seven Fatiha verses remove seven vices: praise dispels desire, Lord of the worlds greed, Judgment Day anger, worship and aid pride and vanity, guidance caprice, the favored path unbelief and doubt, and the final phrase innovation.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The seven Fatiha verses remove seven vices: praise dispels desire, Lord of the worlds greed, Judgment Day anger, worship and aid pride and vanity, guidance caprice, the favored path unbelief and doubt, and the final phrase innovation.

positions.position: Al-Fātiḥa’s twenty-five words contain Qurʾānic sciences: praise, attributes, worship, dependence, guidance, and lessons about rejecters.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (author): Al-Fātiḥa’s twenty-five words contain Qurʾānic sciences: praise, attributes, worship, dependence, guidance, and lessons about rejecters.

positions.position: Umm can mean origin or leading source; al-Fātiḥa’s name may reflect its position and inclusion of Qurʾānic sciences.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (author): Umm can mean origin or leading source; al-Fātiḥa’s name may reflect its position and inclusion of Qurʾānic sciences.

positions.position: It is called the magnificent Qurʾān because it contains praise, worship, dependence, supplication for guidance, and lessons about rejecters.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (author): It is called the magnificent Qurʾān because it contains praise, worship, dependence, supplication for guidance, and lessons about rejecters.

positions.position: Its central purpose is servants' vigilant awareness of their Lord so they worship Him alone; all other themes serve that end.
positions.reasons: BIQAI (author): Its central purpose is servants' vigilant awareness of their Lord so they worship Him alone; all other themes serve that end.

positions.position: These names converge on vigilant awareness of God, the hidden reality sufficient for every aim and the Fātiḥa's central purpose; opening actions without it makes them unworthy of regard.
positions.reasons: BIQAI (author): These names converge on vigilant awareness of God, the hidden reality sufficient for every aim and the Fātiḥa's central purpose; opening actions without it makes them unworthy of regard.

positions.position: The opening praise moves from a particular expression toward the universal, explaining why consequential matters begin with praise; the relation of praise to gratitude is revisited in Sūrat al-Naḥl and Sabaʾ.
positions.reasons: BIQAI (author): The opening praise moves from a particular expression toward the universal, explaining why consequential matters begin with praise; the relation of praise to gratitude is revisited in Sūrat al-Naḥl and Sabaʾ.

positions.position: Prophets, scriptures and laws ultimately gather people to truth so they may know their sovereign and what pleases Him; knowledge and practice together serve the Qur'an's purpose.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (author): Prophets, scriptures and laws ultimately gather people to truth so they may know their sovereign and what pleases Him; knowledge and practice together serve the Qur'an's purpose.

positions.position: Al-Harali contrasts the Qur'an's detailed, dispersed sequence with the Fatiha's seven complete universals, and makes the Fatiha a mirror of the servant's move from misguidance to guidance.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): Al-Harali contrasts the Qur'an's detailed, dispersed sequence with the Fatiha's seven complete universals, and makes the Fatiha a mirror of the servant's move from misguidance to guidance. | mentions 93:7

positions.position: A Prophetic report says he was sent to complete noble character; the author links this completion with the Fatiha's comprehensive opening and the Qur'an's culmination.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): A Prophetic report says he was sent to complete noble character; the author links this completion with the Fatiha's comprehensive opening and the Qur'an's culmination. | mentions 5:3

positions.position: Al-Harali describes the Qur'an's majesty through rulings spanning immediate and deferred realities, witnessed experience, and reports of the past and patterns that recur in time.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): Al-Harali describes the Qur'an's majesty through rulings spanning immediate and deferred realities, witnessed experience, and reports of the past and patterns that recur in time.

positions.position: Al-Harali distinguishes gradual descent that moves understanding between states and rulings from descent from high to low, which may occur with or without intermediaries.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): Al-Harali distinguishes gradual descent that moves understanding between states and rulings from descent from high to low, which may occur with or without intermediaries.

positions.position: The Book functions like a caliph from the resolute messengers, guiding every matter to the right exit: rejecting it fails, hesitation nearly perishes, and accepting it brings piety and excellence.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (author): The Book functions like a caliph from the resolute messengers, guiding every matter to the right exit: rejecting it fails, hesitation nearly perishes, and accepting it brings piety and excellence.

positions.position: Al-Harali maps al-Fatiha's verses to the seven letters: praise, lawful and forbidden, command and prohibition, clear and ambiguous, then the corresponding petitions; its opening gathers all seven.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): Al-Harali maps al-Fatiha's verses to the seven letters: praise, lawful and forbidden, command and prohibition, clear and ambiguous, then the corresponding petitions; its opening gathers all seven.

positions.position: Because praise is the seventh inclusive letter, the Fatiha begins with it and gathers the seven universals diffused through the Qur'an, as the Qur'an gathers earlier scriptures.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): Because praise is the seventh inclusive letter, the Fatiha begins with it and gathers the seven universals diffused through the Qur'an, as the Qur'an gathers earlier scriptures.

positions.position: The first verse contains praise's seventh letter; the second contains the lawful and forbidden letters that Rahmaniyyah establishes for worldly life, allowing enjoyment and removing either prohibition's burden or sin.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): The first verse contains praise's seventh letter; the second contains the lawful and forbidden letters that Rahmaniyyah establishes for worldly life, allowing enjoyment and removing either prohibition's burden or sin.

positions.position: The Qur'an begins with the sixth, ambiguous letter so confessing ignorance and believing without grasping it invites divine gift; this trains compliance with the rest without claiming mastery.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): The Qur'an begins with the sixth, ambiguous letter so confessing ignorance and believing without grasping it invites divine gift; this trains compliance with the rest without claiming mastery.

positions.position: After the ambiguous opening, the Qur'an presents the clear letter in the traits of believers; observance from faith is clear guidance, while external compliance without faith remains mere command.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): After the ambiguous opening, the Qur'an presents the clear letter in the traits of believers; observance from faith is clear guidance, while external compliance without faith remains mere command. | mentions 2:3, 49:14

positions.position: Al-Harali says the alphabetic openings are the roots of God's first speech, translated into Arabic words and composed as the clear Qur'an; in heavenly scripture they signify the whole before its detailed unfolding.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): Al-Harali says the alphabetic openings are the roots of God's first speech, translated into Arabic words and composed as the clear Qur'an; in heavenly scripture they signify the whole before its detailed unfolding.

positions.position: Their comprehensive signs span existence from its hidden center to visible and audible revelation, and they did not appear in earlier books because creation was then incomplete; the final, complete Book fulfills their promised appearance.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): Their comprehensive signs span existence from its hidden center to visible and audible revelation, and they did not appear in earlier books because creation was then incomplete; the final, complete Book fulfills their promised appearance.

positions.position: Baqara answers the Fatiha's plea for guidance by directing worshippers to the Book, describing the guided and denied groups as patterns to follow or avoid; its pious are the straight path and its others the path of ruin.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (author): Baqara answers the Fatiha's plea for guidance by directing worshippers to the Book, describing the guided and denied groups as patterns to follow or avoid; its pious are the straight path and its others the path of ruin.

positions.position: Alternatively, the surah's purpose is solely to describe the Book; it establishes the truth of its meaning, exposes disbelief and hypocrisy to show that inward faith matters, then proves its inimitable form and authority for teaching law.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (author): Alternatively, the surah's purpose is solely to describe the Book; it establishes the truth of its meaning, exposes disbelief and hypocrisy to show that inward faith matters, then proves its inimitable form and authority for teaching law. | mentions 2:21

positions.position: The most specialized form of a fine opening is barāʿat al-istihlāl, which signals the subject to come; al-Bayhaqi cites al-Hasan that knowledge of the earlier scriptures and Qur’an was concentrated into the Fatiha.
positions.reasons: ITQAN (البيهقي): The most specialized form of a fine opening is barāʿat al-istihlāl, which signals the subject to come; al-Bayhaqi cites al-Hasan that knowledge of the earlier scriptures and Qur’an was concentrated into the Fatiha.

positions.position: By signaling all Qur’anic aims, the Fatiha achieves an exemplary opening and combines beautiful words, pleasing cadence, and rhetorical forms.
positions.reasons: ITQAN (author): By signaling all Qur’anic aims, the Fatiha achieves an exemplary opening and combines beautiful words, pleasing cadence, and rhetorical forms.

positions.position: Al-Zamakhshari says the Fatiha encompasses praise, worship through commands and prohibitions, and promise and warning; every Qur’anic verse falls under one of these topics.
positions.reasons: ITQAN (الزمخشري): Al-Zamakhshari says the Fatiha encompasses praise, worship through commands and prohibitions, and promise and warning; every Qur’anic verse falls under one of these topics.

positions.position: Al-Baydawi says the Fatiha contains theoretical wisdom, practical rulings in walking the straight path, and knowledge of the ranks of the blessed and abodes of the wretched.
positions.reasons: ITQAN (البيضاوي): Al-Baydawi says the Fatiha contains theoretical wisdom, practical rulings in walking the straight path, and knowledge of the ranks of the blessed and abodes of the wretched.

positions.position: Al-Ālūsī says al-Fātiḥa gathers praise, worship, and promise or warning; these summarize the guidance sent through messengers and revealed books for worldly and final welfare.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Al-Ālūsī says al-Fātiḥa gathers praise, worship, and promise or warning; these summarize the guidance sent through messengers and revealed books for worldly and final welfare. | mentions 1:2, 1:4, 1:7

positions.position: Praise appears in al-ḥamdu lillāh; worship is taught by its implied command, guidance-seeking, or the declaration of worship, while command entails prohibition.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Praise appears in al-ḥamdu lillāh; worship is taught by its implied command, guidance-seeking, or the declaration of worship, while command entails prohibition. | mentions 1:2, 1:5, 1:6

positions.position: Promise and warning appear in the favored and the angered or astray, and in the Day of Recompense understood as reward and punishment.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Promise and warning appear in the favored and the angered or astray, and in the Day of Recompense understood as reward and punishment. | mentions 1:4, 1:7

positions.position: Al-Ālūsī offers a second map: theoretical knowledge is covered through the Day of Judgment, practical conduct by worship and guidance, and human outcomes by the final verse.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Al-Ālūsī offers a second map: theoretical knowledge is covered through the Day of Judgment, practical conduct by worship and guidance, and human outcomes by the final verse. | mentions 1:2, 1:4, 1:5, 1:6, 1:7

positions.position: A four-discipline scheme maps theology to Lordship and mercy, prophecy to those favored, and the afterlife to the Day of Judgment.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): A four-discipline scheme maps theology to Lordship and mercy, prophecy to those favored, and the afterlife to the Day of Judgment. | mentions 1:2, 1:3, 1:4, 1:7

positions.position: The same scheme maps worship to practical law, reliance and guidance to ethics and spiritual progress, and the final verse to narratives, outcomes, and warning.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): The same scheme maps worship to practical law, reliance and guidance to ethics and spiritual progress, and the final verse to narratives, outcomes, and warning. | mentions 1:5, 1:6, 1:7

positions.position: Quranic composition unites scientific order and aesthetic beauty, surpassing the system of sciences in firmness and literature in variety and resemblance.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): Quranic composition unites scientific order and aesthetic beauty, surpassing the system of sciences in firmness and literature in variety and resemblance.

positions.position: A poet says the cosmos' maiden thought has been torn open while the Quran's meaning still remains veiled in its purity.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): A poet says the cosmos' maiden thought has been torn open while the Quran's meaning still remains veiled in its purity.

positions.position: A second explanation is that Fātiha gathers the Qur’an’s three central aims: praise, commands and prohibitions, and promise and warning; the rest elaborates them.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): A second explanation is that Fātiha gathers the Qur’an’s three central aims: praise, commands and prohibitions, and promise and warning; the rest elaborates them. | mentions 1:2, 1:4, 1:5, 1:6, 1:7

positions.position: Commands and prohibitions guide people toward well-being in both abodes; knowing the divine Commander and hoping for reward while fearing punishment complete the rationale for the Qur’an’s central aims.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): Commands and prohibitions guide people toward well-being in both abodes; knowing the divine Commander and hoping for reward while fearing punishment complete the rationale for the Qur’an’s central aims.

positions.position: Its phrases map onto those aims: praise covers divine perfection, Lord of the worlds divine acts, the merciful names legislation, Master of Judgment the Hereafter, worship and aid religion, and guidance human conduct and past peoples.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): Its phrases map onto those aims: praise covers divine perfection, Lord of the worlds divine acts, the merciful names legislation, Master of Judgment the Hereafter, worship and aid religion, and guidance human conduct and past peoples. | mentions 1:2, 1:3, 1:4, 1:5, 1:6, 1:7

positions.position: Ibn ʿAbd al-Salām distinguishes outward bodily practice as Sharia from inward heart practice as reality; worship expresses Sharia and seeking help expresses reality, together establishing servitude.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (عز الدين بن عبد السلام): Ibn ʿAbd al-Salām distinguishes outward bodily practice as Sharia from inward heart practice as reality; worship expresses Sharia and seeking help expresses reality, together establishing servitude. | mentions 1:5

positions.position: The path of those favored points to the exemplary past of communities and individuals; the final phrase evokes stories and details of misguided nations recounted in the Qur’an.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): The path of those favored points to the exemplary past of communities and individuals; the final phrase evokes stories and details of misguided nations recounted in the Qur’an. | mentions 1:7

positions.position: Harun al-Ataki's accusative reading of al-hamdu lillahi is cited as evidence that al-hamdu is an absolute object.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR-FULL (هارون العتكي): Harun al-Ataki's accusative reading of al-hamdu lillahi is cited as evidence that al-hamdu is an absolute object.

positions.position: The Qur'an's purpose is to guide people; its opening names God as the return of servants, the giver of universal mercy, and the guide to believers' lasting mercy.
positions.reasons: TABATABAI (author): The Qur'an's purpose is to guide people; its opening names God as the return of servants, the giver of universal mercy, and the guide to believers' lasting mercy. | mentions 5:15, 5:16, 7:156

positions.position: He also quotes a Christian's parody of al-Fatiha as another failed counter-imitation.
positions.reasons: TABATABAI (بعض النصارى): He also quotes a Christian's parody of al-Fatiha as another failed counter-imitation.

question: What recitation of al-Fātiḥa is required in prayer?

positions.position: Anas reports that Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, and ʿUthman did not recite the basmala when beginning prayer, evidence for excluding it from al-Fatiha.
positions.reasons: BAGHAWI (أنس بن مالك): Anas reports that Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, and ʿUthman did not recite the basmala when beginning prayer, evidence for excluding it from al-Fatiha. BAGHAWI-FULL (أنس بن مالك): Anas reports that Abu Bakr, Umar, and Uthman did not recite the basmala when beginning the prayer; this is evidence for excluding it from the Fatiha.

positions.position: Na'im heard Abu Hurayra recite the basmala and al-Fatiha, say amin, and perform prayer takbirs; Abu Hurayra said his prayer most resembled the Prophet's.
positions.reasons: DURR (أبو هريرة): Na'im heard Abu Hurayra recite the basmala and al-Fatiha, say amin, and perform prayer takbirs; Abu Hurayra said his prayer most resembled the Prophet's. DURR-FULL (نعيم المجمر): Nuaim heard Abu Hurayra recite the basmala and al-Fatiha through its end, say amin, and describe his prayer as resembling the Prophet's.

positions.position: Al-Shafiʿi and a group require the Fatiha in every prayer unit; others require it in most units, while Hasan and most Basrans require it in one unit.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (الشافعي وجماعة من أهل العلم): Al-Shafiʿi and a group require the Fatiha in every prayer unit; others require it in most units, while Hasan and most Basrans require it in one unit. IBNKATHIR (الحسن وأكثر البصريين): Hasan and most Basrans require the Fatiha in only one unit, relying on the unrestricted wording, “There is no prayer without Fatiha.”

positions.position: A separate report says Muʿāwiya recited the basmala for al-Fātiḥa but not the next sura; the Emigrants challenged him, and he repeated the prayer while reading that sura.
positions.reasons: THALABI (المهاجرون): A separate report says Muʿāwiya recited the basmala for al-Fātiḥa but not the next sura; the Emigrants challenged him, and he repeated the prayer while reading that sura.

positions.position: Those who count it as part of al-Fātiḥa require its recitation in prayer because al-Fātiḥa itself is obligatory.
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD (القائلون إنها من الفاتحة): Those who count it as part of al-Fātiḥa require its recitation in prayer because al-Fātiḥa itself is obligatory.

positions.position: Those who do not count it as part of al-Fātiḥa regard reciting it in prayer as sunnah, while Mālik does not recommend its recitation.
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD (القائلون إنها ليست من الفاتحة): Those who do not count it as part of al-Fātiḥa regard reciting it in prayer as sunnah, while Mālik does not recommend its recitation.

positions.position: Thus Hu is the noblest remembrance in states of divine manifestation and unveiling, provided the reciter understands these subtleties.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Thus Hu is the noblest remembrance in states of divine manifestation and unveiling, provided the reciter understands these subtleties.

positions.position: A higher aim is the honor of serving God: prayer joins awareness of the Lord's majesty and the servant's lowliness, verbal remembrance, and bodily service.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A higher aim is the honor of serving God: prayer joins awareness of the Lord's majesty and the servant's lowliness, verbal remembrance, and bodily service.

positions.position: During drought under Solomon, an ant prayed for God’s favor for His creatures, rain came, and Solomon told people to return because another’s prayer had been answered.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (السدي): During drought under Solomon, an ant prayed for God’s favor for His creatures, rain came, and Solomon told people to return because another’s prayer had been answered.

positions.position: Aisha reports that the Prophet began prayer with the takbir and recitation of al-Fatiha, which opponents take to show the basmala is not one of its verses.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (عائشة): Aisha reports that the Prophet began prayer with the takbir and recitation of al-Fatiha, which opponents take to show the basmala is not one of its verses.

positions.position: Mass transmission establishes that God revealed the formula and commanded its inscription in the codex; the dispute therefore concerns legal consequences such as reciting it and touching it while impure.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Mass transmission establishes that God revealed the formula and commanded its inscription in the codex; the dispute therefore concerns legal consequences such as reciting it and touching it while impure.

positions.position: Al-Shafi‘i’s position entails reading the basmala in every rak‘a; Abu Hanifa is reported both to require it before al-Fatiha in every rak‘a and to require it only at the start of the prayer.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الشافعي): Al-Shafi‘i’s position entails reading the basmala in every rak‘a; Abu Hanifa is reported both to require it before al-Fatiha in every rak‘a and to require it only at the start of the prayer.

positions.position: The Hanafi principle would also validate prayer with matching verses from Torah, Gospel, or ordinary writings, an outcome Razi says is alien to Islam.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The Hanafi principle would also validate prayer with matching verses from Torah, Gospel, or ordinary writings, an outcome Razi says is alien to Islam.

positions.position: Al-Shafi‘i’s newer view requires the follower to recite; his earlier view requires it only when the imam recites quietly, as also held by Malik and Ibn al-Mubarak, while Abu Hanifa discourages recitation behind the imam.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الشافعي): Al-Shafi‘i’s newer view requires the follower to recite; his earlier view requires it only when the imam recites quietly, as also held by Malik and Ibn al-Mubarak, while Abu Hanifa discourages recitation behind the imam.

positions.position: The Prophet recited in prayer, so believers follow him; saying that congregational following blocks recitation merely introduces a counterargument.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The Prophet recited in prayer, so believers follow him; saying that congregational following blocks recitation merely introduces a counterargument. | mentions 6:153

positions.position: The command to establish prayer includes all the Prophet’s prayer actions, including reciting al-Fatiha.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The command to establish prayer includes all the Prophet’s prayer actions, including reciting al-Fatiha. | mentions 2:43

positions.position: The first of six positions denies that recitation is obligatory at all; this is attributed to al-Asamm and Ibn Ulayya.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الأصم): The first of six positions denies that recitation is obligatory at all; this is attributed to al-Asamm and Ibn Ulayya.

positions.position: Al-Hasan al-Basri and al-Hasan ibn Salih require al-Fatiha only once, reasoning that the exception in no prayer without it is fulfilled by one recitation.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الحسن البصري): Al-Hasan al-Basri and al-Hasan ibn Salih require al-Fatiha only once, reasoning that the exception in no prayer without it is fulfilled by one recitation.

positions.position: Abu Hanifa requires reading in the first two rak‘as; in later ones the worshipper may read, glorify God, or remain silent, with another report requiring any two rak‘as without specifying which.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أبو حنيفة): Abu Hanifa requires reading in the first two rak‘as; in later ones the worshipper may read, glorify God, or remain silent, with another report requiring any two rak‘as without specifying which.

positions.position: Sufyan’s position requires reading in the first two rak‘as and regards reading in the final two as disliked.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (سفيان): Sufyan’s position requires reading in the first two rak‘as and regards reading in the final two as disliked.

positions.position: Malik requires recitation in most rak‘as: three in a four-rak‘a prayer, two in Maghrib, and both in Fajr.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (مالك): Malik requires recitation in most rak‘as: three in a four-rak‘a prayer, two in Maghrib, and both in Fajr.

positions.position: Ibn al-Sabbagh introduces Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri’s report as evidence for reciting al-Fatiha in every rak‘a; the report’s wording continues in the next segment.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أبو سعيد الخدري): Ibn al-Sabbagh introduces Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri’s report as evidence for reciting al-Fatiha in every rak‘a; the report’s wording continues in the next segment.

positions.position: Reading al-Fatiha in every rak‘a is the safer view; the standing duty remains until reciting in all units completes it fully.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Reading al-Fatiha in every rak‘a is the safer view; the standing duty remains until reciting in all units completes it fully.

positions.position: Recitation must follow sura order; if the latter half is read first and the first half afterward, only the first half counts.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Recitation must follow sura order; if the latter half is read first and the first half afterward, only the first half counts.

positions.position: Abu Sa‘id reports that the Messenger commanded recitation of al-Fatiha in every rak‘a, obligatory or voluntary.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أبو سعيد الخدري): Abu Sa‘id reports that the Messenger commanded recitation of al-Fatiha in every rak‘a, obligatory or voluntary.

positions.position: The transmitted report itself says that prayer is not established without the Fatiha.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The transmitted report itself says that prayer is not established without the Fatiha.

positions.position: If the superior prayer with the Fatiha discharges the obligation, it does not follow that the inferior prayer with another passage does; the obligation remains due.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): If the superior prayer with the Fatiha discharges the obligation, it does not follow that the inferior prayer with another passage does; the obligation remains due.

positions.position: Calling the Fatiha “prayer” shows that religious law serves human interests: people most need knowledge of God's lordship and servitude, which the surah's two halves provide to fulfill the covenant.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Calling the Fatiha “prayer” shows that religious law serves human interests: people most need knowledge of God's lordship and servitude, which the surah's two halves provide to fulfill the covenant. | mentions 17:7, 51:56, 76:2, 2:40

positions.position: Since God names the Fatiha “prayer,” prayer without its recitation does not occur; Razi takes this to establish that reciting it is a pillar, as his school holds.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Since God names the Fatiha “prayer,” prayer without its recitation does not occur; Razi takes this to establish that reciting it is a pillar, as his school holds.

positions.position: The seven Fatiha verses correspond to the seven bodily prayer acts—standing, bowing, rising, first prostration, rising between prostrations, second prostration, and sitting—as soul to body.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The seven Fatiha verses correspond to the seven bodily prayer acts—standing, bowing, rising, first prostration, rising between prostrations, second prostration, and sitting—as soul to body.

positions.position: The opening formula corresponds to standing: the connected letter bāʾ remains upright, and both the formula and standing begin the acts of prayer and other important matters.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The opening formula corresponds to standing: the connected letter bāʾ remains upright, and both the formula and standing begin the acts of prayer and other important matters. | mentions 87:14, 87:15

positions.position: The seven Fatiha verses are the soul of the seven prayer acts, themselves the soul of seven stages of human formation; God is the soul of souls and light of lights.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The seven Fatiha verses are the soul of the seven prayer acts, themselves the soul of seven stages of human formation; God is the soul of souls and light of lights. | mentions 23:12, 23:13, 23:14, 53:42

positions.position: Prayer was given to Muhammad as a gift for his community because it joins bodily ascent through actions with spiritual ascent through remembrances.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Prayer was given to Muhammad as a gift for his community because it joins bodily ascent through actions with spiritual ascent through remembrances.

positions.position: A report in Ibn Mājah says prayer requires al-Fātiḥa in every unit, obligatory or otherwise.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (أبو سعيد الخدري): A report in Ibn Mājah says prayer requires al-Fātiḥa in every unit, obligatory or otherwise.

positions.position: In Muslim’s prayer instruction, the Prophet tells the worshipper to repeat the prescribed actions throughout prayer.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (أبو هريرة): In Muslim’s prayer instruction, the Prophet tells the worshipper to repeat the prescribed actions throughout prayer.

positions.position: Qurṭubī says 7:204 is Meccan while the prayer speech ban came in Medina; Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib says it addresses pagans.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (سعيد بن المسيب): Qurṭubī says 7:204 is Meccan while the prayer speech ban came in Medina; Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib says it addresses pagans. | mentions 7:204

positions.position: The Kūfans say al-Fātiḥa is not specifically required and any Qurʾānic passage may replace it; Qurṭubī says Prophetic designation refutes them.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (الكوفيون): The Kūfans say al-Fātiḥa is not specifically required and any Qurʾānic passage may replace it; Qurṭubī says Prophetic designation refutes them.

positions.position: Khidāj means deficient: a she-camel may miscarry before term, while akhdajat may deliver early even if fully formed.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (الأخفش): Khidāj means deficient: a she-camel may miscarry before term, while akhdajat may deliver early even if fully formed.

positions.position: Because an incomplete prayer is not validly finished, Qurṭubī says the worshipper who omits al-Fātiḥa must repeat it.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (author): Because an incomplete prayer is not validly finished, Qurṭubī says the worshipper who omits al-Fātiḥa must repeat it.

positions.position: A report from Mālik says recitation is not required; al-Shāfiʿī held similarly in Iraq but reversed this in Egypt.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (مالك والشافعي): A report from Mālik says recitation is not required; al-Shāfiʿī held similarly in Iraq but reversed this in Egypt.

positions.position: The report that ʿUmar omitted al-Fātiḥa in Maghrib and accepted prayer is disconnected and textually objectionable; Mālik removed it.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (عمر): The report that ʿUmar omitted al-Fātiḥa in Maghrib and accepted prayer is disconnected and textually objectionable; Mālik removed it.

positions.position: Qurṭubī says the sound account is that ʿUmar forgot recitation in Maghrib and repeated prayer.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (عمر): Qurṭubī says the sound account is that ʿUmar forgot recitation in Maghrib and repeated prayer.

positions.position: Scholars agree prayer requires Qurʾānic recitation but set no amount beyond al-Fātiḥa; they generally recommend one additional sūra.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (الأمة): Scholars agree prayer requires Qurʾānic recitation but set no amount beyond al-Fātiḥa; they generally recommend one additional sūra.

positions.position: Al-Awzāʿī says another passage can suffice if al-Fātiḥa is omitted, but omission in three units requires repeating prayer.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (الأوزاعي): Al-Awzāʿī says another passage can suffice if al-Fātiḥa is omitted, but omission in three units requires repeating prayer.

positions.position: Abū Thawr and Ibn Khuwayz Mundād require al-Fātiḥa in every unit, the view Qurṭubī calls correct.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (أبو ثور وابن خويز منداد): Abū Thawr and Ibn Khuwayz Mundād require al-Fātiḥa in every unit, the view Qurṭubī calls correct.

positions.position: Qurṭubī prefers Mālik: Qurʾānic status requires definitive mass transmission, not solitary reports.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (author): Qurṭubī prefers Mālik: Qurʾānic status requires definitive mass transmission, not solitary reports.

positions.position: Ibn ʿAbbās calls the names soft, one softer than the other; al-Khaṭṭābī objects and al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl corrects it to “gentle.”
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās calls the names soft, one softer than the other; al-Khaṭṭābī objects and al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl corrects it to “gentle.”

positions.position: Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl says the narrator confused “gentler” with “softer”; gentleness is divine.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (الحسين بن الفضل): Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl says the narrator confused “gentler” with “softer”; gentleness is divine.

positions.position: A report attributed to ʿAlī says al-Fātiḥa, the Throne Verse, 3:18, and 3:26 hang at the Throne without a veil.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (علي بن أبي طالب): A report attributed to ʿAlī says al-Fātiḥa, the Throne Verse, 3:18, and 3:26 hang at the Throne without a veil. | mentions 2:255, 3:18, 3:26

positions.position: Al-Fātiḥa is called al-Ṣalāh because the divine report calls it prayer and prayer is not valid without it.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (author): Al-Fātiḥa is called al-Ṣalāh because the divine report calls it prayer and prayer is not valid without it.

positions.position: Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna calls it al-Wāfiya because it cannot be halved across two prayer units.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (سفيان بن عيينة): Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna calls it al-Wāfiya because it cannot be halved across two prayer units.

positions.position: Mālik requires the imam and individual worshipper to recite al-Fātiḥa in every prayer unit.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (مالك): Mālik requires the imam and individual worshipper to recite al-Fātiḥa in every prayer unit.

positions.position: Ibn Khuwayz Mundād says Mālik invalidates a two-unit prayer if al-Fātiḥa is omitted in one; longer prayers have reports of repeating or prostrating for forgetfulness.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (ابن خويز منداد): Ibn Khuwayz Mundād says Mālik invalidates a two-unit prayer if al-Fātiḥa is omitted in one; longer prayers have reports of repeating or prostrating for forgetfulness.

positions.position: Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, most Basrans, and al-Mughīra hold one recitation of al-Fātiḥa anywhere in prayer suffices.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (الحسن البصري والمغيرة بن عبد الرحمن): Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, most Basrans, and al-Mughīra hold one recitation of al-Fātiḥa anywhere in prayer suffices.

positions.position: Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Thawrī, and al-Awzāʿī allow another passage to suffice if al-Fātiḥa is deliberately omitted.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (أبو حنيفة والثوري والأوزاعي): Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Thawrī, and al-Awzāʿī allow another passage to suffice if al-Fātiḥa is deliberately omitted.

positions.position: Al-Ṭabarī requires al-Fātiḥa each unit but allows an equivalent passage; Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr rejects substitution.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (الطبري): Al-Ṭabarī requires al-Fātiḥa each unit but allows an equivalent passage; Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr rejects substitution.

positions.position: Al-Shāfiʿī first held that a follower reads when the imam is quiet but not loud; in Egypt he gave two views for loud recitation.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (الشافعي): Al-Shāfiʿī first held that a follower reads when the imam is quiet but not loud; in Egypt he gave two views for loud recitation.

positions.position: Qurṭubī prefers al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, and Mālik’s alternate view: al-Fātiḥa is required from everyone in every unit.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (author): Qurṭubī prefers al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, and Mālik’s alternate view: al-Fātiḥa is required from everyone in every unit.

positions.position: Qurṭubī cites Companions who require al-Fātiḥa in every unit.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (عمر وابن عباس وأبو هريرة وأبي بن كعب): Qurṭubī cites Companions who require al-Fātiḥa in every unit.

positions.position: The Fatiha is Makkan, Madinan, or both; Nasafi prefers both: it descended at Mecca when prayer became obligatory and again at Medina when the qibla turned to the Kaaba.
positions.reasons: NASAFI (author): The Fatiha is Makkan, Madinan, or both; Nasafi prefers both: it descended at Mecca when prayer became obligatory and again at Medina when the qibla turned to the Kaaba.

positions.position: Prayer was prescribed in Mecca, and no prayer in Islam is known to have been performed without al-Fātiḥa.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (author): Prayer was prescribed in Mecca, and no prayer in Islam is known to have been performed without al-Fātiḥa.

positions.position: Abu Hanifa and his followers hold that Fatiha is not specifically required in prayer; any Qur'an passage suffices, citing 73:20 and “recite what is easy.”
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (أبو حنيفة وأصحابه): Abu Hanifa and his followers hold that Fatiha is not specifically required in prayer; any Qur'an passage suffices, citing 73:20 and “recite what is easy.” | mentions 73:20

positions.position: The other major view requires the Fatiha in prayer, using the deficient-prayer hadith and reports that prayer does not count without it.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (مالك والشافعي وأحمد والجمهور): The other major view requires the Fatiha in prayer, using the deficient-prayer hadith and reports that prayer does not count without it.

positions.position: Abu Hanifa, al-Thawri, and al-Awzaʿi again hold that another Qur'anic passage can replace the Fatiha, citing 73:20.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (أبو حنيفة والثوري والأوزاعي): Abu Hanifa, al-Thawri, and al-Awzaʿi again hold that another Qur'anic passage can replace the Fatiha, citing 73:20. | mentions 73:20

positions.position: The Fatiha is a treasure, cure, sufficiency, fulfillment, protection and incantation; it gathers praise, gratitude and supplication, with prayer as their greatest assembly.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (author): The Fatiha is a treasure, cure, sufficiency, fulfillment, protection and incantation; it gathers praise, gratitude and supplication, with prayer as their greatest assembly.

positions.position: The Qur'an's arrangement is miraculous, so the Fatiha must retain its required order in prayer; rearrangement or insertion of foreign material invalidates it. Al-Isfahani locates its clearest inimitability in order.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (author): The Qur'an's arrangement is miraculous, so the Fatiha must retain its required order in prayer; rearrangement or insertion of foreign material invalidates it. Al-Isfahani locates its clearest inimitability in order.

positions.position: Al-Harali says the seven repeated verses are the Qur'an's gathered essence and its contents will be disclosed at creation's completion; earlier scriptures progress from changeable scrolls and lasting books to the Qur'an, which completes religion.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): Al-Harali says the seven repeated verses are the Qur'an's gathered essence and its contents will be disclosed at creation's completion; earlier scriptures progress from changeable scrolls and lasting books to the Qur'an, which completes religion. | mentions 5:3

positions.position: Recitation order can differ from revelation chronology; the verse allowing the Prophet to marry certain women was placed before a later restriction.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): Recitation order can differ from revelation chronology; the verse allowing the Prophet to marry certain women was placed before a later restriction. | mentions 33:50, 33:52

positions.position: The Prophet says al-Fatiha is salvation for him, his community, and followers from the Fire.
positions.reasons: DURR (النبي): The Prophet says al-Fatiha is salvation for him, his community, and followers from the Fire.

positions.position: The Prophet told Ubayy that no counterpart to al-Fatiha was revealed in the Torah, Gospel, Psalms, or Qur'an.
positions.reasons: DURR (النبي): The Prophet told Ubayy that no counterpart to al-Fatiha was revealed in the Torah, Gospel, Psalms, or Qur'an.

positions.position: The Prophet describes al-Fatiha as divided between God and the servant; the servant receives what he asks.
positions.reasons: DURR (النبي): The Prophet describes al-Fatiha as divided between God and the servant; the servant receives what he asks.

positions.position: A weak report says the Prophet listened to a man reciting al-Fatiha and said nothing on earth compares with it.
positions.reasons: DURR (أبو زيد): A weak report says the Prophet listened to a man reciting al-Fatiha and said nothing on earth compares with it.

positions.position: Al-Fatiha is reported from the Prophet as a cure for poison; another route attributes the saying to Abu Sa'id and Abu Hurayra.
positions.reasons: DURR (أبو سعيد الخدري): Al-Fatiha is reported from the Prophet as a cure for poison; another route attributes the saying to Abu Sa'id and Abu Hurayra.

positions.position: A report with trustworthy transmitters attributes to the Prophet the saying that al-Fatiha heals every disease.
positions.reasons: DURR (عبد الملك بن عمير): A report with trustworthy transmitters attributes to the Prophet the saying that al-Fatiha heals every disease.

positions.position: Kharija's uncle cured a chained, mentally ill man by reciting al-Fatiha twice daily for three days; the Prophet permitted payment for valid healing.
positions.reasons: DURR (خارجة بن الصلت التميمي): Kharija's uncle cured a chained, mentally ill man by reciting al-Fatiha twice daily for three days; the Prophet permitted payment for valid healing.

positions.position: Al-Hasan transmits that reading al-Fatiha is like reading the Torah, Gospel, Psalms, and Qur'an.
positions.reasons: DURR (الحسن): Al-Hasan transmits that reading al-Fatiha is like reading the Torah, Gospel, Psalms, and Qur'an.

positions.position: Al-Hasan says knowledge of revealed books was condensed into the Qur'an, the Mufassal, and al-Fatiha, whose exegesis equals their exegesis.
positions.reasons: DURR (الحسن): Al-Hasan says knowledge of revealed books was condensed into the Qur'an, the Mufassal, and al-Fatiha, whose exegesis equals their exegesis.

positions.position: A man found Umar praying at night with only al-Fatiha and tasbih; Umar called it the angels' prayer.
positions.reasons: DURR (عمر بن الخطاب): A man found Umar praying at night with only al-Fatiha and tasbih; Umar called it the angels' prayer.

positions.position: Al-Suyuti infers from Umar's report that angels were permitted to recite al-Fatiha alone.
positions.reasons: DURR (author): Al-Suyuti infers from Umar's report that angels were permitted to recite al-Fatiha alone.

positions.position: A Prophetic report compares hearing al-Fatiha from its opening to witnessing a campaign's opening, and hearing it to the end to seeing its spoils distributed.
positions.reasons: DURR (أبو قلابة): A Prophetic report compares hearing al-Fatiha from its opening to witnessing a campaign's opening, and hearing it to the end to seeing its spoils distributed.

positions.position: Shaddad reports the instruction to recite al-Fatiha and another sura before sleep; an angel accompanies the sleeper when he wakes.
positions.reasons: DURR (النبي): Shaddad reports the instruction to recite al-Fatiha and another sura before sleep; an angel accompanies the sleeper when he wakes.

positions.position: The Prophet says there is no valid prayer for one who does not recite al-Fatiha.
positions.reasons: DURR (النبي): The Prophet says there is no valid prayer for one who does not recite al-Fatiha.

positions.position: The Prophet describes prayer without al-Fatiha as defective or deceptive.
positions.reasons: DURR (النبي): The Prophet describes prayer without al-Fatiha as defective or deceptive.

positions.position: Abu Maysara recounts the first call to Muhammad: he was instructed to recite al-Fatiha; Waraqa recognized him as a messenger like Moses.
positions.reasons: DURR (أبو ميسرة عمرو بن شرحبيل): Abu Maysara recounts the first call to Muhammad: he was instructed to recite al-Fatiha; Waraqa recognized him as a messenger like Moses.

positions.position: When Muawiya omitted the basmala and takbirs in prayer, the Emigrants and Helpers rebuked him; he then recited the basmala for al-Fatiha and the following surah and made the prostration takbir.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (معاوية): When Muawiya omitted the basmala and takbirs in prayer, the Emigrants and Helpers rebuked him; he then recited the basmala for al-Fatiha and the following surah and made the prostration takbir.

positions.position: Abū Hurayra transmits the Prophet’s maxim that an important matter begun without God’s name is incomplete; al-Ālūsī interprets it broadly to include trivial matters.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (أبو هريرة): Abū Hurayra transmits the Prophet’s maxim that an important matter begun without God’s name is incomplete; al-Ālūsī interprets it broadly to include trivial matters.

positions.position: The maxim’s variants include beginning with praise, “praise of God,” or another remembrance, and incomplete versus severed; al-Ālūsī calls it unstable in wording and chain but strengthened in meaning.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): The maxim’s variants include beginning with praise, “praise of God,” or another remembrance, and incomplete versus severed; al-Ālūsī calls it unstable in wording and chain but strengthened in meaning.

positions.position: Al-Ālūsī reconciles variants by taking the intended opening as remembrance that manifests divine perfection; matters may be outwardly complete yet deficient in meaning without it.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Al-Ālūsī reconciles variants by taking the intended opening as remembrance that manifests divine perfection; matters may be outwardly complete yet deficient in meaning without it.

positions.position: Al-Munājāt and al-Tafwīḍ name its intimate address to God and the servant’s entrusting matters to Him.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Al-Munājāt and al-Tafwīḍ name its intimate address to God and the servant’s entrusting matters to Him. | mentions 1:5

positions.position: Al-Ālūsī rejects the claim that a prayer without the basmala is incomplete under the “every important matter” report: prayer begins with its required opening takbīr.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Al-Ālūsī rejects the claim that a prayer without the basmala is incomplete under the “every important matter” report: prayer begins with its required opening takbīr.

positions.position: He rejects repeated descent as an explanation reconciling reports: reports can validate an occurrence without causing it, and the alleged repeat lacks a sound rationale.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): He rejects repeated descent as an explanation reconciling reports: reports can validate an occurrence without causing it, and the alleged repeat lacks a sound rationale.

positions.position: The Daraqutni version may describe occasional recitation; it counts the formula because it is obligatory in prayer and deserves attention, not because it is textually part of the Fatiha.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): The Daraqutni version may describe occasional recitation; it counts the formula because it is obligatory in prayer and deserves attention, not because it is textually part of the Fatiha.

positions.position: Muslim's sound report from Abu Hurayra divides prayer between God and servant: three Fatiha verses for God, the middle verse shared, and three for the servant, beginning with al-Hamdu lillah.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (أبو هريرة): Muslim's sound report from Abu Hurayra divides prayer between God and servant: three Fatiha verses for God, the middle verse shared, and three for the servant, beginning with al-Hamdu lillah.

positions.position: Mālik holds that opening basmalas are neither part of al-Fātiḥa or other surahs nor a separate Qurʾānic portion; they are written for separation and blessing and are not recited in prayer.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (İmam Mâlik): Mālik holds that opening basmalas are neither part of al-Fātiḥa or other surahs nor a separate Qurʾānic portion; they are written for separation and blessing and are not recited in prayer.

positions.position: Mālik bases his view on the need for Qurʾānic status to be explicit and mutawātir at every locus and on the practice of Medina’s people.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (İmam Mâlik): Mālik bases his view on the need for Qurʾānic status to be explicit and mutawātir at every locus and on the practice of Medina’s people.

positions.position: Fātiha gives the reciter a general grasp of the Qur’an and invites fuller study according to capacity; this is why it is recited in every prayer rakʿa.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): Fātiha gives the reciter a general grasp of the Qur’an and invites fuller study according to capacity; this is why it is recited in every prayer rakʿa.

positions.position: Some scholars conclude Fātiha descended when prayer became obligatory, so Muslims recited it in prayer from the outset.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (بعض العلماء): Some scholars conclude Fātiha descended when prayer became obligatory, so Muslims recited it in prayer from the outset.

positions.position: Except in Shāfiʿī and Jaʿfarī law, most schools do not recite the basmalah with sūrahs during daily prayers.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (author): Except in Shāfiʿī and Jaʿfarī law, most schools do not recite the basmalah with sūrahs during daily prayers.

positions.position: Anas reports that the Prophet and first three caliphs began prayer recitation with Praise be to God, omitting the basmalah.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (Anas ibn Mālik): Anas reports that the Prophet and first three caliphs began prayer recitation with Praise be to God, omitting the basmalah.

positions.position: Abū Hurayrah recited the basmalah while leading prayer and said his prayer most resembled the Messenger’s.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (Abū Hurayrah): Abū Hurayrah recited the basmalah while leading prayer and said his prayer most resembled the Messenger’s.

positions.position: Al-Fātiḥah means The Opening: it opens the Book, each prayer cycle, many everyday acts, and may open the breast to faith.
positions.reasons: STUDYQURAN (author): Al-Fātiḥah means The Opening: it opens the Book, each prayer cycle, many everyday acts, and may open the breast to faith.

question: Should the basmala be recited aloud in prayer?

positions.position: The basmala is recited aloud in prayer.
positions.reasons: THALABI (author): The author says reciting the basmala aloud in prayer is sunnah, citing commands to read in the Lord’s name and to remember the Lord’s name when praying. | mentions 96:1, 87:15 THALABI (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): A report relayed by al-Mahdī from his father and grandfather, Ibn ʿAbbās, says the Prophet recited the basmala aloud. THALABI (عطاء وطاوس ومجاهد): Al-Layth reports that ʿAṭāʾ, Ṭāwūs, and Mujāhid recited the basmala aloud. JISHUMI (الشافعي): Al-Shāfiʿī holds that it should be recited aloud. JISHUMI (أنس): Anas says he heard neither the Prophet nor Abū Bakr nor ʿUmar recite the basmala aloud in prayer. KASHSHAF (قراء مكة والكوفة وفقهاؤهما): Because they count it as a verse, this group recites it aloud in prayer. KASHSHAF-FULL (قراء مكة والكوفة وفقهاؤهما): They hold that the basmala is a verse of al-Fatiha and every surah; al-Shafi'i and his companions agree and recite it aloud. IBNATIYYA (أبو هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): Abu Hurayra reports that Gabriel taught the Prophet prayer and recited the basmala aloud. IBNATIYYA-FULL (أبو هريرة): Abu Hurayra reports that Gabriel taught the Prophet prayer and recited the basmala aloud. TABRISI (الصادق): Al-Sadiq condemns those who call the basmala an innovation when they recite it aloud, calling it the greatest verse in God's Book. IBNJAWZI-ZAD (الشافعي): Al-Shāfiʿī recommends reciting the basmala aloud; this view is also reported from Muʿāwiya, ʿAṭāʾ, Ṭāwūs, and Mujāhid. RAZI-FULL (author): When Muawiya omitted the basmala aloud in prayer, the Migrants and Helpers rebuked him and he repeated the prayer; Razi takes this as Companion consensus that it is Quran and part of al-Fatiha, and that aloud recitation is preferable. RAZI-FULL (author): Razi holds loud recitation to be Sunna: if the sura is recited aloud, its opening basmala should be too, rather than making only part of a sura audible. RAZI-FULL (علي بن أبي طالب): Ali is reported to recite the basmala aloud in all prayers, a practice Razi says strongly confirms public recitation. RAZI-FULL (author): Since Muawiya was powerful, the Companions’ public protest shows that aloud basmala recitation was established among them. RAZI-FULL (البيهقي): Al-Bayhaqi transmits Abu Hurayra’s report that the Prophet recited the basmala aloud, and reports the same practice from Umar, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, and Ibn al-Zubayr. RAZI-FULL (علي بن أبي طالب): Razi says Ali’s loud recitation is established by mass transmission; he cites the report asking God to keep truth with Ali wherever he turns. RAZI-FULL (أبو حامد الإسفراييني): Abu Hamid al-Isfarayini groups six Anas reports: three support the Hanafi position by omitting the basmala, while three contrary reports recount the protest against Muawiya, loud recitation, or Anas’s uncertainty. RAZI-FULL (الشعبي): Al-Shafi‘i later answers the Umar report by citing al-Sha‘bi that Umar repeated the prayer, or by suggesting he omitted aloud recitation rather than recitation itself. QURTUBI (عبادة بن الصامت): ʿUbāda reports that the Prophet prohibited followers from reciting aloud except al-Fātiḥa; al-Tirmidhī grades it ḥasan. QURTUBI (عمر بن الخطاب): Al-Dāraquṭnī authenticates the report that ʿUmar ordered recitation behind an imam, even when ʿUmar recited aloud. NASAFI (قراء مكة والكوفة والشافعي وأصحابه): Meccan and Kufan reciters and al-Shafi‘i’s school count the basmala as a verse of the Fatiha and every sura, and recite it aloud; they argue the early Muslims wrote it in the Qur’an despite orders to exclude non-Qur’anic material. NASAFI-FULL (author): Meccan and Kufan readers, with al-Shafi'i and his companions, count it as a verse of al-Fatiha and every surah and recite it aloud; they cite its inclusion in the early codices despite the instruction to exclude non-Qur'anic material. IBNKATHIR (الشافعي): Al-Shafiʿi recites the basmala aloud with both Fatiha and the following surah when opening prayer; many early and later authorities also did so. IBNKATHIR (أبو هريرة): Abu Hurayra recited the basmala aloud and said his prayer most resembled the Prophet's; Ibn Kathir cites several scholars who authenticated the report. DURR (سعيد بن جبير): Sa'id ibn Jubayr says the Prophet first recited the basmala aloud in Mecca, then concealed it after Meccans linked al-Rahman to Musaylima. DURR (عبد الله بن مغفل): Ibn Abd Allah ibn Maghfal says his father objected to his reciting aloud, having heard none of the first caliphs do so behind the Prophet. DURR (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas calls loud recitation of the basmala Bedouin-style recitation. DURR (إبراهيم): Ibrahim calls an imam's loud recitation of the basmala an innovation. DURR (النبي): Abu Hurayra reports Gabriel taught the Prophet prayer and he recited the basmala aloud in every rak'a. DURR (العَبَادِلَة): A report says Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, and Ibn al-Zubayr began recitation aloud with the basmala. DURR (النبي): Reports from Ali, Ammar, Ibn Umar, Abu Hurayra, Anas, al-Nu'man, Hakam, and Aisha attest that the Prophet recited the basmala aloud in prayer. DURR (أبو هريرة): Abu Hurayra reports the Prophet recited the basmala aloud during prayer. DURR (أنس): Anas reports the Prophet recited the basmala aloud. DURR (علي): Ali reports the Prophet recited the basmala aloud in both suras. DURR (ابن عمر): Ibn Umar says the Prophet, Abu Bakr, and Umar recited the basmala aloud. DURR (النعمان بن بشير): Al-Nu'man ibn Bashir says Gabriel led the Prophet at the Kaaba and recited the basmala aloud. DURR (الحكم بن عمير): Hakam ibn Umayr says the Prophet recited the basmala aloud in night, dawn, and Friday prayers. DURR (عائشة): Aisha reports the Prophet recited the basmala aloud. DURR-FULL (أبو هريرة): Abu Hurayra reports that the Prophet taught prayer and recited the basmala aloud in every rakah. DURR-FULL (أبو هريرة): A report says Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, and Ibn al-Zubayr began recitation aloud with the basmala. DURR-FULL (علي وعمار): Ali and Ammar say the Prophet recited the basmala aloud in obligatory prayers at the opening of al-Fatiha. DURR-FULL (أبو هريرة): Abu Hurayra says the Prophet recited the basmala aloud in prayer. DURR-FULL (علي): Ali reports that the Prophet recited the basmala aloud in both surahs. DURR-FULL (ابن عمر): Ibn Umar says the Prophet, Abu Bakr, and Umar recited the basmala aloud. DURR-FULL (النعمان بن بشير): Al-Numan ibn Bashir says Gabriel led the Prophet in prayer at the Kaaba and recited the basmala aloud. DURR-FULL (الحكم بن عمير): Al-Hakam ibn Umayr says the Prophet recited the basmala aloud in night, dawn, and Friday prayers. DURR-FULL (عائشة): Aisha reports that the Prophet recited the basmala aloud. DURR-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas calls aloud recitation of the basmala the Bedouin style of recitation. DURR-FULL (إبراهيم): Ibrahim says an imam's aloud recitation of the basmala is an innovation. ALUSI (عبد الله بن المغفل): Ibn al-Mughafal recounts his father’s objection to audible basmala, saying the Prophet and first caliphs began aloud with al-Ḥamd; al-Ālūsī infers they concealed the basmala. ALUSI (author): Al-Ālūsī says the explicit sound evidence for audible recitation is limited; reports of occasional loud recitation can demonstrate that it is read without making it habitual. ALUSI-FULL (الفخر الرازي): Razi cites the report that companions challenged Mu'awiya for omitting the basmala in a public prayer and he repeated it aloud. ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi says only Ibn Abbas's report explicitly supports loud recitation; it conflicts with earlier reports or may describe occasional public demonstration that the basmala is recited. ALUSI-FULL (الفخر الرازي): Razi's second argument says the basmala is praise and glorification and therefore should be spoken aloud, citing the command to remember God intensely. | mentions 2:200 ALUSI-FULL (الفخر الرازي): Razi's fifth proof cites a Bayhaqi report of the Prophet reciting the basmala aloud, also attributed to Umar, his son, Ibn Abbas, Ibn al-Zubayr, and Ali, and says following Ali is guidance.

positions.position: The basmala is recited silently in prayer.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Shafi'i says the basmala is a verse of al-Fatiha and must be read; Malik and al-Awza'i exclude it except in the Quran's Naml passage, with a Ramadan-night exception, while Abu Hanifa orders quiet recitation without stating its status. | mentions 27:30 RAZI-FULL (أحمد بن حنبل): Ahmad ibn Hanbal is reported to count the basmala as a verse of al-Fatiha while reciting it quietly in every rak‘a; al-Shafi‘i counts it and recites aloud, while Abu Hanifa does not count it but reads it quietly. RAZI-FULL (أبو حنيفة): For those who do not count the basmala as a verse of al-Fatiha, Abu Hanifa and several other jurists require it quietly; Malik forbids it in obligatory prayer but permits a choice in voluntary prayer. QURTUBI (حمزة): Readers pronounce seeking refuge aloud at al-Fātiḥa’s start except Ḥamza, who recites it quietly. QURTUBI (أبو هريرة الفارسي): Abū Ḥātim says the imam-responsibility report supports reading behind an imam; Abū Hurayra al-Fārisī advised quiet recitation. QURTUBI (author): Qurṭubī reads “Why do I hear the Qurʾān contested?” as forbidding loud competing recitation, not silent reading. QURTUBI (أبو حنيفة والثوري): Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Thawrī, Aḥmad, and others recite the basmala quietly with al-Fātiḥa. QURTUBI (أنس بن مالك): Anas reports not hearing the Prophet recite the basmala aloud; Qurṭubī prefers quiet recitation to reconcile the reports. IBNKATHIR (مالك): Malik does not recite the basmala in prayer either aloud or quietly, relying on reports that the Prophet and first caliphs began with al-Hamd and did not mention it. IBNKATHIR (author): The legal disagreement is narrow: scholars agree a prayer is valid whether the basmala is recited aloud or quietly. DURR (أنس): Anas says the Prophet, Abu Bakr, and Umar recited the basmala quietly. DURR (أبو هريرة): Abu Hurayra says prayer without Umm al-Kitab is incomplete, repeats the warning three times, and tells followers to recite quietly behind the imam. DURR (الزهري): Al-Zuhri calls reciting the basmala part of prayer's sunna and says Amr ibn Sa'id first recited it silently in Medina out of shyness. DURR-FULL (الزهري): Al-Zuhri calls reciting the basmala part of prayer's sunnah and says Amr ibn Said ibn al-As was the first in Medina to recite it quietly, out of modesty. DURR-FULL (أنس): Anas reports that the Prophet, Abu Bakr, and Umar recited the basmala quietly. ALUSI (أنس): Anas reports that he heard no basmala from the Prophet, Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, or ʿUthmān; al-Ālūsī takes this as silent recitation, not omission. ALUSI (author): Al-Ālūsī lists many authorities for silent basmala recitation, including Sufyān, Ibn al-Mubārak, Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn al-Zubayr, Mujāhid, and Aḥmad. ALUSI-FULL (أنس): Anas reports that he did not hear the Prophet, Abu Bakr, Umar, or Uthman reciting the basmala aloud; Alusi says this does not deny quiet recitation. ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi says concealing the basmala in aloud prayers does not make it merely recommended; the Prophet and early caliphs recited it quietly. ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi reports that a father rebuked his son for reciting the basmala aloud, saying the Prophet and first caliphs began aloud with al-Hamdu lillah; Alusi understands the formula to have been recited quietly. ALUSI-FULL (الفخر الرازي): Razi's first proof of loud recitation is that a basmala belonging to the sura should share its public or quiet recitation; Alusi answers that it is not part of the sura and parts may differ in volume regardless. ALUSI-FULL (author): The silent sin reached through an alif suggests the emergence of what was absent through God; depending on its symbolism, the basmala signals universal mercy or Muhammad’s universal mission. | mentions 7:156, 25:1, 21:107 ELMALILI (Hanefîler): In prayer before al-Fatiha, Hanafis recommend silently reciting isti'adha and basmala. ELMALILI (Şâfiiyye): Shafi'is require basmala in prayer, either silently or aloud. ELMALILI (author): Ḥanafīs say it at the start of each prayer unit’s recitation, not in the middle, and recite it silently even in audible prayers so it will not appear part of the surah. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (Ebû Hanîfe): Because basmalas are separate opening verses, Abu Hanifa says to recite one silently before Fatiha in prayer, but not before the additional surah or verses after it.

positions.position: Another report says Meccan polytheists mocked the basmala because Musaylima called himself al-Rahman, after which the Prophet was ordered not to recite it aloud.
positions.reasons: DURR (ابن عباس): Another report says Meccan polytheists mocked the basmala because Musaylima called himself al-Rahman, after which the Prophet was ordered not to recite it aloud. DURR-FULL (سعيد بن جبير): A mursal report says Meccans mocked the Prophet's aloud basmala by associating al-Rahman with Musaylima, so he ordered it concealed and did not recite it aloud again. DURR-FULL (ابن عباس): A report from Ibn Abbas says the polytheists mocked the basmala because Musaylima called himself al-Rahman, after which the Prophet was ordered not to recite it aloud.

positions.position: Abu Hanifa and his followers share that position and therefore do not recite it aloud in prayer.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF (أبو حنيفة ومن تابعه): Abu Hanifa and his followers share that position and therefore do not recite it aloud in prayer. KASHSHAF-FULL (أبو حنيفة رحمه الله ومن تابعه): Abu Hanifa shares the view that the basmala is not a verse, and his followers accordingly do not recite it aloud in prayer.
