positions.position: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that the Prophet did not recite the basmala aloud; al-Ālūsī reconciles this with occasional audible recitation for instruction.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās reports that the Prophet did not recite the basmala aloud; al-Ālūsī reconciles this with occasional audible recitation for instruction. ALUSI-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas reports that the Prophet did not recite the basmala aloud before his death.

positions.position: In this account, the voice tells the Prophet to recite the basmala and the opening of al-Fātiḥa through its final words, then affirm God’s oneness.
positions.reasons: THALABI (author): In this account, the voice tells the Prophet to recite the basmala and the opening of al-Fātiḥa through its final words, then affirm God’s oneness. | mentions 1:1, 1:7

positions.position: A report says the four ʿAbādila opened recitation with the basmala and voiced it.
positions.reasons: THALABI (عبد الله بن عباس، عبد الله بن عمر، عبد الله بن الزبير، عبد الله بن صفوان): A report says the four ʿAbādila opened recitation with the basmala and voiced it.

positions.position: Al-Ṣādiq calls audible recitation the truth and links it to the verse about people turning away when God alone is mentioned in the Qurʾān.
positions.reasons: THALABI (جعفر بن محمد الصادق): Al-Ṣādiq calls audible recitation the truth and links it to the verse about people turning away when God alone is mentioned in the Qurʾān. | mentions 17:46

positions.position: Anas reports that he did not hear the Prophet, Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, or ʿUthmān recite the basmala aloud.
positions.reasons: THALABI (أنس بن مالك): Anas reports that he did not hear the Prophet, Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, or ʿUthmān recite the basmala aloud.

positions.position: The author says Anas’s report only denies raising the voice; it does not deny that the basmala is part of the sura, and “not aloud” need not mean whispering or omitting it.
positions.reasons: THALABI (author): The author says Anas’s report only denies raising the voice; it does not deny that the basmala is part of the sura, and “not aloud” need not mean whispering or omitting it.

positions.position: Abū Ḥanīfa holds that the basmala should not be recited aloud.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (أبو حنيفة): Abū Ḥanīfa holds that the basmala should not be recited aloud.

positions.position: They hold that the basmala is not a Qur'anic verse, but was written to separate surahs and for blessing; they therefore do not recite it aloud in prayer.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL (قراء المدينة والبصرة والشام وفقهاؤها): They hold that the basmala is not a Qur'anic verse, but was written to separate surahs and for blessing; they therefore do not recite it aloud in prayer.

positions.position: The opposing jurists argue that the early community included the basmala in the codex while excluding Amin, so it must be Qur'an.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL (author): The opposing jurists argue that the early community included the basmala in the codex while excluding Amin, so it must be Qur'an.

positions.position: Aḥmad and the listed Companions and early authorities do not regard reciting the basmala aloud in audible prayers as recommended.
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD (أحمد ومن وافقه): Aḥmad and the listed Companions and early authorities do not regard reciting the basmala aloud in audible prayers as recommended.

positions.position: Because the basmala praises and glorifies God, making its remembrance public is fitting; the Qur’an commands abundant remembrance, as one would publicly honor a beloved father.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Because the basmala praises and glorifies God, making its remembrance public is fitting; the Qur’an commands abundant remembrance, as one would publicly honor a beloved father. | mentions 2:200

positions.position: Open remembrance publicly shows pride in honoring God and indifference to objection; reason commends that, supported by the reported maxim about what Muslims deem good.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Open remembrance publicly shows pride in honoring God and indifference to objection; reason commends that, supported by the reported maxim about what Muslims deem good.

positions.position: Anas reports that the Prophet, Abu Bakr, Umar, and Uthman began prayer with al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin; Muslim versions say they did not mention, or were not heard saying, the basmala aloud.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أنس): Anas reports that the Prophet, Abu Bakr, Umar, and Uthman began prayer with al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin; Muslim versions say they did not mention, or were not heard saying, the basmala aloud.

positions.position: Ibn al-Mughaffal says his father warned him against introducing the basmala, recalling that the Prophet and first three caliphs began with al-hamdu lillah.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (عبد الله بن المغفل): Ibn al-Mughaffal says his father warned him against introducing the basmala, recalling that the Prophet and first three caliphs began with al-hamdu lillah.

positions.position: Opponents cite Qur’anic commands to invoke God humbly and remember Him inwardly as proof that the basmala should be quiet; jurists infer this from the verses and earlier reports.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (المخالف): Opponents cite Qur’anic commands to invoke God humbly and remember Him inwardly as proof that the basmala should be quiet; jurists infer this from the verses and earlier reports. | mentions 7:55, 7:205

positions.position: Conflicting and unstable Anas reports leave the evidence balanced; possible Umayyad pressure against Ali’s practice may explain Anas’s hesitation, and Ali’s lifelong practice should prevail.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Conflicting and unstable Anas reports leave the evidence balanced; possible Umayyad pressure against Ali’s practice may explain Anas’s hesitation, and Ali’s lifelong practice should prevail.

positions.position: If reports conflict, Razi prefers Ali, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, and Abu Hurayra over Anas and Ibn al-Mughaffal because they were more knowledgeable and closer to the Prophet.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): If reports conflict, Razi prefers Ali, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, and Abu Hurayra over Anas and Ibn al-Mughaffal because they were more knowledgeable and closer to the Prophet.

positions.position: Razi invokes Abu Hanifa’s refusal of solitary reports that oppose analogy: the evident rational case favors openly reciting a phrase that honors God.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi invokes Abu Hanifa’s refusal of solitary reports that oppose analogy: the evident rational case favors openly reciting a phrase that honors God.

positions.position: Ali, Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Umar were more learned and eminent than Anas and Ibn al-Mughaffal; their likely proximity, the Prophet’s moderate voice, and gradual increase in volume explain who heard the basmala.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Ali, Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Umar were more learned and eminent than Anas and Ibn al-Mughaffal; their likely proximity, the Prophet’s moderate voice, and gradual increase in volume explain who heard the basmala. | mentions 17:110

positions.position: Al-Shafi‘i interprets Anas’s phrase that the Prophet began with al-hamdu lillah as saying al-Fatiha, named by its opening, came before other suras.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الشافعي): Al-Shafi‘i interprets Anas’s phrase that the Prophet began with al-hamdu lillah as saying al-Fatiha, named by its opening, came before other suras.

positions.position: Ibn al-Mughaffal’s denial of loud recitation can mean only that the Prophet did not raise his voice excessively, as instructed by the Qur’an; an affirmative report outweighs a negative one.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Ibn al-Mughaffal’s denial of loud recitation can mean only that the Prophet did not raise his voice excessively, as instructed by the Qur’an; an affirmative report outweighs a negative one. | mentions 17:110

positions.position: The Shi‘a hold that the basmala should be recited aloud in both loud and quiet prayers; most jurists disagree.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الشيعة): The Shi‘a hold that the basmala should be recited aloud in both loud and quiet prayers; most jurists disagree.

positions.position: Al-Daraqutni transmits the Prophet telling followers not to recite when he reads aloud except Umm al-Qur’an, because prayer is invalid without it.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (عبادة بن الصامت): Al-Daraqutni transmits the Prophet telling followers not to recite when he reads aloud except Umm al-Qur’an, because prayer is invalid without it.

positions.position: Many reports promise great reward for Qur’an recitation and apply to followers, so reciting behind the imam earns reward; Razi says those accepting that reward must accept obligation.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Many reports promise great reward for Qur’an recitation and apply to followers, so reciting behind the imam earns reward; Razi says those accepting that reward must accept obligation.

positions.position: Because Abu Hanifa agrees recitation behind the imam does not invalidate prayer while Shafi‘i holds omission invalidates it, reciting is the safer course.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Because Abu Hanifa agrees recitation behind the imam does not invalidate prayer while Shafi‘i holds omission invalidates it, reciting is the safer course.

positions.position: A follower unable to hear the imam would otherwise remain idle; since Qur’an recitation is the best deed, the reciter’s state is superior and therefore obligatory.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A follower unable to hear the imam would otherwise remain idle; since Qur’an recitation is the best deed, the reciter’s state is superior and therefore obligatory.

positions.position: If congregational following prevented recitation, following would unlawfully block a great act of worship; since following is permitted, it cannot prevent reading.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): If congregational following prevented recitation, following would unlawfully block a great act of worship; since following is permitted, it cannot prevent reading.

positions.position: Abu Hanifa argues from the command to listen and be quiet when Qur’an is recited; Razi says his exegesis of that verse defeats the argument, and al-Bayhaqi weakened the cited reports.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أبو حنيفة): Abu Hanifa argues from the command to listen and be quiet when Qur’an is recited; Razi says his exegesis of that verse defeats the argument, and al-Bayhaqi weakened the cited reports. | mentions 7:204

positions.position: Even assuming the opposing reports sound, Razi prefers recitation because it occupies prayer with worship, is safer, and avoids leaving time empty of remembrance.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Even assuming the opposing reports sound, Razi prefers recitation because it occupies prayer with worship, is safer, and avoids leaving time empty of remembrance.

positions.position: Aisha reports prayer was originally two rak‘as, retained while traveling and expanded at home; opponents infer that only the first two rak‘as are original and later ones allow lighter requirements.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (عائشة): Aisha reports prayer was originally two rak‘as, retained while traveling and expanded at home; opponents infer that only the first two rak‘as are original and later ones allow lighter requirements.

positions.position: Razi answers that his proofs are more numerous and stronger, and his position is more cautious.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi answers that his proofs are more numerous and stronger, and his position is more cautious.

positions.position: Al-Dāraquṭnī calls ʿUbāda’s report ḥasan and its narrators reliable; ʿAbd al-Ḥaqq notes Nafiʿ ibn Maḥmūd’s obscurity.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (الدارقطني): Al-Dāraquṭnī calls ʿUbāda’s report ḥasan and its narrators reliable; ʿAbd al-Ḥaqq notes Nafiʿ ibn Maḥmūd’s obscurity.

positions.position: Al-Dāraquṭnī says “when he recites, listen” is unpreserved because Sulaymān al-Taymī alone transmits it against Qatāda’s stronger students.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (أبو موسى الأشعري): Al-Dāraquṭnī says “when he recites, listen” is unpreserved because Sulaymān al-Taymī alone transmits it against Qatāda’s stronger students.

positions.position: The report that an imam’s recitation counts for the follower is weak; al-Dāraquṭnī says its sound form is mursal.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (الحسن بن عمارة وأبو حنيفة): The report that an imam’s recitation counts for the follower is weak; al-Dāraquṭnī says its sound form is mursal.

positions.position: Abū Saʿīd says worshippers were ordered to recite al-Fātiḥa and whatever else was easy, so the latter means extra recitation.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (أبو سعيد الخدري): Abū Saʿīd says worshippers were ordered to recite al-Fātiḥa and whatever else was easy, so the latter means extra recitation. | mentions 73:20

positions.position: Aḥmad, Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd, and Ibn Maʿīn trust ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd ibn Jaʿfar; Abū Ḥātim calls him truthful, while al-Thawrī criticizes him.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (عبد الحميد بن جعفر): Aḥmad, Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd, and Ibn Maʿīn trust ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd ibn Jaʿfar; Abū Ḥātim calls him truthful, while al-Thawrī criticizes him.

positions.position: Qurṭubī argues generations at the Prophet’s Medina mosque through Mālik’s era did not recite the basmala.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (author): Qurṭubī argues generations at the Prophet’s Medina mosque through Mālik’s era did not recite the basmala.

positions.position: Qurṭubī says the basmala dispute is interpretive, not a basis for declaring Muslims unbelievers.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (author): Qurṭubī says the basmala dispute is interpretive, not a basis for declaring Muslims unbelievers.

positions.position: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr links quiet basmala recitation to Musaylima’s claim to al-Raḥmān; the practice persisted after its cause passed.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (سعيد بن جبير): Saʿīd ibn Jubayr links quiet basmala recitation to Musaylima’s claim to al-Raḥmān; the practice persisted after its cause passed. | mentions 17:110

positions.position: The Prophet promises protection to anyone who says God’s complete words when stopping somewhere; al-Tirmidhī grades it ḥasan gharīb ṣaḥīḥ.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (خولة بنت حكيم): The Prophet promises protection to anyone who says God’s complete words when stopping somewhere; al-Tirmidhī grades it ḥasan gharīb ṣaḥīḥ.

positions.position: Abū Maysara’s account says a voice taught the Prophet al-Fātiḥa and declared him a prophet; al-Bayhaqī calls the report disconnected.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (أبو ميسرة عمرو بن شرحبيل): Abū Maysara’s account says a voice taught the Prophet al-Fātiḥa and declared him a prophet; al-Bayhaqī calls the report disconnected.

positions.position: By consensus, an imam’s recitation covers a latecomer who catches him bowing; one who catches him standing recites.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (العلماء): By consensus, an imam’s recitation covers a latecomer who catches him bowing; one who catches him standing recites.

positions.position: In quiet prayer, Mālik’s school says one should not omit recitation behind the imam; omission is improper but does not invalidate prayer.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (مالك وأصحابه): In quiet prayer, Mālik’s school says one should not omit recitation behind the imam; omission is improper but does not invalidate prayer.

positions.position: Ibn Wahb, Ashhab, Ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥakam, Ibn Ḥabīb, and Kūfans say the follower recites nothing, relying on the imam’s recitation counting for him.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (ابن وهب وأشهب وابن عبد الحكم وابن حبيب): Ibn Wahb, Ashhab, Ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥakam, Ibn Ḥabīb, and Kūfans say the follower recites nothing, relying on the imam’s recitation counting for him.

positions.position: Medinan, Basran, and Syrian reciters and jurists, including Abu Hanifa and his followers, hold that the basmala is no verse of any sura, but is written to separate suras and for blessing; they therefore do not recite it aloud in
positions.reasons: NASAFI (قراء المدينة والبصرة والشام وفقهاؤها): Medinan, Basran, and Syrian reciters and jurists, including Abu Hanifa and his followers, hold that the basmala is no verse of any sura, but is written to separate suras and for blessing; they therefore do not recite it aloud in prayer.

positions.position: Medina, Basra, and Syria's readers and jurists, with Abu Hanifa, hold that the basmala is not a verse of al-Fatiha or other surahs; it separates surahs and is blessed at the opening, so they do not recite it aloud.
positions.reasons: NASAFI-FULL (author): Medina, Basra, and Syria's readers and jurists, with Abu Hanifa, hold that the basmala is not a verse of al-Fatiha or other surahs; it separates surahs and is blessed at the opening, so they do not recite it aloud.

positions.position: Anas describes the Prophet's recitation as prolonged, with lengthening on each word of the basmala.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (أنس بن مالك): Anas describes the Prophet's recitation as prolonged, with lengthening on each word of the basmala.

positions.position: Another group does not recite the basmala aloud; Ibn Kathir says this is established from the four caliphs, Ibn Mughaffal, and other early authorities.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (أبو حنيفة والثوري وأحمد): Another group does not recite the basmala aloud; Ibn Kathir says this is established from the four caliphs, Ibn Mughaffal, and other early authorities.

positions.position: An account through Abū Isḥāq from Abū Maysara says al-Fātiḥa was the first revelation; it describes the Prophet hearing a voice, fleeing, and then the angel's descent and the opening of the sūra.
positions.reasons: BURHAN (أبو ميسرة): An account through Abū Isḥāq from Abū Maysara says al-Fātiḥa was the first revelation; it describes the Prophet hearing a voice, fleeing, and then the angel's descent and the opening of the sūra. | mentions 96:1

positions.position: Al-Qāḍī Abū Bakr calls the report that al-Fātiḥa came first disconnected.
positions.reasons: BURHAN (القاضي أبو بكر): Al-Qāḍī Abū Bakr calls the report that al-Fātiḥa came first disconnected.

positions.position: The views can be reconciled: اقرأ was the first verses, المدثر the first preaching commands, and al-Fātiḥa the first complete sūra revealed.
positions.reasons: BURHAN (القاضي أبو بكر): The views can be reconciled: اقرأ was the first verses, المدثر the first preaching commands, and al-Fātiḥa the first complete sūra revealed. | mentions 74:1, 1:1

positions.position: A report says the mountains roared when the basmala descended; the Prophet said mountains praise with a sincere reciter, though people cannot hear it.
positions.reasons: DURR (عائشة): A report says the mountains roared when the basmala descended; the Prophet said mountains praise with a sincere reciter, though people cannot hear it.

positions.position: Ali says a man who carefully embellished the basmala was forgiven.
positions.reasons: DURR (علي): Ali says a man who carefully embellished the basmala was forgiven.

positions.position: Al-Zuhri attributes to the Prophet a prohibition on elongating the basmala.
positions.reasons: DURR (الزهري): Al-Zuhri attributes to the Prophet a prohibition on elongating the basmala.

positions.position: A mursal report says the Prophet forbade putting the basmala on the ground and said it belongs only in its proper place.
positions.reasons: DURR (النبي): A mursal report says the Prophet forbade putting the basmala on the ground and said it belongs only in its proper place.

positions.position: A report from Anas promises that respectfully lifting paper bearing the basmala earns the rank of the truthful and eases his parents' burden, even if unbelievers.
positions.reasons: DURR (النبي): A report from Anas promises that respectfully lifting paper bearing the basmala earns the rank of the truthful and eases his parents' burden, even if unbelievers.

positions.position: Umm Khalid bint Khalid ibn Sa'id claims she was the first to write the basmala.
positions.reasons: DURR (أم خالد بن خالد): Umm Khalid bint Khalid ibn Sa'id claims she was the first to write the basmala.

positions.position: A report says Quraysh mocked the Prophet in Mecca when he pronounced the basmala.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (ابن عباس): A report says Quraysh mocked the Prophet in Mecca when he pronounced the basmala.

positions.position: The report continues that Meccans said Muhammad called on the Yamama deity and that the Prophet then concealed the basmala until his death.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (سعيد بن جبير): The report continues that Meccans said Muhammad called on the Yamama deity and that the Prophet then concealed the basmala until his death.

positions.position: Ibn Mughaffal called his son's aloud basmala a new practice and said he never heard the Prophet, Abu Bakr, Umar, or Uthman recite it aloud.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (عبد الله بن مغفل): Ibn Mughaffal called his son's aloud basmala a new practice and said he never heard the Prophet, Abu Bakr, Umar, or Uthman recite it aloud.

positions.position: Abū Bakr al-Tūnisī transmits a consensus that God opened every revealed book with the basmala; another report calls it the opening of every book.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (أبو بكر التونسي): Abū Bakr al-Tūnisī transmits a consensus that God opened every revealed book with the basmala; another report calls it the opening of every book.

positions.position: Al-Suyūṭī, citing al-Sarmīnī, reports “the basmala is the opening of every book”; al-Ālūsī cautions that the transmission is the reporter’s responsibility.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (السيوطي عن السرميني): Al-Suyūṭī, citing al-Sarmīnī, reports “the basmala is the opening of every book”; al-Ālūsī cautions that the transmission is the reporter’s responsibility.

positions.position: The Medinese, Mālik, al-Awzāʿī, Abū ʿAmr, and Yaʿqūb hold it is a separate verse revealed to mark sūra openings; al-Ālūsī calls this the common Hanafi doctrine.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (أهل المدينة ومالك والأوزاعي وأبو عمرو ويعقوب): The Medinese, Mālik, al-Awzāʿī, Abū ʿAmr, and Yaʿqūb hold it is a separate verse revealed to mark sūra openings; al-Ālūsī calls this the common Hanafi doctrine.

positions.position: Al-Dāraquṭnī reportedly concluded, when pressed to identify sound evidence for audible basmala, that no report on the matter is sound.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (الدارقطني): Al-Dāraquṭnī reportedly concluded, when pressed to identify sound evidence for audible basmala, that no report on the matter is sound.

positions.position: Another version says Mu'awiya omitted the takbir at bowing and prostration too, so repeating the prayer does not prove basmala membership in the Fatiha; whether he recited aloud remains unclear.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Another version says Mu'awiya omitted the takbir at bowing and prostration too, so repeating the prayer does not prove basmala membership in the Fatiha; whether he recited aloud remains unclear.

positions.position: Razi's third argument says loud remembrance publicly shows pride in God and disregard for those who object, and calls this proof firmly convincing to him.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (الفخر الرازي): Razi's third argument says loud remembrance publicly shows pride in God and disregard for those who object, and calls this proof firmly convincing to him.

positions.position: Some hadith specialists say every explicit report of loud basmala recitation has a flaw in its chain; al-Daraqutni reportedly said no sound report establishes it.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Some hadith specialists say every explicit report of loud basmala recitation has a flaw in its chain; al-Daraqutni reportedly said no sound report establishes it.

positions.position: Alusi rejects the claim that Anas's conflicting versions arose from Umayyad hostility to Ali: the strongest chain favors silence, and accusing its transmitters of lying is less plausible than accusing Anas and the Companions.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi rejects the claim that Anas's conflicting versions arose from Umayyad hostility to Ali: the strongest chain favors silence, and accusing its transmitters of lying is less plausible than accusing Anas and the Companions.

positions.position: He calls al-Razi's suggestion of political intimidation strange, asking why the Medinan Companions would publicly accuse Mu'awiya if they feared him.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): He calls al-Razi's suggestion of political intimidation strange, asking why the Medinan Companions would publicly accuse Mu'awiya if they feared him.

positions.position: Alusi replies that most prayer phrases also praise and glorify God, so this argument would absurdly require reciting all of them aloud.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi replies that most prayer phrases also praise and glorify God, so this argument would absurdly require reciting all of them aloud.

positions.position: Alusi says this does not explain why other glorifications in bowing and prostration should be hidden; he cites poetry on the hidden Night of Decree and concealed nobles to show hiddenness is no disgrace.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi says this does not explain why other glorifications in bowing and prostration should be hidden; he cites poetry on the hidden Night of Decree and concealed nobles to show hiddenness is no disgrace.

positions.position: Alusi says this report is countered by the reports of silent recitation, or the Companions may have inferred omission from other signs without hearing the prayer.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi says this report is countered by the reports of silent recitation, or the Companions may have inferred omission from other signs without hearing the prayer.

positions.position: Alusi says these reports are contradicted, and any loud recitation could have been occasional for teaching; he denies Sunni recognition of tawatur from Ali and criticizes Shi'i claims that all their attributions are mutawatir.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi says these reports are contradicted, and any loud recitation could have been occasional for teaching; he denies Sunni recognition of tawatur from Ali and criticizes Shi'i claims that all their attributions are mutawatir.

positions.position: Alusi says Sunni practice ordinarily follows the two senior caliphs and cites reports successively urging the Companions, the rightly guided caliphs, then Abu Bakr and Umar as guides.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi says Sunni practice ordinarily follows the two senior caliphs and cites reports successively urging the Companions, the rightly guided caliphs, then Abu Bakr and Umar as guides.

positions.position: There is no basmala at Bara'a's opening; in the Asim reading, reciting it between two surahs is recommended, and starting midway or at the end also recommends isti'adha and basmala.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): There is no basmala at Bara'a's opening; in the Asim reading, reciting it between two surahs is recommended, and starting midway or at the end also recommends isti'adha and basmala.

positions.position: On this view the basmala is al-Fātiḥa’s first verse, while anʿamta ʿalayhim is not a verse ending, so they recite the basmala aloud in prayer.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): On this view the basmala is al-Fātiḥa’s first verse, while anʿamta ʿalayhim is not a verse ending, so they recite the basmala aloud in prayer.

positions.position: The author calls continuous Medinan mosque practice decisive: the Prophet, caliphs, Companions, and scholars did not recite the basmala aloud in public prayers, a practice he considers mass-transmitted.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (أهل المدينة): The author calls continuous Medinan mosque practice decisive: the Prophet, caliphs, Companions, and scholars did not recite the basmala aloud in public prayers, a practice he considers mass-transmitted.

turns_on: The transmitted prayer practice and the strength and interpretation of its reports.

question: Must the basmala be recited in prayer?

positions.position: In a report from Jabir, the Prophet instructs him to begin the prayer with the basmala.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (رسول الله): In a report from Jabir, the Prophet instructs him to begin the prayer with the basmala. DURR (النبي): Jabir says the Prophet likewise instructed him to say the basmala when beginning prayer. DURR-FULL (جابر): The Prophet similarly instructed Jabir to say the basmala when beginning prayer. ALUSI-FULL (النبي): A report from Jabir says the Prophet instructed him to say the basmala when beginning prayer.

positions.position: Ibn Umar recited the basmala in prayer at a sura's end and said it was written in the codex to be recited.
positions.reasons: DURR (ابن عمر): Ibn Umar recited the basmala in prayer at a sura's end and said it was written in the codex to be recited. DURR-FULL (ابن عمر): Ibn Umar recited the basmala in prayer at a surah's end, saying it was written in the codex to be recited.

positions.position: Ibn Abbas reports that the Prophet began prayer with the basmala.
positions.reasons: DURR (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas reports that the Prophet began prayer with the basmala. DURR-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas reports that the Prophet began prayer with the basmala.

positions.position: Abū Ḥanīfa holds that the basmala is recited once, in the first rakʿa.
positions.reasons: JISHUMI (أبو حنيفة): Abū Ḥanīfa holds that the basmala is recited once, in the first rakʿa. JISHUMI (أبو يوسف): Abū Yūsuf holds that the basmala is recited in every rakʿa.

positions.position: In a report from Jābir, the Prophet tells him to say the basmala when beginning prayer after Jābir says al-ḥamdu lillāh.
positions.reasons: THALABI (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): In a report from Jābir, the Prophet tells him to say the basmala when beginning prayer after Jābir says al-ḥamdu lillāh.

positions.position: When Muʿāwiya omitted the basmala while leading prayer in Medina, the Emigrants and Helpers called out that he had forgotten it, so he repeated the prayer with it.
positions.reasons: THALABI (المهاجرون والأنصار): When Muʿāwiya omitted the basmala while leading prayer in Medina, the Emigrants and Helpers called out that he had forgotten it, so he repeated the prayer with it.

positions.position: Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq says the Prophet’s family agreed on voicing the basmala, making up missed night prayer in daytime, and speaking well of Abū Bakr and ʿUmar and their companion.
positions.reasons: THALABI (جعفر بن محمد): Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq says the Prophet’s family agreed on voicing the basmala, making up missed night prayer in daytime, and speaking well of Abū Bakr and ʿUmar and their companion.

positions.position: Abū Hurayra reports that Gabriel taught the Prophet prayer, after which the Prophet stood, said takbīr, and voiced the basmala.
positions.reasons: THALABI (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): Abū Hurayra reports that Gabriel taught the Prophet prayer, after which the Prophet stood, said takbīr, and voiced the basmala.

positions.position: Jabir says that when he told the Prophet he opened prayer with al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin, the Prophet told him to say the basmala.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (جابر بن عبد الله عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): Jabir says that when he told the Prophet he opened prayer with al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin, the Prophet told him to say the basmala.

positions.position: The sound hadith qudsi describing prayer as divided between God and the servant quotes the servant beginning with al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin, not the basmala.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (الله تعالى في الحديث القدسي): The sound hadith qudsi describing prayer as divided between God and the servant quotes the servant beginning with al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin, not the basmala.

positions.position: No record says the Prophet or Abu Bakr, Umar or Uthman recited the basmala in prayer.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (author): No record says the Prophet or Abu Bakr, Umar or Uthman recited the basmala in prayer.

positions.position: The sound hadith describing prayer as divided between God and the servant begins its quoted recitation with praise, not the basmala.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): The sound hadith describing prayer as divided between God and the servant begins its quoted recitation with praise, not the basmala.

positions.position: No basmala recitation in prayer is preserved from the Prophet or the first three caliphs.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): No basmala recitation in prayer is preserved from the Prophet or the first three caliphs.

positions.position: The Prophet's saying that an important matter begun without God's name is cut off implies that prayer, the greatest act after faith, is gravely deficient without the basmala; such acknowledged deficiency entails invalidity.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The Prophet's saying that an important matter begun without God's name is cut off implies that prayer, the greatest act after faith, is gravely deficient without the basmala; such acknowledged deficiency entails invalidity.

positions.position: Al-Shafi‘i reports that when Muawiya omitted the basmala and bowing and prostration takbirs in Medina, the Emigrants and Helpers protested and he repeated prayer with them.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الشافعي): Al-Shafi‘i reports that when Muawiya omitted the basmala and bowing and prostration takbirs in Medina, the Emigrants and Helpers protested and he repeated prayer with them.

positions.position: Another report from Mālik says to begin every obligatory and voluntary prayer with the basmala.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (ابن نافع): Another report from Mālik says to begin every obligatory and voluntary prayer with the basmala.

positions.position: Ibn ʿAbbas reports that the Prophet opened prayer with the basmala; al-Tirmidhi says its chain is not strong.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbas reports that the Prophet opened prayer with the basmala; al-Tirmidhi says its chain is not strong.

positions.position: When Muʿawiya omitted the basmala in Medina, the Muhajirun present objected; on his next prayer he recited it.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (أنس بن مالك): When Muʿawiya omitted the basmala in Medina, the Muhajirun present objected; on his next prayer he recited it.

positions.position: The Prophet instructed his stepson ʿUmar ibn Abi Salama to say God's name, eat with his right hand, and eat from what is nearest; some scholars make the basmala obligatory at meals.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): The Prophet instructed his stepson ʿUmar ibn Abi Salama to say God's name, eat with his right hand, and eat from what is nearest; some scholars make the basmala obligatory at meals.

positions.position: A report from Ibn Abbas says Quraysh cursed the Prophet when he said the basmala in Mecca.
positions.reasons: DURR (ابن عباس): A report from Ibn Abbas says Quraysh cursed the Prophet when he said the basmala in Mecca.

positions.position: Ibn Abbas reports the Prophet received two lights not given to earlier prophets: al-Fatiha and the closing verses of al-Baqara.
positions.reasons: DURR (النبي): Ibn Abbas reports the Prophet received two lights not given to earlier prophets: al-Fatiha and the closing verses of al-Baqara. | mentions 2:285, 2:286

positions.position: A weak report says the Prophet treated al-Sa'ib ibn Yazid with al-Fatiha and a light spitting.
positions.reasons: DURR (السائب بن يزيد): A weak report says the Prophet treated al-Sa'ib ibn Yazid with al-Fatiha and a light spitting.

positions.position: A weak report says al-Fatiha and al-Ikhlas before sleep protect from everything except death.
positions.reasons: DURR (أنس): A weak report says al-Fatiha and al-Ikhlas before sleep protect from everything except death. | mentions 112:1

positions.position: Reports from Ibn Abbas variously say al-Fatiha is a third of the Qur'an and, in a weak Prophetic version, equals two-thirds.
positions.reasons: DURR (ابن عباس): Reports from Ibn Abbas variously say al-Fatiha is a third of the Qur'an and, in a weak Prophetic version, equals two-thirds.

positions.position: When Muawiya led prayer in Medina without the basmala or transition takbirs, the Muhajirun and Ansar objected; he included them thereafter.
positions.reasons: DURR (المهاجرون والأنصار): When Muawiya led prayer in Medina without the basmala or transition takbirs, the Muhajirun and Ansar objected; he included them thereafter.

positions.position: Al-Ālūsī endorses the cautious view that omitting the basmala warrants the forgetfulness prostration, against Qāḍīkhān and the author of al-Khulāṣa.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Al-Ālūsī endorses the cautious view that omitting the basmala warrants the forgetfulness prostration, against Qāḍīkhān and the author of al-Khulāṣa.

positions.position: In the sound Muslim report, God divides prayer between Himself and the servant; the three verses before the central pair and three after total seven without the basmala.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (أبو هريرة): In the sound Muslim report, God divides prayer between Himself and the servant; the three verses before the central pair and three after total seven without the basmala. | mentions 1:2, 1:3, 1:4, 1:5, 1:6, 1:7

positions.position: Al-Ālūsī prefers the Muslim version over al-Thaʿlabī’s and rejects readings that make the division merely semantic or mean half the prayer; it does not deny the basmala is Qurʾān.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Al-Ālūsī prefers the Muslim version over al-Thaʿlabī’s and rejects readings that make the division merely semantic or mean half the prayer; it does not deny the basmala is Qurʾān.

positions.position: Al-Thaʿlabī transmits Jābir’s report that the Prophet instructed him to say the basmala when beginning prayer; al-Ālūsī says it does not establish sūra-part status.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (جابر بن عبد الله): Al-Thaʿlabī transmits Jābir’s report that the Prophet instructed him to say the basmala when beginning prayer; al-Ālūsī says it does not establish sūra-part status.

positions.position: Al-Thaʿlabī attributes to ʿAlī the practice of beginning each sūra in prayer with the basmala and saying omission diminishes the prayer; al-Ālūsī does not accept this as proof of inclusion.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (علي): Al-Thaʿlabī attributes to ʿAlī the practice of beginning each sūra in prayer with the basmala and saying omission diminishes the prayer; al-Ālūsī does not accept this as proof of inclusion.

positions.position: Reports say Medinese objected when Muʿāwiya omitted the basmala and he repeated the prayer; al-Ālūsī says this could concern a missed obligatory act and does not prove inclusion.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (معاوية): Reports say Medinese objected when Muʿāwiya omitted the basmala and he repeated the prayer; al-Ālūsī says this could concern a missed obligatory act and does not prove inclusion.

positions.position: Al-Shāfiʿī’s report says Muʿāwiya omitted both the basmala and transition takbīrs, then repeated prayer after objections; al-Ālūsī says this poses no difficulty for his view.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (أنس): Al-Shāfiʿī’s report says Muʿāwiya omitted both the basmala and transition takbīrs, then repeated prayer after objections; al-Ālūsī says this poses no difficulty for his view.

positions.position: Al-Ālūsī notes that prior mention does not prove an event already occurred: 48:1 describes a future conquest in the past tense to assure its fulfillment.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Al-Ālūsī notes that prior mention does not prove an event already occurred: 48:1 describes a future conquest in the past tense to assure its fulfillment. | mentions 48:1

positions.position: Al-Ālūsī says the independent Qurʾānic basmala should be recited in prayer; Hanafis may require it, and caution favors the ruling.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Al-Ālūsī says the independent Qurʾānic basmala should be recited in prayer; Hanafis may require it, and caution favors the ruling.

positions.position: Al-Rāzī’s six arguments for loud recitation fail: membership would not require identical volume, praise may be quiet, and reports and inferred commands are inconclusive.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Al-Rāzī’s six arguments for loud recitation fail: membership would not require identical volume, praise may be quiet, and reports and inferred commands are inconclusive.

positions.position: Umm Salama reports that the Prophet recited the basmala before al-Hamdu lillah in prayer.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (أم سلمة): Umm Salama reports that the Prophet recited the basmala before al-Hamdu lillah in prayer.

positions.position: The prayer-splitting hadith has God call the worshipper's basmala a glorification of Him.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (أبو هريرة): The prayer-splitting hadith has God call the worshipper's basmala a glorification of Him.

positions.position: Abu Hurayra recounts that the Prophet called a prayer cut short when a worshipper began without the basmala, and said omitting it invalidated the prayer.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (أبو هريرة): Abu Hurayra recounts that the Prophet called a prayer cut short when a worshipper began without the basmala, and said omitting it invalidated the prayer.

positions.position: Alusi reports the relied-upon Hanafi view that the basmala is required in a rak'a where recitation is required, citing al-Zayla'i and al-Zahidi.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi reports the relied-upon Hanafi view that the basmala is required in a rak'a where recitation is required, citing al-Zayla'i and al-Zahidi.

positions.position: Ibn Wahban says that if someone forgetfully omits the basmala in every rakaa, prostration of forgetfulness is due.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (إبن وهبان): Ibn Wahban says that if someone forgetfully omits the basmala in every rakaa, prostration of forgetfulness is due.

positions.position: Razi invokes the hadith that an important matter begun without God's name is cut off to argue prayer without the basmala is defective.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (الفخر الرازي): Razi invokes the hadith that an important matter begun without God's name is cut off to argue prayer without the basmala is defective.

positions.position: Alusi says Razi's description of the Hanafi position as neglecting the basmala is extreme partisanship, since many Hanafis require it and he personally adopts the cautious view.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi says Razi's description of the Hanafi position as neglecting the basmala is extreme partisanship, since many Hanafis require it and he personally adopts the cautious view.

positions.position: Alusi objects to Razi's Umm Salama proof: Abu Mulayka is not shown to have heard from her, and the quoted wording is not established among well-known versions, likely being paraphrase.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi objects to Razi's Umm Salama proof: Abu Mulayka is not shown to have heard from her, and the quoted wording is not established among well-known versions, likely being paraphrase.

positions.position: Against Razi's ninth proof, Alusi notes that the prayer is already opened by the takbir and intention; applying the hadith to every consequential act would also require basmala before bowing and prostration.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Against Razi's ninth proof, Alusi notes that the prayer is already opened by the takbir and intention; applying the hadith to every consequential act would also require basmala before bowing and prostration.

positions.position: Alusi doubts the fifth report's wording and says it may be the version transmitted by al-Daraqutni; he does not rely on al-Razi for hadith and lacks al-Thalabi's text to check it.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi doubts the fifth report's wording and says it may be the version transmitted by al-Daraqutni; he does not rely on al-Razi for hadith and lacks al-Thalabi's text to check it.

positions.position: Alusi extends the reductio: if every prayer movement needs a basmala to avoid being cut off, Razi would have to recite it before bowing, prostrating, and every transition.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi extends the reductio: if every prayer movement needs a basmala to avoid being cut off, Razi would have to recite it before bowing, prostrating, and every transition.

positions.position: Alusi says the prayer division cannot concern only a portion that also includes actions and an appended sura; its halves must form a coherent whole.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi says the prayer division cannot concern only a portion that also includes actions and an appended sura; its halves must form a coherent whole.

positions.position: The Mu'awiya report, even if accepted, could show only that he omitted an obligatory basmala and repeated the prayer; the companions may have waited to see whether prostration of forgetfulness repaired the lapse.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): The Mu'awiya report, even if accepted, could show only that he omitted an obligatory basmala and repeated the prayer; the companions may have waited to see whether prostration of forgetfulness repaired the lapse.

positions.position: Razi's fourth proof is the report that the Companions challenged Mu'awiya after he omitted the basmala in prayer.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (الفخر الرازي): Razi's fourth proof is the report that the Companions challenged Mu'awiya after he omitted the basmala in prayer.

positions.position: Outside prayer, beginning a surah recitation with isti'adha and basmala is sunnah according to the majority, while some imams such as Ata consider it obligatory.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (Cumhûr): Outside prayer, beginning a surah recitation with isti'adha and basmala is sunnah according to the majority, while some imams such as Ata consider it obligatory.

positions.position: Malikis recommend omitting basmala in prayer.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (Mâlikîler): Malikis recommend omitting basmala in prayer.

positions.position: The Ṣaḥīḥayn report has God divide the prayer between Himself and the servant, answering each recited passage from praise through the request for guidance.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (أبو هريرة): The Ṣaḥīḥayn report has God divide the prayer between Himself and the servant, answering each recited passage from praise through the request for guidance. | mentions 1:2, 1:3, 1:4, 1:5, 1:6, 1:7

positions.position: In the Muwattaʾ report of God dividing prayer, the response begins after the servant says al-ḥamdu lillāh; Mālik uses the omission of the basmala as evidence.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (أبو هريرة): In the Muwattaʾ report of God dividing prayer, the response begins after the servant says al-ḥamdu lillāh; Mālik uses the omission of the basmala as evidence. | mentions 1:2

positions.position: In a Muwattaʾ and Ṣaḥīḥayn report, the Prophet asks Ubayy how he opens prayer; Ubayy recites from al-ḥamdu lillāh through the end without the basmala.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (أبي بن كعب): In a Muwattaʾ and Ṣaḥīḥayn report, the Prophet asks Ubayy how he opens prayer; Ubayy recites from al-ḥamdu lillāh through the end without the basmala. | mentions 1:2

positions.position: If this interpretation is refused, Anas contradicts his other report that he never heard the Prophet say the basmala in prayer, so the reports would conflict fatally.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): If this interpretation is refused, Anas contradicts his other report that he never heard the Prophet say the basmala in prayer, so the reports would conflict fatally.

positions.position: In a report authenticated by al-Tirmidhī, Ibn ʿAbbās asks ʿUthmān why al-Anfāl and Barāʾa were joined without a basmala; ʿUthmān says their similar subject and the Prophet’s silence led him to join them.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (عثمان بن عفان): In a report authenticated by al-Tirmidhī, Ibn ʿAbbās asks ʿUthmān why al-Anfāl and Barāʾa were joined without a basmala; ʿUthmān says their similar subject and the Prophet’s silence led him to join them.

question: Must a follower recite behind an imam?

positions.position: The hadith no prayer without the Opening is general; Razi says the opposing report exempting those behind an imam has been criticized.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The hadith no prayer without the Opening is general; Razi says the opposing report exempting those behind an imam has been criticized.

positions.position: Al-Shafi‘i’s earlier view excuses a forgotten recitation, citing Umar’s Maghrib prayer; his newer view invalidates it because the general proofs cover both deliberate and inadvertent omission.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (الشافعي): Al-Shafi‘i’s earlier view excuses a forgotten recitation, citing Umar’s Maghrib prayer; his newer view invalidates it because the general proofs cover both deliberate and inadvertent omission.

positions.position: A report says Umar omitted recitation in Maghrib and considered the prayer sound after the congregation confirmed his bowing and prostration were proper.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (عمر): A report says Umar omitted recitation in Maghrib and considered the prayer sound after the congregation confirmed his bowing and prostration were proper.

positions.position: The statement that prayer without al-Fātiḥa is invalid except behind an imam is stopped at Jābir, not soundly traced to the Prophet.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (جابر): The statement that prayer without al-Fātiḥa is invalid except behind an imam is stopped at Jābir, not soundly traced to the Prophet.

positions.position: Abū Salama says an imam has two pauses that worshippers should use for recitation; al-Awzāʿī and Aḥmad favored the report.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (أبو سلمة بن عبد الرحمن): Abū Salama says an imam has two pauses that worshippers should use for recitation; al-Awzāʿī and Aḥmad favored the report.

positions.position: Mālik’s well-known view bars the follower from reciting al-Fātiḥa or another passage when the imam recites aloud.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (مالك): Mālik’s well-known view bars the follower from reciting al-Fātiḥa or another passage when the imam recites aloud.

positions.position: Al-Shāfiʿī’s Egyptian view and Aḥmad require every follower to recite al-Fātiḥa each unit, whether the imam recites aloud or quietly.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (الشافعي وأحمد بن حنبل): Al-Shāfiʿī’s Egyptian view and Aḥmad require every follower to recite al-Fātiḥa each unit, whether the imam recites aloud or quietly.

positions.position: Scholars have three views on whether a follower must recite: that the follower must recite the Fatiha just like the imam.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): Scholars have three views on whether a follower must recite: that the follower must recite the Fatiha just like the imam.

positions.position: A second view says a follower recites nothing, whether prayer is audible or silent, based on “one with an imam has the imam's recitation”; the marfuʿ routes are weak, and Malik transmits it as Jabir's own statement.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (مالك): A second view says a follower recites nothing, whether prayer is audible or silent, based on “one with an imam has the imam's recitation”; the marfuʿ routes are weak, and Malik transmits it as Jabir's own statement.

positions.position: A third view requires the follower's recitation in silent prayer but not audible prayer, combining the general requirement with the command to listen when the imam recites.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (الشافعي في قوله القديم وأحمد في رواية): A third view requires the follower's recitation in silent prayer but not audible prayer, combining the general requirement with the command to listen when the imam recites.

question: May al-Fātiḥa be recited in translation?

positions.position: Ibn al-Mundhir transmits Abu Hurayra’s report that prayer is invalid without reciting the Opening; a Persian rendering is either called Qur’an, which Razi deems ignorant and contrary to consensus, or not Qur’an.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أبو هريرة): Ibn al-Mundhir transmits Abu Hurayra’s report that prayer is invalid without reciting the Opening; a Persian rendering is either called Qur’an, which Razi deems ignorant and contrary to consensus, or not Qur’an.

positions.position: When a man could not recite Qur’an, the Prophet taught him glorification, praise, and takbir instead of a translation, showing the alternative for inability.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (عبد الله بن أبي أوفى): When a man could not recite Qur’an, the Prophet taught him glorification, praise, and takbir instead of a translation, showing the alternative for inability.

positions.position: If Qur’an could be translated as Qur’an, Christians could claim its opening was copied from the Gospel’s matching formula; no one makes that claim.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): If Qur’an could be translated as Qur’an, Christians could claim its opening was copied from the Gospel’s matching formula; no one makes that claim.

positions.position: A Persian rendering of the cave passage or insults and requests becomes ordinary human speech, barred in prayer; the Arabic original remains distinct through its miraculous arrangement.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A Persian rendering of the cave passage or insults and requests becomes ordinary human speech, barred in prayer; the Arabic original remains distinct through its miraculous arrangement. | mentions 18:19, 68:11, 68:13, 2:61

positions.position: The Prophet and Companions recited only Arabic in prayer; the saved group follows their practice. Muslims throughout Islamic lands agree on Arabic recitation, and departing from believers’ way is condemned.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The Prophet and Companions recited only Arabic in prayer; the saved group follows their practice. Muslims throughout Islamic lands agree on Arabic recitation, and departing from believers’ way is condemned. | mentions 4:115

positions.position: Prayer requires Qur’an recitation, and Persian words are not Qur’an: revelation is in clear Arabic, messengers speak their people’s language, and the challenge to produce its like would be contradicted if a Persian rendering counted.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Prayer requires Qur’an recitation, and Persian words are not Qur’an: revelation is in clear Arabic, messengers speak their people’s language, and the challenge to produce its like would be contradicted if a Persian rendering counted. | mentions 26:192, 26:195, 14:4, 41:44, 17:88

positions.position: If every language’s translation were Qur’an, revelation would have more than the seven canonical forms, contradicting the report that it came in seven forms.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): If every language’s translation were Qur’an, revelation would have more than the seven canonical forms, contradicting the report that it came in seven forms.

positions.position: A translation of al-Fatiha reduces it to generic praise found in any sermon; allowing this would make prayer valid with all sermons, an unacceptable result.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A translation of al-Fatiha reduces it to generic praise found in any sermon; allowing this would make prayer valid with all sermons, an unacceptable result.

positions.position: If translation were permitted, the Prophet would have authorized Persians, Romans, and Ethiopians to pray in their languages; such a popular, easier permission would have spread and erased the Arabic Qur’an.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): If translation were permitted, the Prophet would have authorized Persians, Romans, and Ethiopians to pray in their languages; such a popular, easier permission would have spread and erased the Arabic Qur’an.

positions.position: Although a non-Arab may understand meaning more readily in translation, prayer seeks remembrance and reflection; treating translation as valid would perversely make Arabic recitation prohibited.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Although a non-Arab may understand meaning more readily in translation, prayer seeks remembrance and reflection; treating translation as valid would perversely make Arabic recitation prohibited. | mentions 20:14, 47:24

positions.position: Prayer preserves both meaning and Arabic wording: the wording carries the inimitable eloquence, and its required recitation safeguards memorization and fulfills God’s promise to preserve the Reminder.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Prayer preserves both meaning and Arabic wording: the wording carries the inimitable eloquence, and its required recitation safeguards memorization and fulfills God’s promise to preserve the Reminder. | mentions 15:9

positions.position: Abu Hurayra tells a Persian worshipper to recite al-Fatiha silently even when behind an imam; Razi says this contradicts treating that prayer as deficient and supports the questioner’s understanding that recitation is required.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أبو هريرة): Abu Hurayra tells a Persian worshipper to recite al-Fatiha silently even when behind an imam; Razi says this contradicts treating that prayer as deficient and supports the questioner’s understanding that recitation is required.

question: What is the rule for the basmala in ablution?

positions.position: A report promises that honoring a paper bearing Bismillah earns the rank of the truthful and lightens one’s parents’ burden even if they were polytheists.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): A report promises that honoring a paper bearing Bismillah earns the rank of the truthful and lightens one’s parents’ burden even if they were polytheists.

positions.position: Abū Hurayra transmits instructions to say Bismillah at ablution, intercourse, mounting, and boarding a ship, with good deeds counted through each act and even descendants’ breaths.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أبو هريرة): Abū Hurayra transmits instructions to say Bismillah at ablution, intercourse, mounting, and boarding a ship, with good deeds counted through each act and even descendants’ breaths.

positions.position: A report says invoking God’s name in ablution purifies the whole body, while invoking Him from the heart should purify the heart of unbelief and innovation.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): A report says invoking God’s name in ablution purifies the whole body, while invoking Him from the heart should purify the heart of unbelief and innovation.

positions.position: A story says Khalid ibn al-Walīd ate deadly poison after invoking Bismillah and survived by God’s permission, prompting the Magians to accept Islam.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A story says Khalid ibn al-Walīd ate deadly poison after invoking Bismillah and survived by God’s permission, prompting the Magians to accept Islam.

positions.position: Scholars agree that invoking God in ablution is recommended, and most do not require it because the ablution verse omits it.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Scholars agree that invoking God in ablution is recommended, and most do not require it because the ablution verse omits it. | mentions 5:6

positions.position: Literalists require the basmala in ablution, while Ishaq invalidates ablution for deliberate omission but excuses forgetfulness.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (أهل الظاهر): Literalists require the basmala in ablution, while Ishaq invalidates ablution for deliberate omission but excuses forgetfulness.

positions.position: A hadith judged hasan says there is no ablution for one who does not mention God's name; scholars differ over whether it is obligatory when remembered or absolutely.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): A hadith judged hasan says there is no ablution for one who does not mention God's name; scholars differ over whether it is obligatory when remembered or absolutely.

positions.position: The implied action varies with the activity begun—standing, sitting, eating, drinking, reciting, ablution, or prayer—and the basmala seeks blessing, aid to completion, and acceptance.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): The implied action varies with the activity begun—standing, sitting, eating, drinking, reciting, ablution, or prayer—and the basmala seeks blessing, aid to completion, and acceptance.

question: When should the basmala be said outside prayer?

positions.position: Ibn Masud says reciting the basmala protects a person from the nineteen keepers of Hell, one letter serving as protection from each.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (ابن مسعود): Ibn Masud says reciting the basmala protects a person from the nineteen keepers of Hell, one letter serving as protection from each. DURR-FULL (ابن مسعود): Ibn Masud says reciting the basmala protects a person from each of the nineteen keepers of Hell, one shield for each letter.

positions.position: The scholarly consensus that saying “by God” at slaughter does not fulfill the prescribed “in the name of God” supports his distinction between the formula and “by God.”
positions.reasons: TAB (author): The scholarly consensus that saying “by God” at slaughter does not fulfill the prescribed “in the name of God” supports his distinction between the formula and “by God.”

positions.position: The people of spiritual realities say the basmala is for blessing and encourages beginning words and deeds with it, following the Qurʾān’s own opening.
positions.reasons: THALABI (أهل الحقائق): The people of spiritual realities say the basmala is for blessing and encourages beginning words and deeds with it, following the Qurʾān’s own opening.

positions.position: Some connect the basmala's nineteen letters with the nineteen guardians of Hell, assigning one angel to each letter as a source of their strength.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (بعض الناس): Some connect the basmala's nineteen letters with the nineteen guardians of Hell, assigning one angel to each letter as a source of their strength. | mentions 74:30

positions.position: The Prophet promises absolution for a child, the child's parents, and the teacher when the child learns and recites the basmala.
positions.reasons: TABRISI (النبي): The Prophet promises absolution for a child, the child's parents, and the teacher when the child learns and recites the basmala.

positions.position: The opening formula marks the beginning of all good deeds and commanded acts.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The opening formula marks the beginning of all good deeds and commanded acts.

positions.position: Razi rejects the suggestion that Solomon put his own name before God's: the hoopoe laid the letter on the queen, who first identified its sender as Solomon and only after opening it read the basmala.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi rejects the suggestion that Solomon put his own name before God's: the hoopoe laid the letter on the queen, who first identified its sender as Solomon and only after opening it read the basmala. | mentions 27:30

positions.position: Scholars recommend beginning every activity with the basmala, from sleep and waking to worship, entering and leaving home, eating, drinking, giving, and receiving; they also recommend it at birth, death, burial, resurrection, and the gathering.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Scholars recommend beginning every activity with the basmala, from sleep and waking to worship, entering and leaving home, eating, drinking, giving, and receiving; they also recommend it at birth, death, burial, resurrection, and the gathering.

positions.position: Ibn al-Mubārak and one Shāfiʿī view cite the report that the Prophet recited a newly revealed al-Kawthar beginning with the basmala.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (أبو أنس): Ibn al-Mubārak and one Shāfiʿī view cite the report that the Prophet recited a newly revealed al-Kawthar beginning with the basmala. | mentions 108:1

positions.position: Another scholar says the obligation applied only to the Prophet, with the community following his example.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (غيره): Another scholar says the obligation applied only to the Prophet, with the community following his example.

positions.position: Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn Shihāb, with al-Shāfiʿī and others, require the basmala.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (ابن عمر وابن شهاب): Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn Shihāb, with al-Shāfiʿī and others, require the basmala.

positions.position: ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa uses basmala as a verb in poetry, describing Laylā as having said it.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (عمر بن أبي ربيعة): ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa uses basmala as a verb in poetry, describing Laylā as having said it.

positions.position: The law recommends basmala at the start of eating, drinking, slaughter, intimacy, purification, travel, and other acts.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (author): The law recommends basmala at the start of eating, drinking, slaughter, intimacy, purification, travel, and other acts. | mentions 6:118, 11:41

positions.position: On the reading “your gods” in 7:127, Ibn ʿAbbās and others gloss it as “your worship.”
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (ابن عباس): On the reading “your gods” in 7:127, Ibn ʿAbbās and others gloss it as “your worship.” | mentions 7:127

positions.position: Kaʿb al-Aḥbār assigns basmala letters to divine glory, majesty, and sovereignty; another reading maps each letter to a divine name.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (كعب الأحبار): Kaʿb al-Aḥbār assigns basmala letters to divine glory, majesty, and sovereignty; another reading maps each letter to a divine name.

positions.position: Al-Kisāʾī reports an Arab reading al-Raḥīma al-ḥamdu; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says no reader transmitted it.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (الكسائي): Al-Kisāʾī reports an Arab reading al-Raḥīma al-ḥamdu; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says no reader transmitted it.

positions.position: The Basrans parse ism as nominative in an implied nominal sentence, approximately “my beginning is fixed/stable in the name of God”; Abū Ḥayyān weighs this against the verbal parse.
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN (البصريون): The Basrans parse ism as nominative in an implied nominal sentence, approximately “my beginning is fixed/stable in the name of God”; Abū Ḥayyān weighs this against the verbal parse.

positions.position: A report recommends beginning a sermon with the basmala and calls an affair begun without it defective.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): A report recommends beginning a sermon with the basmala and calls an affair begun without it defective.

positions.position: The basmala is recommended before slaughter according to al-Shafiʿi and a group; others require it if remembered, and some require it absolutely.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): The basmala is recommended before slaughter according to al-Shafiʿi and a group; others require it if remembered, and some require it absolutely.

positions.position: A report promises four thousand good deeds, erasure of four thousand sins, and four thousand ranks for each basmala letter.
positions.reasons: DURR (ابن مسعود): A report promises four thousand good deeds, erasure of four thousand sins, and four thousand ranks for each basmala letter.

positions.position: A report to Muawiya gives letter-shaping instructions for the basmala and recommends putting the pen by the left ear for memory.
positions.reasons: DURR (النبي): A report to Muawiya gives letter-shaping instructions for the basmala and recommends putting the pen by the left ear for memory.

positions.position: Matar says the Prophet directed Muawiya to join the basmala's letters and not elongate God's names.
positions.reasons: DURR (النبي): Matar says the Prophet directed Muawiya to join the basmala's letters and not elongate God's names.

positions.position: Sa'id ibn Jubayr says the basmala marked the end of one sura and beginning of another in the Prophet's time.
positions.reasons: DURR (سعيد بن جبير): Sa'id ibn Jubayr says the basmala marked the end of one sura and beginning of another in the Prophet's time.

positions.position: Al-Dahhak is reported to give the same letter-by-letter interpretation of the basmala as the report about Jesus and his teacher.
positions.reasons: DURR (الضحاك): Al-Dahhak is reported to give the same letter-by-letter interpretation of the basmala as the report about Jesus and his teacher.

positions.position: Al-Ālūsī takes dhū bāl as comprehensive—anything that enters the mind—rather than restricting it to dignified matters, since God’s aid matters in small acts too.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Al-Ālūsī takes dhū bāl as comprehensive—anything that enters the mind—rather than restricting it to dignified matters, since God’s aid matters in small acts too. | mentions 6:38

positions.position: Ibn Jarīr supplies an implied “I recite,” the specific act of the person uttering the basmala; al-Ālūsī finds this broad and contextually apt.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (ابن جرير): Ibn Jarīr supplies an implied “I recite,” the specific act of the person uttering the basmala; al-Ālūsī finds this broad and contextually apt.

positions.position: Al-Farrāʾ, with a view attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, supplies an imperative addressed to people, urging them to begin in God’s name.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (الفراء وابن عباس): Al-Farrāʾ, with a view attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, supplies an imperative addressed to people, urging them to begin in God’s name.

positions.position: Al-Ālūsī favors placing the implied act before the basmala: God’s name precedes it in rank, and the order suggests beginning through divine aid.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Al-Ālūsī favors placing the implied act before the basmala: God’s name precedes it in rank, and the order suggests beginning through divine aid.

positions.position: Alusi prefers Ibn Jarir's specific recitation verb because it makes the whole recitation occur with God's assistance, whereas beginning only links the formula to the initial moment.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi prefers Ibn Jarir's specific recitation verb because it makes the whole recitation occur with God's assistance, whereas beginning only links the formula to the initial moment.

positions.position: Alusi says beginning here is specifically the beginning of recitation, not a generic action; the basmala itself already makes the reciter a beginner, so no hidden act is needed to establish that.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi says beginning here is specifically the beginning of recitation, not a generic action; the basmala itself already makes the reciter a beginner, so no hidden act is needed to establish that.

positions.position: Bal means a state or affair of consequence that occupies the heart; another explanation likens a great matter to something possessing a heart through implied metaphor.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Bal means a state or affair of consequence that occupies the heart; another explanation likens a great matter to something possessing a heart through implied metaphor.

positions.position: Asking for small things does not violate reverence: the Qur’an finds no disparity in creation, and a discerning believer sees no created thing as insignificant.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Asking for small things does not violate reverence: the Qur’an finds no disparity in creation, and a discerning believer sees no created thing as insignificant. | mentions 67:3, 67:4

positions.position: Reports vary between beginning with praise, the basmala, or remembrance, and between descriptions such as cut off or amputated; the hadith is textually and transmission-wise unsettled, but leniency applies in merits and semantic corroboration strengthens it.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Reports vary between beginning with praise, the basmala, or remembrance, and between descriptions such as cut off or amputated; the hadith is textually and transmission-wise unsettled, but leniency applies in merits and semantic corroboration strengthens it.

positions.position: He directs readers to later discussions of isti'adha at 16:98, general naming at al-Alaq, slaughter at al-Anam, and basmala again at al-Naml.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (author): He directs readers to later discussions of isti'adha at 16:98, general naming at al-Alaq, slaughter at al-Anam, and basmala again at al-Naml. | mentions 16:98

positions.position: Abduh says customary in the name of means acting for an authority, by its command and on its behalf; the Muslim's basmala can express beginning an act for Allah and by His command.
positions.reasons: ELMALILI (Şeyh Abduh): Abduh says customary in the name of means acting for an authority, by its command and on its behalf; the Muslim's basmala can express beginning an act for Allah and by His command.

positions.position: Ibn ʿĀshūr suspects the formula continues Abrahamic monotheist practice: Abraham invokes the Merciful and the compassionate, and Solomon opens his letter with the basmala, likely inheriting that prophetic tradition.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): Ibn ʿĀshūr suspects the formula continues Abrahamic monotheist practice: Abraham invokes the Merciful and the compassionate, and Solomon opens his letter with the basmala, likely inheriting that prophetic tradition. | mentions 19:45, 19:47, 2:128, 27:30, 27:31, 22:78

positions.position: Most scholars say early muṣḥaf scribes wrote the basmala at every sura except Barāʾa; its presence at Fātiha’s beginning is undisputed but is not itself a sura divider.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): Most scholars say early muṣḥaf scribes wrote the basmala at every sura except Barāʾa; its presence at Fātiha’s beginning is undisputed but is not itself a sura divider.

positions.position: Anas reports that the Prophet, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar began recitation with al-ḥamdu lillāh and did not mention the basmala at the beginning or end.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (أنس بن مالك): Anas reports that the Prophet, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar began recitation with al-ḥamdu lillāh and did not mention the basmala at the beginning or end. | mentions 1:2

positions.position: ʿĀʾisha reports that the Prophet began prayer with the takbīr and began recitation with al-ḥamdu lillāh.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (عائشة): ʿĀʾisha reports that the Prophet began prayer with the takbīr and began recitation with al-ḥamdu lillāh. | mentions 1:2

positions.position: Ibn Mughaffal reports that he heard none of the Prophet, Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, or ʿUthmān say the basmala, and advises beginning with al-ḥamdu lillāh.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (عبد الله بن مغفل): Ibn Mughaffal reports that he heard none of the Prophet, Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, or ʿUthmān say the basmala, and advises beginning with al-ḥamdu lillāh. | mentions 1:2

positions.position: He conjectures that the Companions lengthened the basmala's letter in al-Naml to mark the opening of Solomon's quoted letter, then retained the form as a marker of new suras or topics.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR-FULL (author): He conjectures that the Companions lengthened the basmala's letter in al-Naml to mark the opening of Solomon's quoted letter, then retained the form as a marker of new suras or topics. | mentions 27:30

question: What reports link the basmala with first revelation?

positions.position: Ibn Abbas reports that the first thing Gabriel brought down was the basmala.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas reports that the first thing Gabriel brought down was the basmala. IBNATIYYA-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbas reports that the first words Gabriel brought were the basmala.

positions.position: In some versions of Khadija's taking the Prophet to Waraqa, Gabriel first tells the Prophet to say the basmala; the Prophet says it, then Gabriel commands him to read, and he replies that he cannot read.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (خديجة عن ورقة): In some versions of Khadija's taking the Prophet to Waraqa, Gabriel first tells the Prophet to say the basmala; the Prophet says it, then Gabriel commands him to read, and he replies that he cannot read. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): A report in some versions of Khadija's account also has Gabriel tell the Prophet to say the basmala before commanding him to recite.

positions.position: Ibn Abbas says the first revelation began with the command to say the basmala and to read by remembering God, rising and sitting in His remembrance.
positions.reasons: IBNABIHATIM (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas says the first revelation began with the command to say the basmala and to read by remembering God, rising and sitting in His remembrance.

positions.position: In the first-revealed surah, placing the command to read before the basmala is more fitting because the reading command is paramount.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL (author): In the first-revealed surah, placing the command to read before the basmala is more fitting because the reading command is paramount. | mentions 96:1

positions.position: One analysis makes the name relate to reciting as a pen relates to writing: the believer makes the act God's by beginning with His name, as a prophetic report says.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL (author): One analysis makes the name relate to reciting as a pen relates to writing: the believer makes the act God's by beginning with His name, as a prophetic report says.

positions.position: A report from the Prophet says that an important matter begun without God's name is cut off.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): A report from the Prophet says that an important matter begun without God's name is cut off.

positions.position: The other analysis treats reciting as occurring in the blessing of God's name; al-Zamakhshari calls this account more idiomatic and better.
positions.reasons: KASHSHAF-FULL (author): The other analysis treats reciting as occurring in the blessing of God's name; al-Zamakhshari calls this account more idiomatic and better. | mentions 23:20

positions.position: Amr b. Shurahbil reports that Gabriel first came to the Prophet saying, “Say: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Compassionate.”
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (عمرو بن شرحبيل): Amr b. Shurahbil reports that Gabriel first came to the Prophet saying, “Say: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Compassionate.”

positions.position: ʿAmr ibn Shurahbil reports that Gabriel first came to the Prophet and told him to say the basmala.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL (عمرو بن شرحبيل): ʿAmr ibn Shurahbil reports that Gabriel first came to the Prophet and told him to say the basmala.

positions.position: ʿAmr ibn Shurayḥil says the first revelation was al-Ḥamd lillāh; after Muhammad confided his fear to Khadīja and consulted Waraqa, Gabriel instructed him to recite Bismillah and the Fātiḥa.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (عمرو بن شرحبيل): ʿAmr ibn Shurayḥil says the first revelation was al-Ḥamd lillāh; after Muhammad confided his fear to Khadīja and consulted Waraqa, Gabriel instructed him to recite Bismillah and the Fātiḥa.

positions.position: A report from Ibn ʿAbbās says the Prophet recited Bismillah and Quraysh cursed him.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (ابن عباس): A report from Ibn ʿAbbās says the Prophet recited Bismillah and Quraysh cursed him.

positions.position: The Qur'an uses human creation to prove the Creator, as in the command to worship the Lord who created people and the first revelation about creating humanity from a clot.
