positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The Qur'an uses human creation to prove the Creator, as in the command to worship the Lord who created people and the first revelation about creating humanity from a clot. | mentions 2:21, 96:1, 96:2

positions.position: The proof from creation is also a blessing: it teaches the servant that God exists and gives a great benefit, so it is both evidence and grace.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The proof from creation is also a blessing: it teaches the servant that God exists and gives a great benefit, so it is both evidence and grace.

positions.position: Al-Fatiha gathers what people need to know about the origin, the middle of servitude, and the return; Razi begins its proof of the Creator from human creation, citing Abraham and Moses.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Al-Fatiha gathers what people need to know about the origin, the middle of servitude, and the return; Razi begins its proof of the Creator from human creation, citing Abraham and Moses.

positions.position: The Qur'an repeatedly establishes the Creator by reflecting on human creation: Abraham says his Lord gives life and death and created him, and Moses says his Lord gave each thing its form and guided it.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The Qur'an repeatedly establishes the Creator by reflecting on human creation: Abraham says his Lord gives life and death and created him, and Moses says his Lord gave each thing its form and guided it.

positions.position: Al-Thawrī reads al-Fātiḥa and a sūra in the first two units; in later units tasbīḥ or recitation is optional.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (الثوري): Al-Thawrī reads al-Fātiḥa and a sūra in the first two units; in later units tasbīḥ or recitation is optional.

positions.position: Abū Qatāda reports the Prophet recited al-Fātiḥa and two sūras in early units and al-Fātiḥa in the last two.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (أبو قتادة): Abū Qatāda reports the Prophet recited al-Fātiḥa and two sūras in early units and al-Fātiḥa in the last two.

positions.position: Most scholars say recitation beyond al-Fātiḥa is not obligatory; Abū Hurayra’s report says al-Fātiḥa suffices and more is better.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (الجمهور): Most scholars say recitation beyond al-Fātiḥa is not obligatory; Abū Hurayra’s report says al-Fātiḥa suffices and more is better.

positions.position: Reports differ on the first revelation: al-Muddaththir, “Read,” or al-Fātiḥa.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (القاضي ابن الطيب): Reports differ on the first revelation: al-Muddaththir, “Read,” or al-Fātiḥa. | mentions 74:1, 96:1

positions.position: If the account is preserved, Qurṭubī says it may describe al-Fātiḥa’s descent after “Read” and al-Muddaththir.

positions.position: The name relates to recitation as oil relates to growth in ‘it grows with oil’: reciting with God’s name seeks blessing and teaches worshippers to honor it.

positions.reasons: NASAFI-FULL (author): In “Read in the name of your Lord,” the verb is brought forward because reading was the central command of the first-revealed surah; “read” may also mean perform reading absolutely, or take the following phrase as its object. | mentions 96:1

positions.position: The overt iqra bism rabbik is explained either by the priority of reading in the first-revealed sura or by attaching the phrase to a later iqra; the latter creates a long interruption and makes the second iqra redundant.

positions.position: A report from Burayda says the basmala was revealed to Muhammad and Solomon alone.

positions.position: In a report on the first revelation, Gabriel tells Muhammad to say the basmala and explains it as beginning, standing, and sitting in remembrance of God; Ibn Kathir elsewhere calls the report weak and disconnected.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (ابن عباس): In a report on the first revelation, Gabriel tells Muhammad to say the basmala and explains it as beginning, standing, and sitting in remembrance of God; Ibn Kathir elsewhere calls the report weak and disconnected. | mentions 96:1

positions.position: Ibn ʿAbbas's reading “wa-yadharuka wa-ilahatak” is explained as “your worship”; Mujahid gives the same gloss.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (ابن عباس ومجاهد): Ibn ʿAbbas's reading “wa-yadharuka wa-ilahatak” is explained as “your worship”; Mujahid gives the same gloss.

positions.position: Al-Razi also cites 19:65, “Do you know anyone like Him?” as evidence for an un-derived name, but Ibn Kathir finds that argument debatable.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): Al-Razi also cites 19:65, “Do you know anyone like Him?” as evidence for an un-derived name, but Ibn Kathir finds that argument debatable. | mentions 19:65

positions.position: One view makes the Fatiha the first revelation, based on a report in al-Bayhaqi and listed by al-Baqillani among three views.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): One view makes the Fatiha the first revelation, based on a report in al-Bayhaqi and listed by al-Baqillani among three views.

positions.position: A second view makes “O you wrapped up” the first revelation, based on Jabir's sound hadith.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): A second view makes “O you wrapped up” the first revelation, based on Jabir's sound hadith. | mentions 74:1

positions.position: Ibn Kathir says the correct view is that “Read in the name of your Lord” was first revealed.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): Ibn Kathir says the correct view is that “Read in the name of your Lord” was first revealed. | mentions 96:1

positions.position: Ibn Kathir distinguishes the Muwatta's Abu Saʿid, a Successor and client of Khuzāʿa, from the Companion Abu Saʿid ibn al-Muʿalla; the former report appears disconnected unless he heard it from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (author): Ibn Kathir distinguishes the Muwatta's Abu Saʿid, a Successor and client of Khuzāʿa, from the Companion Abu Saʿid ibn al-Muʿalla; the former report appears disconnected unless he heard it from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb.

positions.position: Ibn ʿAbbas reports that Gabriel announced two lights given to Muhammad alone: the Fatiha and the closing verses of al-Baqara; each letter brings a response.
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbas reports that Gabriel announced two lights given to Muhammad alone: the Fatiha and the closing verses of al-Baqara; each letter brings a response. | mentions 2:285, 2:286

positions.position: The Qur'an's recited order differs from revelation order: the first revelation to the Prophet was the clear command to read, while the first public warning was the command to rise and warn of the afterlife.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): The Qur'an's recited order differs from revelation order: the first revelation to the Prophet was the clear command to read, while the first public warning was the command to rise and warn of the afterlife. | mentions 96:1, 74:1, 74:2, 34:46

positions.position: The warning came first for the community because afterlife reform is most important and also sets worldly affairs right; the Prophet rendered warning and prohibition with one sense, though the first addresses instinct and the second understanding.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): The warning came first for the community because afterlife reform is most important and also sets worldly affairs right; the Prophet rendered warning and prohibition with one sense, though the first addresses instinct and the second understanding. | mentions 29:25

positions.position: Al-Qadi Abu Bakr argues that the disconnected letters challenge opponents to use the remaining half of the alphabet to produce a rival discourse; al-Zarkashi transmits the claim.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (أبو بكر): Al-Qadi Abu Bakr argues that the disconnected letters challenge opponents to use the remaining half of the alphabet to produce a rival discourse; al-Zarkashi transmits the claim.

positions.position: Abu Bakr says every book has an essence and the Qur'an's essence lies in the opening letters of its surahs; Ali likewise calls the alphabetic openings the Qur'an's selected core.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (أبو بكر): Abu Bakr says every book has an essence and the Qur'an's essence lies in the opening letters of its surahs; Ali likewise calls the alphabetic openings the Qur'an's selected core.

positions.position: Ibn al-Qayyim reads Alif-Lam-Mim as the three articulation zones in order, symbolizing creation, worldly life and its laws, and resurrection; the Qur'an gathers what all humanity needs.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (ابن القيم): Ibn al-Qayyim reads Alif-Lam-Mim as the three articulation zones in order, symbolizing creation, worldly life and its laws, and resurrection; the Qur'an gathers what all humanity needs.

positions.position: Al-Harali gives metaphysical senses to Alif, Lam and Mim: encompassing authority, the link between hidden and manifest, and the perfected manifestation, with examples including Adam, angels and Muhammad.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): Al-Harali gives metaphysical senses to Alif, Lam and Mim: encompassing authority, the link between hidden and manifest, and the perfected manifestation, with examples including Adam, angels and Muhammad.

positions.position: Al-Harali says these signs are names when pronounced as alif, lam and mim; they are called letters only as word-parts without separate meaning, following al-Khalil's account of their names.
positions.reasons: BIQAI-FULL (الحرالي): Al-Harali says these signs are names when pronounced as alif, lam and mim; they are called letters only as word-parts without separate meaning, following al-Khalil's account of their names.

positions.position: A weak report from Ibn Umar says Gabriel first conveyed the basmala when bringing revelation.
positions.reasons: DURR (ابن عمر): A weak report from Ibn Umar says Gabriel first conveyed the basmala when bringing revelation.

positions.position: Ibn Abbas reports that the first revelation began with Gabriel telling Muhammad, “Bismillah”; the command means to read in God's name.
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas reports that the first revelation began with Gabriel telling Muhammad, “Bismillah”; the command means to read in God's name.

positions.position: Fātiḥat al-Kitāb means the opening of the Qurʾān in its received order, not the first lesson taught or the first sūra revealed.
positions.reasons: ALUSI (author): Fātiḥat al-Kitāb means the opening of the Qurʾān in its received order, not the first lesson taught or the first sūra revealed.

positions.position: The claim that the basmala was the first revelation is weak; even if it came first, that would not prove it belongs to a sura.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): The claim that the basmala was the first revelation is weak; even if it came first, that would not prove it belongs to a sura.

positions.position: Alusi says preposing God's name can sever claims of self-power and makes sense for the messenger's mission, while the first revelation preposes the verb because its context was prophethood rather than disputation or public preaching.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi says preposing God's name can sever claims of self-power and makes sense for the messenger's mission, while the first revelation preposes the verb because its context was prophethood rather than disputation or public preaching. | mentions 96:1

positions.position: Beginning in God's name expresses the first major Islamic worldview principle, God's oneness and proper reverence; comprehensive mercy expresses the second and defines the bond between God and servants.
positions.reasons: QUTB-ZILAL (author): Beginning in God's name expresses the first major Islamic worldview principle, God's oneness and proper reverence; comprehensive mercy expresses the second and defines the bond between God and servants.

positions.position: Beginning in God's name is the etiquette revealed to the Prophet at the first revelation and accords with God as First, Last, Manifest, and Hidden.

positions.position: Fātiha is first in the Prophet’s reading order, not the first revelation; sound, widespread reports make al-ʿAlaq the first revealed passage, after which God ordered Fātiha to lead recitation.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): Fātiha is first in the Prophet’s reading order, not the first revelation; sound, widespread reports make al-ʿAlaq the first revealed passage, after which God ordered Fātiha to lead recitation. | mentions 96:1

question: How did the formula of the basmala develop?

positions.position: Ibn ʿAbbas says the Prophet recognized the end of a surah only when “In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful” was revealed.

positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Another explanation is that Solomon wrote his name on the letter’s outside and began the inside with Bismillah, which Bilqīs read in that order. | mentions 27:30

positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): A third explanation says Solomon put his name first because he feared the unbelieving Bilqīs might insult God if His name appeared first. | mentions 27:30

positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Since God exists before all created things, rational propriety requires mentioning Him before others; what Muslims deem good is good before God, so the basmala should precede recitation and belongs to al-Fatiha.

positions.position: Reports trace the Prophet’s written invocation from “in Your name, O God,” to “in the name of God,” then the full basmala after revelations.

positions.position: Al-Māwardī notes the coined verb basmala for saying “in God’s name”; linguists document related devotional abbreviations.
positions.reasons: QURTUBI (الماوردي): Al-Māwardī notes the coined verb basmala for saying “in God’s name”; linguists document related devotional abbreviations.

positions.position: Al-Suyuti, as quoted by al-Sarmīnī, reports that the basmala opens every book; al-Sarmīnī takes the formula as particular to this community.

positions.position: Al-Sarmīnī argues that if the nested meanings of Qur'an, Fatiha, and basmala belonged to earlier books, their meanings would be in every book, which is false.

positions.position: Alusi answers that the staged commands do not prove earlier books lacked the formula, since its use then may simply have been unknown.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi answers that the staged commands do not prove earlier books lacked the formula, since its use then may simply have been unknown.

positions.position: Alusi says the Qur'an's distinctive feature is the Arabic wording in this order; earlier scriptures were non-Arabic and Qur'anic quotations from them are translations.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi says the Qur'an's distinctive feature is the Arabic wording in this order; earlier scriptures were non-Arabic and Qur'anic quotations from them are translations.

positions.position: Alusi notes that the report that the formula opened every book itself weighs against claiming it was exclusive to the Qur'an.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (author): Alusi notes that the report that the formula opened every book itself weighs against claiming it was exclusive to the Qur'an.

positions.position: Razi uses the report that the Prophet wrote bismika Allahumma to argue that the complete formula belongs to the Qur'an and cannot be excluded.
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL (الفخر الرازي): Razi uses the report that the Prophet wrote bismika Allahumma to argue that the complete formula belongs to the Qur'an and cannot be excluded.

positions.position: Ibn ʿĀshūr conjectures that the elongated bāʾ was first written in Solomon’s letter to mark its opening, then copied as a sign of a new discourse at sura beginnings.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): Ibn ʿĀshūr conjectures that the elongated bāʾ was first written in Solomon’s letter to mark its opening, then copied as a sign of a new discourse at sura beginnings. | mentions 27:30

positions.position: Muslims agree the basmala is Qur’anic because it occurs in Solomon’s letter; beginning important acts with it is also established, though the cited hadith is described as ḥasan and is not in the Sunan or Mustadrak.
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR (author): Muslims agree the basmala is Qur’anic because it occurs in Solomon’s letter; beginning important acts with it is also established, though the cited hadith is described as ḥasan and is not in the Sunan or Mustadrak. | mentions 27:30

positions.position: The report that any important matter begun without the basmala is cut off is described as ḥasan, though major Sunan and Mustadrak compilers did not include it.

positions.position: The only occurrence inside a sura is in Solomon’s letter to the Queen of Sheba, raising the possibility that suras were treated as written documents from then on.

question: How does the basmala separate sūras?

positions.position: Ibn Masud says the basmala showed where one sura ended and the next began.
positions.reasons: DURR (ابن مسعود): Ibn Masud says the basmala showed where one sura ended and the next began.

question: What benefits or virtues are ascribed to the basmala?

positions.position: Teaching a child to say the basmala brings release from the Fire for teacher, child, and parents.
positions.reasons: DURR (النبي): Teaching a child to say the basmala brings release from the Fire for teacher, child, and parents. DURR-FULL (ابن عباس): A marfu report promises the teacher, child, and child's parents immunity from the Fire when the teacher teaches the basmala.

positions.position: One possible reading makes al-Salām a divine name: “adhere to God’s name” after a year, with the command for adherence delayed in the wording; Ṭabarī finds this likelier.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): One possible reading makes al-Salām a divine name: “adhere to God’s name” after a year, with the command for adherence delayed in the wording; Ṭabarī finds this likelier.

positions.position: A second possible reading is a protective invocation: may God’s name be upon the two addressed people against harm.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (author): A second possible reading is a protective invocation: may God’s name be upon the two addressed people against harm.

positions.position: A report says Jesus explained the letters bāʾ, sīn, and mīm as God’s beauty, splendor, and dominion when a teacher asked about bism.
positions.reasons: TAB-FULL (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): A report says Jesus explained the letters bāʾ, sīn, and mīm as God’s beauty, splendor, and dominion when a teacher asked about bism.

positions.position: The Prophet did not include the basmala in his exchange with Ubayy because he was identifying the special surah and its virtue, whereas that purpose was absent in the instructional exchanges with Jabir and Abu Hurayra.
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA (author): The Prophet did not include the basmala in his exchange with Ubayy because he was identifying the special surah and its virtue, whereas that purpose was absent in the instructional exchanges with Jabir and Abu Hurayra.

positions.position: The implied verb with the basmala means beginning acts with God’s help; hearing it teaches dependence on divine protection from sin and aid for good, making its recitation a call to the best good rather than an innovation.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The implied verb with the basmala means beginning acts with God’s help; hearing it teaches dependence on divine protection from sin and aid for good, making its recitation a call to the best good rather than an innovation.

positions.position: Whether meat from an animal slaughtered without the basmala is lawful is a famous dispute, with Qur’anic commands both to invoke God over offerings and not eat what was not named over.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Whether meat from an animal slaughtered without the basmala is lawful is a famous dispute, with Qur’anic commands both to invoke God over offerings and not eat what was not named over. | mentions 22:36, 6:121

positions.position: The basmala at the gathering is said to distance the fire from the speaker by its blessing.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The basmala at the gathering is said to distance the fire from the speaker by its blessing.

positions.position: Razi rejects translated Qur’an as sufficient for prayer for both able and unable reciters; Abu Hanifa allows it for either, while Abu Yusuf and Muhammad allow it only for the unable.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi rejects translated Qur’an as sufficient for prayer for both able and unable reciters; Abu Hanifa allows it for either, while Abu Yusuf and Muhammad allow it only for the unable.

positions.position: Razi calls Abu Hanifa’s view far from sound; al-Samarqandi and al-Dabusi explicitly abandoned it.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): Razi calls Abu Hanifa’s view far from sound; al-Samarqandi and al-Dabusi explicitly abandoned it.

positions.position: The Prophet prayed using the revealed Arabic Qur’an throughout his life, so believers must follow that practice; Razi notes the irony that Abu Hanifa treats habitual head-wiping as a condition but not habitual Arabic recitation.
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL (author): The Prophet prayed using the revealed Arabic Qur’an throughout his life, so believers must follow that practice; Razi notes the irony that Abu Hanifa treats habitual head-wiping as a condition but not habitual Arabic recitation. | mentions 6:153
